en: First Canto:
Having drunk the stories of that protector of the earth, the wise no longer value even the nectar of immortality.
Nala, whose circle of fame was shaded by a white umbrella, was a mass of splendors, most brilliantly radiant. ||1||
That King Nala, whose virtues were marvelous, became a sovereign whose stories— composed of aesthetic flavors— held even nectar in contempt;
he was shaded by a single white parasol upon a golden staff.
The orb of whose fame is a blazing circle of the radiance of majesty. ||2||
In this age, the story of whom— when remembered— is spread as a purifier throughout the world like the washing away of impurities;
how then could it not cleanse even my turbid speech?
He will purify only those who serve him.
By means of the four conditions— study, comprehension, practice, and propagation—
he established the state of fourteenfoldness; why did he do so himself?
I myself do not know the fourteen branches of knowledge. ||4||
The knowledge of this man, like the triple Veda brought to expansion by the excellence of its constituent parts, became eighteenfold through the desire for conquest, dancing at the tip of his tongue.
Of the various glories of victory over the eighteen islands. ||5||
That Lord of the quarters, whose majesty was a portion of the host of world-protectors,
possessed two extra eyes that restrained the spreading of desires, [and he] bore the scriptures.
which makes known her own nature as an incarnation of the Three-eyed One. ||6||
When the Kṛta age was made firm by him through four well-performed steps, who did not undertake ascetic penance?
For he touched the earth with only the tip of his big toe.
Even Adharma, being emaciated, assumed the state of an ascetic. ||7||
That very dust, which rose up from his military expeditions with the beauty of smoke from the blazing fire of his prowess,
having traveled on, fell into the ocean of nectar.
It bestows upon the moon the state of having its spots turned into a row. ||8||

In battle, hundreds upon hundreds of the flames of his own fiery energy were expended by the heavy rain of powerful arrows from that cloud-like foe, which thundered with the roar of flashing lightning.
Others spread their infamy like glowing coals. ||9||
Having circumambulated the blazing circle of the earth with his own glories— which were as radiant as the fire that consumed the cities of his enemies— he was created for the sake of victory.
That slayer of kings shone with the lustration ceremony. ||10||
When the entire surface of the earth had been rendered free from pestilence by him, excessive rains were warded off; yet, surely,
those rains did not abandon it, for they found no other refuge.
The glances of the deer-eyed women of the opposing kings [fell upon him].

On the battlefield, she, acting as a weaver, wove a vast garment to cover the limbs of the lady of the quarters with the white-rayed threads of his virtues, using the Great Śiva’s matted locks as her shuttle.
The loom for the cloth of fame was the skillful shuttle of those warriors.
What fear can there be from that [enemy],

even though he is abandoned by friends, since he— like kings who have turned against their own subjects— is a conqueror of enemies and a conqueror of friends through his prowess, even though possessed of contradictory qualities?
The movement of his analytical vision and his far-reaching gaze proceeded as well. ||13||
Whenever he thinks in his mind that these two [the moon and the sun] exist in vain compared to his own power and fame,
the sun expands its halo under the guise of a solar aureole.
Then the ritual procedure [is performed] for the coiling of the moon as well. ||14||
He, who had belittled the wish-granting kalpa-tree, did not make false the decree of fate inscribed upon the foreheads of supplicants— that they would become poor.
Nala brought about the state of extreme poverty [among his enemies]. ||15||
That he did not divide Mount Meru for the sake of suppliants, nor that he did not turn the ocean into a desert through the expenditure of water from his gifts—
these two were considered by him to be his own twin stains of infamy.
The hair, bound in two tufts, rests upon the head. ||16||
Passing his time with increasing proficiency, this King, together with the poet and the wise scholar who had attained constant practice, spent his moments in nothing but joy.
The glorious rising of the Lord of Day occurs day after day.
Because he placed the lotus and the sprout below and bestowed his head upon all sovereigns,
the Creator ordained that this [lotus] should remain above.
Why is its foot marked with an upward stroke? ||18||
By means of that [conquest], he established an inexhaustible treasury; though still in the bloom of youth,
he was like the spring season bringing a forest to fruition, a friend to the Lord of Love.
Then his youth embraced his body. ||19||
Compassion was held by his foot upon lotuses; how could there be even a fraction of the shade of his body upon a sprout?
Even in the service of his mouth, [the lotus] attained the status of a servant.
Nor was he the autumnal moon, the lord of the night. ||20||
Did the Creator not count his virtues with millions of lines on his skin under the guise of body hair?
Or did the Maker of the World not [count them] under the pretext of the multitude of his pores?
And what fault is there in these drops being devoid of defects? ||21||
In the plundering of his enemies' fortresses, the long and thick mass of the bolt was surely grasped by his two arms;
and there, the splendor of his chest shone like a gateway.
She extended herself across the door, making it difficult to force open. ||22||
[To her] whose smile, a mere fragment of her own play, puts the moon to shame;
whose lotus-like wealth of eyes is surpassed by her own rays;
and who possesses an inner beauty so lovely that it triumphs over that pair [the moon and the lotus].
There is no likeness of his face among the moving and the unmoving.
His lotus-face was surpassed by his very glance, and even the splendors of the moon were conquered by his smile alone;
where, indeed, could there be anything more auspicious? Oh, how magnificent!
There is poverty in the comparison of her face. ||24||
The yak-cow, desiring to equal her own heavy tail with the hair growing from his head,
confesses her childish fickleness to one who is innocent of offense.
Again and again, under the pretext of wagging his tail. ||25||
And because of that king's beauty which rivaled the God of Love,
and his own heart's longing for him,
the inhabitants of the three worlds were divided twofold toward that monarch.
In those women with arched brows, there arose the amorous agitation of the God of Love. ||26||
Having drunk him in deeply with eyes that have abandoned their closing, the gods have acquired such a mastery;
these [eyes] now manifest that very intensity of practice.
Even now, with eyes that have lost their power to blink. ||27||
"Thus has our life become fruitful, having heard this;
and thus has our pair of eyes become fruitless, not having seen it. So they spoke regarding Nala, the beloved of the serpents.
They praise and they revile from their hearts that very Self. ||28||

By mortal women, through the power of constant meditation, he was beheld even during the closing of their eyes; thus, not even the slightest obstacle arose for them in seeing him, even when blinking occurred.

Which woman did not see him in her dreams at night? And which woman did not call out his name when she stumbled over his clan-name? And which woman, whose husband was meditated upon as being identical with him, did not call out to him during lovemaking?
He neither acted nor failed to act upon the arising of his own mind-born passion. ||30||
Beholding him in her hand, which fair woman— devoid of pride— did not hold it, thinking, "I am worthy of his splendor," while looking at herself? Yet she abandoned Damayantī.
The mirror was not made soiled by breath. ||31||

Just as the city of the son of Virocana was forcibly entered by the consumer of enjoyments [the demon Bali] while being carried away, so too was Madana introduced by Youth alone into the heart of the daughter of Vidarbha, which was already besieged by Love.
When that king, who was worthy of her own excellence of form,
had heard [her praises] many times,
that daughter of King Bhīma distinguished him above all others.
The mind is subject solely to the power of the ignorance born of the mental faculty.
Attending upon her father's worship, she grew increasingly enamored day by day with those bards as they recited at the appropriate moments the praises of rival kings.
Her hair stood on end as she listened for Nala.
During conversations with her friends, when even the name "Nala" was heard from the mouth of a companion regarding a blade of grass,
that slender woman would quickly shake off everything else and become absorbed in it.
With joy, her ears were then poised to hear it.
"She said, 'I am afraid of Smara, the enemy of Parāśara, who has unblinking eyes; therefore, describe him.
At that, the people, praising the young man, consecrated the King of Niṣadha as the illustrative example for his station."
Under the pretext of inquiring about Nala’s virtues, messengers, brahmins, bards,
and minstrels who had come from Niṣadha drank in those accounts of his fame through her.
She remained for a long time, feeling dejected. ||37||
"Paint two figures, a man and a woman, who possess the splendor that conquers the three worlds, upon the wall of this pleasure-chamber.
Thus was she addressed by the preeminent artist.
And she perceives the friendship between Nala and herself. ||38||
Where did she not see Nala as her own husband during the night through the power of her longing?
For by the influence of unseen destiny, one may perceive even that which is not before one's eyes.
Sleep makes the sight of people its guest. ||39||
From his pair of eyes closed by sleep,
and from his heart likewise sealed by the silence of the external senses,
he was seen while being concealed— never before beheld.
That great lord of the earth knew her profound secret. ||40||
Oh, how her greatness was attained day after day even during the onset of winter for her who was tormented by love;
for even at the height of the summer season, she possessed a fullness of fat.
They were borne by the nights. ||41||
Sometimes, it bore the beauty of a thread within itself, serving as a string for the pearl-necklace of the multitude of his own splendor and fame—
a necklace that occasionally robbed the fortitude of young women.
Nala also heard from the people a multitude of praises regarding her virtues.
Then, having found that very opportunity, Smara—
feeling envious because his own bodily beauty had been surpassed—
[acted] with his own unfailing power in embodied form.
With her, she desired to conquer the King of Niṣadha. ||43||
The king made his virtue a guest of the ears of that ruler,
whose arrow was aimed at the expenditure of Bhīma’s daughter’s lofty fortitude.
And by Smara, [he was made] the support for his own bow. ||44||
Then, indeed, that reckless warrior, making his bowstring resound with arrows for the sake of conquering that steadfast hero,
cast his own fame into jeopardy.
O Lord, you who have acquired [these] for the sake of conquering the three worlds! 45.
That [armor] shone forth because of the infallible will of Fate, who was thus about to unite him with the daughter of Bhīma;
for even by those arrows of the Bodiless One (Cupid), which were made of flowers, his armor of fortitude was pierced.
What else remains even now? For behold, scorched by his weapon,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) still takes refuge within the lotus,
concealing himself from him by making his own body its shadow!
I suspect that Nala was unable to leap over it. ||47||
Was her youth blooming with a pair of breasts formed upon her chest as a fresh offering?
Having crossed even the river of bashfulness, she—
That slender woman entered the heart of Nala. ||48||
The witness to the suffering of his wakefulness perceived that which the God of Love had wrought for him, as he denied his own lack of fortitude to the people.
And the night and the bed are as soft as the moon. ||49||
Though tormented intensely by love, that lord did not beg the King of Vidarbha for his daughter;
for the proud abandon their lives and even their happiness,
but they do not abandon their singular vow of never begging.
By means of feigned dejection and falsehoods, he concealed in certain places the succession of sighs born of separation;
and by applying an ointment containing an excess of camphor,
he explained away his paleness.
She was unable to conceal that from her beloved;
for he spoke to her who had been falsely watched by him in the very assembly while the lute-players were playing, and he fainted during the fifth musical modulation (*mūrcchanā*).
That king, whose reputation stood at the forefront of those who have conquered their senses,
felt shame as the unrestrained prowess of Śiva— the enemy of Śambara—
gradually became manifest there.
Indeed, these virtues, headed by discernment, were not at all able to restrain his fickleness;
for that Love creates one who is truly "unrestrained" (aniruddha) in passion—such is the very nature of creation. 54.
Since he was unable to remain in the assembly even with great effort because of the mark of his bodiless state,
he then went for a moment under the pretext of wandering in the garden.
He desired to resort to a desolate region. ||55||
Then, having been rebuked by Śrī, he whose emblem is the fish, together with his companions who knew his secret intentions,
reportedly went to look at the grove on the outskirts of the city.
He gave orders to his attendants to prepare the vehicle. ||56||
Then they brought him that white horse, adorned and superior in both speed and stature, with its constant flickering [of the tail].
The interior of the stable was trampled by the hooves of the horses.

Then, it was illuminated by the rays of the mane-hairs rising from the neck like rays from a divine gem, resembling the day of the lord of the night (the moon) traveling along the path leading to the Avatū region.
He was attended at his feet by the dust raised from the incessant striking against the edges of the earth,
as if by the minds of people who had arrived with the speed of their utmost effort to study the science of *aṇimā* (the power of becoming minute).
With its bill moving restlessly back and forth, it seemed eager to speak to the mountain of its pride in its own speed;
"Enough with words," [the mountain thought], "for he surely knows my intention."
And he himself maintained silence regarding the horse. ||60||
On the path of the great chariot-warrior, the universal monarch, white fame arose from his independent bearing of others; it appeared, as it were,
under the guise of the brilliant rays of his tusks, for such [fame] is not seen in others.
Laughing within, he was the inner strength of the sun's horses. ||61||
And by the pretext of its white luster reaching a state of flickering in its tail and mane,
it clearly did not conceal its status as a king among horses through the signs of its pair of waving chowries.

Moreover, he attained the status of a rival to Garuḍa— who had been forcibly conquered by the pride of his own speed— by means of the long and beautiful reins attached to his mouth, which served as the prowess for swallowing the double-tongued serpents.
The large-eyed lord of the earth, who had conquered all kings, mounted that horse born in the Sindhu region— a brother to the moon in its whiteness, which bore away the splendor of Uccaiḥśravas.
Like one's own rays surrounding the sun of piercing brilliance,
the horsemen surrounded him as he rode upon his swift steed, his lotus-like hand clearly marked with a blooming lotus.
Having the nature of light, they followed the lord of men. ||65||
Adorning his swift horse as he rode, Nala— graceful in attire suited for his own charioteer—
was gazed upon by the city-dwellers with eyes whose lashes were motionless from joy.
Then, in an instant, he who possessed the splendor of the Lord of Night and the prowess of Indra, with a horse whose speed was to be mastered only by the Wind-god,
emerged from the city together with those showers of glances from the people.
Then, shouting "Receive!
and "Strike!", the two armies of horsemen, with their sword-blades flashing like sprouts against one another, playfully staged a mock battle at the vanguard of Nala out of curiosity.
"How much ground is there for us to travel? Let even the ocean become dry land!"—
as if thinking thus, the horses, proud of their own speed, galloped on.
The dust, raised up, was capable of obstructing the ocean.
When Hari ascended to the sky with a single step,
even as he was proceeding with four steps,
those horses turned back with their faces bowed down in shame, having taken only half a stride toward the heavens.
The cavalrymen of that king, like Saindhava horses through their faith in the words of the Jina,
formed circles even with their many steeds upon reaching that pleasure ground.
As if thinking, "The very quarters have been overstepped by his enemies,
and the ocean itself has been turned into a cow’s footprint by his glories," the circle of kings disregarded the [raining] stream.
The ground was adorned with horses by the splendor of their movements.
Nala caused the horse to perform beautiful circles beneath his own royal umbrella;
does the wind even today not learn from them by spreading its movements in the form of whirlwinds?
Then, desiring comfort, the lord of the earth went and entered the Vilāsa grove;
and desiring sleep, he entered that place which was suffused with the glow of young coral shoots.
Hari [is like] the ocean, which possesses the shadow of wealth. ||74||

Having reached the edge of the forest, as he gradually entered the range of vision, the multitude of citizens— acting as kinsmen to the assembly of relatives who were following him— turned back their streams of sight with longing.
Then, as the flower and the lovely fruit were being presented by the hand of the forest-guardian with his fingers pointing toward them, that lord of men—
He gazed upon the loveliness of the forest.
Fruits and flowers were held by those standing on branches shaken by the wind arising from the onset of old age,
having gathered them due to the senescence of the great seers.
In the forest, he then received hospitality from the trees. ||77||
There, out of curiosity, he beheld a *ketaka* flower that bore, under the guise of bees clinging to its unblown petals, the wandering ill-fame acquired by the moon-crested Lord for abandoning it.
Since you, a barbed arrow, are placed by Smara with its barb facing inward as a bitter thorn in the hearts of those destined for separation,
you are therefore reviled by the burner of Manmatha’s own body because of your difficulty in being drawn back.
With you as his assistant needle, the Mind-born God sews the garments of ill-repute upon lovers;
clearly, with his arrows taking the form of saws, he acts cruelly upon the wood that is the hearts of those separated from their beloveds.
"Even though his hands are moistened with honey from his bow, the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) makes me subject to his arrows by dusting the daughter of Bhīma with your pollen"—
thus was the *kaitaka* flower reviled by him in anger.

He beheld the fruits of the pomegranate tree— which was being fumigated with incense as a ritual for its first-fruits— hanging head-downwards as they drank the smoke; they appeared like water-jars performing intense penance to attain the lofty height of the breasts of the fair-browed maidens of Vidarbha.
He beheld a pomegranate tree, like a woman separated from her lover, whose thorns had clearly bristled at the memory of her beloved;
it was one whose breasts were its fruits, which had burst open with passion, and into whose heart the parrot-like mouths of parrots— acting as the god of love’s *kiṃśuka* arrows— were entering.
He beheld a fragment of a stalk attached to a *palāśa* flower, which resembled the crescent-shaped arrow of Smara; for those who travel on the road, it clearly serves as food when they are emaciated.
[It is] born from the black spot [on the moon], which shatters the hearts of those separated from their lovers. ||84||
The fresh creeper, kissed by the wind and its limbs drenched with droplets of nectar,
was gazed upon by the king with an eye whose corner was beautiful with a smile.
Trembling with fear, she drank [it] with great longing. ||85||

He beheld rows of campaka buds like sacrificial lamps of the enemy of Śambara (Kāma), which, under the guise of the black soot of bees, seemed to be accumulating demerit through the act of harming travelers and moths.
He thought that the pollen within the flowers,
which causes blindness to those separated from their lovers,
had been released by Smara against the Enemy of the Cities in former times.
It was as if the ashes from his body had become attached to the arrows.
In the forest, while the cuckoos heard the "huṃ" cries of the bees, their state of compassion for the separated lovers rose upward;
there, the distressed Nala beheld a land-lotus plant stretching out its hand of blossoms in a gesture of indifference.
To him, the mango tree appeared like one hissing with rage at the sound of buzzing bees,
its flower-buds trembling in the wind for the sake of the separated lover.
As if desiring to give [something] to the people, she made this gesture of threat. ||89||
"Day by day you must grow thinner, and again and again you must faint and suffer the heat!"—
it was as if the parrots, those twice-born birds, were thus cursing the travelers; he beheld them with eyes reddened by distress.
Having drunk in with an agitated mind the *cāmpeya* flower, which formed a high crest upon her creeper-like brow like a bud,
he suspected it to be a comet risen for the destruction of those separated from their lovers.
He beheld the *nāgakesara* flower, its pollen scattered by the whirling movements of swarms of bees clinging to it as they fell,
appearing like a whetstone with glowing sparks flying from the friction of Cupid’s arrows.

Then, seeing the swarms of bees humming as they flew toward her limbs, touching the clusters of flowers with their fragrant wings, Smara was ashamed, thinking they were arrows discharged from his own bow.
Wounded by the thorns of the swaying sprouts in the breeze, and exuding the fragrance of the finest sandalwood rising upward,
it resembles the breasts of the women of the harem.
He saw a ripe mālūra fruit. ||94||

Having mentally transformed the cluster of *pāṭala* flowers into the arrows of the God of Love— with his mind blinded by fear— he trembled, for its deep interior was not empty of blossoms suitable for plunging the hearts of the two youths.
In the forest, the dark-hued son of Siṃhikā (Rāhu) perceived the sage as a tree budding with buds;
he seemed to be vomiting the collection of lunar digits that had been devoured by the peak of the waning fortnight.
In former times, when the creepers were covered by a white canopy of hailstones suddenly cast down,
the playful movements of the wind, as it watched with closing eyes, produced a blossoming of joy within those flowers.
Since the trees have attained such vastness upon her lap, how could they not honor their nurse with their heads bowed down by the weight of their fruit?
He greeted those who were paying him homage. ||98||
For that king, the day was cooled by forest breezes,
made sweet by the nectar of flowers,
and rendered white by the pollen of ketaka blossoms.
To one separated from his beloved, the joys of the Kaumudī festival were not granted. ||99||
Even as the king, who was not a practitioner of yoga,
gazed upon that very face which was like the moon itself,
the cuckoo, its eyes repeatedly reddened with rage, [cried out].
The moon's enemy (the owl) was summoned by the sound "ku-hū-ru-ta."
He regarded the Ashoka tree— which possessed a name corresponding to its purpose, which was a refuge for those grieving for their homes and wandering in the forest,
and which seemed to offer a mass of blazing weapons of Kama through its sprouts— as if it were a vast mountain.

In the forest as well, the threefold symphony of music was performed for him: the playing of the waves on the banks of the pleasure-pool, the singing of the swarms of cuckoos, and the grace of the peacocks’ dance.
Where does a person of fortune not find enjoyment? (102)

For that purpose, having been taught by the people, parrots released in that forest praised him with eloquence; likewise, mainas, made into singers of his prowess, sang to him with the nectar of their voices. (103)
Thus, as he wandered through the forest rich with desirable fragrances— though already celebrated by the songs of cuckoos and praised by parrots—
he found no external abundance of fragrance.
There is no interval [of time] due to separation from the fair-browed lady of Vidarbha. ||104||
Holding his own emblem, the fish, in his trunk with the suspicion that it was water from the basin of a tree,
Smara— as if seeking his friend Madhu there amidst the cloud thick with all seasons— was thus conjectured. 105.

The forest breeze, a master of the art of dancing for the young vine-maidens and a thief before one's very eyes of the massed fragrance of tree blossoms, attended upon him with playful baths in the waters scented with honey.
Then, having taken his own [essence] due to fear, the ocean of waters— which had been collected for a long time in greater abundance from churning—
was seen by the king as a lake in the forest, appearing as if it were submerged within that very essence.

He bore, under the guise of a mass of lotus stalks rising from the ground at the edge of the shore and half-submerged in water, rows of teeth from the mouths of the serpent Abhramu as she lay submerged in the milk-ocean, possessing the brilliant luster of the tail of the serpent Ananta.
By kissing the clear reflections of the throngs of horses resting on its banks,
it shone as if it were supporting a thousand Uccaiḥśravas horses, struck by the lashes of its moving ripples.

Bearing beneath the guise of its multitude of white lotuses the dense mass of the moon, which is crowded with dark spots of equal luster, it shone with its interior beauty turned dark by that swarm. 110.

He was followed by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow— who possesses the discus (rathāṅga), who is associated with Lakṣmī (kamalā), and who is a friend to swarms of bees (śilīmukha)— under the guise of a cluster of lotus stalks,
appearing like a serpent remaining only as its coils (mṛṇāla).
He bore wave-ridges that were like his own beloveds resting on his lap;
and he bore a multitude of coral sprouts in the form of clusters of half-opened *kokanada* buds. (112)
Nala imagined that the great orb of lotuses, white and dark,
was emitting the radiance of the moon and the Kālakūṭa poison as they lay hidden within the water.

Where the successions of young *śaivāla* creepers were set in motion by the play of the waves, they surely assumed the appearance of the thick-smoking fumes rising from the presence of the submarine fire (*vāḍava-havyavāṭ*). (114)
Having fully attained the sun, manifesting an abundance of fragrance intermingled with thorns,
she displays during the day a physical form that is the abode of manifest splendor.
Sarojinī, from whom [the river] originated, acted like an Apsaras. ||115||
The tree on the bank, its long reflection cast in the flood of water and trembling from the waves stirred by the wind,
seemed to possess wings as it submerged and shook them while remaining within the Maināka mountain.
In that playful pond which stole the splendor of the ocean, he [heard] the sweet, respectful calls of female swans eager for sport;
there, near him, [he saw] one wandering in a wondrous manner.
The prince of Niṣadha recognized the golden swan.
Upon his beloved young wives, who were capable of sexual dalliance,
he bore the sprouts of the tree of passion produced by Love— the tree that had already put forth two leaves and begun to bud.
And by means of a pretext, [he touched] the two feet and the two beaks. ||118||
The great lord of the earth, though deeply distressed by his separation from his beloved, gazed for a moment at that bird which provided such singular solace to his mind.
His mind became slightly overcome with curiosity. ||119||
In whatever direction the Creator’s desire runs— unrestrained by the grasp of even those fated for liberation—
it is followed by that [desire] as the wind follows a blade of grass.
By the mind of people, which is utterly lacking self-control. ||120||
Then, having perched for a moment on one leg, the bird fell asleep by the pond;
he lay with his neck bent sideways and his head—
Covering [her] with his wing, he was languid from the exhaustion of passion. ||121||
Did you not perceive that golden lotus, adorned with a coral stalk, which— having surpassed the luster of its own self by means of its stalk—
was bowed down with shame?
Did he drink that water, or was it perhaps the lord’s fly-whisk?
Then, as he had dismounted from his horse, the two shoes shone upon his feet; did they perhaps put on armor,
desiring to fight with the sprouts of those two forests and the lotuses?
Having assumed by means of a ruse a dwarfed form that mimicked the Destroyer of Bali himself,
he approached with his silent foot.
The king grasped the moth with his hand.
Realizing then that he had been captured, he attempted again and again in his agitation to leap away;
but finding no hope of flight,
he cried out and merely bit the hands of his captor.
The lake, agitated by flocks of birds flying up and falling down in alarm, out of a sense of compassion for the king who had fallen into its depths,
[rescued] him with its wave-tossing [hands] from being seized by the birds.
He warded it off with lotuses as if with his hands. ||126||
Deceived by that beautiful winged bird,
the lotus-like feet of the departing Goddess Śrī slipped from the pond, as if to imitate the tinkling of anklets on moving feet.
On the bank, a flock of kalahamsa geese warbled. ||127||
"O friend! This earth is no longer fit for habitation, since its lord is such as you, who has abandoned all moral conduct!
Thus did the birds, having left the earth and taken to the sky, surely reproach him with their cries.
Then, praising repeatedly, "This quality of being born from gold is not seen in a twice-born man," he was addressed by that resident of Lake Mānasa:
The lord of people [was touched] by that which brushed against the cage of his hands. ||129||

"Fie upon your mind, so restless with craving! Having observed my wings born of gold, how much increase could there be for you from these [wings], which are like the spray of frost to the ocean? (130)

Not only is the killing of living beings a slaughter for me, but even more so is the destruction of one whose inner self has placed trust in you through the mere sight of you— a destruction censured by those whose wealth is dharma.
Especially for those enemies who have placed their trust [in him]. ||131||
At every step there are warriors fierce in battle,
yet this passion for violence is not satisfied by them; fie upon such wicked prowess of yours, O King!
Toward that wretched bird who was the object of his compassion. ||132||
Since my livelihood, like that of a sage, depends thus upon the fruits and roots of water-born plants,
even upon such a person as me you have today laid hands with the staff of punishment.
How is it that the Earth does not feel ashamed before her husband? ||133||

Having thus composed these words for the king— which produced wonder, embarrassment, and compassion— the bird then made his own voices, like rivers of the essence of mercy, guests in that ocean-like heart.
The mother has but one son and is afflicted by old age; the female crane has recently laid her eggs and is pitiable.
This man is their only refuge; alas, O Fate, your lack of compassion is not restrained as you crush him! (135)

O Mother! My friends, whose companionship is compassion, will find relief from their flowing tears after censuring you for only a moment; however, this ocean of grief for my son is impossible to cross except by you alone. (136)
When you asked how far away my beloved was— his gait slow as a lotus stalk due to his message for me—
I looked toward the weeping birds.
"O beloved! What will that moment of yours be like? (137)
O Creator, how is it that from my lotus-hand— craftsman of coolness and softness for your beloved—
there has emerged a message of harsh syllables burning the forehead, saying: "You shall be separated from your beloved"?
O tremulous-eyed one! Alas, you have undoubtedly described this news of mine today— resembling a wound from a thunderbolt— to the faces of the quarters by your fellow travelers.
You will perceive even the ten [directions] as empty. ||139||
O lady of variegated limbs! If you should perish through my own grief, with your chest torn asunder, then I,
though already struck by fate, am truly ruined— alas, utterly ruined!
For it is evident that those children have passed away.
Alas, alas! Even those birds of yours, distressed by hunger, rolled about in their nests on the riverbanks;
though found after many long-felt desires, they have vanished in an instant before my very eyes, their vision unopened.

"O sons! Having called whom for so long with cooing sounds, and having made whose faces tremble, toward whom shall you now discourse?"—closing his eyes thus, he awoke from the sprinkling of the king's tears. 142.
The protector of the earth, out of compassion for the wretched, released him as he was thus lamenting; having said, "I have shown my form because you were held captive;
now go wherever you wish," he let him depart. (143)

Under the pretext of his wheel-like circumambulation, he performed a lustration ceremony for his kinsmen, whose eyes had previously shed streams of tears out of grief, but whose paths were now followed by tears born of joy.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the circle of kings among poets, begot Śrī Harṣa—who has conquered the host of his senses—and Māmalladevī;
this first canto has concluded in the beautiful epic *Naiṣadhīyacarita*, which is the fruit of meditating upon the *Cintāmaṇi* mantra, composed in the style of the erotic sentiment. 145.
The Second Canto: Having then obtained liberation from that Puruṣottama, the sovereign lord of the world, he—
That Brahmin attained that bliss which is not even within the range of words. ||1||
The bird shook its body, which was covered in bristling feathers, many times within the cavity jagged by the pressure of his talons.
And she scratched her two wings with the tip of her beak. ||2||
At that very moment of his stumbling, he took refuge with one of his hind legs, which had its knee raised high and its shank and foot extended upward.
With his head quickly scratched, he went to his dwelling. ||3||
Somewhere, that wise man, whose skin was only slightly itchy, brushed away the biting insects that were difficult to catch due to the inaccessible thickets of the Garuḍa forest.
By the pecking with the tips of their sharp beaks. ||4||
Having approached, he was quickly surrounded by the birds of the pond who were filled with suspicion;
then, due to his grasping at their feet with a distorted form, they flew up with loud cries.
Bearing the mark of many śaivala plants and possessing bees clinging to his rudrākṣa beads,
that bird went to the hand of Nīla.
Again, as if from the delusion that it was a red lotus in a lake. ||6||
Has that bird perhaps attained such extreme confidence through being caressed for a long time? ||7||
With his mind like that of a celestial being (Mānasa), he spoke while immersing the king’s heart in the waves of the nectar of curiosity,
making it as if it possessed two jars in the form of the cupped ears.
Hunting is not censured even by kings who have mastered the essential points of the scriptures on dharma;
for [O Smarasundara! you [have struck] me...
Your sacrifice is that very dharma, radiant with the arising of compassion. ||9||
Fish that devour the weak of their own kind,
birds that damage the trees of their own nests,
and deer that ravage blameless grasses.
It is not for kings who are engaged in the act of hunting [to kill]. ||10||
Whatever unpleasant thing I have spoken to you, I intended it to bring you what is beneficial;
it is like the heat produced by the sun for the sake of a tree’s growth.
Having showered [him] with nectar, like the sun. ||11||
It is not even now appropriate for you to reject this beneficial advice, which has come unasked from Fate itself, acting as an intermediary personage like a hand.
For that acceptance was obtained from one who was pure. ||12||
"O Lord of the World, having rendered service to you, what more could be required of me, a mere bird?
Thus I know; yet they do not abandon me."
Even so, you desire to repay me for that. ||13||
One should, without delay, perform a reciprocal service for a benefactor according to one's own means;
whether that service be great or small, the wise here do not hold fast to such distinctions. (14)
Even if this speech of mine is not charming to the discerning mind, it should still be heard,
for it is the voice of a bird.
Why will it not bestow joy, like the song of a parrot? ||15||
Victorious is that King Bhīma, whose name has indeed been rendered meaningful by his success against the host of his enemies;
having obtained him as her lord, the land of Vidarbha laughs even at heaven, whose master is Śakra.

From the ascetic Tathyagiri, who was pleased by his self-restraint despite his natural lack of it, he obtained a daughter whose excellence of virtues was peerless throughout the three worlds ordained by fate. (17)
Since she arose with the splendor of her body, this Damayantī became the intoxication of loveliness for the fair-browed women of the three worlds.
Thereupon, he bestowed upon her the name Damayantī. ||18||
Know that she is indeed the supreme Fortune arisen from the ocean of virtues of the lords of the earth;
for who does not know the digit of the moon residing upon the crest of Śiva, even though it is separated by a vast distance? 19.
Victorious are those masses of hair which that learned lady bears upon her head;
who would wish to compare them with a yak-tail whisk, even one held aloft by a beast? 20.
Under the pretext of scratching themselves with their hooves, the deer provide consolation to their own eyes,
which have been conquered by the rising drowsiness [of the day].
Out of fear of the splendor of that magnificent gaze. ||21||
Even the two worlds, even her eyes, and even the qualities of a beautiful woman previously heard of or seen,
were surpassed by the fame of Damayantī reaching the ears.
O Lord of the Earth! They shine forth all the more intensely. ||22||
His two eyes, though adorned with collyrium, reveal a lotus that is soiled; they touch not the doe, yet they even surpass the khanjana bird.
They bring about that which is difficult for pride in one's own taste to overcome. ||23||
Because the fruit called *bimba* is indeed inferior (*adhara*) to this [lip],
it appropriately receives the derivative name *adharabimba*.
They call her lip "the foot. ||24||
The orb of the moon, its essence extracted by the Creator for the sake of Damayantī’s face,
is seen with a hollowed center.
Possessing the deep blue-black hue of a deep, dug-out mine.
The Creator turns the large ceremonial lamp used for the lustration rite of Vidarbha’s daughter— a vessel smeared with cow-dung bearing the mark of the moon and white with a garland of moons.
In an examination regarding supreme beauty,
the entire lotus was surpassed by her face;
even now, it does not possess the auspicious marks [of that excellence].
Clearly abandons its emergence from the water. ||27||
Her two eyebrows arose like the bows of Rati and the Five-Arrowed One for the conquest of the world;
her high nose was not a mere tube [for arrows].
In you, there is neither falsehood nor desire for liberation. ||28||
O hero! That [lotus] of yours is truly comparable to the lotuses that dwell with their friends, for its arm-like stalks surpass those of the lotuses situated within the watery fortress.
He who, with the mere play of his hand, seizes hold of the goddesses of fortune. ||29||
O beautiful one, the two stages of life— childhood and that which follows it— desire to establish their own dominion even by means of fate,
yet not even by a line of hair.
Having established the boundaries, they divide [the territory] and take pleasure [in it]. ||30||
Furthermore,
as Love and Youth both surged forth within her form, they were indeed rendered unfathomable by the cascades of her radiance.
Your two breasts are like swimming jars. ||31||
Does the quality of causing the wheel to rotate, produced by its own cause— the rod— reside in the water-jar?
For that quality, becoming manifest in her two high breasts, spreads a whirling motion like a circle of streams of light.
Indeed, the peacock, whose plumage is eclipsed by Damayantī’s tresses, resorts to the six-faced god (Kārttikeya);
likewise, the lord of elephants, whose temples have been surpassed by the beauty of Damayantī’s breasts, resorts even to Indra, the enemy of Jambha.

With her fist, the palm of which was pressed against her back so that the middle of her abdomen was indented, Damayantī’s belly was made to shine with three folds emerging from its center at the distance of four finger-breadths. 34.
Does some curious person measure Damayantī’s belly with his fist?
For it is measured by her folds, which seem to hold its four fingers, together with the golden girdle.

By means of his training in the art of crafting the sun’s chariot, did the Creator perhaps wish to fashion a single-wheeled chariot for the God of Love, using her broad and rounded hips as the material? (36)
With her pair of thighs as thick as a tree-trunk, does the beautiful woman surpass even the tall *rambhā* plant?
Indeed, she alone would conquer even a young woman.
Her breasts were the fruit of the penance performed by the children of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Those two who, through service to the Sun,
attained the state of being his very feet—
surely they have now become the Creator’s own pair of swan-consorts, having reached the Lake of Milk along with their cries.
O lake of merit, you who are frequented by rivers— how could meditative concentration not spend the entire night there?
May the lotus attain its beautiful course.
In the birth named Damayantīpada. ||39||
Having made many villages my destination in order to visit lakes,
she was brought within the range of my sight as a guest.
Her belly is the domain of doubt regarding existence and non-existence. ||40||
Having ascertained that she had studied together with even the young women of heaven, I wondered: "Which husband dwells in the heart of the Creator for her? (41)
Then, examining him to see if he was suitable for all the other youths— who were unable to remove his status as a mere prima facie opponent—
I established my conviction that you were the final conclusion.
By this limit of your beauty,
my latent impressions have been awakened;
though she was gazed upon long ago, she is [as if] seen today.
She of the pure smile has ascended into my memory. ||43||
O hero! Damayantī’s amorous agitation (kilakiñcita) truly shines supremely in you;
it truly glows only upon the breast of a young woman.
The beauty of the rows of jewel necklaces. ||44||
This form of yours is fruitless without her, like a flower on a barren tree;
this earth, though rich in wealth, is in vain.
And what is this forest where even the cuckoos are singing together? 45.
Union with her, who is desired by the gods, will not be easily obtained by you,
who are enclosed by wealth like a cloud at the onset of the rainy season.
Like a night-lotus by the light of the moon. ||46||
Therefore, I shall perform your praise in the presence of Damayantī in such a manner that you,
once placed within her heart, cannot be removed even by Indra himself. (47)
Fie on this report submitted merely to obtain your approval!
For the virtuous demonstrate their own utility through action, not by words from their own throats. (48)
Having drunk this clear nectar of speech uttered by the lord of birds,
he produced [this work] out of extreme satisfaction.
He [emitted] that white smile like a belch. ||49||
Having caressed the bird with his hand, which was like a red lotus, the King of Niṣadha softly uttered words for its delight.
They are wells of nectar for pleasant speech, born from their throats. ||50||
Your form is not within the scope of a scale, nor is your virtuous character on the path of words;
that "your virtues are of the same nature as your example" is a seal that stamps the very essence of all comparison.
Is it not the case that your body alone is not made of gold, but rather even your speech is likewise?
Is it not the case that your partiality extends beyond the pathless road, reaching even to one such as me? (52)
Carrying intense heat, I have encountered you, O Wind, who possess the essence of coolness;
for while the wealth of the wealthy is otherwise, for the virtuous, the very presence of one endowed with excellence is their true treasure.
That great medicine for deluding the three worlds has already reached my ears hundreds of times; yet,
by this praise of yours, it is [renewed].
I know her to have been attained by my own vision alone. ||54||
For those wise men who perceive everything clearly through their friends and their own hearts,
there is no witness more subtle than this, even though it is close at hand.
The two eyes are merely ornaments for the face. ||55||

O bird! When people have made the story of that immeasurable nectar a guest in my ears, it becomes a kindling verse for igniting the fire of passion; shame on me, who possesses such lack of fortitude! 56.

O Heaven! The wind arising from the direction of Yama’s consort is unfavorable to me; it consists of the poisonous hissing of the circle of Malaya serpents and serves as fuel for the fire of separation from her.
O bird! Since this lord of the night assails the lord of the day month after month, will he not then burn me with his even more intense rays that steal away my fortitude? (58)
If the arrows of Smara were indeed flowers and not thunderbolts born of poisonous creepers, then they would not have bewildered my heart.
And that which has passed away excessively. ||59||
Therefore, as I am sinking here into the shoreless ocean of the affliction caused by the arrows of Kandarpa, may you be my support like a boat.
The proximity [of the cause] is produced by a rule without a specific occasion. ||60||
Or rather, why does this urging of yours not merely grind what is already ground for us?
For the altruism of the virtuous exists by its very nature.
For the validity of apprehensions corresponds exactly to their being in accordance with reality. ||61||
May all be auspicious on your path;
may our reunion be swift.
O friend! Accomplish, accomplish your desire.
We are the youth who should be remembered at the proper time.
Having thus dismissed him, that steadfast king, a Bṛhaspati in truthful speech,
entered his forest dwelling, filled with wonder by the cries of the swans that remained fixed in his memory.
Then, in order to make that very day fruitful by beholding the daughter of Bhīma,
he [set out] toward that which served as the ornament of the circle of the earth.
Maṇḍaja went to the city of Kuṇḍina. ||64||
First, on the road, he beheld before him a water-filled jar, a guest to his eyes, foretelling the success sought by the traveler.
That kalahamsa bird began to utter its call. ||65||
Having paused for a moment in the sky, languid with the sentiment of wonder at the desire to behold it,
he descended into the Vilāsa grove of the mountain king.
He beheld the fruit joined with the mango tree. ||66||
That bull among birds beheld a city with many watchtowers, attended by clouds like playful elephants in the sky.
[He saw] a hyena and a serpent hidden by the branches. ||67||
With the base of his wings shaken, he flew for a moment,
then for a moment he was difficult to discern as he soared upward,
spreading his broad, motionless pinions.
For a moment, he granted the curiosity of light. ||68||
With a slender stream of light moving swiftly,
he seemed to rub the gold of his wings against the surface of the sky, which resembled a shining touchstone for the purpose of testing the world.
With birds swooping downward from above, suddenly alarmed by the fear of a hawk's descent, he was watched with a single gaze as his trail of fluttering leaves made a whirring sound.
He was not seen by the people on earth because, at that very moment,
they cast their eyes toward the sky and in all directions upon seeing his shadow.
His range of vision was swiftly swept away by a great velocity. ||71||
On his journey, he never took shelter in a forest that was exceedingly beautiful with its lofty trees,
nor did he converse with any kinsman.
Or [he uttered] a cry, with a radiance spreading from the speed of his movement. ||72||
Then that city, protected by the arm of Bhīma and ruled by Dharañjaya,
came within the range of vision of the bird.
It shone with palaces resembling the mountain of Śiva. ||73||
Where the crystal stone forms shone like continuous waves of joy and laughter of the earth directed toward her beloved.
The houses had walls that were unmarked by the moon. ||74||

Where, out of fear of the sun, even during the day, darkness— arising from the constant recurrence of its absence— dwelt for the sake of refuge, serving as a pretext for the luster of the king’s sapphire palaces.
In that mansion fashioned from white, radiant jewels, where the expanse of the floor was laughing with its blossoming lotuses,
the single lunar day of the full moon alone attended as a guest throughout the entire night.
There, the pond, its depths stained by the saffron rubbed off from the bodies of beautiful women bathing therein,
did not clear itself even throughout the entire night, like a stubborn, sulking woman.
By her, who was silent for a moment at night and who wore the series of ramparts as a yogic cloth,
the spotless palace of jewels appeared as if it were a mere reflection.
Some indescribable light within, beyond the external, is worshipped. ||78||
In one place, the sky, as if reflected within the depths of the lake,
sported upon the water that was clearly manifesting its own reflection under the guise of a moat.
As he traveled through the sky, the strikes from the staff-like hems of the fluttering garments on the rows of houses provided rest for Aruṇa,
who was driving the team of the Sun’s horses.

Indeed, she was born from the essences of all the worlds— those situated below, in the middle, and above, which are filled with the earth, the womb, and the sky respectively— and who bear their own distinct emblems. (81)
Bearing the state of having a throat as dark blue as a cloud,
and possessing a body radiant with exceedingly pure nectar—
how could that [glory] not be attained?
The mountain-king’s palace attained the state of being the abode of the moon-crested Lord.
The dark spots on the moon-like faces of the statues of various forms were like the Rāhu-demons swallowed within the bellies of the lions carved upon the many necks of the palaces.
Nārada, whose speech was ever truthful, declared that Bali’s abode was heaven, and even above heaven; yet by that very declaration,
it was rendered inferior.
She was born from that which is contrary [to worldly norms], as an ornament of the earth. ||84||
From the fragrance of roasted barley flour used to call out to travelers, rising from the water-mills along the market road,
there was no quarreling with the clouds.
Even now, he lets out a gurgling sound as he abandons [his life]. ||85||
The Vindhya mountain, with its wings of doors made of dense jewels, [seemed to] receive the proud lady of gold who had come from the lap of heaven, the king of the immortals.
Embracing and consoling her, he dwelt with her. ||86||
Surrounded by fires born from the surfaces of blazing sun-stones that formed a halo,
the city of Bāṇa attained the status of being the most excellent, surpassing even the city of the Sun, which experiences rising and setting between dawn and dusk.
The ocean of that marketplace resounded loudly, where the multitude of crabs— hands engaged in counting numerous conchs, jewels, and cowries— moved about amidst the white sands of Himalayan musk.
Because her waters were swollen by the moonstones trickling from the floors of the houses and towers,
the celestial Gaṅgā did not abandon her conduct befitting a devoted wife at every rising of the moon.
Where, it is said, the rays of the setting sun, having lost their support, stumbled and became homeless;
for the evening streets of the saffron shops served as their place of refuge.
Where all the merchandise spread out for sale in the merchant's shop is gazed upon by the people as if by the sage, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu.
The objects of the world are within the belly of Hari. ||91||
When the merchant weighed [the flower] in his shop against emeralds and rubies, it did not ring out with the noise of people, being rendered motionless by its greed for fragrance.
Even though it is buzzing and soiled with blackness. ||92||
In former times, for those traveling at night during the winter, there was a bridge made of sun-stones that remained warm throughout the entire day due to the heat imparted by fire.
Wherein the cold does not pain our feet. ||93||
At the onset of the summer heat, that path, composed of moonstone and cooled by the water born of lightning’s radiance, was as cool as the character of Nala.
The heat did not burn with such intensity as it had before. ||94||

Under the guise of a circular moat, she— difficult to penetrate due to the complex arguments of the commentaries spoken by the Serpent (Patañjali)— has been brought to a state of coiled enclosure, so that she is no longer within the reach of capture by enemies. 95.
There, the daughter of Bhama herself adorned her face, hands, feet, and eyes with lotuses, while her other limbs were decorated with campaka flowers.
The beauty of the flower garlands for the worship of Smara. ||96||
Unable to sport in the sky because of the weight of their hips and breasts,
the Apsarases have surely descended to this city.
Her circle of friends occupied the space in between them by the hundreds. ||97||
How could that which is not composed of variegated colors not possess all its hues in a stable state?
How could it undergo a change in its tone?
Possessing many voices of various kinds, or not. ||98||
Thirsty from having met the sun during the day with its banner red with its own radiance,
they licked the moon in many ways.
At night, their dwellings were made of rubies. ||99||
At night, the moon, parched by the rays of the sun, licked with its tongue-like banner of its own radiance the nectar-bearing orb.
That which was produced from pure ruby at the king's palace. ||100||
The mark of the moon, possessing the luster of nectar, was joined by a yellow banner on the turret of the palace as he lay upon Śeṣa, who had coiled himself into a circle.
He first established friendship with the one clad in yellow garments. ||101||

In former times, the daughter of Gādhi, having slightly commenced her descent, was perhaps released as the Mandākinī; for her silken stream, swaying in the wind atop his palace, played in the heavens, while the celestial rites were interrupted by the multitude of faces of the gods— Brahmā and the others— who, their tongues purified by tireless recitation of the Vedas, offered profuse hymns of praise.

Rolling about on the palm of the sun’s lap, the daughter of Yama attained childhood—a state where her radiance was shimmering with the beams from his exceedingly pure blue chambers, and she was like a garland of cloth upon a white palace. (103)
A passionate woman, having climbed to the top of her own pleasure-palace, was eager to welcome as a guest the rain-cloud that had arrived at the turret of her lover’s palace;
she became like a celestial nymph whose chariot had ascended into the sky, for she did not even blink as she traveled along the path with the speed of a cloud out of delight.
On the pleasure-mountain of Vidarbha, from the emerald peaks, rays of light rose up like blades of *darbha* grass.

By these, whose tips reached the face of the celestial cow Surabhi as she stood with her mouth upturned in the sky, the merit of his vow to grant morsels of grass to cows expanded without ceasing—she who had cast down her head in shame because her pride was shattered by the blow of the universe. (105)
By means of tree basins fashioned from moonstones, filled with the exudations of their own essence through the embrace of the moon's rays,
the laborious ritual of watering them was rendered fruitless.
There, his heart was captivated by the forest of Damayantī.
Then Kanakapatra beheld that princess in the assembly, shining with a luster equal to her companions,
her beauty capable of emulating the crescent moon situated in the midst of the host of stars. (107)
Somewhere below, a bird, its golden luster scattered by the speed of its circling flight, seeks a place suitable for landing; meanwhile,
another hangs down, eager to attend upon this moon-like face of hers.
He spread it out like the halo of the moon above.
"Thus Śacī experiences the intense joy of the Nandana grove together with her companions headed by Ghṛtācī"—
such was the thought that arose in the bird upon seeing the daughter of Bhīma engaged in play with her friends in the forest.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this second canto, naturally radiant, has reached its conclusion in his beautiful epic poem, the *Naiṣadhīyacarita*. (110)
The third canto: Then, having descended with speed from the expanse of the sky by means of his two contracted wings, he—
With his wings shaken by the wind from the region where he had alighted, the swan fell to the ground near the daughter of Bhīma. ||1||
Then, the sudden sound that arose from the earth being struck by the hollow of her wings caused her to quickly cast her gaze elsewhere.
He caused his inner mind to become utterly bewildered. ||2||
The eyes of the princesses of Vidarbha, having abandoned their respective graspings for external objects,
attained that one whose form is beyond description.
Like Brahmā, he [knows] the minds of those who are firm in their vows. ||3||
The crane,
desiring to seize the swan moving within its own body, acted with the same lack of respect as a sage’s mental faculty toward the *haṃsa* residing within his own person.
With effort, he attained a state of immovability. ||4||
Having inferred from her gestures that she was composed of illusion, he did not fly up into the air; instead,
by the lightness of his leap, he rendered futile her hand as it was about to fall upon him.
Having thus concluded that her resolve had been rendered futile by that bird,
they clapped their hands against one another.
At that time, the rows of trees were made to resound by the bees.
Now, you must drive him away with the clapping of hands;
he who follows me harms me as much as he does you.
Thereupon, her circle of friends was reproached by her with the word "here. ||7||
Then the dark-complexioned maiden, her slight anger restrained by the laughter of her friends, followed him like a shadow follows one approaching the sun,
until the swan reached its destination.
Marked by bashfulness, she followed behind. ||8||
"O Teacher, you shall not go toward the swans again," she was teased by them with this playful jest;
she replied, "It would certainly not be an ill omen for me."
This swan is a foreteller of future delights. ||9||
Even that swan, as it moved gracefully before the fair-toothed maiden who possessed a swan-like gait,
appeared to falter out of a sense of embarrassment at her movement.
Mocking him loudly, as if imitating him right before his eyes. ||10||
Just as she surely perceives that [the mango fruit] will be within reach at every step as it unfolds,
so too does she move playfully among the creepers.
Having deceived her with that, he dragged away the slender-limbed woman.
When he perceived her, accompanied only by her shadow, with her kinswomen forbidden by his anger,
her limbs were then adorned with drops of perspiration from fatigue.
He spoke in human speech like Kīra.
Ah! How far do you go? Why do you weary yourself thus in vain?
O young girl, does fear even arise within you?
She did not gaze upon the dense rows of forest trees.
Behold, as you are vainly setting foot upon the wrong path,
this breeze restrains you with the trembling of its hands— its swaying sprouts— like a female friend.
The forest grove resounds with the cooing of pigeons.
"How can I, who roam the sky, be supported by you, who have the earth as your only path?
Oh! Your childhood has not been diminished."
By this very youth, which is also the friend of the God of Love.
We are like the wings of the swan, belonging to the lineage of the thousand-petalled lotus-throne;
for those such as us, the nectars of eloquent flattery are difficult to obtain elsewhere than in the world of the gods. (16)
May we enjoy a perfection of bodily form corresponding to our food— the golden lotus stalks of the celestial river— [we] whose arms are like the tips of those very stalks.
For one learns qualities from the cause in the effect. ||17||
By the decree of fate, among these golden swans who have come here to frequent the pleasure-lake of Nala,
I alone remain.
I wander, eager to behold the world of mortals. ||18||
Once, during the playful wandering of the Creator, he granted rest to his own shoulders for those who were weary from their great burden; from that time on, it has been so.
I am weary, even though I travel everywhere without resting. ||19||
No one, even one who has acquired human prowess through snares and the like, can bind a celestial being or a beast;
for a man, that [prowess] is effective against none other than one such as me.
The fortune of one's own enjoyments belongs to that which arises rarely. ||20||
Subdued by Nala’s sacrifices and meritorious works,
even the immortals here provide him with celestial enjoyments;
for trees, through the power of being watered during their period of longing, put forth buds out of season.
Descending quickly from the golden mountain, we fan him with drops of water from the celestial river at the time of amorous play.
And with wings that had formed a friendship with fly-whisks, they fanned the king.
If an investigation into the correct declensions were to be undertaken,
then that individual [the feminine gender] would be the primary object of expression,
she who accomplishes the forms *sva*, *au*, and *jas* through her various charms.
For that long, patience would be a state of great abundance. ||23||
That king, a performer of sacrifices who protects the assembly of gods,
enjoys his kingdom as if it were the very sovereignty of a sacrifice, having entrusted his royal fortune to learned Vedic scholars.
But previously, the final [moment] was entirely the remainder of the day. ||24||

To that beloved deity, who is contented with his desired objects, and whose vow is like an unfailing cloud raining down floods of wealth upon the multitude of supplicants to dispel their poverty— him [I praise].
Who indeed in the world does not seek refuge in the Lord of the World? ||25||
It is said that Rambhā, having long made Nala’s incomparable splendor nectar for her ears,
became enamored of him there; yet, failing to obtain him, she resorted to another.
She [spoke] that name, "Nalakūbara," and [offered] food and fragrance. ||26||
When we departed from here for the world of the gods, having drunk in the excellence of his singing during our dalliances, he was grieved by that [departure] as he sang out, "Alas! Alas! (hā hā).
By his very name, Hāhā became a singer of Hari. ||27||
Hearing of that noble disposition of Pulomajā’s daughter, the world-protector, his hair bristling with joy again and again, did not look at her while he was with his wife, owing to his own merit.
His garland of eyes was veiled by tears of joy. ||28||
While the Lord was listening to the multitude of his own qualities—
which forcibly captivate the mind— Pārvatī, sharing half of Śambhu’s body, covered her ears with her fingers.
When [will it be] not under the pretext of scratching? ||29||
Enough with the ritual of composing poetry; the Creator restrains my speech under the pretext of silence.
Therefore, embracing his throat, may I be satisfied with the essence of aesthetic flavor.
He, dull-witted from his Vedic learning, does not perceive that crookedness.
There was no injury whatsoever to the vow of that devoted wife, for she was the very ground for the embrace of Śrī;
nor did it result in the destruction of all beings, because she was the self of all beings.
By even a slight atom of jealousy on the part of her husband. ||31||
Fie upon that shameless hand of the Creator who fashions the full moon on the day of the lunar festival; I believe he is truly wise, for his memory of the beauty of her face remains ever fresh.
Having performed this, he cast half of it upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Deprived of its luster by shame upon hearing of our moon-like face— which has conquered it— the moon hides itself from our mouth even within the flood of the ocean at sunrise.
Once, within the womb of a cloud that was wandering through the sky, ||33||
Having consoled us— our own banner-bearing retinue— the Enemy of the Daityas,
for the sake of praising his exceedingly lotus-like face, [drank] from that [nectar] which was swallowed by the lotus of his contracting navel.
The element, being shameless, delights in Ramā. ||34||
Within his mouth, as it were by means of the thirty-two lines formed by his teeth,
there are fourteen and eighteen branches of knowledge.
The Creator declared that she exists in both ways. ||35||
Beholding the two splendors of that lord of men, we do not even remember the God of Love or the Lord of the Immortals;
and because of his perfect dwelling in forbearance, we truly do not apply our minds to the knowledge of Śeṣa.
Without wings, by the sons of Vinatā; by winds, which can only be inferred by their effects;
or by minds, which are not of minute dimensions—none of these surpassed the direction reached by his horses. (37)
On the battlefields where the rivers have been formed by the blood of enemies,
[he becomes the refuge] for those whose food is the wind and rain from the streams of his arrows.
There was an abundance of food through the vital breaths of those belonging to the royal lineage. ||38||
The fame that arose for him in battles through his arm, which possessed a restless longing for combat,
spread to the rivers of the quarters solely because of its quality as a cause.
His addiction to eroding the riverbanks. ||39||

If the three worlds were intent on counting, and if there were no end to their lifespan; and if the calculation reached beyond the *parārdha*—even then, he would possess infinite qualities, for his virtues are entirely beyond measure. (40)

Because the doors were never barred, we slender-waisted women entered the inner apartments of that king among the animals; and as they departed for their delightful dwellings, we taught them an even greater degree of excellence.
We immerse ourselves within the ocean of their aesthetic flavor with secret tales of the exquisite beauty of Rambhā and others, which are like streams of nectar flowing from their lips.
Let him create poetry with poetry through his devoted efforts. ||42||
By which [words] there might I not have been made a merchant for depositing the trust of fresh amorous commands?
For no animal ever feels shame before anyone, nor does any animal feel abashed by that [shame]. (43)
Even a rumor does not reach another person when one restrains it within a heart that is without cracks through yoga—
a heart cleansed by the teachings from the various mouths of Brahmā.
His ears were filled with the hearing of the treatises on meditative concentration. ||44||
Alas, by taking refuge in Nala, you obtain the enjoyment of the third heaven, which would otherwise have been unattainable for you—
just as the night-lily does through the embrace of the moon.
[He is] like a rare festival of moonlight for a lotus plant. ||45||
Therefore, that happiness born from our flatteries— which would otherwise be difficult for you to obtain because you have not married a Nishadhan—
is like a mango grove frequented by bees.
Like a spring that has not attained its full splendor. ||46||
Or rather, will you not go into the very hand of that Creator himself?
For who has seen his mind after entering it?
You have not yet even taken a husband's hand.
And it is the substratum for the excellence of the nature of form. ||47||
The effort of even the Creator to unite the night with the moon, the Lord of the Mountain with Śivā, and Hari with Śrī, is recognized as being entirely natural.
For the sake of a mutually suitable union. ||48||
You, whose lute is the ocean of feminine virtues that transcend all bounds, are not fit for union with anyone other than Nala;
a tender jasmine garland cannot be woven with a cord of darbha grass that is exceedingly rough.
I indeed inquired about the ritual for the bride’s departure— the one suitable for Nala’s dalliance—
whose syllables, like those of your name, were drunk by my ears.
I am sporting with him upon the wheel of the wheel. ||50||
Or, if you are united with another husband, so that your reputation for wisdom may cause your life to end,
it will be to cross over the ocean of public scandal.
Of the three ways of the Creator, which one would it be? ||51||
Let that be; enough with this irrelevant reflection.
O slender one! You have been exhausted by me to an extreme degree. I am he who now desires to wipe away that offense.
Tell me what you desire, and I shall grant it to you.
Having spoken thus, the bird fell silent,
desiring to know the heart of the princess;
for both the deep lake and her heart had been entered.
For the virtuous indeed praise the undertaking of a task. ||53||
With her head slightly tilted and trembling,
that daughter of the lord of the earth reflected for a moment in her mind upon what was to be said, and then addressed the bird.
He spoke with a face that treated the moon as mere straw. ||54||
Fie on your fickleness and lack of affection for your child, by whose instigation you have become so agitated, like a ripple of water stirred by the touch of the wind!
I have assailed you while you were standing on the sidelines. ||55||
Through your clarity, you attain the state of a mirror; indeed, you are truly worthy of being beheld by the virtuous.
Yet, you place blame upon me, who am already guilty.
In whose self this [world] is reflected—[to him you bow]. ||56||
O gentle one, may you forgive me for this ignoble conduct practiced by a young girl; for you,
being a portion of a god, are worthy of my veneration even as a swan.
For the form of the Fish is indeed like the Śrīvatsa mark. ||57||
What pleasure do you wish to bestow upon me? May the joy of beholding you surpass even that which my eyes experience from the sprinkling of their own nectar;
for does the moon ever create anything distinct for living beings other than the moistening of their eyes with its own ambrosia? (58)
But as for that which the mind never abandons—how could such a desire ever reach the path of the throat?
What girl indeed, without shame, would speak of her longing to take the hand of the Moon, the king of the twice-born? (59)
Having drunk in her soft speech,
which possessed a flavor equal to that of the grape, that swan abandoned his delight in the warbling of the cuckoo.
And he felt loathing for the sound of the lute. ||60||
When she had spoken with her voice faltering due to bashfulness and had silenced her speech, the swan,
feeling some doubt regarding what she had indicated, [reflected].
With his speech, he joined this [man] to the lotus-face. ||61||
I am not even able to drink with my two ears that very matter which you, so full of longing, have thus spoken of as if wishing to seize the moon with your hand.
Is it like the final phoneme of a word within a sequence of sounds? 62.
Or what is there to be gained by so much, since that which exists even within the single path of your mind is where,
it is said, there is darkness even for the intellect?
Even that Brahman is attainable by those who are not excessively crooked. ||63||
In the midst of the manifestation of the sovereignty of Īśāna, in the midst of the worlds of the Lords of the World,
I bow even to the animal, who is ignorant yet possesses the reputation born of knowing the taste of falsehood.
Sarasvatī, the dweller in our mouths, stands as the neighbor in the midst of the other Śrutis;
yet she truly seems to shrink away from them out of modesty.
Just as a path is bound together by the quality of association with the virtuous. ||65||
If your mind, longing even for the city of Laṅkā— whose lap is occupied by Sarasvatī seated in the paryaṅka posture—
should turn toward any other object whatsoever;
Know that too to be lying dormant within its own bed.
Thus addressed by that bird,
the daughter of Bhīma, both abashed and delighted, replied:
"My heart desires Nala."
And it has no longing for anything else whatsoever. ||67||
Having reflected upon the mountain of the character of foolish folk—
where the elephant of passion sinks in the river of shame—
that lord of the swan-like birds spoke clearly to her who remained silent.
The king’s mind, desiring her hand in marriage, longs for Nala, thinking, "She is mine";
yet it has not been embraced by you, the poet of intimacy.
What can I, though wise, say regarding the meaning of these two verses? //69//
But having anticipated a reversal of the steadiness of your mind, I was indeed ignorant of what was to come;
for the hearts of young women are fickle by nature toward their object of desire.
Even the God of Love might have his arrows miss their mark. ||70||
Indeed, how can the moon-like King of Niṣadha, that great lord of the earth, be informed of this matter in such a manner?
For such a purpose is one fraught with uncertainty.
Like an ordinary person, so am I. //71//
Whether by your father’s command or by your own desire, if you choose another young man,
my conviction is that this act of supplication was undertaken solely for your sake.
What kind of impression would I leave upon the Lord of Niṣadha?
Was this drunk because of some suspected agitation in you,
or was it not fit to be poured into such a subject?
Yet, whatever else you seek apart from this—
O daughter of the lord of the earth! I shall perform all of that. ||73||
Shaking off those words as if they had entered her ears,
with her head shaken by disagreement, she spoke, her regard for modesty itself loosened.
Again, she is the daughter of the Earth and of Indra. ||74||
As long as this conceptualization of giving other than me remains in your heart, O Veda,
even the night will harbor the suspicion that its lover is someone other than the Moon.
One should place the syllable *oṃ* at its forefront. ||75||

"Without considering that her heart's passion for Sarojinī has no contact with the sun [of another suitor], she suspects that I might take the hand of someone else; oh, how great is your audacity! (76)
It is well that you have reasoned thus:
"I shall indeed resort to fire itself;
for without it, I cannot strike at my own self."
I shall not make you a speaker of falsehood before the king. ||77||
Furthermore, as for that reasoning which you have stated to deceive me— is it mute regarding the statement of its own result,
since its cause is incapable of being suspected of deviation?
If speech were not the Vedas, what then would they be? ||78||

"Father, why does he offer [my life] as a sacrifice solely for the sake of the son of Nala? Why does he not reduce me to mere ashes in the fire? Surely he has mastery over my body, born from his own loins."
Nevertheless, Nala is the lord of my life. ||79||
Since my desired goal is lofty— the state of being her sole maidservant— it is fitting that you act to accomplish it;
what indeed can a lotus do for those who are not suns?
Even by the moon, the maker of nectar. ||80||
In my heart, which is greedy for that alone, there is no thought of obtaining even the priceless *cintāmaṇi* jewel;
for in my mind, that lotus-faced one alone is the treasure-trove containing the essence of all the three worlds. (81)
He has been heard of and seen in all directions; yet, through delusion, he remains far away, having blocked the flow of my intellect.
Today, either I shall attain him or my life shall perish.
In your hand lies a pair, with one remaining.
Let merit be accumulated, arising from the fulfillment of my promise and from the gift of my own life;
O Noble One, let this groundless suspicion be dispelled!
O auspicious one! O you who are not made of clay! How very beautiful you are! ||83||

Enough of overstepping, O wise beloved! Even after making various requests, you must observe silence regarding that which is to be done, lest you fall from the path of glory due to the state of being untrustworthy.
Indeed, from the play of stumbling, falling, and false speech. ||84||
Shame on you, who are so tight-fisted, that you feel no shame in giving even your own suffering life for the joy of others,
yet desire to withhold my very life-breaths from me.
Dharma, cleansed by fame, slips from the hand. ||85||
Having given my own life to you, the giver of life, I am purified; but by what means can I be purified when I have given more than my life?
Therefore, O Creator, make me so that I may discharge my other debts to you.
[She] was submerged in a vast ocean of unsealable poverty. ||86||
Buy my very life as the stake;
if there is nothing else, let that be a meritorious act.
O Giver of Life, if you do not grant it to me—
I am even able to sing the praises of Yaśas. ||87||
The wealthy do not honor those who are grateful even for a small favor worth a single cowrie,
yet they themselves skillfully claim their own lives as the price for such help.
But alas, the virtuous purchase those very things! ||88||
That king is all eight world-protectors; through them, my mind, fixed on that single point, was graced. For it is not possible for anyone other than him to come here.
Be yourself my guarantor for attaining that. ||89||
O Hero, although you have become the very root of the vīraṇa grass grown by the Self-born Creator for my sake,
why do you not attain the state of a nalada for me?
The agent performs the act of applying sandalwood paste to the heart. ||90||
Enough of delaying; for it is indeed time to hasten.
Deliberation is appropriate only in a matter that can endure stability;
[otherwise,] the sharp [intellect] is like a reflection of the teacher’s instruction.
Death never waits for the right time. ||91||
That king should not be entreated by you on my behalf while he is in the inner apartments;
for he is constrained by the courtesy shown toward the faces of his beloveds.
In that case, there would arise the prohibition of other wives. ||92||
