O King of Niṣadha, who is utterly delighted by the enjoyment of the inner harem, this matter should not be spoken to you;
for a stream of water is of no use to one already satiated with water.
Sweet, fragrant, and cool, it is indeed delicious.
You must not utter words on my behalf with anger in the heart of the King of Niṣadha;
sugar, even when placed in a tongue scorched by bile, becomes bitter.
O ornament of the swan race, he acts like a bitter [drug]! ||94||
O Earth, you who are weary of bearing burdens, do not grant my request with a mind distracted by other affairs;
for that would be the sleep of ignorance regarding what has been asked of you.
He bears the mark of one who acts with contempt. ||95||
This must be made known by a wise person to the lord of men;
therefore, you, having considered the present moment,
[should advise him] regarding ultimate non-attainment and delayed attainment.
The auspicious splendor of every single task shines forth. ||96||
Since she abandoned her modesty after speaking thus,
let that impropriety remain in our minds;
let Cupid, however, be the witness to its innocence.
Having become intoxicated, he played those various [instruments]. ||97||
Having encountered the madman [the spring], both Hara and Smara experience boundless joy;
the former, out of rivalry with the latter, surely [seeks] the flower.
The second [act] concerns one distressed by the pain of separation. ||98||
Then, having determined that the princess who spoke thus was bound by passion for the King of Niṣadha,
the seal of silence upon the bud of his beak was released.
Laughing once more from the sky, he [spoke] further. ||99||
O daughter of the king! If this is the truth,
then I see no course of action for myself in this matter,
as I am causing both you and the king such intense suffering.
This [world] was indeed produced by the five-arrowed one alone. ||100||

Today you have attained [the state] of those who possess the satisfaction of immortality through ascetic penances, whose external senses have become steadfast like yours, and who observe the vow of fasting.
May he attain his own divine state, having fulfilled his purpose. ||101||
"Our forms were once equal; yet while mine was consumed by fire, his was not even scorched.
Thus he seemed to feel envy at the heat of his own body.
Because of her separation from you, she makes [her body] non-limbed. ||102||
Drinking you in with his eyes—though you are but a painting adorning the wall—the king gazes with unwinking devotion;
does he not bear the passion of his own eyes, bestowed by the streams of his gaze, as if it were painted there by you? (103)
The king, with eyes that had closed out of reverence, remained gazing at you as if you were a painting; for he thought, "This is mine," regarding the flow of tears from his eyes.
There is a dispute regarding the interruption of joy by the blinking of the eyes. ||104||
O daughter of Bhīma! You have entered her heart; though you have gone outside, you have become as vital as her breath through the passage of her nostrils.
It is no wonder that the painting there takes on life.
This is the mind which exists as a single function. ||105||
You constantly ascend that long and distant flight of stairs which is his stream of thoughts; he,
for his part, sheds profuse sighs when he attains a state of being composed of you through longing for you.
That which her heart whispers in secret, her mouth proclaims aloud;
this is indeed the fitting conduct of her face, whose friendship with the moon— the friend of the flower-weaponed god— is well known.
She who, while he stands by his bed at night,
plunges his mind into delusion and kisses him as she embraces him— she is the one who closes his eyes.
Neither sleep nor a woman is possible for me now without you. ||108||

Having carved her away with his arrows in vain, Smara has reduced her to a state of emaciation where only her beauty remains; for even though he himself is now attaining bodilessness, she alone is left as the residue of loveliness.
She does not abandon her rivalry with him. ||109||
Since he does not even fear sin that might prevent him from attaining you, and yet feels no shame even in being your servant—
having been so deeply carved by the sharp arrows of Smara— [he is yours].
Even its own nature, once cut away, how much of it remains? ||110||
As the collection of perfected physicians treated the shameful one for the terrible fever of love,
the vast [city] remained silent regarding its diagnosis.
His shame was like an infectious disease. 111.
He fears suddenly that you are angry; he laughs without cause that you have indeed departed; and he follows after you as if you were going away, for no reason.
He answers you in vain with exactly what you have said.

Alas, alas! This elephant among the warrior-kings, finding no refuge, sinks into the thick mud of the great darkness of a swoon—a continent of fainting—within the river of Yama, whose current is a stream of piercing pain caused by separation from you. 113.
Among the ten states that resounded individually with the five arrows of the Five-Arrowed One, discharged alternately from the right and left,
that state which remains is indeed the final one.
By that bud, let the sky blossom.
I have been dispatched to you by that mountain-king, who is ever-smiling at his affliction caused by love;
having arrived, may my presence bear fruit for you.
Through the perception of existence, she becomes one who covets qualities. ||115||
Blessed are you, O Princess of Vidarbha! For by your noble virtues, even the King of Niṣadha was drawn away.
Beyond this, what praise indeed can there be for the moonlight?
That which even makes the ocean surge.
As the night shines with the moon and the moon with the night, so may he shine with you as his wife and you with him;
may the Creator join that pair together again and again.
Desiring to unite, he now attends upon you two who are worthy.
O slender one! If the broad expanse of your two breasts alone should be obtained by the King of Niṣadha,
it will increase his already vast store of cleverness.
The winding of the rows of petals reaches its conclusion. ||118||
A single moon can by no means suffice to satisfy both of your eyes; therefore, let there be one that is ever-satisfying to your gaze.
Accompanied by Nala, who was like a second moon.
Oh, how wonderful! Your asceticism is a wish-fulfilling tree, possessing the beauty of sprouts shimmering at the tips of your fingers;
indeed, the pair of your eyebrows is its two young leaves.
That your lower lip is reddened like a kalamba fruit. ||120||
That which has sprouted anew by your two hands, that which remains as a bud by your smile,
and that which has blossomed through the softness of your limbs.
He who has borne fruit through the beauty of your breasts alone.
Indeed, the circle of the moon was turned into bell-metal by Smara with its mass of clinging rays;
and his own bowstring was made into the very balance-beam for the arrows.
In the equalization of mutual passion, you two are [the standard]. ||122||

During the festivals of love, the decorative leaf-patterns on your breasts, having adhered and then risen from his lotus-like hands— which were thick with the honey of perspiration flowing from his body— remain visible.
May those who have emerged from it enter it once again. ||123||
In the pleasure grove, the gods, delighted by various wrestling matches rich in acrobatic feats,
rained down a shower of flowers that seemed like a repeated offering of pearls.
"Accept her, O Bhaimī! You two are young men. ||124||
Now, by the power of their mutual union, let the minds of both you and him shine forth with blossoming charm,
like a pair of atoms engaged in forming a dyad at the very beginning of creation, intent on fashioning once more the body of the Mind-born God.
Desire, having obtained you— the king whom even the flower-bowed god finds difficult to conquer— as its bow-creeper born of a flawless lineage and endowed with excellent string, exults;
for you shine with the vine-like silk ribbon adorning your neck, which hangs slightly down your back, radiant as if it were a streak of vermilion resting upon a line of scars.
Know that the pearl-like clusters of your limbs are the pellets for that royal swan—the Lord’s mind-born god—who is to be pierced; and know yourself to be his lovely bow-creeper.

For it is upon this creeper, constantly cherished by its dwelling on his lap and being strung by the bowstring of his arms, that the line of hair resting in the cavity of your radiant navel center assumes its entire graceful beauty.
He who, defeated by you, cast a multitude of arrows into your tresses, his bow at the base of your forehead, and his body into the fierce fire of your eye—
now bodiless, having lost all hope, he takes refuge in you to conquer that very [fire].
The row of leaves upon your breasts, resting on those mountain-like mounds, acts as a leaf-hut for her.
When the bird had thus addressed Bhaimī there, her friends, after a long time, returned to her, intent on reconnecting with her;
he too, having uttered, "May you be blessed; release me," departed.
He went with speed to the capital city of the lord of Niṣadha. ||129||
Tasting again and again that honey from the flowers of the arrows born of her heart— mixed with the milk of the cow of the sun-bird (Cakravāka) sent by her beloved, which was as sweet as butter—
she attained no satisfaction despite its boundless flavor and desired fragrance; instead, she experienced intense inner heat and even reached the state of fainting.
As she followed the kinsman of the king, her gaze was not long restrained;
for even though he was at her side, he was drawn away from the range of her vision.
It is separated even by a distance, but not from the mental state itself. ||131||

Then, clearly proclaiming the existence [of his power] through the various tremors of his position as the means to accomplish his purpose, he set out alone to relate this entire account to the King of Niṣadha:
"O dear friend! You have gone out into the wilderness; have you forgotten the path, O simple one?"
"Do not weep," said her friends, their voices faltering as they led her away to another.
In that lake he saw the king; there, at the foot of an aśoka tree on its bank, trembling with love,
he found him lying upon a bed of tender leaves that were beginning to wither.
Of him whose crown is adorned with flowers that rival the blazing arrows of the god of love. ||133||
"O Damayantī, who belongs to another! I shall say nothing to you;
come quickly! O swan, tell me, what did she say to me? While Nala was speaking thus, the bird approached and related it to him.
For those who act virtuously, there is indeed no delay in attaining what they desire. ||134||
Although it had been told, the king could not believe it;
asking "What? What? he inquired about his beloved's speech.
Then, having understood it, he became intoxicated by the thick wine of bliss.
He himself also recounted that very thing in that same manner a hundred times.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered his senses;
this naturally radiant third canto has reached its conclusion in his beautiful epic poem, the *Naiṣadhīyacarita*. (136)
The Fourth Canto: Now, the Self-born [God of Love], taking Nala’s every virtue as his fragrant bow and his fame as its flower, [prepared to strike].
Having quickly fashioned that arrow from the path of his hearing with a well-disposed mind, he conquered her.
As she immersed herself in the lake of the nectar of her beloved’s stories— which was cooling to her body—
the fever that had long scorched her heart suddenly subsided.
The transformation turned out to be adverse. ||2||
Surely this slender-waisted girl has studied impatience from the speed of her beloved’s messenger as he flew by,
for she now acts in contradiction to her own steady nature.
For that which arises immediately after another is said to be produced from it. ||3||
Then her face became utterly dull-witted,
incapable of even remembering a fragment of a smile;
her eyes, like *khañjana* birds, became lame, unable to take even a single step in wandering about the courtyard of their own outer corners.
Did those two physicians of heaven, Smara and Nala, enter within her to probe her,
desiring to treat her quickly with remedies directed toward that [fever]?
They were commissioned by the lord of the gods, the consumer of oblations. ||5||
Her face, tender as a lotus, was observed to be increasingly tormented day by day by the heat born of the flower-bowed god; it bore an ever-increasing intensity.
The state of the moon when it is withered by the rays of the sun. ||6||
May that pair of her jar-like breasts, whose firmness was fashioned by the radiance of the youthful sun,
never undergo the heat of contact with fire produced by the playful hand of the potter Cupid.
When her pair of thighs was roasted by the God of Love in the heat of separation,
the plantain tree now suffers that same torment.
If it is defiled by the parched, saline soil scorched by the desert sun. ||8||
The pair of hands of Damayantī, afflicted by the fever produced by the strike of Love’s arrows,
seemed to mock the sun’s heat as it fell upon them without any covering.
A lotus from a lake whose essence has been drunk by the sun. ||9||
That the heart of Damana’s sister did not burst asunder under the weight of the fever of love was due to the constriction of her two firm, full breasts.
She binds the transgression of the body with her own element. ||10||
If even the tip of a grain of awn, when it enters the foot, causes how much pain?
But how could the Mountain, having entered and remained within her tender heart, not cause that same [intense] agony? (11)
As her two eyes, filled with longing, yearned to behold the beloved who seemed to dwell within her mind,
they acquired the power to perceive him.
Nor even with respect to an object that is present before one. ||12||
In Damayantī’s heart, which was drenched by a torrent of tears, the reflection of her husband’s face— bent down due to the pain of separation—
shone as if to kiss the one who resided within her own heart.
Having approached Nala, she indeed came to his presence. ||13||
In order to raise up the fire of love— the friend—
within the heart of the deer-eyed woman by means of the wind of her sighing,
the smoke was inferred from its exit, yet it was disguised as the act of concealment.

Indeed, that female painter—using the pigments of the paleness of separation, the redness of passion, the blackness of the ink of darkness, and her own natural yellowish hue—painted the ten directions as portraits of Nala. (15)
The wind of her sighs, as if repeatedly speaking of the state of her heart brought about by love,
caused a trembling in the garment resting upon it.
Who would not tremble when their own support is destroyed? (16)
In the fever of separation from her beloved, the hands, feet, face, eyes, and soles of the fair-limbed maiden have,
after a long time, drunk in the light of the sun as if it were a great draught.
Under the pretext of the heat of the sun, it was released. ||17||
That wonder arose among the women on that mountain,
as they reflected upon what was inferred even from the observation of tears.
Nala moved about without being seen by the two of them, yet he caused them no distress. ||18||
Striking the heart of the princess of Vidarbha with arrows for the sake of the lord of Niṣadha,
the Lord of Rati caused her own deep wounds to be inflicted upon him by those very arrows entering within her.
Indeed, the bank of the river Phaladānī did not at all lose its luster. ||19||
If the sun was considered by her to be separated [from his wife],
how then, alas, did he cause that heart of hers to blaze with its rays— [a heart] which had become like a stone made manifest by the weight of separation as it shattered? 20.
Where could there be a likeness to her, who is submerged in separation and holds a lotus to her heart— compared to her embracing the beloved’s bow with her chest during the night?
Did she wish to follow him in death upon the flames of the funeral pyre? ||21||
This woman, residing in her own home, did not perceive the secret of separation— that it is of an insufferable nature—
since she desired to cast away her life-breaths there, having offered blades of grass as a means for their pacification.
How can that quality which belongs to women not be their very nature, since even with arrows made of flowers, he has pierced this heart called "tender"?
It was well-revealed by the wise one, the mind-born [Kāma]. ||23||
Did the moonlight,

fearing that she might otherwise attempt to prevent him from leaving, pierce her with rays through the holes in the lattice windows as she remained within the house, unable to depart? Or rather, was she even more distressed because she could not escape?
Assuming the guise of a Vaiśya, he entered in order to cause a feverish affliction.
In her heart, which was filled with tears, the god of love clearly reflected her downcast face—
her eyes, mouth, and lips— having planted them there.
All his arrows are like flowers of that [same] kind. ||25||
Reflected upon the surface of Bhīma’s cheek, which was pale from the pangs of separation,
the moon rendered her face indistinguishable from its own whiteness.
He bestowed his own friend, Sukha, upon the lap of Mṛgā. ||26||
Tormented by the heat of separation, she adorned her body with sandalwood dust until it assumed a pallid beauty;
wearing ornaments of lotus stalks that resembled venomous serpents, she bore the marks of her grief.
[This was] a terrifying spectacle displayed by Śambhu toward the Lord of Rati. ||27||
The sandalwood paste applied to her heart shone like a bubble,
as she approached her friend, the lord of her heart, who lay within her own bosom.
Like the moon separated from its companion, the night. ||28||
By her, ignited by the fire of love,
a lotus full of nectar was repeatedly held midway,
as if to take refuge before reaching its destination.
Abandoned, it rustled with the sound produced by its own sighing. ||29||
"Will you thus obtain a grasp of what is dear? Why does this pair of yours languish?"—
thus did they speak as the two lotuses were placed upon her heart.
[He embraced] her of broad breasts with the bud-like throbbing of passion. ||30||
As if to inform the Lord of her Heart, Nala, who was seated within her heart— that no other than you has been held by me even in my mind—
she awakened him in the fire that consumes the oblation of love.
[She perceives] her own purity through the paleness caused by separation. ||31||
Did the lotus plant, placed upon her body which was scorched by the heat of separation,
attempt to remove his intense fever with its closing buds as if with fists,
or did it seek to overcome that great affliction? (32)
Overwhelmed by the spreading poison of separation caused by the wounds of the serpent-like rows of Cupid’s arrows,
whom did she— who resembled a crescent moon afflicted by the rays of the sun— not cast into the ocean of compassion? (33)
Burning with the pain of love in her own heart,
she placed a fresh lotus stalk against her chest out of shame before her two conquerors standing nearby.
The two arms attained an extreme state of impurity. ||34||
The moss placed upon her heart by her, which trembled as she sighed, shone as it moved,
like the banner of the god of love who was constantly fixed within her heart.
As if stolen away by that which rubs against the thick mass of its own body. ||35||
Surely Nala’s mind did not perceive that face, which was like a moonstone, through the power of delusion;
otherwise, upon the rising of the moon, how could he have remained so?
How did he shed milk consisting of tears? ||36||
Just as the arrow of the victorious weapon of the Lord of Love triumphs, so too does that daughter of Bhīma;
for from her, as if from her own shafts, the five [arrows] emerge.
He certainly intended to employ her for that purpose. ||37||
Perceiving the moon to be the rising fire-weapon of the Mind-born God, that woman separated from her lover suddenly [assumed] a watery nature under the guise of tears.
He took up a corresponding weapon for each of those. ||38||
Beholding the cloudless new cloud raised as a weapon by the bodiless one,
that fair-limbed woman discharged against him a fitting weapon in the guise of long-drawn sighs. (39)
Perceiving the Malaya breeze to be a weapon of the wind-god seized by her husband Rati, the fair-toothed lady,
out of fear of its great heat upon him, took it up as if it were a lotus-stalk— a serpent-weapon.
Two things were planted in her heart like thorns:
her state of separation and yet her continued life;
what then did the Lord of Vows do there, but strike down and bury that pair with the two bilva fruits from her breasts?
Madana made her an even more perfect target by exhausting all his flower-made arrows;
he clearly did so even while discharging his fruits.
The placing of a pair of breasts upon his chest while making a sucking sound. ||42||
Then, as she repeatedly censured the moon while praising Rāhu,
she fell down, struck by a disease consisting of the fever of love.
The female friend spoke, her face drenched with tears. ||43||
Just as the *yuga* of humans, gods, and those born from the lotus (Brahmā) is measured by a certain duration of time,
why is that same duration not calculated in the science of mathematics as consisting of moments (*kṣaṇa*) for those who are separated from their beloveds? 44.
Satī, tormented by the thought of him, took birth from Himavat, yet she did not respect his greatness;
for it was the separation from Satī alone that burned on the surface of Hara’s forehead, and not his eye.
The agony of fever born of fire is not as great as the agony of separation; if it were not so,
why would women enter the fire so swiftly?
They were intent on attending upon their beloved, who was about to depart from life. ||46||

O friend! Behold the misconduct of the Moon: these digits, stained by the mire of the murder of women separated from their lovers, roll about within his heart; yet those that formed friendships with the night-lotuses have been cast out. 47.
O Moon! Ask the Preceptor clearly from where you learned this generosity of burning;
for by you, the poison that withered Śiva’s throat was consumed.
O dull-witted one! Is it from the ocean, or rather from the submarine fire? ||48||
This man, having indeed fallen from heaven due to the sin of killing a non-yogi, is now whirled about;
he makes the sky appear more star-spangled with the multitude of sparks flying up as they burst against the stone of the dark night. (49)
O friend, speak to the Moon on my behalf:
"Why do you act in such a manner?
If your birth in the ocean was not taken into account,"
Even the ground upon which Śiva’s head rests has been forgotten.
O moon of rabbit-mark! Though falling into the ocean, you were not ground to powder by Mount Mandara;
nor did you meet with digestion in the gastric fire of the Sage.
O Vāyu, you have gone away; you have not drunk from the ocean of milk. ||51||
O fool! Do you think that by wasting my life-breaths, the mind of Bhīma’s daughter will sink into me?
For it is said that my Veda has that very thing as its purpose.
The wise god of love took her as his supreme moon-faced Nala. ||52||
Sound the great drum of your own fame;
now illuminate the lineage of the ocean!
And take up, too, the manliness of slaying a bride.
O Moon! Cease this torment! ||53||
O Moon! at night, assume the guise of the sun; O wicked one, while the true sun is absent, torment me!
I shall, however, behold you during the day when your pride has been eclipsed by the lord of the day.
O moon, you who bear the mark of a hare! O terrifying one!
Since you blaze at night while taking refuge with a king, such is the nature of a ghost that you have become for one supported by him.
She is the maker of reality and the shaker of the supreme head. ||55||
O friend! Place the sprouts of tamāla leaves, filling the ears, into the mouth of the deer-marked moon;
for he has become somewhat swollen and is concealing it.
Instantly, by that, I breathed for a moment. ||56||
Surely my intellect falters at an inopportune time, for if this new moon had already reached my hand,
it would have returned again and been held back.
O friend! The face of the moon shall never again be beheld.
Oh! This young cakora bird of mine does not become a disciple of the sage who drinks the ocean;
for he has studied how to swallow the sea himself.
How many droplets of the moonbeams are being drunk? ||58||
Make my hand a mirror for the moon of your face,
and place it outside;
as soon as the moon enters therein, [it will reveal its reflection].
O friend! Quickly abandon that which is harmful to your happiness. ||59||
Why was the moon, as uneven as the submarine fire, not held within the belly of the ocean?
Even though it was released by him like poison, it did not [kill him].
Did the all-pervading Lord, the Destroyer of Smara, consume this [world]? ||60||
Even when consumed by a single demon, this moon did not become foul poison; yet,
even after being drunk by the gods and thus undergoing diminution, it remains pure.
It rises by itself as a new ocean once more.
Behold the full moon, a sinner who torments the multitude of those separated from their lovers by his addiction to killing them,
and who is the source of the sin from which the gods drank the nectar.
How can those who know the planets speak contrary [to the truth]? ||62||
The month of Bhādrapada (Bahula-pakṣa) has indeed become preeminent here, for it was in this month that those separated from their lovers attained great esteem,
since its duration was measured by all of them together.
And was that lunar day fashioned by him as one devoid of all form? ||63||
Is it because of the confusion caused by his own son, the sharp-sighted Sudarśana,
that Rāhu swallows the moon?
Otherwise, how could the moon have fallen into his mouth?
It abandons its own likeness to curdled milk and whey. ||64||
Without doubt, Rāhu does not release the moon from within his mouth by his own will; rather,
it dissolves away only after being swallowed.
O friend! Without the path of the hollow of the throat-pipe... ||65||
Those who know the past and possess upright vision indeed declare the Slayer of Madhu to be the one who severed Rāhu’s head;
yet they do not say that this [present] head belongs to one separated from his body.
Where indeed is the moon, if it were the fire within his belly? ||66||
The two physicians of heaven, who were friends of Smara, immediately joined together with their radiant splendors the head of the sacrificial deer that had been split by the enemy of Smara.
O friend! Who indeed can do the same even for darkness? ||67||
Does the head of the enemy, whose neck has been severed in battle by Nala,
not join with his headless trunk as it leaps upward violently out of fear of death?
With that head of obstinacy, firmly bound by the blood of attachment.

O friend! Ask Old Age: even while bearing a head identical to that of Darkness, why does it assume the state of a headless trunk (*kabandha*), like the pair of chest-plates on the body of the King of Magadha?
Thus, he does not interweave with his banner. ||69||
Speak, O friend Rāhu! Why do you abandon your enemy at my words, thinking him to be the king of the twice-born?
Does such a one ever return again to heaven?
For he has fallen after having indulged in the wine of Varuṇa.
This [fire] indeed burns the throat; why then, like Garuḍa, do you abandon your habitual enmity toward birds?
O Rāhu! Its nature is simply to burn.
Tell me, what offense have I committed that you should act so falsely toward me? (71)
Indeed, having been fashioned by Yama with every single part of his fang,
he was created as the instrument for devouring the multitude of women separated from their lovers.
The sacred tradition states that the moon is the king of the twice-born. ||72||
The Moon was fashioned by the Creator from the blazing fire of Śiva’s eye as the face of Smara,
due to his manifold sins of killing those separated from their lovers.
Then, it was marked with the blackness of a hare's flesh. ||73||
His body was turned white by leprosy arising from the sin incurred by devouring the wives of the twice-born;
[he was driven] by a desire to consume the moon-like faces of women separated from their lovers.
"This is Rāhu; it is not the moon," she thought,
reflecting that her various words of reproach against the moon were in vain because he was out of sight.
Experiencing an exceeding fever of separation,
she reproached the God of Love who dwells within her heart.
O Anaṅga! If you take refuge in my heart, why do you thus burn it? Having yourself consumed your own fuel in an instant, where indeed will you go?
O destroyer of enemies, you shall become like the sacrificial fire! ||75||
O Smara! You were rendered invisible by the Destroyer of Cities out of fear that you might be overwhelmed by his third eye;
yet, you were not destroyed by anyone else.
What is the use of three eyes if you do not look at me?
"It is well known that you are the companion of Rati; yet, even though you dwell within me, why is there no passion in me?
Or perhaps there is no union at this time, for she has surely not followed after you in death. (77)
O you who are devoid of passion and ignorant of yourself and others! Why have you scorched me as if you were yourself?
Otherwise, how could my heart be burning from contact with you, who are free from all heat? (78)
O Māra, did you not reflect: "How could she, though renowned for her supreme delight in passion, be so devoted to her husband?
How can I, a sinner who slays such a helpless young wife, [be called righteous]?"
Were you abandoned even by that beloved? ||79||
Since the Sugata himself, having conquered and subdued his senses, destroyed the body of your vast fame,
he left behind only your physical form.
The Lord took away the earth consisting of the elements in that assembly. ||80||
O Ananga! Since you obtained the fruit by using flowers while contending with the Three-eyed One,
the Goddess of Policy (Nīti) has consequently incurred fear from him.
Nor does he desire a body even with flowers. ||81||
Tell me, how did you reach that state— even while drinking nectar from the Three-Eyed God like the other gods—
out of your devotion to the flavor of Rati’s lower lip?
Having obtained the nectar, you surely did not drink it out of compassion. ||82||
O deceased one! What sin born of deluding the world did you commit that you have become a Piśāca,
now stained by the impurity of separation?
O Smara, you wander about, overwhelming those like me! 83.
Alas, O Smara! You grant not even death;
yet your bow does not slip from your hand through lack of compassion.
Now you are dead, and by dying, one is released.
Indeed, a fist that has been clenched cannot be unbound. ||84||
When practiced by others who are not liberated, it pacifies defects of vision, untimely death,
and deformity, as well as extreme blindness, physical injury, and pallor.
Remember! [For] they become so for one who worships you. ||85||
Remember! You are the most cruel of beings; therefore, the Creator made the *sumanas* flower your weapon, for had he given you a firm bow, swift arrows, and iron shafts...
It may create for you the dissolution of the three worlds, yet it shall pass away. ||86||
"May the fire of your anger burn even the three worlds, just as the fire of Shiva’s wrath once burned the cities.
Thinking thus, did the Creator fashion your arrows from flowers?
Not yet satisfied, he sprinkled [him] within with honey. ||87||
Having perceived that the minds of people are indeed indivisible and cannot be pierced, Fate surely fashioned the target [of the bow] as a mere hundred thousand;
for had he not done so, he might even have given you the thunderbolt.
He too would have been slain by your arrows. ||88||
O Smara! Even after fashioning your swift arrows from flowers, the Creator did not attain satisfaction;
for he bestowed those five upon you only after restraining her [the mind].
Alas, by them even this world has been shattered to pieces. ||89||
How many flowers do the five celestial trees not offer to some fortunate recipient?
Yet, because of your lowly state, each one offers you only a single blossom.
"Alas! Even this much censure of yours is not enough, my dear! (90)
Did the Creator, having bestowed upon you even a flower that causes such extreme misconduct,
take away his bow? Or did he do this because your face alone is the sole abode for both?
For now, the two eyebrows of Nala have indeed become a pair. ||91||
Out of compassion, the six seasons, who delight the Nandana grove with their flowers in turn, each give one flower to you;
yet you make them into six.
Like a bow with five arrows, he [pierced] them with those [five]. ||92||
Since you are bodiless, this is for the benefit of the world;
where is that sage who endures your blows?
For if your arrow were to reach its full length, extending even to the ear...
You are able to abandon this wondrous state that does not waver. ||93||
O Smara! Along with her, you instantly became ashes when you aimed your arrow at Paśupati;
surely that arrow of yours has now become bodiless.
That fifth note is indeed your own cuckoo’s call.
Remember! That labor of yours in burning even the Blessed One was rendered fruitless by my misdeeds;
yet, for the welfare of the gods, you have once again offered your own body as an oblation.
Did you not indeed attain birth in heaven at that very moment? ||95||
At the rising of the moon, that breeze from the direction of the West was not favorable to the lover who was turned away in separation;
for it bent the bow of the God of Love, whose flowers are his arrows, toward the dancing girl.
But if this right arm of yours [is truly so]... ||96||
Why is it not sung that the Lord of Umā conquered you alone— intoxicated with pride and the destroyer of those who have not attained yoga?
It is for this very reason that he is not so praised.
That Blessed One is the conqueror of Mada, Andhaka, and Mṛtyu. ||97||
O Manmatha! No one like you has ever been seen or heard of as so skilled in harming others;
you burn with a self-kindled fire that blazes forth from within.
He who, having embraced the worlds, causes them to blaze. ||98||
It was fitting that Śambhu made you the sacrificial oblation for the fire-offering of world-pacification within the flame of his eye; yet,
having cast aside your friend Madhu, you have [consumed] the honey.
Alas, what has been done by Hari, who is possessed of a head? ||99||
Thus, with only so few words, that face— so intensely thirsty for the lip of his beloved— was instantly covered in dust,
as if struck by the drying arrows of the God of Love ignited by her unpleasant speech. (100)
Then, together with her circle of dear friends,
she composed verses by means of half-verse completion (ardhasamasyā),
while her heart’s core was pierced by the arrows of the god of love.
She was most severely wounded and unable to speak much. ||101||

In this calamity, it was through my own innate fortitude that I preserved my life from the pitiless forest fire whose arrows are its flames; yet today, those very vital breaths have become my enemies.
"O friend! Why do you tell me to protect my enemies? ||102||
O compliant one, why do you not listen to beneficial words?
Even by force, preserve your own life,
my friend, if you are to be so well-disposed toward me!
You desire my life, O enemy! ||103||
O daughter of Vidarbha! This is the nectar-rayed moon;
why do you suffer from its rays? O friend, if the moonbeams were truly nectar, they would not cause death.
Where does the hare die then? ||104||
Take heart and cast off this groundless fear;
here rises the gentle-rayed sun,
clearly setting the air ablaze with the waves of his heat.
O friend! You are subverting direct experience with mere words. ||105||
O friend! I swear by your very heart that if you are not within the range of the lover's desire,
then the fruit of that desire is surely seen [only in you].
It inflames the skin and agitates the vital breaths. ||106||
O friend, do you not indeed desire the cuckoo, who proclaims the lunar day that opposes the moon? What is the use of searching for the meaning of her speech?
She scatters this mass of misfortune upon me. ||107||
That beloved of yours is indeed within your heart;
even so, O Damayantī, why do you despair?
He truly dwells in the heart alone, and not without.
Friend! Poison is being drunk from that very same [milk]. ||108||
The necklace-jewel bursts from the heat of passion, and today even your heart is no longer adorned;
O friend! I am ruined if it is so even within your heart.
That most beloved one of mine has been separated from me. ||109||
Having uttered this, her mind instantly fainted, for the fire of love within her was already smoldering;
where indeed could she find the strength to endure such a severing of even a fragment of support?
She was exceedingly pained by the thought that [rebirth] was impossible for her. ||110||
One friend placed water upon her face;
another smeared her breasts with lotus petals;
and yet another applied the breeze of a fan to her heart.
A certain woman placed snow upon the breasts of her fair-bodied daughter.
In that manner, her circle of dear friends gradually attended to her for a long time with soft and cool lotus stalks, lotus fibers, water, and other such things.
Just as she regained her consciousness quickly. ||112||
Now, O Kālī! clearly perceive that he breathes;
O Cañcalā! observe that his eyelashes move; O Menakā! raise up his trembling lower lip.
O Kalpalatā! Listen to what she says. 113.
O Cārumatī, arrange a covering for your breasts; O Keśinī, bind your disheveled hair;
O Taraṅgiṇī, restrain the wandering of your eyes!
"Waterfalls!"—such were the cries heard. ||114||
Then a great clamor arose from the mouths of her companions as they spoke with haste; having heard it,
he went to his daughter's quarters.
That Indra of Vidarbha, his fear dispelled, [spoke]. ||115||
When no calamities befell the king despite his efforts to afflict the maiden’s inner apartments, the two foremost ministers and the physician spoke equally to him:
"O King, listen; through the *Suśruta* as taught by Caraka, I know everything."
Without *nalada*, there would be nothing capable of allaying her feverish distress. (116)
Though spoken simultaneously by those two, their words were mutually contradictory, as they excluded one another;
yet not a single word of theirs reached the ears of that king.
Of him who was distressed, fearing hundreds of undesirable things regarding the daughter of Bhīma. ||117||
Although the signs of separation had quickly vanished from her, the king perceived his daughter, bowing at his feet,
as one submerged in the ocean of the god of love.
For the wise indeed perceive the intentions of others instantaneously. ||118||
Then her father, suddenly raising the head of his daughter who stood with bowed face, bestowed a blessing upon her:
"O Svayaṃvara! May you yourself choose a beloved husband who possesses all virtues!"
May you attain this within a few days. ||119||
Thereupon, he said to the friends of his daughter:
"Indeed, when winter has passed, even a flower acts like an arrow upon the bodies of such women as these."
As he was performing the customary attentions toward her in a fitting manner... ||120||
In a few days, your friend herself will choose for you a most excellent husband of her own accord; therefore,
it is fitting that those like you should find pleasure in this [emaciation] as a means to alleviate your thinness.
Thus, while the king was speaking, he did not ask his daughter about that which was a source of shame;
for he attributed her delusion to love, inferring it from the paleness and feverish heat of her body,
and he uttered a blessing— a fitting consolation in such a situation— under the pretext of a formal benediction.
By that thought, her circle of friends churned the ocean of her mind with both joy and bashfulness. ||122||
Śrī Hīra, the diamond ornament upon the crowns of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the collection of his senses;
here, in this great poem, the *Naiṣadhacarita*, which is the brother to the treatise on the investigation of stability (*Sthairyavicāraṇaprakaraṇa*), ends the fourth canto, naturally radiant. (123)
Then, while that lord of the earth was awaiting the arrival of the kings for the sake of the great Svayaṃvara festival, the fifth canto begins.
At that very moment, the sage Nārada, desiring to see Indra, went to the abode of the thirty gods. ||1||
It was no wonder that Parvata followed after him, for he was indeed his winged companion;
but Nārada, the preceptor of the world, soared high into the sky to the great amazement of all.
While traveling on the road, that sage traversed the sky even without a celestial chariot;
for such a restriction applies only to other people regarding the means of accomplishment.
But for yogins, all perfections arise through austerity. ||3||
This Sage bypassed the celestial palaces, which had lost their pride as the abodes of Indra and others;
even when entreated by their lords who bowed at his feet, he did not accept the status of a guest.
Out of fear of being scorched by him, the Sun contracted his own flames for exactly as long as it took for the day to pass, like the moon.
He was not instantly scorched by that very splendor.
Alas, because the sun then overwhelmed the king of birds with its rays,
the king of birds indeed overwhelmed him in turn with his own talons.
Who here does not experience the karma they themselves have created? ||6||
He offered a seat with rows of kuśa grass from the riverbank, water for the feet and the respectful offering (arghya) with plants growing on the marshy shore,
and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with the nectar from clusters of lotuses.
To him, the guest of the celestial river Aditi.
Having traversed the profound expanse of the sky, he reached the abode of the Lord of Heaven;
having crossed the ocean of worldly existence, he was no longer afflicted by suffering.
The Brahman, bearing auspiciousness, was as beautiful as a wandering ascetic. ||8||
Indra honored that guest with exceedingly lofty and beautiful rites of worship; for indeed,
it is the duty toward a virtuous person to offer him what is appropriate.
It leads to the removal of transgression, not to excellence. ||9||
Then he immediately took refuge with the sage who was like a friend to the mountain Nāmadheya-samatā;
for how could even Mount Parvata not receive honor when he [the sage] had obtained the status of a twice-born lord of the gods? 10.
From that arm, which had been offered such supreme service, the Lord of Sages perceived even the trees of heaven,
through the skill learned by dwelling together with him.
[He sees] them as generous solely through the perfection of giving. ||11||
Having silenced conversation with other people, the enemy of Bala (Indra) spoke to Nārada,
he who is a mine of many stories concerning himself and others.
For generally, there is cohabitation between two friends. ||12||
While she was thus deeply engaged in the curiosity of long conversation arising from the continuous flow of their talk,
[he asked] the reason for the kings' long absence.
Desiring to know [the truth], Śatakratu spoke.
Do royal lineages no longer produce heroic offshoots now as they did in the past— those who, in their final stage, [perish] by the weapons of their enemies?
Wounded, they fall upon the surface of the earth. ||14||
For in battles, heroes cast off their earthly bodies— which, due to their weight, obstruct upward travel— and abandon them far behind.
The excellence of the hospitality shown to guests performed by me. ||15||
O Blessed One, since those guests do not approach me today as if under a curse,
I do not hold this prosperity in high regard.
Miserly in its effort to sustain only its own belly. ||16||
The masses of glory obtained through the expenditure of the wealth of former merits, when scrutinized, are nothing but calamities;
their true purpose lies only in being offered into the lotus-hands of worthy recipients.
In those [circumstances], the ritual for pacification is prescribed according to the rules. ||17||

Having quickly wiped away that great evil, which is the artisan of my doubt regarding this matter, may it be purified today by the words of the Blessed One— the essence of the Vedas— which are like the *aghamarṣaṇa* verses.
Having spoken thus, Maghavan, increasing the excellence of his disciple’s discipline with a weight of profound attentiveness,
[gazed] with his thousand unblinking eyes.
Having fixed [his gaze] upon the mouth of the sage, he remained standing. ||19||
Having observed his maturity in discipline,
even though he was touching the station of Indra,
Nārada spoke with words faltering from joy:
Filled with wonder, he spoke, preceded by a smile. ||20||
The Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices has begged for that merit which you,
knowing its exertion, possess as your own power;

Since the portions of her lower lip near its center appear somewhat swollen,
have I perhaps not offended her by the bites of my teeth during our union in a dream? (40)
"How many sciences, each possessing its own internal distinctions, dance upon the lower lip of the daughter of the Lord of Vidarbha?"—
as if with this thought, he effortlessly delineated them with lines.
The Creator, full of curiosity, has numbered them. ||41||
This sweet-lipped woman, whose lips possess such boundless beauty and whose teeth are so white, was experienced by me in a dream this very night while enjoying her company.
Or how could it be practiced by me alone? ||42||
If she were to bestow even a thousandth part of her smile upon the moon,
it would turn that very light into a mass of moonlight.
By virtue of his aspiration, that god made his birth fruitful. ||43||
This slightly elongated second drop of perspiration, falling before me, surpasses the moonlight of her face— which is brighter than the moon— by its density compared to the rays [of that moon].
The multitude of drops dances upon the row of teeth. ||44||
This twilight, which brings about the dawn of light after the darkness of my swoon from the pain of separation from him, now appears before me,
painting the quarter of the great Indra with its glow.
Being attended by these twice-born ones. ||45||
That here, during the night, the royal teeth of the twice-born bear the grace of Vedic scholars,
being pure and bright through the cleansing away of agitation, passion, and other such stains.
I know these four to be liberated. ||46||
The Creator, having fashioned every limb of her— more delicate even than the calyx of a *śirīṣa* flower—
has reached the pinnacle of excellence in the creation of the tender.
He brought to an end the seal of softness upon his speech.
Is she not some Upaniṣad spoken by the twice-born cuckoo, who asserts the non-duality of the one whose arrows are flowers;
or is she perhaps the moon, the king of the twice-born?
One who subsists on alms does not study under trees. ||48||
Beholding Lakṣmī, whose dwelling is marked by a lotus, as his co-wife due to her devotion to the one Viṣṇu alone,
this man’s moon-like face enjoys the victory over the lotus.
What is the use of Sarasvatī’s desire to conquer that? ||49||
Since the clever Sarasvatī dwelling in her throat plays the lute,
that very sound becomes speech in the mouth of this deer-eyed woman.
It becomes like the essence of nectar within the ears of the listener. ||50||
Having raised her face, has the Creator himself gazed upon it at the completion of its perfect beauty, since this radiance arising from fortitude shines upon her chin?
In the low [register], it is like a slight constriction of the fingers. ||51||
Having become the face of his beloved and being thus happy, this moon triumphs through the disappearance of fear from Rāhu; he now bears the grace of the orb of her lower lip.
His very circle of hands is like a circle of cakra-birds. ||52||
Let this face not possess the fullness of the full moon;
for its greatness, having surpassed the full moon,
remains even while bearing the mark of a crescent eyebrow.
Indeed, his forehead constitutes the third part. ||53||
The Creator fashioned her lotus-face as the sovereign over the entire family of lotuses;
for the two royal lotuses [her eyes] create their own sovereignty within that very family.
Therefore, one should perform service to those who are designated by the term "eyes. ||54||
Day and night, fearing the sun and the moon respectively, deposit their own splendor into the moon and the lotus;
when that splendor is not in them, it is then [transferred] to her face. Yet, even with only one source of beauty, how could this [face] ever not be lovely? (55)
Surely the lotus and the moon, having entreated her father, the water, and their friend, the mirror, respectively, bear the very reflection of the beauty of her face.
Ornaments that are borrowed are, at best, merely temporary. ||56||
While standing for the sun as their lord during their aquatic play, the lotus plants, measured by bees with their eyes, [seemed to] envy the beauty of Damayantī’s face.
They entreat with hands extended like lotuses. ||57||
Having conquered him by her face alone— which possesses the luster of saffron-paste like the wrath of an eternal rival—
the moon, being forcibly bound, shall surely remain with his halo serving as a tethering rope. (58)
Month after month, during the new moon nights, Brahmā repeatedly effaces hundreds of the moon’s orbs;
yet why is it that this [face] of hers remains with its splendor unbroken?
He left only his moon-like face remaining. ||59||
From the makara on the leaf-design of his cheek comes his banner;
with his bow, he desires to conquer the worlds from his brow.
Here, the god of love takes his stand, having found delight.
Possessing two lips that are like honey. ||60||
Are her two ears, with their lotus-eyes filled with tears of separation, like sacrificial cakes (*pūpa*) offered as flowers by the Lord of Love and his consort?
Such indeed is the craftsmanship of the Creator.
Here, this stream of nectar flowing from the essence of the multitude of scriptures, though following a most winding and unclear path,
runs toward the hollows of her ears like a channel through the pair of her ear-leaf ornaments.
When the eighteen branches of knowledge were divided and the two Vedas each took half of them,
they left deep furrows carved within her ears.
Is his number indeed new, or is it the digit nine? ||63||
I believe that with these two ear-creepers, which are unbreakable snares,
he has conquered Varuṇa, who possesses but a single noose.
The Lord of Love, having undertaken a succession of efforts, [attained] delight. ||64||
Your father’s very self was born as Cupid, who is worthy of his four arms;
for the two creepers of his ears serve as the bowstrings for the two bows of his eyebrows.
Why are her two ears flat, like bamboo shoots? ||65||
This very neck, though adorned with the *avaṭu* mark,
is further embellished by this young student; though not embracing him, it seems to hang down as if to embrace him.
Her entire upper body possesses a portion of exquisite beauty. ||66||
The Creator has placed poetry, song, pleasant speech, and truth upon her throat,
under the pretext of marking it with the three lines.
He divided the boundaries for the sake of habitation. ||67||
The beloved’s arms conquer the lotus-stalk;
there is no cause for wonder in such victory in a duel. But it is truly marvelous that even this [lotus-stalk] has been broken by them.
That which is perceived within without distress. ||68||
Was this lotus-stalk, beautiful with its whorls and navel-like nodes, conquered by her two arms so tender as to be like lotus-fibers?
For it now lies here, threadless, amidst thick mud and clay.
It is not submerged in that [world] when infamies have become embodied. ||69||
Under the guise of his five fingers,
which are reddened by his nails, he possesses a golden-feathered arrow with pure joints within a quiver made of two lotuses.
The five arrows of Smara [were] in the hands of Priyā. ||70||
The sprout that once attained the state of childhood through the power of its intense rivalry with her hand,
has now surely grown up again to take pride in its likeness to her lower lip.
How could he, while doing this, not be a sprout? ||71||
"The creation of this lotus for your hand is my preliminary sketch for the sake of its production"—
thus did the Creator say regarding the fawn-eyed maiden.
What is the use of making a written copy of her in this [world]? ||72||
Is this the Narmadā river of mine,
whose lotus-stalk-like creeper-arms are visible on all sides? Have her breasts risen above her inner garment?
The stream of his youth was drying up under the heat of passion. ||73||
A palm tree may be able to imitate these two when they are standing firm, but not when they have fallen;
moreover, it cannot do so without relying upon a great tree.
The breasts of the slender-limbed woman are high by their very nature.
Because it rivals these breasts, the jar has attained the status of a well-known illustration in the treatises;
and from that craft, the maker of water-jars and such [is derived].
He became a potter known by that very name. ||75||
O fair-browed lady of Vidarbha, whose smile is like a ruby, you are marked by clusters of pearl-like foam resembling drops of the purest water from a cluster of lotuses.
Upon her breast grows the beauty of a young sprout. ||76||
This orb of the moon has risen here in the form of her face, with its lotuses closed without fear;
yet it is a marvel that the pair of breasts remains like a pair of ruddy geese.
It does not undergo even the slightest separation. ||77||
The beauty of these two breasts is taken away from those two elephant-ivory temples, because those two have their pearls hidden out of fear,
while these two have their ornaments clearly displayed.

If one were to compare those two breasts with the hands of Śiva, whose fingertips are ever-active with his hundred million hands, then even the entire fruit of the *śrīphala* tree would appear intoxicated by comparison.
Now, even a mere pill has become unobtainable.
In the hollows of her breasts, which are smeared with sandalwood paste,
there appear lines of stumbling— resembling streams of light from the gems of her pearl necklaces— left by the hearts of young men who have fallen upon them. (80)
That which is not overcome by the folds of age, even when the waist has become thin and the belly remains,
occurs when all limbs are pure— that is the kingdom of the Bodiless One (Kāmadeva).
A wondrous display has unfolded here upon the earth of Bhīma. ||81||
If the Creator had not thinned her waist and set aside this lovely portion of hers,
by what means could she now possess such breasts in her youth?
He would create [her], whose slender body has no equal.
"Perhaps like Gaurī, fortunate with her husband, I too might one day perform this composition of a body joined in half"—
as if thinking thus, the Creator fashioned her in the middle.
The line of hair on her body is like a dark thread. ||83||
If one’s thirst for the sight [of her] were to cease upon reaching the rope of the line of body hair, the two jars of her breasts, and the deep well of her navel;
Alas, this protection for them by means of a garment is not [sufficient]. ||84||
With its hitching post and navel-like depression uprooted, and its chain-like line of hair broken and hanging loose—
this is that very elephant of passion in its state of intoxication.
May their breasts be as high as the mounds of a sleeping serpent. ||85||

It is a marvel that the victorious hero, the progenitor of Rati, remains triumphant even with these weapons— his line of body hair, his eyebrows, and his flower-arrows— which, though scattered across her waist, forehead, and head respectively, still constitute his bow, string, and shafts.
The flowers are his arrows, the ornaments of her breasts are his bow, the brow adorning his forehead is the string,
and the line of hair is the ornament of his waist.
Nevertheless, the Conqueror is the source of delight through these very things. ||87||
Indeed, by means of the reflection of the jasmine clusters bound in her braided hair,
this eulogy of the God of Love is inscribed in silver letters upon the golden tablet of her back.
Having seen the entire universe conquered by his father’s Sudarśana discus in battle, he who has the fish as his emblem now desires to conquer the world with this [discus] upon his hip.
What is the use of one whose sight is so difficult to obtain? ||89||
The young woman possesses both the string and the water of loveliness upon the wheel of her hips, which are marked by the lines of body hair—
she who is the creator of the jar-like breasts of the embodied form of youth.
He bears a circle of auxiliary causes for his spear. ||90||
Is some particular limb being sought for her to conquer this trembling leaf,
unless it be because it differs from other leaves?
But how could there be any trembling on her part out of fear? ||91||
Her eyebrows are Citralekhā, her face is Tilottamā, her nose is Rambhā, and her thighs are the creation of Urvaśī;
therefore, when seen, she alone fulfills all [desires].
The curious glances of a single apsaras. ||92||
Does even Rambhā mark her own trunk?
Nor is this [trunk] her own thigh,
since she places it above her very self.
The petals remain awake through the delusion of these two. ||93||

If the kadalī tree were to place its head above [the thighs], abandon its state of passionlessness through austerities, and not experience numbness, then only would it be as beautiful as these thighs. (94)
The trunk of the elephant was surpassed by the two shapely thighs of the slender maiden;
it was only fitting that it felt shame under the guise of curling its trunk.
He protects his own lotus-like face. ||95||
I suspect even the sages are deluded by her;
for even the great Bhṛgu, who dwells upon the mountains of her breasts,
has not taken refuge on her thighs, though her face delights with its various rows of teeth.
Vyāsa is the one fit for the composition of the Mahābhārata. ||96||
Does her wisdom know that the fullness which has gradually spread to her shanks is like one climbing a tree,
even though her limbs are concealed by the various turns of her girdle?
The garment is skillfully fashioned from entwined creepers. ||97||
This fourteenth lunar day is indeed appropriate here for Arundhatī, Kāma’s beloved, Lakṣmī, Janabhadrī, Dviṣaddārā, and Navāmbikā,
since the power of invisibility extends even to their two ankles. (98)
We believe that the sprouts of trees acquired the name "pallava" (sprout) because they became mere fragments in comparison to the great beauty of her feet. (99)
Because this [goddess] placed her lotus-foot upon the heads of the wives of the world out of pride in her beauty,
it is now colored by the intense red of thick vermilion powder.
It is certainly as intensely red as a fresh sprout of coral. ||100||
The goddess Śrī, flushed with anger, chose as her abode the feet of Damayantī, who surpassed her in all virtues;
for it was certain that she (Śrī) had deceived him (Brahmā).
This foot, possessing such a state, shines with an intense crimson hue.
I know that the slender lady’s two lotus-feet, which surpass the lordly elephants with their gait and possess perfectly pure heels,
do not wish to be served by me.
With his head bowed, [he asked] which king? ||102||

The Creator fashioned a second [face] right here for him— who conquers all his own equals by means of his ears, eyes, lips, arms, hands, feet, and so forth— because that [first face] was subject to the agitation of pride regarding its own duality.
Now, for the Creator who desires to restore the race of lotuses that was completely destroyed by the frost,
the splendor residing in her five hands and feet is like the honey-gathering bee.
Kings afflicted by love will come from the ends of the earth in such numbers as to defy counting, seeking to enter for refuge into these two lotus-feet which were created even by Brahmā himself.
There are exactly as many lines here as there are fingers. ||105||
Fate has brought joy by making this moon possess ten auspicious digits, having turned its beloved [the night] into nails;
otherwise, how could it possess the fortune of the beauty of red lotuses disguised as its spots? (106)
May the sixty-four arts take up their residence in her, she who bears four full moons: her fame, her big toe, her nail, and her face.
How indeed could he not be devoted to her, that fair-browed woman? ||107||
Having first created the entire universe by the Creator himself,
youth has now surpassed even that; having instructed it in the art of cleverness, the Mind-born God [Kāma] has taken its place.
She has been brought to the very further shore of the path of speech.

Thus describing her, whose eyes were like those of a doe, from the hair down to the nails, the lord of the earth— his mind wandering within the ocean of wonder, his joy overflowing as it filled his heart— assumed a state of emotion when she became the object of Bhīmajā’s gaze while surrounded by her friends. (109)

Śrī Hīra, the diamond ornament upon the crowns of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who had conquered the host of his senses; in this beautiful epic poem concerning the life of the son of Vīrasena, composed by that [Harṣa] as a brother to the panegyric verses of the Gauḍa kings, the seventh canto has come to an end.
The Eighth Canto:
Then, [he beheld] this youth, whose eyes were fixed in wonder and whose hair stood on end.
All those of beautiful form were rendered harsh by his glance, as was the daughter of Bhīma, the lord of the earth. ||1||
How long, indeed, can the words spoken by the gods possibly succeed in concealing him?
For he is like a fire covered by a mass of straw.
The young sugarcane attains its brilliance. ||2||
Even before the ray of Nala’s eye reached the corner of his vision as he longed for the daughter of Bhīma,
the arrow of Love struck that fair-browed maiden.
It submerged limb by limb, up to the tips of his feathers.
Since the five-arrowed god, due to the equality of his power to stride, treated both [the two worlds] simultaneously,
how could he not have caused discord between them?
With arrows that took up half of a half-division [of the army]. ||4||
At that moment, she felt a surge of passion, thinking, "This is Nala," but for a moment she remained indifferent, wondering, "Where could he be here? Then again, his heart turned back toward her.
Then, by means of this messenger, he returned once again. ||5||
Upon seeing Nala, one maiden felt bashful; another sank into her heart as she gazed upon him;
and yet another maiden considered him to be the god of love himself.
Another woman fell under the sway of the god of love.
Due to the overwhelming burden of their lack of eloquence, they were never able even to ask him "Who are you? or "From where do you come?";
rather, they rose up as if desiring to offer him a formal welcome.
Not remaining on their own seats, those slender-limbed women were filled with manifold emotions. ||7||
Upon beholding him, Damayantī experienced an indescribable freedom that was the pinnacle of successive joys,
just as a river of waters attains great velocity.
Having reached the time for the play of the rain-cloud. ||8||
Immersed in that very state, she saw nothing else before her; her vision did not turn toward any other limb,
had her stream of consciousness not been withdrawn from it.
After long intervals, the blinking of the eyes occurs repeatedly. ||9||

Even with her glance, she did not seize his body, which was already embraced by the horripilation on the parts of his limbs perceived first; but when another part was seen immediately thereafter, [she did so].
Having turned back, he did not remember what had been seen before.
Leaving aside one part of her body, her gaze entered the boundary of the enjoyment of another limb;
for a long time, it remained there out of greed to obtain both simultaneously.
Fickle by nature, they come and go. ||11||
Drinking in his limbs with her eyes— both those she gazed upon and those she did not see— with impetuous haste,
she experienced an identical bliss.
The fair-browed daughter of Vidarbha perceived no difference between them.
Having fallen upon her thick, fine tresses of hair, becoming utterly motionless,
[the eyes] were unable to move away without breaking their connection with them.
It was not possible for those two eyes, which were like *khañjana* birds. ||13||
Having obtained the embrace of the lotus-like face, hands, and feet of that lord of the earth,
the row of lotuses that was Damayantī’s gaze did not for a long time relinquish its connection with her kinsmen.
At that moment, becoming filled with bliss and possessing an even more inexpressible delusion,
she [stands] between the two essences of the states of liberation and worldly existence.
He enjoyed the sweet delight of the double-taste. ||15||
Surely, fearing that she might become stained with blemish due to her future affection for the messenger who bore Nala’s splendor,
she did not create an illusory body of the King of Niṣadha.
Brahmā himself sent this Indra as a messenger to her. ||16||
Whose mind, even that of a sage, would not be inclined toward merit?
For it is the Supreme Lord who remains the authority even when one runs after what is harmful;
yet the mind that contemplates Him is indeed the Supreme Lord himself.
With his heart filled with compassion for the devotee, he restrains [himself]. ||17||
O Sālīka, just as one intoxicated by passion cannot maintain silence even when faced with the most modest person,
so too she could not maintain it before the real Nala.
In those who are deluded, what discernment can there be between truth and falsehood? ||18||
Then, as her friends were rendered speechless by trepidation, she— her efforts to conceal her inner state rendered futile— spoke with a voice that was faint and faltering.
He himself spoke to him, his moon-like face bowed low. ||19||

Having bowed, even with the luster of the jewels upon his head, he offered water for the feet to the guests according to the rules of etiquette; and even with the stream of the essence of the strings of his beloved words, he offered them hospitality.
The satisfaction from the *madhuparka* offering is to be performed according to the prescribed rule. ||20||
One’s own self should be made as lowly as a blade of grass through one's conduct; even one's own seat should be relinquished and offered;
and even tears of joy may serve as the water for the offering.
Inquiries should be made with words as sweet as honey. ||21||
Even the failure to bow at the offering of one's feet may be considered an offense due to the haste of the waters; therefore,
it is fitting to remedy this by joining the palms in salutation.
One's own accumulation [of merit] and even one's straightforwardness [are required]. ||22||
Formerly, having abandoned me, you left your own seat; why then do you not for a moment grace this place,
even though it is unworthy?
And if there is a desire to depart elsewhere as well. ||23||
Alas, let it be announced: how far must these two feet travel in their exertion, as they rival the radiant whiteness of the buds of the *śirīṣa* flower?
Your mind desires that hollow compassion. ||24||
"Which region has been brought today by you to the state of a forest abandoned by spring?
Having obtained you as its appointed rendezvous, it has achieved its purpose."
Even this designation is not to be heard by such people.
Has he not already crossed the ocean itself?
For his entry here was well-guarded;
what, then, is the fruit of this rashness?
Even now, I have not yet reached a firm conclusion. ||26||
I consider that my own past merits are the cause for your entrance here; even so, they have not been noticed by the guard-soldiers with these two eyes of mine.
You are yellow-hued, having surpassed the flower-bowed god with your body. ||27||
Whatever your form may be, or whatever power you possess to blind the gatekeepers,
you are lovely with splendors that surpass gold.
Thus you are a kinsman to those who feed upon nectar. ||28||
You are not Manmatha, for he is bodiless;
nor are you the son of the Aśvins, for he is not peerless.
Or rather, what need is there for other signs? This [form] of yours—
Śrī herself is the superior distinction between those two. ||29||
O You who satisfy the world with light! Who runs to vie successfully with Him who brought forth this moon of nectar-like rays?
Indeed, this lineage is possessed of water. ||30||
Furthermore, considering that beautiful Nala to be a god because he was bound by the eyes of the guards, the young woman,
under the pretext of hospitable flatteries, [addressed] her [situation].
That [beauty] is indeed the very essence of his beloved's splendor.
If silence is maintained toward a subject of wonderful virtues, the fruitlessness of speech becomes an unbearable thorn;
yet if even a few words are spoken, it is mere wickedness.
Let that, then, be merely a ground for the confusion of bards.
I believe that it was Kandarpa himself who, through his merit, found you again in this other birth within the sacrificial pit of the fierce fire of Caṇḍīśa’s terrible eye.
He offered it as a sacrifice to the temple of the senses. ||33||
By means of your splendors and fame, you cause Mount Śiva (Kailāsa) to bow its head in shame;
and you have made the two Aśvins (Dasrau) deficient in their beauty by forcibly seizing their fortune.
Even Kandarpa, who had abandoned pride in his own beauty. ||34||
I recognize these white rows of swans as the flickering chaff of the fame of your beauty;
having flown up, it is fitting that they have fallen and now float about the full pools at the river's edge. (35)
Fortune, though she rests even upon your big toe, was certainly not attained by the flower-armed god;
for indeed, the emblem of the conqueror of Rati’s lord is truly present here.
Narēndu remains there, wearing the guise of a jackal. ||36||
Does the king of the twice-born,
having thinned his full body through austerities month by month, become invisible during the new moon nights?
He attains union with your face. ||37||
Having made your two eyes variegated with many colors, did the Creator fashion a half-moon for those two black antelope eyes by means of the lines of the channels of the pupils shimmering nearby? 38.
Deluded by infatuation, he gave up his beautiful body rather than the bow for the arching of your eyebrows—
since the god of love is already conquered by the play of your brows.
In this form, he existed at that time and at that moment. ||39||
The pair of eyes of the deer is visible upon your face, which is inferred to be the moon; and that very [deer], now disguised in the form of your shimmering mass of hair, is present there.
This is his tail, with its cluster of shimmering chowries. ||40||
Let the ancient saying that "Smara is not visible because he was not accepted by Bhava" remain as it is; rather,
it is because he has taken refuge in your very body that he is [visible] as Śrī.
Let it be; the argument that an object appears as an object [is not yet established]. ||41||
Since the moon, by whom the essence of beauty was gathered from the world by you, adopted the practice of gleaning grains,
even that boy has been placed upon your head.
Even in the sovereignty over sacrificers, he was [consecrated] by Maheśvara. ||42||
Having rendered the God of the Flower-Arrows destitute of any talk of beauty by burning his body,
the Lord [Śiva] once again, through the craftsmanship of your limbs, [restored him].
After a long time, I realize that you have compassion for the world. ||43||
The earth has achieved its purpose if you are a human;
heaven has triumphed if you are someone among the immortals;
and the serpent race has been adorned by you if you are of their lineage.
Nor is the world of the Nāgas situated beneath anyone else. ||44||
This mental state of mine incurs no great inconsistency when you are being meditated upon;
for that very ocean was contained within my hollowed palm.
By you, the seal of profundity and greatness has been assumed. ||45||
I know that the reflection of your son, the prince of the Vīraseṇis, is awake here in the ocean of saṃsāra; for,
apart from the original object and its reflection, there is nothing else for the Creator.
Never has a creation been seen that possesses such a resemblance. ||46||
Ah! By whom on this earth has such great merit been performed, that even your feet, O King, begin to weave a garland of lotuses from the dust of their path? (47)
"What does she say to me? I do not know what this consciousness is, as it hangs upon the swing of doubt.
Are you the guest in the house of some fortunate person, or is this enough with such false imagination? (48)
By the mere attainment of your creation of form, my vision has drunk its fill and realized the fruit of its birth;
let my two ears likewise honor the nectar of your name.
If you would grant them your gracious word. ||49||
Thus, emitting a honey-like nectar,
the five arrows of the flower-arrowed god, released from the bow of her Bandhūka-flower lips, [struck] from her ear.
Under the guise of her speech, she entered his mind. ||50||
Having drunk in his beloved’s sweet words as if they were nectar up to his throat,
he found that praise which tastes delicious even when it comes from the mouth of an enemy.
That sweetness of yours is immeasurable in the face of the beloved. ||51||
Just as the lord of the day accepts the respectful offering brought by the people from the eastern mountain,
so now do you accept this hospitality.
He took the seat offered by his beloved. ||52||
There, having taken hold of that very ground— the Bhaimī herself— his fortitude and the god of love engaged in combat;
therein, the bow of Smara was held within him.
The news of victory or defeat regarding her eyebrows was cut short.
Then, disregarding Smarajñā even though he was being enticed by her words like one played upon by a lute, he spoke from his fortitude,
his inner self washed by hundreds of streams of discernment.
Desire does not defile the virtuous. ||54||
Welcome me, who have come as your very own guest, from the assembly of the lords of the quarters; I carry within me a weighty respect for you.
Like his own vital breaths, [he spoke] the words of the Lord of Heaven.
Let this worship that has been performed be concluded;
please take your seat—why have you abandoned it?
That mission of ours which must be made fruitful remains to be carried out.
That very hospitality of Pṛthu was the source of his great prosperity. ||56||
O auspicious one! Are your limbs well?
Is your mind free from distress?
Enough of this delay; speak my words.
Listen, O lady with eyes as long as the banks of an ear! ||57||
From your youth, your hosts of virtues have carried away the sovereignty held by the lords of the quarters—
the king of the gods and the lord of the waters.
And [he saw] Hutāśana and Āryamanandana. ||58||
As you have long moved through childhood and youth, now partaking in sovereignty, their hearts suffer distress because of you, who are a greater thief of their radiance.
His wealth of fortitude has been plundered by the five-arrowed one. ||59||
Now, it is said that in their hearts only that hope for you shines forth incessantly;
yet that hope, failing to find those noble bodies, remains unfulfilled.
The directions beginning with the east, as well as the self and one's wife, are to be understood as before. ||60||
O slender one! Along with this youth of yours,
the unbreakable love of Indra has ascended to the highest pinnacle toward you.
And even the excellence of the flower-arrowed god's bow [is lost]. ||61||
As you have departed toward the east, this [person], suspecting the moon because of its heat and its form due to the pain of separation,
attributes your transgressions to the sun.

even though he beheld that primordial nature (prakṛti) which had approached him.

but as for what another might say,

"Bring her here; do not fall into despair."
Beyond this, she abandons even the vital breaths for that which is supreme.

For the minds of the virtuous have purity as their own witness. 129.

Having bowed with his mind to the lords of the quarters, the king—

Or rather, let them show mercy through their guileless mission as messengers.

I experienced a sensation born of lack of discipline;
this intoxication was for my own benefit,

He felt compassion for you out of concern for himself.

Having reflected upon what must be done, act; do not let it be performed in vain.
Having felt remorse, he has made a rear-attack against you.

Then, for the sake of attaining purity in your love. ||135||
Thus addressed by the nectar-like truthful words of the son of Niṣadha,

Like the notes of the cuckoo, which expand far and wide. ||136||

Remaining steadfast with a mind that censures lust.

Having awakened Nala by my very self, she lamented;

The sequence of his own delusions and errors as he spoke them himself. ||140||

That channel of the essence of honey has been set in motion. ||155||
