Having made the spring season his ally and having moved within the forest groves, what indeed has he done?
The green one (the parrot) steals the life-breaths of his friend; may they enjoy your fame.
Then, with his head bowed in shame, he [Yudhiṣṭhira] recalled that private conversation held with Bhīma’s sister (Draupadī),
as well as his own conduct in the assembly of kings alongside the immortals.
The lord of the earth, having approached, departed. ||157||
With her mind intent on attaining her beloved the next day, she shed streams of tears like a river of reeds, as the downy bristles on her high and swelling cheeks rose up;
though the night consisted of four watches, it became difficult to exhaust for her due to the pangs of love, yet out of compassion for her, the Creator made that entire night last but three watches.
Then the Lord of the World, in accordance with the nature of beings, immediately proclaimed here the entire truth regarding his own role as a messenger;

he did so swiftly before Indra and the other gods, who were rendered devoid of joy by their realization of the actual state of affairs concerning the conduct of all people throughout the three worlds.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
herein ends the ninth canto, naturally radiant, in his beautiful great poem *The Deeds of Nala*, which describes the Ocean. 160.
The tenth canto: Then the princes, born of noble lineage, who had reached the further shore of both weapons and sacred scriptures, set forth on chariots.
The self-choice marriage of her whose splendor was the array of the body of the enemy of Śambara, she who surpassed the King of Yakṣas in beauty. ||1||
There was no spot that was not the range of Love’s arrows; there was no noble-born prince who did not come as a suitor; nor did even a grain of dust remain upon the earth that did not tread the path.
As the kings' caravans were traveling simultaneously toward their respective settlements.
By the worthy heroes going forth to choose the king’s daughter, by those unworthy ones seeking to carry her off by force,
by others coming to witness them, and by yet others to obstruct them.
The quarters of the sky became reduced to their own measure alone. ||3||
When all the world-regions, having taken refuge in her who is free from all dependence, set out in every direction,
the divisions of the quarters found relief from the exhaustion caused by their respective constraints. (4)
Just as sesame seeds scattered on a surface do not remain there, so too did the royal highways become cleared of troops;
there, he considered himself as if he had already recovered the daughter of Bhima.
Who was it that previously attained the status of a mountain? ||5||
A certain king, his path obstructed by those stationed in front and being pushed from behind,
[performed] the consecration upon the feet of Siddhārtha while he was situated in the mechanical device.
Even having obtained it, he considered himself unsuccessful.
The banners of the city of the Lord of Vidarbha, which were moving slowly due to their heaviness as they followed the kings along the road, seemed to beckon them with the trembling of their tips.
Having previously been Karkoṭaka, he dragged away that great Nāga-force along with Kambala—
the force of kings traveling from the surface of the earth toward Kuṇḍina.
And Aśvatara followed after Vāsuki. ||8||
The beauty of the faces of the quarters of the sky, turned pale by the dust raised by the advancing army of Duryodhana,
clearly revealed their appearance as befitting the state of having abandoned their husbands. (9)
By the four guardians of the quarters— Ākhaṇḍala, Daṇḍadhara, Kṛśānu, and Pāśin—
who were drawn as if by Damayantī herself through the power of her own virtues, [he was surrounded].
He went there to the svayaṃvara, not with the others. ||10||
Where could a Rākṣasa enter that city of Bhīma’s priest, which was protected by mantras?
Thereupon, the Lord of the Quarters exerted his effort.
Therefore, a Yātudhāna can never go there. ||11||
Because the wind, threatened by the lotus-eyes of Damayantī, was unable to turn the deer toward her,
it carried her away to Vidarbha for her marriage on that very mount.
That perverse one is not inclined toward birth, nor wealth, nor virtue; he is devoted solely to beauty—
like a statue of Kutsa seen upon the clear slopes of his own mountain.
Kubera returned to that most excellent woman. ||13||
Why did the body of the daughter of the Mountain, which was half the body of her husband, tolerate the marriage on the floor?

for upon whom else could that serpent—who alone endures the weight of the earth—transfer his burden before departing? (15)
Having reflected upon this, the Lord of the Upper Direction (Indra),
who had examined the treatises on dharma, did not attend the svayaṃvara; for it was neither seen in the world, nor in the Śrutis, nor in the Smṛtis.
Where is there an equal marriage with the grandfather? ||16||
Having learned from the mouth of their messenger that they had been rejected by the daughter of Bhima, the world-protectors headed by Indra,
displaying dejection on their faces and in their hearts, went to the assembly of kings. (17)
There remained a lingering hope among that quartet of gods, headed by Mahendra, that Damayantī might perhaps choose them through a delusion regarding Nala.
A certain fourfold [classification] is of a false nature. ||18||
As the gods strove to become like him,
having looked at and questioned one another,
the attainment of equality with Nala was not at all approved.

They made their faces like the full moon, and again they turned their faces into blossoming lotuses;
then, they gazed at their own faces in the surface of a mirror.

Then,
those [ladies] being unable to obtain the splendor of Nala’s face with their own mouths were not able to avoid the fault of tautology.

From the *vaila* plant boiled by separation from their beloveds, from the moon afflicted by the eclipse of Rāhu, and from the essence extracted by Bhava as he was incinerated— recalling these,
they fashioned for themselves a semblance of Nala.

having caused even the lords of the quarters to engage in rivalry with her.

while hosts of serpent-kings uttered cries of "Be gracious! and "Live on! as if addressing their own dependents. (25)
From other continents,
that city was reached in an instant by kings from the lands of the gods;
at that moment, what youth did not take hold of it?
It is like a tuft of cotton tossed by the wind from the wings of Cupid’s arrows. ||26||

By settling him in delightful palaces, with hospitable service, and by means of affectionate speech, gifts, attentiveness, and humility, that lord of the city of Kuṇḍina graced the circle of kings with his charming conduct.
In the inner apartments of kings, where the moat is the four oceans and fame is the wedded wife,
charity, compassion, truthful speech, and hospitality [are the attendants].

On the pure road, the gate-houses there were made variegated as if out of a desire for festivity;
even the sky was made speckled by them.
by the radiance of the ornaments of the kings. ||31||

The gods and the god-like kings did not distinguish between them there. ||33||
While those kings, having assembled from all directions, were conducting their affairs through refined languages out of fear of not understanding one another's dialects;
The host of celestial beings was not distinguished by the people. ||34||
There, beholding the wondrous deeds of the daughter of Bhīma depicted by the citizens in paintings within the city,
they passed both day and night.
Through the playful arts of enjoyment in that dream. ||35||
Even while she was in a dream that night, she bestowed upon those kings who sought her hand the very illusion of having obtained her; thus, she was truly generous toward those petitioners.
Being virtuous, she fulfilled his desire. ||36||

On the following day, that place where the people were gathered for the svayaṃvara was made magnificent by those heroes, who were summoned by the entreaties of the Vaidarbha messenger and who manifested the various nuances of the erotic sentiment.
Even though he was highly adorned with ornaments,
upon seeing him, the Lord of the Gods conceived the very notion that he was a commoner (prākṛta); thus did that assembly shine with Nala, who surpassed the Flower-Arrowed God.
When that moon among kings, adorned with fragrant unguents and possessing celestial splendor, kissed that assembly hall,
alas, [the night] departed, leaving the range of our eyes.
Where is the splendor of the lunar lineage of the Kṣatriyas? ||39||
The glances of the kings, instantly filled with wonder and longing, fell upon him; but immediately thereafter, those of them whose brows were knit in frowns [fell otherwise].
The corners of their eyes were utterly turbid with jealousy. ||40||
"This first one on earth is the moon," "Is this not the second, Smara?
"This third one is the Aśvins"— thus did the lords of the earth [perceive them].
Under the pretext of praise, the envious ones reviled him. ||41||
"This is the first birth of the Moon upon earth; this youth is the second form of the Beloved of Rati;
he is the third embodiment of the two Aśvins"—thus was he praised by those who were filled with envy.
By means of the illustration of the fire of illusion, they said to one another, "How many are there who are equal to him?
For when their own self is diminished, the remedy for the envious is to compete with an enemy. (43)
To point out a fault in a person who is blameless in some quality is indeed the wickedness of that person; for it is like criticizing the beauty of one who is already irreproachable in his form.
That which was censured by the gods as being human nature—of that [he was free]. ||44||
The truthful Nala spoke to those untruthful men, who were well-dressed and seated nearby:
"Are you not both the Earth and the God of Love?"
Sirs, you are not joined with untruth. ||45||
In this assembly, they spoke thus: "No one at all has been born here in Ilāvṛta;
we stand in your presence without the god of love."
No one here maintains any falsehood. ||46||
Among them, choose for yourself one whose food comes from others, who has surpassed the god of love with his splendor;
wandering through this assembly where there are many such men, you shall find him.
It is said that this daughter of Bhīma will unite with one among us. ||47||
"O King, fie on us who have fallen into such vain hopes! For though we have attained this form of yours here, we have resorted to a state of childish delusion."
Fie on this so-called wisdom of ours! May it cease to be. ||48||
That speech was utterly disregarded by Nala, who suspected no guile in their words;
for, being immersed in the effort to obtain that jewel among women, nothing else appeared to him.
He who, out of rivalry, desires his own status through another, he alone proclaims that other's loftiness;
for what is the rival, who has thereby brought about his own self-inflicted ruin?
In such a situation, one should not show excessive disregard. ||50||
Then Keśava joyfully beheld him, whose fame was praised in songs by the goddess of speech, and who was acting out the graceful play of the lightning-like Goddess Śrī.
Standing in the sky, he witnessed the grand spectacle of the *svayaṃvara*. ||51||
Then the Lord, desiring to behold the assembly, commanded his eight eyes to look toward the eight directions—
even he who, though not having seen the splendor of Śiva’s head, [nevertheless beheld it].
In his view, he is like a *ketakī* flower that speaks falsely. ||52||
With one form he encompassed the mountain,
while with another he became the eye of Murāri;
with those remaining ten forms, the twelve-fold Ātman beheld the ten directions filled with people.
Even though the Lord of the Night always circumambulates the mountain— the abode of the gods— from left to right,
he shall yet behold it as the very form of the vision of Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra.
He did not experience the torment of obstacles to seeing him. ||54||
There, the celestial nymphs (apsaras), longing for the aesthetic delight of the moment, beheld the splendor of the excellent world and cast their own faces into the ocean of people.
They spread forth groves of lotuses. ||55||
Was it not perceived by hundreds of thousands of yakṣas? Or was its perfected beauty not inhabited by the siddhas?
Was it not frequented with passion by the kinnaras?
Neither by Harṣa nor by the great sages was he seen. ||56||

Vālmīki praised her, through whose throat— the path by which the divine speech descended from heaven to earth without effort— there flows a royal row of trees of the three Vedas with their many branches. (57)
Even the Preceptor of the Assembly,
the refuter of all the Cārvākas,
praised her beautiful tongue as a throne for his own eloquence.
I know [this] of the presiding deity of speech. ||58||
He who was a poet among poets, acting as a master in the art of composing garlands of speech that shone even in the celestial realm;
he who was a caravan leader on the path of the Daityas’ policy.
That Kāvya addressed the assembly with eloquence.
King Bhīma did not merely assemble them,
nor did he simply draw them in through his own power of subduing;
even the Creator himself, having reflected upon this, brought these youths together.
He showed us the entirety of his own artistic skill. ||60||
In former times, it was by his solitary state that the Enemy of Tripura reduced the five-arrowed one to the five elements;
this body of his is the means for counteracting that fear.
Are these youths merely playing at belonging to a religious order? ||61||
I believe that the Creator, having set aside somewhere the orbs of the full moons of each month,
the artisan fashioned with those very discs these faces composed of loveliness.
It is in vain that these [fools] have placed jewels upon their heads, for they themselves are those very jewels.
In the self-luminous awakening of the Supreme Self, no other cognition is required for the sake of manifestation.
If this great multitude of beauties were to enter together with mutual joy,
even the two Aśvins would not be able to distinguish them from one another, though they were mixed together, even in the course of thousands of years.
Even though Kāma has been burnt by so many young and clever men standing here, what loss is there for the world?
Who would proclaim the calamity of drying up a full ocean from the loss of a single drop of water? (65)
Thus praising with multitudes of "huṃ" sounds, he was accompanied by the host of gandharvas as they sang;
likewise, he was honored by the assembly of great sages as they recited the Vedas with an abundance of the syllable "oṃ."
Then the King of Vidarbha seated those lions among kings upon a multitude of thrones,
just as the gods are seated upon the peaks of Mount Meru.
It beautified the mountain of refined gold.

Having reflected upon those who had come from various worlds— whose deeds and lineages were celebrated by the immortals— the king was distressed, wondering, "How indeed can these be described to my daughter? (68)
Then, while the wish-fulfilling tree of the Discus-wielder was being fashioned according to the resolve of the faithful,
he became anxious regarding his own family deity.
With his mind one-pointed, he extended his mindfulness for a moment.
Immediately after that thought, the Lord said to Sarasvatī with a smile:
"O Vāṇī, at the self-choice ceremony, I shall make you here the narrator of the lineages and deeds of the assembly of kings."
You know the lineage, the character, and the strength of these youths who have come from various worlds;
therefore, act as their spokesperson.
What occasion is this for you to act like a mute? ||71||
This assembly, adorned by the jewels of scholars from the three worlds, has never existed before nor will it ever exist again;
it exists only under the pretext of making the virtues of kings known.
Make the learned hear the introductory remarks. ||72||
Thus addressed, she, being free from pride, took the pollen from his feet— the remnant of what had been rubbed by the crest-jewels of the gods—
and, together with his grace and command, bore it upon her head.
The young woman, whose neck was like that of a *gandharva* or *vidyādhara*, descended into the midst of the assembly;
her folds of skin had become as if composed of the three Vedas.
The waves of vision produced by literature. ||74||
Then there was Atharvan, possessing the triple power and the three Vedas;
having emerged from the root and spreading forth,
he possessed a dark splendor suitable for various magical rites.
The Veda is the line of hair upon her belly.
Her very conduct was the direct embodiment of the Śikṣā,
her ritual procedure was the splendor of the Kalpas, and indeed, the science of Nirukta reached its full perfection through her, in the form of the etymological explanations of all meanings. (76)
His pair of arms became a meter, distinguished by both birth and conduct,
destined to find its rest in the pauses between the halves of verses.
The middle [point] is the clear sign of the junction between the two lunar phases. ||77||

Without a doubt, was her girdle fashioned by grammar— that which produces long vowels through its qualities and possesses an expansive reach, serving as the creator of successive series of sounds? (78)
I suspect that the necklace, remaining upon her throat and transforming into a circle of rising stars,
has become a luminous knowledge (*vidyā*) for her worship, held within her lap against her midriff.

I recognize that those two treatises on the prima facie and conclusive positions were his very lips, shining with the intense passion for their respective sides held by the proponent and the opponent. (80)
Dividing her own body into two parts according to the distinctions of the Veda— namely, that for the sake of Brahman and that for the sake of ritual action—
she fashioned it so as to be beautiful with a supreme concealment.
[He beheld] her pair of thighs, fleshy through [the practice of] Mīmāṃsā. ||81||
By means of the sixteen categories taught in two ways— both in the section on enumeration and in the section on definitions—
he [Vātsyāyana] polished the ivory-like teeth of the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī).
We recognize that as being embraced by the desire for liberation. ||82||

His arguments are like the teeth of his mouth; otherwise, how could his power in debate be inferred by them? Where else could he find a leaf to offer, were it not for this cluster of virtuous qualities?
Where, then, is the power to refute him through debate? ||83||
That [universe], along with its sprouts, produced by Vyāsa and Parāśara, becoming twofold through its inherent nature,
is characterized by the Fish, the Lotus, and other such forms.
That pair of hands which existed from of old. ||84||
I behold her whose head is graced by the Veda as its root, and who possesses a multitude of Dharmaśāstras that are free from interruption until the end of the aeon.
Whose joy would it not be to have such conduct situated upon their throat? ||85||

The Creator fashioned her eyebrows from the two petals of the *praṇava*, a *tamāla* leaf for the mark on her forehead from its *bindu*, and the bow for the plectrum used to strike the lute from its crescent moon. 86.
Her two earrings are the completion of the circular script;
her fingers are golden pens;
her hair is ink; and the luster of her smile is the lead pencil.
Whose body was fashioned from the very essence [of all things]. ||87||
She whose face consists of the Soma-siddhānta, whose interior consists of the doctrine of the void nature,
and whose innermost core consists of the totality of consciousness.
As if the entire world were composed of the realization of having form. ||88||
Bhīma was addressed by her: "This is indeed the time for you to rejoice; therefore, enough with despondency!
I must now speak to the lords of the earth."
Their lineage and conduct are diverse. ||89||
The Mandākinī found the grace of nectar in his lotus-feet;
she descended here for the purpose of praising his virtues.
I am some unknown woman who has fallen under the power of the kings' command. ||90||
Having perceived that she had been obtained through omens, sounds, and other signs to be realized at that very moment, the king—
who alone bears the burden of protecting the world— ordained for her the honors appropriate to her status.

Then that lord of the earth summoned his own daughter into the midst of the great kings— a perfected spell for the art of attraction, drawn from the farthest reaches of the quarters of the world. (92)
Born among the maidservants moving at the front of the procession, she gradually grew up among her female companions;
now, as she was being gazed upon, she caused the spectators to overflow with a wondrous ocean of beauty arising from her own limbs. (93)

She possessed the luster of a fine cloth polished by the rays of gems through the effortless removal of the oily film of deceitful water; she was mirrored by her own circle of friends, who were like clear reflections in the water of the brilliance of her jewelry.
By the bee,
the messenger of the Lord of Love, who arrived with the fragrance of his body’s ointment and crawled upon the lotus that served as her ear-ornament, [the word was whispered] into her ear.
As if speaking something in secret. ||95||
Beholding the spectacle of the wrestlers— the radiance of the gems in her ornaments of clashing colors— was she perhaps moved by the delusion that they were the bow of the God of Love?
She who bore eyebrows curved with playful grace. ||96||
Her limbs were perfumed by the pollen of fragrant flowers,
and she was attended by swarms of bees resting on the tips of young branches;
like the Fortune of Spring herself, she was honored by those kings.
Desired even by the wish-fulfilling trees.
By the rays of her jewels— shining yellow, white, crimson, and blue— which overspread her body,
she rendered redundant the applications of yellow pigment, sandalwood, saffron, and musk.
To Nala, who she did not believe could conquer Cupid with his flowery bow,
she offered her own ornament, which was a masterpiece crafted from the rays of light.
[She] was offering her bow to the enemy of Bala.

The splendor of the royal assembly was inferior to that of the ornaments, inferior to that of the garments, and even more so than the dense radiance of the jewels; yet, it was not entirely absent from anywhere.
To drink [the light] held by the Creator within the space of her gaze. ||100||
First, the falling showers of flowers from the sky did not allow [the Creator] to see; then, the bees [did not allow it];
and finally, by his face being distorted with fear of them—oh, how the efforts of Fate to obstruct one's desires are thwarted!
She cast from the corner of her eye a glance that was received as a guest by the heart's desire of the king, who thought, "May I become this very person."
The flow of camphor and musk. ||102||

She gently stirs the moonlight within their hearts, while the lotus-faces of the lords of the earth are delighted by the mass of rays from her teeth that have become partially unveiled as her lips quiver with the desire to smile.
By means of the guise of the bright jewels adorning her limbs,

she caused the eyes of the people to remain fixed upon her; and by the rays of the emerald at the center of her necklace, which shone brightly, she filled the hollow of her navel with a deep, thick darkness.
To imitate the beauty of the moon’s trembling head— astonished by her bright, essential smile—
the rows of chowries, adorned with their own paleness, performed a playful dance like a flock of various swans.
Among the celestial nymphs who sang the series of his bodily enjoyments— yet whose eloquence was stunted by the sequence of his descriptions— he himself accepted the favor offered by them.
Bestowing upon the heart the ornament of modesty.
She who surpasses Tārā with her teeth, the moon with her face, and the sky with the luster of her hair—
may she fill my two eyes with honey up to my throat.
Whose kings would she not cause to feast? ||107||
Her limbs were adorned with wonderful ornaments, her beauty was manifest before the eyes of those superior to her in praise,
and she was entering this assembly hall by means of a celestial chariot.
Then the row of kings [regarded him] with sinful side-glances. ||108||
There was no king present there who, at the sight of the wonder arising from the beauty of his form,
did not have his limbs thrill with joy, bristling with the sprouts of hair standing on end. (109)
Pressing with the tip of his thumb and the middle part of his middle finger,
he clapped his hands there while looking at the daughter of Bhima.
By what person indeed is the index finger not [raised] as a threat? ||110||
In this assembly, having gazed upon that woman with eyes like the *khañjana* bird, by whom was the head not shaken again and again by the lord of men?
Or, alternatively, there may be two [types of eyebrows], those with more upward-curving arches. ||111||
Then, perceiving Damayantī as she was approaching the courtyard of the svayaṃvara, the lords of the earth,
their minds overwhelmed with joy, uttered these words with tongues faltering from the saltiness of sugar-candy. (112)
"Let not this earth become empty of those travelers to the realm of the gods who have performed their deeds out of desire for Rambhā and others"—
with these words, she deprived even the men of heaven [of their presence].
In the Rasā [region], there is discord with the Apsarases. ||113||

That form which we heard about from the mouths of people and for which we came from various distant quarters is not at all inferior to this [form] being experienced as the very essence of beauty. (114)
Where indeed does the great ocean exist for that which is known as the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*)?
Otherwise, from what ocean could this Fortune—treasury of beauty and ingenuity—have arisen? (115)
The face of the daughter of Bhīma is clearly the moon itself, while the moon in the sky is merely a figurative designation; her eyebrows are the primary bow of the bodiless god of love.
The flower, moreover, functions by means of its mere qualities. ||116||
Did the pair of earrings held by that fair-toothed woman serve as two quivers for the god of love?
Were the arrows discharged from them moving back and forth right within those two? (117)
Alas, this very woman spreads ill-fame for the flower-arrowed god, since her ear-ornament of blue lotuses has struck his arrow off course.
The wicked man makes that known by means of these two. ||118||
Having abandoned his own ancient flower-throne, which was frequented by six-legged insects and marked with dust,
let that self-born god today accept the throne of Damayantī.
The pair of eyebrows is the bow held within the clenched fist. ||119||
In the autumn, the Creator gathers the khañjarīṭa birds from the lotuses and, taking them with him,
nourishes these two eyes of his with that essence abundantly every year. 120.
"Let people ask the difference between these two bees who know each other's qualities and the lotuses"—
as if thinking thus, the Creator has fashioned a state of neutrality between male and female here in this pair of eyes, using the stars as the bees.
Her youth, devoted to Rati and Kāma who dwell within her heart, has fashioned a palace for them;
who would not regard her breasts as two large golden jars standing at its entrance? 122.
The lotus flower, which surpassed the beauty of a lotus stalk by her two arms, was grasped separately by her hand;
for who would not say that it is here desired by the Goddess of Fortune, or that it is indeed her very hand? 123.

That [lotus] born of Śambara is indeed a mere deception; let this lotus of the lotus-pond rather dwell upon the tips of her arms, for it possesses bristling thorns through its upward growth from the stalk, while this one has sharp-pointed nails as its thorns.
Among mortals, we have no perception of any suitable counterpart for her;
yet, if she exists in heaven or in the world below, then there would be no obstruction from people coming from anywhere. (125)
Salutations be to the hands of the Creator, or let them not exist; for this [work] has not even been touched by his intellect, much less by them.
Indeed, through touch, this craftsmanship would become distorted.
It is fitting for the mind-born [god of love] because of his bodilessness. ||126||

The Creator did not fashion this woman with his two hands, which have become calloused from sitting upon kusha grass; nor did he create her with his mind, that tree on the path of tranquility where the stream of passion finds no rest.
Was she weighed by the Creator in his hand upon her hips, or was she heavy at her breasts?
For that reason, the play of the three folds of her waist has arisen from the space between those three fingers. (128)

Having made her body composed of fresh butter rising from its own nectar, and having gradually manifested a golden luster upon it, the moon became her face; this was impossible for the sleepy lotus to achieve on its own.
The lovely artisan of this [body] fashioned her breath with the Malaya breeze,
and she composed these limbs with flowers.
He uttered a sound with the fifth note of the cuckoo.
This is the handiwork of Smara alone, not of a Creator;
for no other artisan could be its craftsman, nor even the Creator himself in his prime could master the craft of such beauty.
He is subdued by the servant of Love. ||131||

Even for the Guru, the exertion of speaking this [mantra] with his lips and throat was solely the labor of Smara (the God of Love), intended to humble the pride of etymological interpretation, having abandoned [the state of] Bhava (Śiva).
For the sake of preventing regret in those who have attained liberation. ||132||
To describe Damayantī, who had been entirely swallowed by the multitude of eyes of those whose gaze was fixed upon her single form,
Indra adorned his moon-like face with the playful artistry of the nectar-like composition of verses.

With her smile she is Gaurī; with her deer-like eyes, she is Hariṇī; with the resonance of her melodious throat, she is Vīṇāvatī; and with the radiance of her body, this slender woman is like gold in every limb.
Not even a single thought occurs to my mind.
While he was thus offering praise, Indra was observed by Nala, whose mind was filled with apprehension;
having explained the meaning of the verse as applicable to a mortal, Indra dispelled his doubt.

Alas, having assumed his own status as a Nishadhan, did not even the Fire-god, though he was not [actually] Anala, incur the fault of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) for the sake of his mission?
Furthermore, he has received such a prophecy. ||136||

"This one here, charming in her attire, goes along the street; that is Urvaśī herself entering the sacrificial altar of the earth"—by such joyful shouts raised by the people, the impact of hearing descriptions of another woman than Bhaimī was shattered within Nala’s heart. (137)
The diamond that adorns the crest-jewel of the lineage of king-poets, Śrī Hīra, begot Śrī Harṣa—along with Māmalladevī—who subdued the host of his senses;
and for him, whose exertion was peerless even in logic, this tenth canto, naturally radiant, has been completed in the beautiful great poem *Naiṣadhīyacarita*. (138)
Thereafter, the daughter of King Bhīma attended the royal assembly hall of that excellent man, who held her in his heart for the sake of obtaining her as a prize.
Reflecting their own bodies under the guise of their own forms upon the walls of her stainless limbs and within the jewels of her ornaments,
those youths did not merely plunge into that fair-bodied woman with their eyes or with their hearts alone, but rather with their entire being.
If the son of Gadhi had created another world between heaven and earth,
it would have been as beautiful as those celestial chariots which appeared like clouds for the gods who had come to behold him.
Bestowing the fragrance of their own being,
they offered a torrent of wind from the moving fly-whisks of the circle of kings to the gods traveling through the sky to behold them.
Therein, the ritual of worship took place with incenses for the preliminary consecration.

There, following the path of the arrows of the god of love, the swarm of bees, having blocked the fragrance carried by the current of the wind— which bore the scent of the sandalwood paste and unguents belonging to the multitude of lords of the earth—
plunged into that very perfume.
Their wisdom as virtuous men was awakened by the method of echoing all the rhythmic melodies of the loud sounds of auspicious drums;
I believe they displayed their own mastery in the art of *tāṇḍava* dancing among the people through the floating banners of their rows of palaces.
Having engaged in conversation appropriate to her, the Goddess of Speech addressed the one whose neck was bent with modesty—
the one who is honored by the people of the fourteen worlds— saying:
Therefore, seated in the assembly, she relies upon its right wing. ||7||
This multitude of guests with uplifted faces has arrived here, such that a separate description of them would exceed even a hundred years;
from among them, choose someone after reflecting in your mind, whomsoever your heart's inclination pursues. (8)
Just as their natural blinking has ceased due to the pleasure of gazing upon you,
so too, indeed, has it ceased at your face through the enjoyment of your lower lip.
O innocent one, let even the drinking of nectar be twofold! ||9||
Among these mountains, that tree which bears every kind of jewel as its fruit is surely the five-branched [Pañcaśākha] tree from which, in former times, the Earth-cow Surabhi was milked.
Displaying pearls that bear their name through the very act of bearing fruit, it shines as if sprinkled with droplets from the ocean.
Then, placing her joined palms upon her own head— palms which were capable of creating the illusion of a pair of lotuses closing their petals due to the proximity of the moon of his face—
and looking about with eyes trembling from fear of her offense,
she was graciously permitted by the gods to depart elsewhere.
The bearers of the palanquin perceived not even the slightest sign of that detachment arising within him,
whereas the drivers of the chariot understood it through inference from the dejected faces of their leader, which suggested Nala’s dispassion toward Damayantī.
Having observed his own protection against Rākṣasas, he turned away from the Vidyādharas because of their physical inferiority compared to Damayantī;
nor did he find even a trace of the fragrance of his voice in the assembly of Gandharvas.
Having reflected upon this, her group of vehicles turned away. ||13||
Although the poor were present, the Yakṣas— who guarded their wealth and the fruits of their labor— did not even show their faces to Damayantī out of sheer shame;
for did they not know her to be as devoted to her husband as the Lord of the Celestial Trees?
That wish-fulfilling creeper, which had not yet descended to the earth.
Then, the lord of the serpents (Śeṣa), born from that [lotus], beheld the hosts of gods whose feet possessed the beauty of madder-red luster;
he was like a fresh collection of all waters to the mind [of those gods].
The thick clouds caused her to vanish like a flight of swans. ||15||
Furthermore, that Sovereign Goddess, whose manifestation is proclaimed by the sages to be this entire expanse of speech,
possesses a forehead as precious as the rising half-moon of nectar.
The woman, who was always eloquent in assemblies, spoke to Bālā.
That [necklace], which possesses a crimson beauty from being embraced by the silk thread and stained with the saffron from the breasts of the Mountain-Daughter (Pārvatī) during their embrace,
serves as the sacred thread for Śambhu.
This Vāsuki, possessing white splendor, is intent upon services. ||17||
Upon the hand of the Lord, this serpent attains the state of a charming bracelet, beautiful with its lovely jewels;
worship this one who has reached the further shore of the various functions of the Lord of Beings—serving as his crest-ornament, his bowstring, and his meditation-band. 18.

If this double-tongued serpent were capable of determining the supreme distinction between these two, he might do so by holding the nectar of the Lord’s moon with one tongue and the taste of your lower lip with the other, tasting both simultaneously. (19)
The act of biting your lip by a venomous serpent is not to be counted as a misfortune for you;
for it is unable to cause any pain to your lower lip.
His power is effective when joined with the essence of nectar. ||20||
Then, observing her trembling and the bristling of her hair out of fear caused by the sight of his flickering hoods,
and perceiving that these were transformations of the *sāttvika* emotion, he [instructed] his own servants.
The lord of the serpents, feeling ashamed, forbade the dances.
Seeing that, the serpents, despairing of their own choice, sighed and created something detrimental to themselves:
that the carriers of their celestial chariots, though their minds were intent on departing, remained fixed in place.
Alas, alas! Due to the ill omen of the contrary wind, they did not proceed. ||22||
The celestial chariots bore her away from the chief of serpents, whose many hoods were shrinking in shame,
just as one might lead a woman away from a lotus whose petals are closing at twilight.
Like moonbeams upon a white water-lily, it possesses the radiance of a smile. ||23||
The Goddess said: "O timid one, be attentive; behold the gaze of these kings upon the one with the formidable form.
Drink in again with your eyes this very gaze, even as it looks back at you."
Desire does not depart even in ten million years.
He who, with five arrows, made even Lokeśa, Keśava, and Śiva possess states of passion, tranquility, and intense peace— the five senses of the worlds— [is the one].
Agitating the expansive world, may he extend your own great pride. ||25||

O lady with a waist as slender as a double atom, you who take delight in the creation of love, bring these lords of the islands within the range of your eyes— those whose power has been pacified and reduced to ashes by the force of the *huṃ* mantra chanted over showers of arrows by the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma). 26.
May your playful sports in the waters of the ocean of sweet water be auspicious for you along with Savana; therefore,
accept him as the lord of that Puṣkara island.
O you whose eyes are capable of eclipsing the luster of a lotus free from sleepiness! ||27||
In this whirlpool-like navel-cavity, which brings about the wondrous existence of all beings,
you yourself acquire sovereignty over the celestial realm; do not seek the fortune belonging to that [world].
Accept this splendor of Śacī within your home. ||28||
It is said that the self-existent God himself dwells there, beneath the cool shade of a banyan tree; having beheld you two, whose own craftsmanship is peerless, he—
May he strike pride into all the Karus with his hand. ||29||
Like a nyagrodha tree falling from heaven with its heat and rays,
or like a nyagrodha supporting itself by bearing its own weight through its aerial roots— him [he recognized] by the luster of his ripening fruit and his dark foliage.
Behold the parasol made of peacock feathers over the island. ||30||

How could his fame, the beloved of the royal swan, not move through the worlds in whiteness? Yet it is a marvel that, entering into the non-dual purity [of milk], it does not distinguish between the milk and the water as separate from one another. (31)
Even though he was a hero, honored at the forefront of the assembly of wise men, sweet with the grace of erotic sentiment, and a master of the arts—
even so, she incurred that very same reproach from him.
That which is indeed tender is not called "hard" (nala). ||32||
Then, skilled in discerning signs, she made the undulation of her creeper-like brow and the contraction of her facial features a token of her disregard;
likewise, the fire of the king's anguish born from not obtaining her [blazed up].
The smoke from the soot on her face became a visible sign of her soiled complexion.
Then the bridegroom’s attendants led this moon-faced bride toward the king, who was facing them, solely out of their knowledge of his heart;
for when there is a capable servant, there is indeed no occasion for the words of the principal to be required regarding a matter already accomplished.

The Blessed Lady spoke again to the king, pointing out another who was most worthy of being seen and whose lineage was honored by the Aśvins: "O Noble One, let this man, who is distinguished by his noble family and character, be beheld."
Having cast aside the natural modesty of her face, she revealed the orb of her own countenance.

In this sky, already so crowded with the grandiloquence of the unwearying throng of bards reciting before me, there is not even room for my footsteps to arise; nor is there any purpose for my words, which would fall into the trap of needless repetitions.
Indeed, here in this land known by the celebrated name of Havya,
which is ruled by Śākadvīpa, even this Jayā— who has become wise among the wise— acts as a bard proclaiming the titles of his majesty’s arms.
O King, is there no difference between you and a passionate man? ||37||
There, a tree bearing a garland of leaves with a luster like the wings of a parrot will captivate your heart;
for by the manifestation of their embrace with a profusion of sprouts, the quarters of the sky shine forth, celebrated throughout the worlds as "the green ones" (haritaḥ). (38)
It is said that there, the breeze arising from the touch of those tree leaves bestows an indescribable joy;
having experienced that curiosity, you should do so once again.
[One should cultivate] faith even within the narrative of the Parāśara Purāṇa. ||39||

O long-eyed one, may the milk-ocean there emulate the playful splendor of the flashes of light from your side-glances, through the beauty and flickering motion of its variegated masses of waves that kiss the reflections of the forest thickets on the shore. 40.
In this [ocean],
whose great form is unbroken and perfectly circular, he is nourished by a continuous supply of life-sustaining water-juice, brought forth by the movement of a multitude of surging waves.
The king of serpents is being occupied by the slayer of Madhu.
May Kamalā, her suspicions aroused by the sight of the perfection of Your form, long remain attentive here, caressing Your lotus feet with the fingers of her hands.
In order to comply with her husband's persistent urge for sleep. ||42||
Let the rocks of the Sunrise Mountain there experience twice the appearance of artificial red ochre by the morning suns—
even by the lac-dye from your toenails, which falls as you walk about in your playful grace, carrying the sweat born of that exertion.

O lady of faultless legs, as you wander there upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise, may your face— delightful with its application of saffron paste— arouse in men the suspicion that it is the rising moon,
mingled with their overflowing joy. (44)
By this, you have already experienced the fire of separation,
which surely bears your own name as its lineage;
if you were to accept it, then [the grief] would be shared by your sons, Nandana and the others.
Surely let him extend his own lineage, which has already been obtained. ||45||
Although his tree-like arms were the support for the creeper of Fortune, and although his beautiful lotus-face was the abode of the Goddess of Speech,
she perceived there only one single fault.
Maghavan did not become a seeker of wealth when that god [was his]. ||46||
Having drawn from this foremost among flowers— the abode of the play of Lakṣmī— that [fragrance] which had attained renown for its qualities upon the earth,
the bearers of the celestial chariot then led it to another place, just as the winds lead the fragrance of the Surabhi cow to a different location.
Then, that goddess of all speech, whose bodily luster was comparable to gold, spoke further to her:
"To this one, who has repeatedly warded off his enemies with his own arms..."
Fix your mind upon it, O lady with teeth as beautiful as kuruvinda gems! 48.
Behold with the playful flicker of your restless glances this beloved, radiant Krauñca island,
within whose circular expanse that [sun] is situated in its orb-like form.
The pale flood of the ocean of curd-masses shines resplendently.
There stands a mountain, Kr̥auñca, which yearns for the sport of your feet; it shall manifest your virtues through the vocal echoes of the clamorous cries of rows of swans.
Desirous of piercing through the multitude of arrows belonging to Skanda by means of his own openings.
O Vaidarbhi, perform the worship of that moon-crested Lord, by even the mere offering of a blade of darbha grass to whom a person, once conceived in his womb, never again returns to a mother's womb.
That region has as its deities and its people only those who belong to that [specific] measure. ||51||
On that mountain-like palace,

which is as beautiful as golden liquid ornaments and serves as a crest-jewel for the Child-Moon (the infant Śiva), whose nature is like the mountain of sunrise kissing the tips of his topknot— there, fashion rows of golden jars as its decorative finials.

O young woman, may the breeze from the whisks of the rolling waves of the vast ocean of curd— mingling through the lattice-windows— sever for you that pearl-ornament consisting of drops of sweat born from the play of love, as if it were a thief.
Indeed, this ever-new fame of his, assuming the guise of a swan,
acquires practice by means of traveling great distances across ponds, in order to cross the oceans.
And to travel from here to all the ends of the quarters without fatigue. ||54||
Although that king was filled with virtues beyond counting, the slender maiden did not find a bond of affection in his heart;
for when fate obstructs, even the most excellent qualities fail to serve as a means of connection.
Alas, human efforts do not become harsh through exertion. ||55||
Those men, bearing the palanquin as an ornament upon their shoulders, carried the king away from that place,
just as the rays of the moon carry away a streak of frost from the ocean.
The men who were his subordinate scribes [placed] the head of Giriśa [upon their shoulders]. ||56||
To her, who was abandoning one after another— each possessing marvelous qualities and having shaken off all blemishes— by approaching yet another,
the Goddess whose lotus feet are honored by the world spoke:
She was like a lotus fallen from the embrace of Acyuta. ||57||
If you desire the Lord, whose body is marked with the sign of the Kuśa island, who reclines upon a bed that resembles a lotus,
O you who know the truth, divert your mind to the shores of the ocean of clarified butter. ||58||

There, a clump of *kuśa* grass, its tips kissing the sky, will be for your wonder as it is drunk in by your eyes— a clump whose topmost blades, swaying in the tossing of the wind-waves, pierce the mass of clouds and drench themselves with the water falling from them. (59)

O moon-faced one, sport there with your husband in the caves of Mount Mandara— caves purified by the offering of lotus feet to the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī) who arose at the time of churning the depths of the sea— and experience bliss through amorous pastimes.

O lady with limbs as fair as golden ketakī flowers, there stands a mountain— once shaken by the ocean— whose body is beautified by rows of steps that shine like streaks of rays; it appears ready for your ascent, having been polished by the hundred-fold friction of the coils of the Lord of Serpents.

May that Mount Manthāna—the Lord of Serpents, whose white streams of waterfalls are streaked by the friction-marks of his coils—create the illusion that his body is encircled by the remaining limbs of Śeṣa, whose head is constrained by its own weight, as he serves as the churning-stick for your two eyes. 62.
With this pair of breasts, let him remember the two frontal globes of the divine elephant;
with his two hands, the sprouts of the celestial trees;
and with his mouth, the [nectar] arising from the churning of the ocean.
O beautiful one, even Mount Mandara [could not hold] the moon that moved according to its own will. ||63||
To the Blessed One who bears the moon upon his crest, whose jewel of fame was established by all the Vedas and words,
and who exerts himself eternally for the sake of others even without a cause—
just as the Mīmāṃsā [system] does for the Lord.
That monarch did not receive her consent in that matter. ||64||

Therefore, that common folk, without reflecting on their request, led away this slender lady from the king and took her to another prince, even though she had set her foot toward the state of being a wife.
Like a seeker of wealth who turns away from one who is destitute, he turned back from him who was rich in riches.
The Goddess, whose left side was sanctified by the presence of the Four-Armed One,
spoke again to her who was delightful in her majesty: "Of this one,
whose hand is armed with a merciless sword against his enemies..."
From the taking of hands [in marriage], favor the multitude of virtues.
O Lord, you are the master of this celebrated continent known as Śālmala,
which is encircled by the ocean whose waters are wine;
do you not feel wonder at this embodied one who is an ocean of virtues?
Is it a red nose like a sesame flower, or is it simply a nose? ||67||
While the ocean was drinking one of those five [rivers] and they were trembling, the Sindhunadi did not fear among them;
yet in that very place, you were [frightened] by him and by your own kinsmen.
Together with her, engage in sweet sports of drinking honey-wine. ||68||
There, O Mountain, Droṇa will bestow upon you a gift consisting of the beauty that is obtained through good fortune;
he who is as beautiful to behold with his crest-locks as a lamp on an island, where the collyrium of clouds meets [the peaks], illuminated by the radiance of medicinal herbs. (69)

At the time of your playful excursions, may your footsteps be placed upon the surface of the earth, which has become soft with the masses of śālmali-cotton from that island-ornament, beautifully scattered by the wind.
These are suitable for you, as soft as the breast of a graceful female crane.

As they carried the king from one side to the other, the palanquin-bearers observed his inner state— which was indicated by the contraction of the corners of his eyes expanding at the moment he heard of these virtues— and which was pleasing to the Cakrin.

Bhāratī spoke again to her: "O Bhaimī, why do you not direct your affection toward this king, whose attachment to his subjects is like the thick mud of Kashmir, and whose arms shine with the rows of fame from his world-conquests that seem as if smeared with sandalwood paste? (72)
The lord of the island rules over the land marked by the Plakṣa tree; O Earth,
you who have been created for his happiness, shine upon the breast of this Medhātithi.
Just as Kamalā herself was present in person before the enemy of Yama and Arjuna.

Indeed, upon beholding that vast Plakṣa tree, which serves as a parasol for the circle of the earth and inspires love in all people by means of swings suspended from its branches where they dangle their entire bodies in play, your mind too will surely be inclined to sport there.
Having drunk the nectar of your lower lip, let the moon, that jewel of the earth, no longer have faith in the flavor of the waters of the sugarcane-ocean,
which serve as the halo surrounding that island.
O you with eyes as tremulous as those of a cakora bird struck with wonder! ||75||
Just as one who knows no other gods does not eat without beholding the sun or the moon, so too for that lunar [being],
there is no eating without the very sight of your face.
Even for one who has committed an emission during the New Moon sacrifice, the state of being an *avakīrṇin* does not occur.
Alas, for those two eyes of yours, that river which was not even a mere raft during the *utsarpiṇī* age has now become the *Vipāśā*;
let there be a fresh row of lotuses to serve as its lustration lamps.
Devote yourself directly to this king while he shines in his sovereignty.
May the swans in all the waters, rendered into milk by these [king’s] glories, be bewildered by the inability to distinguish between the two;
for even in the word *kṣīra*, which denotes both milk and water, there is a dual meaning.
Let this subject of various lexicons be false speech today. ||78||
We say this to him who desired to summon even Nala:
both he and this king commanded him to simultaneously perform the feat of scaling the coastal mountains on the far shore of the ocean that bounds his own island-continent.

Then the fair-browed daughter of Vidarbha, radiant as the interior of a lotus, gazed upon that king— who, though possessing the form of a youth, had surpassed the three worlds with his beauty— now rendered harsh by his world-weariness.
His gaze was like the flower-bow of the enemy of the three cities (Śiva). ||80||
Then they drew her away from that very place— the sole lamp of the world— while the poles of their own celestial chariots rested upon the surface of their shoulders;
like the crescent moon rising toward the sun,
she was the sprout of merit for the longing night-lotus grove.
Then, with not even the slightest attention paid to those kings,

that fawn-eyed woman was addressed once more by that goddess of speech, who stood there in wonder, having rendered the sound of the lute held in her hand as insignificant as a blade of grass by the excellence of her own voice.
O you who are delighted by the crest-jewel of the earth, this very Jambudvīpa shines with young men gathered for your sake;
it appears like the world of the God of Love fallen from the sky after shattering, trembling with the fear of existence as it swings to and fro.
Surrounded on all sides by his attendants in the form of these islands,
O Princess, he shines like their sovereign,
with Mount Hemādri serving as his great golden-handled parasol.
Marked by the whorls of chowries from the mass of rays of Mount Kailāsa. ||84||

O young woman, this royal rose-apple tree shines here; having examined its fruits, which resemble massive boulders, the Siddha women say this pleasant thing: "By what path did the herds of elephants climb this tree? (85)
The earth known as Jāmbūnada attains renown in the world because its entire soil has been surpassed in splendor by your radiance;
for the water that flows from it is like nectar produced from the juice of the Jāmbava fruit.
O lady with a neck like a conch shell, the river Jambū flows at your boundary.
In this world, thousands of lords of the earth have triumphed over those enemies whose wives were drenched in tears;
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, look with joy at a few of your own heart-stealing forms, and I shall describe them to you with delight. (87)

In this King of Avanti, who is like a garland of *tāmāla* trees upon the crest-jewels of his youthful enemies, and who is a sun of valor that steals away the mass of closing darkness— [in him, there is] a succession of virtues.
O you who subdue the mind in the abode of rest, what more do you desire? 88.

There, O Śiprā, at the time of water-sports, you shall be the companion of your friend [Ujjayinī], bestowing embraces with your wave-arms upon the ascetics and brahmins dwelling in the forests along your banks.
Her lotus-face is beautiful, accompanied by her smile. ||89||
O deer-eyed one, Bhavānī, who is the crest-jewel of all fortunate women, remains ever watchful while reclining upon this city of Ujjayinī;
for her sake, O fawn-eyed one, your husband has joined half his body with hers.
And you shall become a disciple for a long time through devoted service as well. ||90||
Having observed there, in the hearts of those fair-eyed women, that the beloved of Rati had sprouted forth without hesitation through the sprinkling of the nectar of his own moonbeams, Lord Rudra—
Do we not know the fruit that results from the burning of his body? ||91||
Even though he commits a hundred offenses, his beloved women, their desires fully kindled, do not utter a single harsh word to him;
for there, the crescent moon resting on the head of Hara— the very symbol of the lunar day that causes a month-long cessation of study— never departs.
That daughter of the lord of Kuṇḍina did not look at the king, though he was deeply enamored of her from afar;
perhaps because looking at him would have been rendered tasteless by her affection for another.
I know that right observation alone is truly delightful. ||93||
Although the bearers of the palanquin could not perceive Damayantī’s gestures directly in any way whatsoever,
they nevertheless understood them through her reflection in the jewels of the ornaments of the kings standing nearby and facing her.
The people accompanying the bridegroom brought the daughter of Bhīma,
just as the lamp of Raghu’s lineage brought Gaṅgā to the surface of the earth;
she whose pair of jar-like breasts had been drunk by the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma), and who was adorned by her union with Hāra and Cūḍā.
The Goddess of Speech addressed her, whose eyebrows were illuminated by the luster of a bow marked with the sign of a fish:
"O you who are paralyzed by shame, if there is something in your heart, indicate it with your mind."
Here you carry the flavor of playfulness toward the powerful kings of Gauḍa and Viḍa.
Truly, by their spotless glories, these lineages have rendered the rays of the moon like blades of grass;
it is therefore fitting that he dwells there in that ocean of nectar-water.
The deer, out of a longing to devour that forest of sprouts; ||97||
Embraced by you with hands like lotuses, let this dark youth shine like a fresh rain-cloud resting upon a peak of Mount Sumeru;
let him be enveloped by the luster of your limbs, as if by a garland of campaka flowers adorning the hair of the God of Love.
By this [description], the pearls released from the frontal globes of elephants meeting face-to-face shone as they were cast off by the blows of his sword;
scattered by those [pearls] which were utterly unable to endure the heat of his arm.
Like drops of perspiration from the Fortune of the enemy kings. ||99||
It is a marvel that from his pair of arms reaching down to his knees, his majesty has arisen and pervaded the limits of the quarters;
and from the sacrifice performed with a pure heart, the cloth of his fame, born of the seven-threaded rite, has spread across the fourteen worlds.
Perceiving that Damayantī had cast upon him a gaze marked by emptiness, supported by a consciousness of indifference,
the groom’s party led her away; for to one who understands, a mere gesture is indeed sufficient in place of words.

O lotus-faced one, speak again these words skillful for a youth: "Exert yourself fully in the playful embraces of his gaze, which is expertly trained in the art of friendship with the uncontracted lotus. (102)
This King Mathura, a mountain that churned the ocean of his rival monarchs, does not resemble the moon,
whose body is mottled by a dark spot and who has not yet grown a beard; rather, his lotus-face follows the example of the moonless night.
O child, look at his hand, which surpasses various kinds of coral with its lower lip; it holds the magical charm for conquering the world—
a gem that, darkened by the scar born from striking the bowstring, acts like a comet portending the destruction of enemy kings.
Indeed, the scar from the bowstring upon his arm is a streak of smoke arising from the fire of valor produced by the fire-drill of his own arms;
it was created by her, as if desiring to provide a swarm of gnats for the lotus-eyes of the wives of his enemies, so that they might shed tears.
In that central region, the Yamunā was darkened by the washed musk-pastes of the women of Mathurā,
attaining the beauty of a navel with the great Kālīya lake as its center.
You shall behold it as if it were the line of hair upon the earth. ||106||
In that Vṛndāvana, where snakes have been driven away by the roaming of flocks of peacocks on the Govardhana mountain, and which is dense with fragrant blossoms—
there, together with him, enjoy without hesitation the delights of wandering through the forest. (107)
Your future hand, though still a bud among the sprouts of fingernails, will be easily recognized even amidst the cluster of the creepers of your fingers;
it shall bear the mark of an ivory bracelet that resembles the moonlight of frost, its essence having been stolen away by your face.
A thirsty traveler, his gait faltering due to a wind born of the intense perspiration from the joy at the end of lovemaking, will wander across your breast—
its surface bristling with horripilation— and drink without hesitation even the mud of musk, though it be thick with deer-scented ointment.
Those hands of the learned, which possess the stainless luster of lotuses and are useful in the ritual of worship for the enjoyers of sacrifices,
daily acquire fortune by means of the [gifts] bestowed by him.
They have interiors as pale yellow as bright gold coins made of refined gold.
This sole hero of the earth’s circle, who finds no satisfaction in anything while failing to obtain the fortune of his enemies in combat,
may now find contentment upon attaining you— he who flows with a multitude of falling Cupid-arrows— just as one drinking honey does.
Therefore, having had her eyes turned away from the king, she observed the path being traversed by the succession of monarchs;
those appointed to carry the palanquin then made manifest their proficiency in discerning his state of mind solely through their own actions.
Once again, the Goddess of Speech addressed another king, whose eyes were as restless as those of a startled deer:
"O lady with eyes as beautiful as a *khañjana* bird, having beheld the splendor of this King of Kāśī, grant joy to your eyes. (113)
Kāśī is the ancestral capital of this lord of the earth, the boat of Dharma for crossing over worldly existence belonging to the Enemy of Smara;
it is to her that even those whose minds are filled with evil have come.
Having cast off long-accumulated evil, they become free from passion. ||114||
Having beheld the sufferings of the world’s creation brought about by future agents of ritual action, Rudra wept out of sheer compassion;
that he gave her the name "Purī" was merely a pretext, for he created her as a boat for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. (115)
Vārāṇasī does not reside upon the earth;
there is the abiding of the enjoyers of sacrifices, and their dwelling is in the world [of Brahmā]. Therefore, for those whose bodies have been liberated at that sacred site, there is liberation.
May he rise to a station higher than heaven; for what joy could there be otherwise? 116.
Having reached that city of the Lord of Mountains, which is the mistress of the ocean of existence, the daughter of the King of Mountains attains union with Bhava;
she thereby acquires the capacity to denote all beings, just as the verbal root *as* (to be) acquires the sense of "becoming" (*bhū*) upon reaching the feminine form *bhavatī*. 117.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of residing in Kāśī without weariness, and having sported with their partner as they desired,
that couple attains at the time of death a state of singular oneness even greater than the union of Gaurī and the Lord of the Mountain— a state enveloped in waves of bliss.
If you do not believe me, then let there be my silence; it must be told by your own experience, which is the most authoritative for you.
For if Kāśī were not indeed the youngest [of all cities], [this would not be so].
The earth possesses a king by means of the cloud-decorated bow [the rainbow]. ||119||
O noble lady, you are preeminent in wisdom and preeminent in meritorious deeds;
what need is there for further words regarding your duty?
For while one [aspect] of yours constantly grants fearlessness to all people, O blessed one, the other carries on an unceasing sacrificial feast of nectar for those who seek it.
"O deer-eyed one, become the personified Rati to this lord of the earth; let him be your very self incarnate as the Flower-Armed God (Kāma).
For it appears that those two, having formerly offended Śiva, have now descended quickly into that city to propitiate him. (121)
Having thoroughly mastered the hundred instructions on love,

he shall now honor your breasts in private with nail-marks that resemble the crescent-moon mark of Śiva, mingled with the red dye from the saffron-paste on the feet of the angry Daughter of the Mountain.

May this lord of the earth dispel the fever of love within you by embracing you—his beautiful bow being the fly-whisks of his mass of fame, and his prowess spreading forth like sharp-edged arrows that sever the neck-stalks of enemies encountered in battle. (123)
Even from the intense separation from you, his chest has not been rent asunder;
it acts like a diamond, for the weapons of his enemies are blunted upon falling against it.
It is because of the sprouting forth of those two arms that his splendor does not [diminish].
Even by the water of the eyes of the wives of his enemies, the fire bows down.

Are there not hundreds of thousands of trees awake in this world that provide the same enjoyment of fruit for both cuckoos and crows? Yet it is the Kalpa-tree alone that is worthy of praise, for it bestows its fruit upon the gods whose sole sustenance is nectar.

Why should kings not offer tribute to him, since his very sword stood as the guarantor for that? When by fate they do not pay it, then his mercy does not prevail; instead, his own sword seizes them by the hand.

By means of his horses— whose streams of movement traversed the sky solely as an object for the eyes, and who, out of a passion for speed, did not even complete the momentary duration of their touch with the tips of their hooves upon the earth— the pride of the thousand-eyed Indra was shattered.
At the very moment of that description, she cast her gaze upon the assembled beauty of the world;
yet, because he was disregarded by her— who was a knower of virtues—
he withered in the assembly of kings as if by infamy.

Having abandoned with her mind all those who partake of the world’s blessings— the infinite, the unattainable, the radiant, the friends, and all the gods of wind and earth— who though possessing unequal virtues were equally objects of her longing;

she, of hidden intent and auspicious form, remained solely devoted to that one Supreme Person who exists beyond the reach of speech, who is the ocean of consciousness and boundless bliss, thus becoming once more like the Upanishads themselves.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
in this beautiful great poem, the *Naiṣadhīyacarita*, which is cool with the nectar of the erotic sentiment, the eleventh canto—naturally radiant—has thus come to an end. 130.
The twelfth canto: Having embraced his beloved with modesty, the graceful one lingered there, making her the very ornament of Kuṇḍina.
Then, other kings from the ocean arrived at that assembly in their most excellent chariots. ||1||
Then, in that assembly, the svayaṃvara of the daughter of Bhīma proceeded, surrounded by kings who were sighing deeply—
kings who had arrived long ago and had suspected her lack of interest in them.
With ever-new, surging oceans of bliss. ||2||
With his feet trembling from the pressure of those [other] feet, he made the assembly of kings sit down on the bare ground;
for even while traveling in a vehicle, she had become exhausted.
Having spoken thus, that man, a leader among deceitful people, [addressed] his wife with guile. ||3||
Approaching the kings who were seated upon their decorated thrones, that eternal Sarasvatī gave birth to eloquent speeches—
speeches that seemed like streams of nectar rising fresh from the lakes of ambrosia, as if her very body were still moist with them.
Choose King Ṛtuparṇa, who is honored for his complexion that rivals the hue of a golden *ketakī* flower;
absorbed in meditation upon you, this lord of the earth no longer even thinks of his own purifying city of Ayodhyā. (5)
Let this moonlight from her moon-like face not be drunk by the tongue of the cakora bird at all;
why then do you not cause your eyes to sip it?
For a long time, [the gaze] of the cakora bird has touched your face.
While you sport in the waters, let the rising spray of droplets create the illusion of a pearl necklace upon your body;
let that spray, born from the waves crashing against the slopes of your two firm, full, and high breasts, produce a sound as resonant as the *sāra* lute.
The ocean was dug out and filled by the Gaṅgā;
yet in his lineage, he will surely bind it by force—
oh, how his fame shall surpass even those hundreds!
The prowess of the virtuous runs directly toward the great. ||8||
This speech of poets plunges into the unfathomable depths of the ocean of his fame;
it is the falling of the marks used in counting his virtues.
It wears away the chalk-like reputations of one's adversaries. ||9||

How can this hero, who bears the status of a crest-jewel upon the radiant solar dynasty, be described? For even his hair on the battlefield has reached nearly ten million hairs, which are sprouts of courage.
Furthermore, when the mantra consisting of the sequence of syllables of his name is brought to the ears by bards in combat, it causes the serpent-like pillar-arms of rival kings to become paralyzed.
I recognize his agency in the creation of such a long day for Brahmā;
I suspect that the submarine fire within the depths of the ocean's flood is but his reflection;
and he is the one who eclipses the star-like glories of the enemy kings who pervade the sky.
The heat of Kāśmīra’s prowess does not reach the further shore of words. ||11||
When the river consisting of the rows of his fame met upon the battlefield with the Yamunā of the ill-repute of his enemies,
the warriors of that king plunged into it and began a grand display of sporting in the Nandana grove— the abode of the bliss of embracing Rambhā.
Thus, having tasted the praise of those virtues through the Vedas,
the daughter of Bhīma, out of wonder at the ocean of Sarasvatī’s eloquence,
merely shook her head from side to side.
He did not approve of that lineage of Manu.
Then that sovereign of speech, who surpassed the intoxicated cuckoo with the nectar of her own voice, spoke to another youth,
as if her hand were joined with his direction.
Toward this woman, who is like the very face of the kinsman of the night-lord (the moon). ||14||
O fawn-eyed one, ornament of the Pāṇḍya land, you do not even desire to gaze at this king with your eye;
yet you wish to behold his face, which shines like the moon.
She caused the radiance of her eyes to ripple through the direction of her sidelong glances. ||15||
Having wandered upon the earth, she has become intent on a succession of practices to roam unsupported in the sky;
oh, how she has taken refuge in this great lineage!
The dancer of fame dances with joyful excitement. ||16||
Out of fear of this, kings wandering from forest to forest attained the status of vast wildernesses;
yet even that city of their own was, after a long time, reclaimed once more.
Again, he entered his own pleasure-palace. ||17||
There was a hero whose fame served as the cosmetic sandalwood paste for the entire circle of the earth’s surface;
whose prowess with the bow was loudly sung by the dense crowds of people dwelling on the shores of the seven oceans;

and whose moon-like nails were intensely delighted by the service of the rays from the moon-gems in the crest-jewels of kings falling simultaneously at his pair of feet—who could be greater than this hero? (18)
The fire of his majesty blazes within the *tinduka* forests of the ranks of enemy soldiers, who are as dark as ink from the stain of defeat and infamy.
From it spring forth sparks that flash across the lap of the world—clearly manifesting as the eye on Shiva’s forehead, the sun, the sacrificial fire, and the thunderbolt of Indra. (19)
Having observed that the entire earth was embraced by the strength of his tusks at the edge of the battlefield— tusks which produced the illusion of a multitude of moving mountains—
King Pṛthu, moving amidst the rows of gods who had descended to witness this fierce battle, again set his mind upon hurling the mountain.
The maidservant, skilled in interpreting gestures, described the daughter of Vidarbha: "O Mistress, behold this marvel!
Even though the hem of the cloth on this dancer atop the palace roof is moving, this crow maintains his grip upon it. (21)
Then, because of the laughter of the members of the assembly arising from those irrelevant remarks, that assembly became white;
consequently, the pallor of this king became manifest.
For from coldness, visibility arises clearly. ||22||

Then, by that certain woman who was the very embodiment of supreme consciousness, who was the sole object of worship for the world, and whose forefinger was bent in a gesture of humility, the Goddess addressed Mahendra, the Indra of the city of the earth. (23)
O daughter of Kaliṅga, at the great festival of your self-choice marriage, choose Mahendra himself as he has arrived from the Mahendra mountain, [to rival] the beauty of your own pair of breasts.
Listen there to the *kali* of elephants at their temples. ||24||
"Alas, this enemy has arrived!"— out of fear of such words from the citizens, his foe fled to the forest in vain;
for even there in the woods, he was terrified by parrots reciting those very same harsh words he had heard while sleeping at ease.
Then, abandoned by the mountain king who fled in terror from that place,
the beloved was seen by the forest-dwelling people; questioned, she recounted the wonder born of her own land.
Indeed, [he] possesses the cool nature of the moon's radiance. ||26||
Why do you not show your heroism even in this regard—
by making kings submissive through the excellence of your bow, arrows, and virtues,
and by establishing them firmly through your pure merit?
Nevertheless, Urvaśī, the mistress of the circle of the earth, brought him under her control.
The wives of the enemies, terrified by this [king] and forced to flee through mountain caves where daylight was fading, called out loudly as they emerged;
their young children, clutching at the moon with the delusion that it was their own pet swan, cried out for it.

As the children’s laughter—delighted by the nearness of the reflections of the moon-swans mingling with the tears from their mothers’ eyes—filled the air, the women were both comforted and further distressed.
The Earth, the wife of the lords of enemy lands, experiences a tremor— a *sāttvika* emotion— while meditating, "May this man be my husband when he is intent on his conquest of the quarters.
This occurs because she will fall face-down in battle before him, seeking her own elevation [to heaven].
A path consisting of holes is seen by rival kings in the sun. ||29||
When the entire host of enemies has fled in terror from the battlefield, if some warrior, preeminent in fame throughout the world, should turn back again out of anger,
even as he approaches face-to-face, he encounters only a turning away from them.
Instantly, by means of this dagger, his head was severed with a sharp *ṭhaṇ* sound as it rolled away.
Then, as if out of wonder at the virtues of that lord of the earth,
she placed her finger-lotus upon her own lotus-face, saying,
"Let this seal be placed upon your mouth."
She spoke to her with gestures full of cleverness. ||31||

Immediately thereafter, Sarasvatī, whose stage was the shimmering waves of her glances directed toward another king on that path, spoke to her, making the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) seem as insignificant as a blade of grass.
The surface of the earth was overwhelmed by his exceedingly fierce splendor. ||32||
Why then is that very thing not done? What harm is there if he desires it through the mouth of your messenger?
Be gracious; let this Indra of the city of Kāñcī forcibly seize your girdle. (33)
"Stability with me is obtained only through humility; indeed,
it is through arrogance that one oversteps the bounds"—
as if saying this, he held his bow and discharged his arrow.
He correctly instructed the enemies in this method.

In the waterfall of the tears shed by the wives of his enemy hosts, the row of swans that is his fame sports, stealing the lotus-stalks and conch-shells from the arms of the young heroines who were slain before him in battle. (35)

As his elephant— its head charming with the luster of vermilion, its dark hue extending from the shoulders down to the base of the trunk, and reaching toward the very limits of the sky— rushes forth eager for the start of battle,
we wonder whether the thousand-rayed splendors of the arms of all the warriors are setting, as if out of the mistaken notion that twilight is mingled with the darkness of evening.

Having abandoned the chest of the enemy of the Daityas as her own abode— wherein the Kaustubha gem has become like a white parasol fashioned by monkeys and insects, clearly crumbling due to the defect of emptiness—
and having likewise forsaken her own home, the lotus, which is now rendered visibly covered within by the threads of a spider, Fortune today finds rest within his arms.
The ocean has emitted this victorious, purifying, and wondrous flood of fame, wherein the worlds bathe; what poets are there who would not remain silent before it?
Even the moon, entering its water, becomes invisible as it approaches the splendor of a single drop.
Upon whose crystal ground that Lord of Sacrifice (Yogeśvara), the deity of the waters, remains awake. ||38||

He does not veil his eyes with tears of inner satisfaction so that he may hear [the praises] with them; nor does he produce a series of horripilation—the very root of bliss—upon his body, for he is devoid of hair;
nor, fearing a collapse of the earth, does he nod his head. Thus we do not know how the Lord of Serpents manifests his joy while listening to his glories. (39)
That he, skilled in victory, plunged these firm spear-shafts up to their very crests into the frontal globes of the elephant-herds of enemy kings during his fury—that was his great service;
yet for that reason, he is not pleased with you. Why? Because he has wielded these spears, and even harsher punishments, against those [breasts] of yours which are so greedy to rival your own.

With the beauty of her smile resting upon the corners of her mouth— as if bestowed by the very bliss of his virtues— she mocked him with words regarding the greatness of his fame, for the majesty of the Lord of Niṣadha lies beyond the reach of speech. (41)
With the deer-cubs that were her own eyes smiling, she addressed another scorcher of foes,
having first pointed him out with her brow— the ground for the beauty of the turning of that direction— while he was honored by the assembly.
