Alas, alas! Your compassion for kings is nowhere to be found; yet, O you whose eyes are full of aesthetic flavor, let at least the corners of your eyes be directed toward those who bow their heads.
The protectors of the kings of Nepāla, who were worthy of being drunk from [as if they were vessels]. ||43||
His upright conduct, silence, and mastery of the Vedas—
these very qualities, which inspire the utmost confidence, were indeed intended solely to destroy him.
That hypocrite possesses great abundance. ||44||
This arrow, though it reached its enemies and became defiled by contact with them, did not violate its vow of pleasing the people;
for in battle, having cut down even those who were utterly disaffected, it made them appear more red than blood itself by drenching them in gore.
If this brilliance of his were ever to fall upon the fire, then the sun would surely suffer the calamity of becoming a moth, having accepted the fate of a moth;
for Fate was unable to acquire glory equal to his own.
In some way, even the ocean of milk was made a substitute for it. ||46||

As long as the two mountains, Setu and Prāleyaśaila, serve as the upper garments for the two lions—the hair-tufts on the flanks of Rāvaṇa and Hari—while they range over the lands of the descendant of Pulastya; and as long as both mountains bear the crimson beauty of their peaks, fashioned by the lovely banners of twilight, acting as the pillar-marking the commencement of the cities of the lords of the eastern and western quarters; so long shall the fame of this king endure.
Having fought face-to-face in battle, and having perceived the internal difference between himself and the enemy, he released volleys of arrows at those falling [upon him];
or else, his own fear became bowed down as it was severed, or he was exhausted by the weight [of the combat].
By this king, the heads of his enemies were forcibly rolled upon the ground.

Neither when he draws from the quiver, nor when fitting the string, nor when drawing it back to the tip of his ear, is anyone’s gaze fixed upon his arrows—neither in the sky, nor on the target, nor on the ground.
Men do not see his shafts anywhere; rather, their inference is that they perceive the arrows through the cavities of the chests of fallen enemies.
Perceiving the mind of Damayantī’s sister, the jestress said to the queen: "How much will you say about him?
O Noble Lady, tell me: while the world abounds in virtues, why is there such a suffering of dwelling in confinement?"
"This maidservant here says something utterly improper; she is even more insolent than that!"—
thus spoke those who were angry, while saying, "Oh, what a virtuous assembly!"
The people there forbade these followers of the king. ||51||
Then, turning her face toward the direction of another king, that compassionate goddess spoke to Damayantī.
By her speech, she surpassed the splendor of the God of Love. ||52||

Casting aside your modesty, look at me from behind the pretext, with the white rays of moonlight traveling along the path of your outer corners— rays perfumed by their dwelling in the blue-lotus eyes.
The earth is the dwelling place of the earth, and the garland is the dwelling place of radiance. ||53||
Having abandoned this [earth] after the enemy was broken in battle,
he entered his own refuge in vain; for, filled with pride, he did not know that he could not protect himself from this [consequence].
It cannot be traversed even by a difficult mountain path. ||54||
By this king, you— who are thick with the roar of clouds and heavy with the weight of age— have been rendered unfortunate among supplicants;
likewise, Mount Vidūra shall be brought from afar to nearness.
In such a way that he shall become your pleasure-mountain. ||55||

O lady with eyes like those of a deer, this lord of the earth bears a pair of warlike arms that act as serpents; their rows of toenails play the part of the moon by falling within the shadows of the swarms of bees formed by the fading lotus-faces of rival kings, and they are swollen from the abundant drinking of the wave-like nectar of the life-breaths of arrogant enemies.

Where in this world does this flood of fame not remain ever-awake? It is a supplement to the crescent moon on the head of the Destroyer of Smara; it is a multitude of serpent-hoods more befitting the body of the serpent Śeṣa; and it is a manifestation of forms that serves as the means for the Ocean of Milk to avoid being swallowed by the sage Agastya’s cupped palms.

What need has he for a hundred kings who wields the *śataghnī* weapon? What is the use of hundreds of thousands of those who pierce the target, when he conquers ten million lotuses with his own lotuses? Even with a *parārdha* [of enemies], it would be impossible to overcome him who cuts through all opposition.
Alas, for those who hate this [teaching], there is no way out whatsoever without the removal of that very number.
Then Sarasvatī, having spread a smile, addressed Damayantī’s friend who understood her intention:
"Behold, even those beyond this point are making their request."
[He expresses] his eagerness to make his own announcement through your mouth. ||59||
"Here, the Queen has been appointed as the authority over speech; who is there to give an answer, or what answer can she give?"— with these words,
her frown turned back the king's attendants who had spoken thus.
The Goddess of Speech addressed the King of the Earth with words of profound significance directed toward Damayantī, as indicated by his body slightly turning toward her.
He was indicated as a king by both his lineage and his conduct. ||61||
Why have you made such a vow not to look upon him who has come from the world of the gods?
Even this [vow] regarding this Indra of the city of Mithilā—
It would be better for your gaze to become slack after drinking [it]. ||62||
"Protect me! Protect me!"—because he spoke thus to that enemy, O lip, it has become so for you through that very act;
in anger, on the field of battle, he bites his own lip with his teeth while gnawing upon the heads of his adversaries.
Even as his right arm was receding,
he took up the bow along with the string and arrow for it to advance forward;
out of joy in that great battle, he seemed to offer an embrace to his left arm.
The fame of this lord of the earth, which rivals the splendor of the full moon and dispels the pride of the white beauty of Mount Śarva (Kailāsa) radiant in every limb—
is it perhaps the reflection of the autumnal clouds in his conch-shell neck?
Is it a synonym for the waters of the milk-ocean, or is it a restatement of all things? ||65||

By whom has this hand of his not been observed, scattering heaps of pearls from the hollows of the frontal globes of enemy elephant herds shattered by his sword—pearls that seem to sow a multitude of seeds for the trees of fame upon the earth, which is furrowed by the hooves of horses galloping in battle against his fourfold army? (66)

While this king, who bestows excessive charity, stands here, let that celestial wish-granting tree (kalpadruma) somehow remain bowed down under the pretext of the weight of its fruit, which increases as it is plucked by supplicants;

but how can the Mountain of Jewels (ratnācala) endure, for he is exalted by the rising of a wealth of jewels that never diminishes, yet is thick with shame due to the ill-repute of being avoided by the throngs of beggars?

When her friends asked her with gestures, "Shall I create an obstacle to this praise of the king?", the bride turned her face away to smile; that very act was perceived by the king as a sign of her aversion.
Having pointed out another king to her with a glance,
she whose voice was like honey and who was the sovereign of speech caused the daughter of Vidarbha to hear his praises.
With utterances that are like the nectar from his own moon-like face. ||69||
Alas, this lord of Kāmarūpa, who is superior even to the realm of desire (Kāmarūpa), is not even looked upon by you;
yet you are his most worthy beloved.
For another equal to its rival is extremely difficult to find. //70//
Alas, while his enemies— having reached a state where their limbs were severely lacerated by arrows that missed their mark due to the absence of a helmsman, and being deprived of a rudder—
were creating a breach in the ship of the sun;
Having plunged into it, he has crossed the ocean of worldly existence in battle. ||71||
Since the summer season itself is produced in the enemy's palace by the heat of the arms of this ruler of the earth,
let not the wretched wives of his enemies provide water-stalls there with the waters residing in their lotus-eyes.

To whom did this mass of dust raised by the hooves of the multitude of horses in his vanguard not cause the illusion of smoke rising from the fire of his fierce majesty—blazing with the abundant fuel of the royal lineages of his enemies whose blood flowed from the sword-strokes he dealt—as they beheld the burden of his battle in the conquest of the quarters? (73)
Having churned the waters of the Ocean of Milk, when the gods fashioned a throne out of the dregs of that churning, they created for this fame a lion-throne made of the Ocean of Milk.

For whom among the people of the world did the festival of its consecration not arise—a festival wherein their thirsty ear-vessels were filled by being immersed in the stream of the nectar of his poetry? (74)

Upon the stone-like chests of hundreds of thousands of deer-eyed wives of rival kings—suddenly split open by the impact of their hands upon hearing of his fall—the panegyric of his fame was, as it were, inscribed with the sharp chisels of the nails from their hands agitated in the act of beating their breasts. (75)
Having placed the betel-roll in the hollow of her hand,
the bearer of the betel casket spoke to Bhāratī, having perceived the intention of Damayantī’s sister.
By this or that [method], bring rest to the fatigue of the mouth.
Turning her face toward another king who was like the god of love, Sarasvatī raised her own arm;
thereupon, the eyes of that girl became like those of a trembling young deer.
He praised the woman who delights the company of people. ||77||
This man from Utkala, whose eyes long for the nectar of beholding your face and who is enamored by the flood of your virtues— surely let them touch him at this pool of the nectar of beauty.
Even for you, there are such breakages of waves upon the surface. ||78||
By this [act], the wish-fulfilling cow and the celestial tree— the former who fulfills all needs and the latter who brings wealth to those who seek it—
have both reached the height of their generosity by mutually bestowing upon one another the milk for watering and the young shoots for eating. (79)
With his two hands, this king lifted up those kings who were falling at his two feet;
by the rays of the rubies in their crests, [he seemed to hold them aloft].
This coloring of his hands and feet is clearly evident. ||80||
That the sun does not maintain its stability in any direction whatsoever,
and that the forest fire has arisen finding refuge solely in the dense woods—
this is indeed the fitting consequence of those two being utterly defeated by the splendor of his arms.
Fie on that submarine fire which, out of fear of its enemy, has entered back into the waters! ||81||
I foresee that when the season of frost begins with the spray from the elephants of this sovereign’s spreading army,
let the soldiers of rival kings not tremble within, let the lotus-faces of their wives not wither, and let it not be a day of ill omen for them.
Oh, how truly fitting it was for this king— who has elevated his virtues within himself—
that he caused the destruction of his enemies by avoiding certain limbs;
for with that heart which repeatedly struck them down, and with those shoulders which did not bend, he shattered their vital organs piece by piece with a multitude of arrows effective in battle.
The white lotus wanders far away from the fame of your arms—which bears the mark of victory over those possessed of pride—fearing it even at night and finding no sleep;
the jasmine garland in your braided hair hides itself out of fear;
and the cool-rayed moon, harboring dread, perspires under the guise of trickling nectar.
This scent-elephant, his body submerged up to the throat in the water out of thirst, is whitened by froth that rivals the fame of his victory in sport over the elephants of the quarters;

appearing as if he has four tusks due to the reflection of his own pair of tusks in the water, he extinguishes the ocean’s grief of separation from Airāvata under the guise of the spray from his trunk. (85)
Then, as if to savor in her heart this marvel of the description of the lord of the earth,
she closed her eyes while muttering the name of the King of Niṣadha with a garland of honey.
With the flame of meditative concentration clearly manifesting before him.
To praise the Lord of the World, the Conqueror— who delights the assembly, who triumphs through his splendor, and who conquers the world—
he uttered those same words as before.
She is the deity of the time of the evening twilight at the end of the day. ||87||
Therefore, O lovely one, act in such a way that he, who has long desired you and is now filled with longing, may receive you;
for his eyes are eager to perform a dance upon the stage of their outer corners.
The streams of your sidelong glances [are like rain] upon the lord of the Aṅgas. ||88||
Is this the mark upon the moon, the enemy of the night?
Is this the face of that enemy?
Frightened by his glories that pervade all the worlds, the ink of darkness flees away. (89)
This Rohaṇa mountain, abandoned by suppliants seeking it from kings and growing instead with sprouts of jewels,
will cover the sky in a few days;
in vain did the sage Agastya obstruct the Vindhya range.
With what words can we praise the glories of this Bhūśakra, acquired through the weight of his valor, which vie with the tusks of the great elephant Airāvata?
Though the Golden Mountain (Meru) was turned into mere silver by the liquid quicksilver of the fame of other kings, it has been fashioned anew as gold by the fires of his majesty.
Since she has led her husband on this military expedition, she is surely Indra’s earth,
now smeared with the ashes showered by Maghavan like the soot from a forest fire;
alas, may she quickly take up the vow of Śambhu, the twilight dancer!
The earth, the very form of the eight-bodied one, dances with the thought that it is the twilight of a shower of blood.
Before the Creator fashioned this body with its moon-like face, the entire treasury of all splendors— even that which was employed in the creation of the fathomless world— dried up;
or perhaps, due to the exhaustion of his entire orb of light, it has become difficult to find even a trace of it.
Is the remainder, consisting of hair, fashioned from the mass of blinding darkness? ||93||

This king creates darkness with the dust raised by the tips of the hooves of his horses, which are exultant in their expeditions for victory over various quarters— a darkness as if born from the fire of the majesty of his enemies already extinguished.

His body, whose form is to be inferred through the science of illusions consisting of the shadows of the earth’s sphere, has been summoned to battle by the spreading webs of his fame, as if by moons, like Rāhu.
The three worlds remain supported within this cave-like belly of Viṣṇu;
yet, due to the weight of their vastness, his glories are unable to fit here.
Having filled that very belly, these glories—as if emerging from the Destroyer of Madhu through the path of the navel—have assumed the guise of white lotuses, resembling the tusks of an elephant.
His sword, drawn from the hollow of its own scabbard, shimmering with blackness and performing a tremulous,
curved, and playful dance, strikes terror into those kings;
for in battles, it is like a great medicinal creeper of perfected power residing upon his own fingers.
By whom, indeed, was the state of a snake-charmer not assumed by placing [venomous snakes] upon their own mouths? ||96||

He who shows his back against rows of enemy warriors in battle, he who maintains a crookedness toward them, and he who emits a harsh and cruel sound— of such a bow that possesses these faults, this king alone is clearly renowned as the supreme limit of those who appreciate virtues, for he accepts its string.
O King, when the enemy’s arrow and this king’s shaft fall together in battle,
neither produces a whistling sound nor does either suffer a tremor;
yet it is not fitting that there should be no difference between them once released, for while one pierces a friend, the other pierces an enemy— this is truly marvelous.
Blinding the heavens with dust, deafening the quarters with the clatter of its hooves, crippling the wind with its swift speed in battle, and silencing its praisers with its virtues—
mounted by this king who has engaged the world in the worship of Dharma,
even the horse mocks the earth with its deep leaps as it attempts to touch her with its hoof.
Alas, even on this earth— the very abode of people who witness the spectacle of battle— no one remained merely to look upon the wondrous dance commenced by rival warriors whose throats were severed,
for they were shrouded in the darkness of the thick columns of dust rising from the surface of the earth as it was pulverized by the hoof-strikes of horses galloping with unrestrained speed.

This pond was excavated by him—a pond whose waves are made resonant by the gusts of wind rising from the wings of flocks of birds sporting in its belly, which is overflowing with the fragrance of the opening petals of playful blue lotuses; and which, with its shores embraced by rows of trees filled with fresh green leaves upon their many branches, has bestowed delight upon the eyes of travelers whose fatigue is soothed by its presence. (101)
This ocean is an old man, bearing a pale body with wrinkles like waves; he possesses such great age that he is supported by a staff in the form of a flight of white swans,
and he bears a head of hair turned white by the moonlight, which is joined in a fitting and radiant union with his blossoming locks.
He was constantly devoted even to bowing his head before righteous men who performed the ritual bathing at sacred sites. ||102||
O young girl, sport with this youth in the waters during the hours for sporting in the water; let there be no distinction between the blue lotuses there and your eyes, as they reflect your image.
Let the shadow of your body alone take the place of those goddesses of the waters.
And may the consecration of your face take place in that kingdom of blossoming lotuses. ||103||
All the dark forces of the worlds, having been banished from the three realms washed clean by the revolving waves of his fame, found rest only in mere stories. Oh,
from this man who was composed entirely of glory, there arose such a weight of fear that infamy— possessing a soiled luster— could no longer even establish its presence upon the path of his legend.
Then Bhīma’s daughter said, prompted by a gesture:
"If infamy among people is not desired for him,
then indeed I too shall certainly not desire that [union] with another."
[The assembly hall] was entwined with Mālava creepers that filled its windows. ||105||
The infamies of this lord of the earth, which have been rendered into numbers by the highest possible count, appear like darkness when scrutinized by the eye of wisdom;
indeed, they are sung by a multitude of mute sons born from the wombs of barren women on the shore of the milk-ocean of female tortoises, while they modulate the eighth musical note.
Having drunk in that assembly with his glances— whose faces were smiling and filled with wonder at those syllables—
he [asked] him whether this laughter had arisen here for the first time or not.
The daughter of Vidarbha also gazed upon the king. ||107||
The pupil of Damayantī’s eye, which was the abode of deep blackness, indeed did not cast its gaze upon anyone other than Nala;
it performed service worthy of its pure redness.
But when the King of Niṣadha was nearby, her sidelong glances met his.
With his glance as an arrow kissing the ears, and his hand possessing a wheel as a bow bent in the guise of a discus, Smara assumed the state of an archer through the limbs of others.
Then the bodiless god of love himself tormented Janīman. ||109||
With its bristling thorns, its shimmering rows of brilliant petals, its abundant fragrance, and its exceeding whiteness, that most fair woman,
perceiving Nala as the enemy of Rudra’s wrath,
sought refuge with him like a golden ketakī flower.
With her mind entirely fixed on the stalk of that lotus, she did not turn her gaze even slightly toward the four clever Nishadhan princes standing before her;
having plunged deep into the ocean of bliss, she gave the people the illusion that she was a daughter of the underworld (Pātāla), as she became an ornament for its floor.
The king, having bestowed upon her— the very essence of his heart— the gift of joy for his gaze,

attained that sight which was a cherished guest, difficult even for the gods to obtain, surging with the waves of her sidelong glances; yet, through the blindness of bliss, he rendered fruitless all other descents of Rati’s intentions.
He was swiftly licked by her husband with an arrow fashioned from the swirling streams of nectar. ||112||
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the circle of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this twelfth canto, naturally radiant, has thus concluded in his great poem *Nalacampū*, which is like a garland at the lotus-feet of his mother. 113.
The thirteen cantos:

Then, like fragrances from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) leading a swarm of bees away from a multitude of ordinary, censurable trees, the bearers of the celestial chariot led that [Sītā] away from the assembly of kings and brought her to the five heroes who had assumed human forms. (1)
Having directly perceived the conduct of all the people in the world, she spoke there concerning the lord of heaven in such a manner that he was identified as the husband of Śacī,
yet the illusory form of the Nishadhan king was not revealed.

O lady of excellent complexion, what need is there for us to describe the rise of this Vīrasena, whose manliness triumphs over the forces of his enemies, and by the scent of whose ichor—emanating from the faces of the elephants serving in his army—the glory of battle was rendered fragrant? (3)

In the assembly hall and on his expeditions, he is attended by female fly-whisk bearers who possess the luster of sun-gems set in rainbows kissing the breasts of necklaces that steal the beauty of clusters of bright moonbeams, and who are adorned with many ornaments.

Having performed the amputation of the wings of those mountain-like kings—whose bodies were incomparably harsh and who possessed millions of lions and elephants of unrestrained pride—the one of exalted strength rescued the world, which had been submerged in an ocean of calamity. (5)
Know that this conqueror of assemblies of kings is Indra himself, free from any decline;
O lady with breasts rivaling jars, you do not perceive his hidden, extraordinary excellence consisting of his arms and eyes. 6.

O lady of shapely hips, the lines on his hands and feet bear a reddish hue, indicative of the abundant enjoyments of a kingdom richly endowed with power and other such riches; therefore, together with this husband, may you experience joy like Śacī with Hari. (7)
Having heard this entire speech, which was identical whether applied to Indra or to Nala, the fair-toothed maiden,
perceiving that the beauty was equal in both cases, reached no certain conclusion through her ears nor through her eyes.
Having observed Damayantī’s mind wavering as she wondered, "Is this Śakra, or is it the lord of Niṣadha?",
the Goddess directed her toward the friend of Pavana (the Wind-god) and once more released a garland of words.
This one is a treasury of splendor and ever possesses upward motion; what wealth indeed has not been acquired by this Dhanañjaya?
Obtain abundant gold from this pure one; no one else possesses such a wealth of radiant form as he. (10)
O fair-eared one, the prosperity arising from various royal foundations— which is swallowed up by the sharpness of his arrows—
serves even for this ascetic to produce a cosmetic ointment for the body of Maheśvara.
This entire assembly of the wise, headed by you, maintains a neutrality toward him that exceeds even that of Yama and Mahendra.
Approach this radiant one, O daughter of the Sun, who is always exceedingly fierce, for it is by him that the splendor of his hand is held, O mother of the ancestors.
This cloth possesses no brilliance when on the loom of one of little intelligence; even while dwelling amidst the fire, its enemies are but blades of grass.
Yet, once it has risen here as something powerful, by what adversary can it ever be overcome? (13)

Having drunk in this common speech from both Uṣarbudha (Agni) and Naiṣadha (Nala), her mind—failing to perceive any distinction—declared "This is Nala" regarding him, while her other [mental faculty] said "This is not fire. ||14||
Then, observing her whose mental state was variegated by doubt, wonder, and fear, Sarasvatī proceeded to address the Lord of the Quarter, the son of the god who causes the lotus to bloom. (15)
Oh, he wields the rod of punishment over this world; therefore, there shall be no falling into the mire for the entire universe, which would otherwise be trembling with fear.
Is there any among the immortals who is not subject to the diseases of this king, diseases that bring about even the loss of the pride of the two physicians of heaven? (16)
To whom among people has his reputation for producing friends and pleasing them not been heard?
And such a shadow of his has never been seen anywhere as was produced by the heat of the penance performed by him alone through self-restraint and discipline.

Moreover, what power does not appear to inspire awe in anyone—the Lord, whose father is the Sun, whose splendor surpasses all royal majesty, whose form is beautiful, and who possesses a blackness that he employs against his enemies to strike them down? (18)
One attains power over the king of the departed; O charming girl, fix your mind here upon him as the lord of life, he under whose sway all beings indeed come to abide. 19.

The composition of words was common to both Śamana and Naiṣadha; yet it was this very composition that, in the mind of the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha’s land—whose suspicion had been aroused by the sight of many similar reeds—crushed what was already crushed. 20.
Thereupon, the lady, perceiving her intense hesitation regarding the cessation of both injunctions and prohibitions,
extended her hand with the index finger pointed toward her husband and began to speak what was appropriate for the occasion.

That army of his, which stands facing every direction with its various divisions, which triumphs with the roars of its aquatic creatures, and for which the vast ocean is but an object of perception beyond which there is no further shore—[that army] is victorious. (22)

At the vanguard of his army, the lord of rivers—possessing a deep roar, accompanied by crocodiles and aquatic monsters, and bearing water along with Dānavas—brings forth great joy, like a friend to the forest of blooming lotuses, as he attains the state of an ornament through his jewels. (23)
What river does not spread its current against the flow by means of flowing boats, even bearing his name?
O playful woman, how could we be the sands of that river, which are coarse and exist in such great abundance? (24)
Behold his quality, which is red and devoted to his feet; moreover, Sarasvatī herself is intent upon serving him.
O fortunate one, worship this lord of the world; for who, possessing a heart like a lotus, would not worship him? (25)
May this indistinguishable speech of his increase the creeper of doubt, which clings to many branches;
yet it is a marvel that it grew equally toward both Nala and the Lord of Waters regarding the daughter of Bhīma. (26)
Seeing that the young girl was not deceived even by those cunning gods who had disguised themselves as false Nalas,
the Goddess, pointing toward the Lord of Niṣadha who sat within the circle of the royal assembly, spoke to her.
O Great Lord of the Earth, why is it that you do not recognize this king as a worthy object of affection, whose expansion of victory has been won through extraordinary exertion?
Because of his conduct toward the enemy Dānavas, in whom he has placed his trust, whom does he not cause to think of him as Jīmūtavāhana? (28)
Since he became one whose splendor blossomed through the consecration to the sovereignty of the many deep sacrifices of the Lord of the Gods,
it was indeed fitting that I should have addressed Nala here by name in this manner, following his inclination.
Having understood his addiction to the rites of fierce sorcery and his underlying intent, as well as his devotion to the South,
you ought to offer yourself to this King of Dharma, Nala, out of the weight of your innate passion for him.
Is your mind such that it would be free from the bond of forming a marriage alliance with him according to his own inclination?
Is it right to say that he does not protect those humans wandering through the world, and that there is no true humanity in him? (31)
In this verse, she first recognized him as Hari; from the second [verse], as Agni; from the third, as equal to Yama;
and from the fourth, as having an identical nature with Varuṇa. Knowing this, she spoke again to that bewildered one. (32)
O you who claim to be a seeker of Nala, how could your self-surrender to him lead to any good, while these four—
Indra, Agni, Aryaman, and Varuṇa— are shining here in this assembly, having attained a uniform appearance?
O learned lady, this god is not determined by the world of mortals to be the Lord; why then is he not chosen by you?
Surely this is not Nala, for it would be a loss to you greater than a great fire if you abandon him; what other suitor could be better for you? (34)
Then, having weighed that speech equally upon Nala by means of Indra, Agni, Yama, the Lord of the Southern Quarter,
and Varuṇa, the daughter of Bhīma— she who was the very source of beauty— suffered an indescribable anguish, like the river Sindhu’s current when it encounters the submarine fire.
The King of Niṣadha did not bestow her upon any of the four suitors, nor upon the fifth alternative which promised her acquisition;

rather, he placed his faith in the sage who was beyond dispute, just as people place their trust in the more real non-dual reality (advaitatattva) despite the existence of conflicting doctrines. ||36||
The Kali age will bring about the humiliation of Nala, while Dvāpara previously tormented that fair-limbed lady;
for these two malevolent ages, Dvāpara and Kali, cannot endure the marriage of Damayantī and Nala in this world.
Arousing longing for each of these separately and simultaneously bewildering them all at once with his arrows,
we know that the five-arrowed god attained the fruitfulness of his name— his possession of as many shafts as there are sages— only when he was directed toward her.
This fair-browed daughter of Vidarbha, though she possessed the splendor of the King of Niṣadha, did not fall in love with Nala because of his physical beauty;
for the affection of one person for another arises only from the ripening of karma acquired in a previous birth. (39)

"Where can that bird be found? Let him be questioned, for I trust his word as much as I did Nala's before," said the lady with curly hair, whose mind was filled with longing, as she called to mind the swan from the abode of the gods regarding the prince of Niṣadha.
She gazed at each one of them again and again with great reverence, yet she perceived no distinction whatsoever among the five.
Then, as her mind—bestowing hundreds of doubts and then withdrawing them—acted like one possessed, she spoke this: (41)

There exists the cognition of two moons for people, and in that error there is the flattening of the corners of the eyes and so forth; likewise, there is the approaching of a clear surface in the conceit of a reflection. Yet, regarding the delusion of difference among these [reflected] objects, I have no cause [for such an error]. 42.
Or perhaps that playful Nala himself has spread this web of poetry over me as a jest;
for does he, who possesses the majesty of supreme knowledge, not possess that very art, just as one who knows the disposition of horses possesses the science of horsemanship? (43)
Is this one Nala? Or is he another? Is he Aila? Or perhaps Kāma? Or are these two the sons of the Aśvins?
Am I experiencing this delusion that they are Nala because they are all equal in the perfection of their physical beauty, or is it truly him? (44)
Previously, though unable to endure separation, I beheld this beloved, the sovereign of Niṣadha, here and there;
has that same state of mine returned once more, by whose play I now see false Nalas? (45)
"How can I, being so simple-minded, entertain such a suspicion? This is clearly a ruse devised by Indra and the others;
for it was by this very goddess that their verses were composed in such a way that they even touch upon the lords of the quarters. (46)
While my Lord resides within this group of five deceivers of the mind, how indeed can the mark of a human being shine forth?
Alas, do these gods of the east not bear those very marks, beginning with the state of having shaken off the dust from their bodies? (47)
Should I beg Nala, or rather the gods? Enough of them, who have been fruitless despite my constant worship;
their hearts are as formidable as deep ocean caverns, from which the waters of compassion have been drunk away by the falling arrows of Kandarpa that dry up all mercy.

Having reached the land of Nala, the sovereign of the quarters, you who possess the splendor of the Vedas and are endowed with virtues—how is it, alas, that your commitment to altruism has vanished like books falling into the blind wells of fools? 49.
Whatever has been written by the Lord upon one’s forehead shall come to pass for that person, setting aside whether it is suitable or unsuitable.
What desire could I harbor here in my heart? A lotus does not suffer scorching from the sun’s rays, nor does it experience burning from snow.
Thus, I think that because of my ill fortune in this world, even that wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), when entreated by me,
surely becomes a closed-fisted hand toward me, its fingers and sprouts withering from the fever of contraction.
"Or rather, let me place this garland of choice into the hand of the Goddess, saying: 'Whosoever here is the son of Vīrasena, let it rest upon him.
By doing so, she would be made an enemy of the gods by me; yet I would not strike down a jewel of a kinsman for the sake of a mere blade of grass. (52)
"If he among these were truly possessed of the fire of supreme passion, let him accept this garland for my sake; I shall then send it to him.
But if I cast aside my shame and do so, alas, what a mockery would that be for the world to hear! (53)
For what reason does this Nala, whose other limbs are not equal to fire, bathe my heart with nectars?
Or rather, when the number of syllables in the first and last words is equal, the splendor of alliteration shines forth in the latter. ||54||
Thus, with mental constructs arising in her mind, Damayantī, though striving to abandon them, could not reach a certain conclusion anywhere;
then, her joy assailed by distress, she reproached her own face, which was like the moon when its splendor has been eclipsed by the sun.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crowns of the lineage of sovereign poets, and Māmalladevī begot Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this ocean of aesthetic flavor, the thirteenth canto designated as the "Sweet," has thus concluded in his great poem, the *Nalacampū*, concerning the life of Nala. (56)

Canto Fourteen Then, in order to find the Lord of Niṣadha, she resorted to the propitiation of the gods; for Surabhi was created by the Creator as the wish-fulfilling cow for the gods, but she [the maiden] was created for men. (1)

Indeed, our grove of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma) are the gods themselves, yielding desired and delicious fruits through circumambulation, treading upon the ground, offering water-basins, ointments, incense, and the sprinkling of water. ||2||

Becoming filled with faith, she bowed to those gods, beginning with the utterance of their names; for among the deities, bowing down with faith is the combined prerequisite for the accomplishment of all goals.
By the power of her meditation, she directly perceived all those [deities] within her own heart;
for they, being witnesses to her, became the guarantors of her desired goal, since those who are seen grant the highest boon.
While she watched them with wonder at that assembly, she bestowed her honor upon them;
for when the fruit is attained, one is gladdened by flowers alone, even as she was by those very flowers.

Then she honored them with fresh clusters of flowers of praise, which were clear and pleasing to the heart, delightful in their softness, fragrant, born of various species, and accompanied by bees in the form of songs.
Then, having established these [objects] within the abode of the heart-lotus through her intellect, she meditated with one-pointed concentration;
for a clear visualization of the deities is indeed the precursor to the realization of the fruit. (7)
Then, by that very devotion, the four gods themselves became pleased with her;
for what need indeed could there be for blowing upon fire that is already intent on bursting forth by its own nature? (8)
Having attained grace bestowed by the gods, she remembered the creation of Sarasvatī’s eloquent speech;
for the gods grant nothing else, but when they are pleased, they bestow a virtuous intellect.
Then, as each verse capable of identifying Nala was uttered by the god against the remaining suitors, Damayantī connected that specific verse with the one who was not among them.
Those quarters of the sky, which had each adopted the status of a devoted wife toward one of the world-protectors individually,
were then known by him to have united as a single song, becoming submissive to that one Nala alone, like so many directions.

She considered that very same verse to have been joined with Nala’s own, as if by Varuṇa holding his noose, Indra holding his thunderbolt, Yama himself, or Agni; yet even so, it was still insufficient for her to distinguish Nala at that time.

Having ascertained that the king was still alive, she—her inner being overflowing with joy at the words of the queen whose meaning had been clearly discerned—spoke with a mind like a sea-monster in the ocean of anxiety. (13)

There is indeed some extraordinary artistry in her speech, for this very goddess of eloquence, having spoken in a manner that was ambiguous regarding Indra and the other gods, yet specifically singled out Nala for my sake. (14)
By my grace, she has composed these four garlands of words to clarify [the matter];
two of them are capable of identifying Nala, yet this delusion of mine—alas!—is truly great. (15)
That these words of hers flow together is indeed the play of that poetic power;
for even the guardians of the world, though distinct from one another, enter into the playful roles of kings.
Did she applaud the abandonment of the quartet beginning with Mahendra, indicated by their sequence?
Or did that eloquent speech of hers urge her toward Nala? What is this delusion of mine? (17)

At that time, she saw the earth being regarded as another's wife by the gods who refrained from touching her, while she herself was placing her feet upon the feet of her husband Nala out of devotion. 18.
Facing the mountain-king, she did not perceive the blinking of his eyes among the gods;
rather, she beheld it as if speaking by granting a sign, saying: "Come here and meet Nala."

The foolish women did not perceive that the dust of the earth had settled upon those awakened ones; however, she [Damayantī] undoubtedly perceived it upon the Nishadhan prince as he offered an embrace to the Earth, for her body was in direct contact with his.
As if wishing to extinguish the heat of separation from her own body, she beheld perspiration on Nala— just as a sprout of diamond might appear upon beautiful gold— but not upon the gods.
Seeing the garland spotless among the gods, yet becoming soiled upon the fire, she thought as if out of anxiety:
"Thinking 'Having encountered this soft girl today, will Nala now believe in me? (22)
"Let them enjoy prosperity; how much of this does Nala possess? Even so, they do not have his shadow.
As if saying this, she gazed at that prince of Niṣadha, but not upon those gods.
Through these signs, her first-born consciousness attained correspondence with Nala;
she understood that the favor of the gods had been obtained precisely through the manifestation of these marks.
Then, as she was about to place that marriage garland upon Nala, Smara (the God of Love) urged the beautiful woman forward;
yet bashfulness restrained her. Thus, she maintained a state of equilibrium, caught between the demands of both.
Out of passion, she made every effort to embrace her beloved with the garland;
yet, due to paralysis and shame, not even a slight movement occurred in her lotus-like hands.
While her heart was being made to swing in the playful motion of a swing by both shame and the god of love,
the splendor of the Lord of the Earth embraced the erotic sentiment, which remained there under the royal parasol of the deer-marked moon.
Her hand, more busily occupied with her garland and turned toward her beloved, paused once more;
and her exceedingly restless sidelong glance went halfway toward the face of her lover and then returned again.
Her dear heart was indeed inclined toward him, yet her eye did not venture to go;
at that moment, the popular saying that "shame resides clearly in the eyes" was proven true by her. (29)
Having somehow or other made the lotus-face of the Lord of Niṣadha appear with its beauty slightly visible,
she, bashful and full of meaning, cast a glance at the moon-like orb of the Goddess of Speech.
As if not knowing, she said this to her; the Queen, having understood her intention, replied:
"The state of your heart is not permitted to be perceived even by me, being hidden behind the curtain of your own bashfulness. (31)
As soon as the name "Nala" was heard by the Goddess, she was swallowed up by shame;
then, touching her fingers with her fingers, she bent them far away.
Having been held by the hand by the Goddess of Speech with a smile, she was made a traveler on the path of Indra;
thus, she bore the very name "Vāmā" (the Left-handed one), sharing it in common with ordinary women.

Then, smiling, the Goddess drew her by the hand and set out to lead her toward Mahendra; but she, as if bewildered, thought "this has been given to the body of a serpent" and, recoiling in astonishment, pulled her hand away.
Beholding Bhaimī facing toward Indra, the Fortune of Sovereignty felt envious;
then, seeing her turn away from him, that Fortune, being devoted to Indra, was overcome with shame.
Having been addressed by the Goddess, "Tell me from whom you heard 'no,' O Nala," Damayantī—
she who was the battleground for the duel between Modesty and Love— then spoke of the Prince of Niṣadha with her very eyes.
When the gods had placed Bhaimī’s hand in their own hands, she, out of passion for the celestial nymphs,
embraced them and led them along the path between the royal families of the world-guardians, making it difficult for travelers to pass.
Then, seeing her move very slowly even though she had been directed toward Nala’s direction,
he again urged her from mid-path to lead her back to those very gods.
Making her lotus-face— its stalk swaying as she turned it away— alternately visible and invisible by the humming "ali-hūṃ-hūṃ" sounds,
Damayantī pushed back that firm embrace of the Goddess, just as a newlywed bride pushes back the firm embrace of her husband.
The Queen, her corners of the mouth moistened with a smile, somehow turned her gaze toward that goddess and said to me:
"What further suspicion can you have even regarding me, whose face-disk surpasses the moon?"

Without having prostrated at their feet and without having properly obtained their permission, how can this desire of yours to choose the son of Virasena amidst the enmity with the gods be considered appropriate? (41)

When this was said, the Goddess took that woman—who had now regained her confidence—by the hand; and having caused her to bow before the gods in heaven, she said to them: "This devotee now deserves your compassion. (42)
"O Guardians of the World, this virtuous woman does not choose many, nor does she choose even one among you for fear of insulting the rest;
therefore, she seeks you all together to choose portions of yourselves for this king."
By creating the garland for the daughter of Bhīma on the road, the Creator previously brought about her svayaṃvara;
by means of an embrace, he has now brought about union with him. What remains, then, that you all strive so much to destroy? 44.
Because Nala did not falter from the path of conduct prescribed for his caste and stage of life even while with his own subjects,
the Earth— pleased by such a turn of events— seemed to desire to bestow her fame upon you through this very circumstance.

When she had heard these words, she made her bimba-like face playful with a smile; then, once they had given their consent through the gestures of her arching brows and significant glances, she led her away to Nala.

She brought the hand of that moon of the earth— sweet with its garland of *madhūka* flowers— to the vicinity of her neck, even though it was difficult for the mind-born god (Kāma) to incite, as her body was motionless with bashfulness.
Then, as if presenting a royal decree inscribed with the letters of her own acceptance,
the bride placed a garland of madhūka flowers— abundant with sprouts of dūrvā grass— around Nala’s neck.

The king wore around his neck that garland, exceedingly dark with dūrvā grass, beautiful with its appearance resembling the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra), and possessing the luster of the noose of the flower-weaponed god (Kāma). ||49||

I think that she, her face bent down with pride, looked with envy at that flower garland—which was like a row of horripilation bristling on the tips of dūrvā grass—as it gleamed intensely from Nala’s body against his own limbs. (50)
That auspicious song which they sang, with syllables seemingly emerging indistinctly due to their intense joy,
issued forth from the mouths of the city beauties as a loud ulūlu cry.
That Madhūka garland of his, resting upon her stainless heart and reflected therein, appeared like a row of arrows from the flower-bowed god—partially submerged and partially immersed. (52)

All her hairs of the body, eager from childhood to behold that supreme splendor, then experienced as it were the act of stretching their necks upon her slender frame, which was bristling with thrill. (53)
With her entire body bristling with hair-shoots and possessing lovely lips, she shone most brilliantly,
like the altar for the worship of the god of love, adorned with the beauty of ornaments and supported by the shafts of arrows.
Then all her movements vanished, as if shaken by the arrows of the God of Love;
or rather, they were carried away for a moment by Kali, who had been entreated to exert himself greatly for his own gain.
The five-arrowed god (Kāma), who caused Nala’s sweat to arise upon his hand as it touched the garland placed thereon,
produced the water for the hand-offering (*hastodaka*) of the great festival of their future wedding.
Let her softness be weighed against cotton, and let her tremble be stirred by the winds of Cupid’s arrows;
yet it was a marvel that Nala, the great mountain-king, experienced such intense trembling from them.
As if placed upon their eyes, the reflection of the garland appeared in the tears of the kings out of passion;
it seemed as though it were being grasped within the very eyes of the king who had drunk it in, for it was a fitting object to be held.
The pillar, which had been touched by Nala as a favor granted through the joy of Damayantī’s touch,
long bore the semblance of a pillar fixed for the purpose of being made a target for the God of Love.
Then, like kings renouncing sovereignty for alms, or like youth passing away into old age,
the lords of the quarters abandoned that beautiful form as it departed and resumed their own bodies.
As she cast off her illusory nature, the eyes of Indra, hidden within her previously,
manifested themselves as if out of a competitive desire to behold the beauty of the emotional state (*sāttvika-bhāva*) arising from Damayantī.

In that marriage which was contrary to the suitability of their lineages—as if he were a family enemy due to such incompatibility—he placed his chosen groom before him; yet as he approached, he beheld him as a friend through her eyes.
As if desiring to extinguish the great darkness of his own delusion caused by passion with lamps,
the friend of the wind (the fire) spread his own body, variegated with rising flames.
When Bhīma’s daughter had chosen her husband and not the fire, that light which she had quickly concealed by her own splendor became, alas, unmanifest;
for, out of shame before the people, it remained hidden from view.
At that time, Kāla assumed a body that was fierce with eyes red as lac and accompanied by his staff, spreading forth darkness;
it was as if he had approached to preside over the hearts of the kings like their own wrath.
Then Citragupta, the scribe of great merit who was his subordinate, came within the range of his vision;
one of them held an ink-pot above a leaf, while another placed the leaf over the ink.
At that moment, as if to release the mind’s bondage that had been performed, the Lord Pracetas appeared,
having assumed a watery body while holding a noose bound to his hand.

Accompanied by his wife, he approached another woman; thus that man of poor intellect disregarded the instruction on policy, wondering how one who already has a wife could seek another—yet the Lord of the Waters remained truly without a companion.
The Goddess also manifested her divine form, creating joy for the Wielder of the Discus;
perceiving her through unmistakable signs, the young woman became slackened in her wonder at his words.

In this assembly of spectators who were observing the curiosity of the transformation of forms, Indra and the other gods indeed caused an obstruction by destroying the livelihood of those skilled in the art of illusion. (70)

Then the Lord, the sovereign of the Jāmbūnada mountain range, beholding those two who had attained their difficult-to-attain desire and were delighted by the essence of mutual love, spoke with a joyful mind.
"O Vaidarbhi, this boon, difficult to obtain, has already been granted to you by the lord of the earth himself;
as for the fact that you have performed the office of messenger, this favor toward you is mine. (72)
Having taken recourse to your form, which is directly perceptible, I shall enjoy the offerings made in sacrifices;
for we have doubts regarding the sacrifice being consumed when it is not seen, given the status of the deity as being superior to the mantras.
May you and your beloved both attain union with Śiva and Śivā;
for the anxiety, "What shall I become after death? spreads torment within a living being. (74)
Formerly, there existed a city named Upavārāṇasī where you dwelt;
though you desired to rest there, you passed it by for fear of being constrained by union with the daughter of Bhīma. ||75||
Then Suparvan, his beard made of columns of smoke, said to him who knows the taste of sacrifices:
"May your prosperity flow like the milk from my cow of plenty, which consists of the sacrificial initiation. (76)
May that body of mine which is fit for burning and cooking become subject to your will;
through it, may you, as its master, become superior to that Anaṅga whose body has been consumed by her.

Let the food prepared by you—consisting of fish, juices, and other delicacies—be superior even to the essence of nectar; for we know, O King, that your character is characterized by a keen curiosity for the arts of a cook.
The god Vaivasvata himself, being pleased, spoke to that lord of the earth:
"Because of your noble deeds, this tongue of mine has long been eager to grant you a boon. (79)
May all weapons manifest from the wheels on your limbs, O conqueror of enemies;
for there is nothing further to be attained by those consecrated in the vow of heroes. (80)
Even when you have fallen into the ripening of adverse circumstances, let not your mind waver from the Dharma;
for one who does not abandon merit and is devoted to nothing else, the three aims of life remain as if residing in the very palm of his hand. (81)

With a serene mind, the wise sage addressed these words, smilingly, to the king: "Having now bestowed the daughter of Bhīma upon you, I shall grant you two boons as a token of my affection for this wedding gift."
Wherever you have a desire, let there be water quickly even in a desert;
for in this world, the waters sustain the course of life, whereas no other elements do so in such a manner. (83)
May the desert, its heat dispelled by the pure-rayed sun, attain once more the state of an ocean through even a slight arising of the thought of you, becoming as it was before the abode of camels.

May there arise from contact with your limbs upon flowers both freshness and a divine abundance of fragrance; for I have seen nothing else comparable to a flower that is so effective in producing both spiritual merit and worldly pleasure. 85.
The Goddess of Speech also, preceded by a smile, spoke impetuously to the king of the earth:
"Is there nothing at all that you would not accept from me, as I bestow this joy upon your beloved?"
Even a trifling gain that arrives unexpectedly should not be disregarded by the wise;
for I consider it a gift of affection bestowed by the venerable Ordainer, and thus worthy of great esteem. (87)

O King, that form which is designated as the Blessed One (Bhagavat)—which, though a single whole, becomes twofold through the union of both aspects within its own left and right halves—within that [form] is my mantra, consisting of the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva), together with the Moon, stainless and formless; chant this constantly, O virtuous one, and may it be successful for you. (88)
With speech moistened by the nectar of rasa pervading every limb, he is the Lord of Speech; he acts like Māra for the sake of subjugating even the fawn-eyed women of heaven.
Whatever anyone desires from him, they obtain that very thing—indeed, much more—by means of this Cintāmaṇi-mantra of his own heart, which resides within that fortunate one. (89)

If a devotee, having worshipped me with flowers and other beautiful perfumes, and while I am departing on my lovely swan as the embodiment of the mantra, recites the mantra while fixing his mind on me alone, then at the end of that year, whoever he places his hand upon the head—even if that person be anyone at all—will spontaneously compose beautiful verses; this is the wondrous sight of her power. (90)

O ornament of kings, I shall daily take refuge in the playful embrace of the Vaidarbhi style—known as the "woman" who is the abode of all virtues, overflowing with aesthetic flavor within you and in your conduct as a poet—to fashion it ever more intensely around my own neck. (91)
As I, the poet, praise your life with my voice constrained by you, may these meritorious verses arise for your intense joy and for the joy of all people;
thereby, you shall become known as "Puṇyaśloka" (the one of holy fame) to the world of mortals on earth, like Hari, the remover of the impurities of the Kali age.
The Goddess and they spoke to him, the jewel upon the head of the world: "Tell us, what desire shall we grant you?
For nothing is difficult to attain for you, a woman devoted to her husband; alas, let him who wishes to violate your vow be reduced to ashes! (93)

Seeing that you do not bear a physical body after having abandoned your illusory form, I am struck with wonder; may the power of knowledge arise in your heart as well, so that you too may attain the desired embodied form. 94.

As they thus traversed the excellent sky and took their place, a vast clamor suddenly arose from the calls of the attendants of the kings as they rose up—a sound dense with the resonance of the drums beaten by the hosts of celestial dwellers. (95)

Out of malice, the rival kings did not utter even a single faultless word against the one of virtuous fame (Nala), who had obtained excellent weapons; nor did they say anything appropriate for the commencement of battle. Instead, they filled the heart of Damayantī—which was already overflowing with love—with their own sighs.

Having been granted by the kings the status of the personified goddess of the river of the sentiment of compassion (karuṇa-rasa), she immediately requested her father to give her suitable female companions to them;

and those kings, their desire for departure having been thwarted by the failure to obtain the princess of Vidarbha, had their hearts' longing for life destroyed by these friends who, having mastered the sciences, were ever-emulating the behavior of their mistress.

Then, as Nala was established in his own abode together with Maghavat—the two being equal in the establishment of their glory—a rain of flowers fell from the sky like the embodied fame of the Lord of the Immortals, shedding tears of nectar from the bees clinging to them. (98)
As the gods abandoned this portion of the king to their own immortality, they experienced only the agony of being severed from a part of him;
even Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, looked back again and again as she departed, longing for Bhaimī, who was the very abode of her own grace.

At the joyful festival of his daughter’s wedding, King Bhīma, as well as the Queen of Vidarbha and the Lord of Niṣadha, performed auspicious rites for the cleansing away of the ill-omened words uttered by the kings;
and as the monarchs departed toward their respective camps—one by one, two by two, and in groups—the king first performed, then they created, and finally they repeated those auspicious ceremonies.
Śrī Hīra and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, whom the diamond that adorns the crowns of the kings of poets begot and who has conquered the collection of his senses;
this is the fourteenth canto of his work, whose verses are as pure as the moonlight of autumn.
Thus ends the naturally radiant canto in the beautiful Mahākāvya, the Naiṣadhīyacarita. 101.
Fifteenth Canto:
Then the lord of the Niṣadha land, honored by the garland of choice, went to his own residence.
He showered very many riches upon the bards who were preeminent in proclaiming the virtues of the daughter of Bhima. ||1||
Likewise, he bestowed such generosity upon the road that the Magadhas, by the acquisition of an excessive burden,
held the great mass of jewels in utter contempt, as if they were mere blades of grass.
The world, long eager for the gleaned harvest, has now gathered it. ||2||
If he were to be ashamed, there would be no [reason for him to appear] in the assembly because of his association with women;
how then could a person of such exceeding beauty be a vessel of happiness? Such is the case through the descriptions of poets and bards.
The worldly speech of King Karañji was silenced.
The false attribution of even a speck of fault by enemies only reveals the faultlessness of the virtuous;
for as long as a truth remains uncorrupted, there can never be a blameless effort to impose a falsehood upon it. (4)
The King of Vidarbha also,
entering his own inner apartments with his daughter, joyfully announced [the news] to the Queen, whose doubts had now vanished.
Accept Nala as your son-in-law, O eager one!
He who, with his slender radiance, makes even a blade of grass a god of love;
he who, by the glory of his lineage, has purified our family;
[he is] the bridegroom in the assembly of the lords of the three worlds.
Only those who have heard the supreme Veda are able to discern such a thing.
Let the fawn-eyed women perform the rites appropriate for the auspicious ceremony of taking the hand and consistent with the conventions of womankind;
as for us, we shall attend to the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
He spoke thus regarding the ritual injunctions and then departed. ||7||
Having emerged, she whose face was gazed upon by the king announced to the assembly of astrologers that the auspicious moment was free from blemish due to its many excellent qualities.
Then he proceeded to give away his daughter.
Then, speaking through the mouth of his messenger, he said to the King of Niṣadha:
"May my lineage and this young maiden be shown compassion;
let the sprout of our long-suppressed desire today be made into a tender leaf by the water used for washing your feet."
Having thus drunk in from the cave of the messenger’s mouth the echo of those terrifying words as they arose—
"I am going; I bow at the feet of my guru"— he [departed].
Having spoken thus and having given him many [gifts], he sent him away.
Then, having drunk in the messenger’s speech, the lord of Vidarbha awaited Nala at the end of the night,
having heard the cry of the cock.
Just as the wheel of a chariot holds the sun with devotion. ||11||
In one place, she was honored by one skilled in the art of applying ointments, who displayed a certain pride;
in another, she received respect from one clever at making cakes due to being seated upon a high throne. (12)

The faces of that city, as well as those of all its houses, shone, suffused with the joyful laughter of rays of light emerging from pearl-encrusted archways that had adopted the playful grace of travelers. 13.
Then, as they were being led along the path,
the canopies— free from the fear of the sun’s heat and casting a delusion even upon the honey-bees— were likewise carried forward.
Garlands made from cloth rags, seasonal flowers, and wild flowers [are permitted]. ||14||
The people shone as if clad in armor by their ornaments, and the houses gleamed with the luster of various paintings; in that city, everything was transformed by jeweled pavements.
His own body was comparable to the overturned earth. ||15||
Then the *ghana* drums resounded most deeply,
the *tata* lutes vibrated intensely,
and the *suṣira* wind-instruments attained a high-pitched resonance.
He was led away by the measure of his own pride. ||16||
He was not covered by fine silk, nor by bamboo flutes; he was not [pleased] by sublime songs, nor even by cymbals;
he was not [pleased] by the *huhukka* drum, nor was he [pleased] by the *ḍhakka*.
Neither she [is reached] by drums, nor are they [reached] by the large kettledrum. ||17||
The clamor from the faces of the multitude, swelling with the resonance of various musical instruments and spreading to great distances,
could not be contained within the ears of the elephants guarding the horizons.
Resonant with an echo like the swelling tide of the ocean. ||18||
Then, having set aside the jars made of gold within the interior of the altar-platform, which possessed the beautiful luster of a fourfold arrangement,
[the priest] performed the rites for the daughter of the lord of the earth according to the family tradition.
The group of matrons bathed her. ||19||
Having been conquered by the pair of her breasts as if they were female slaves, those mango branches were made to carry water;
with their faces bent down, they seemed to cast their crests downward out of the exhaustion of shame.
Having repeatedly received the sprinkling of water, she gradually became radiant with her white silk garment like the moon;
thus, she embodied the simultaneous characteristics of both the rainy season and autumn.
He firmly bound his kinship with the twilight.
In former times, she reviled the sky— which was once as beautiful as the moon’s radiance but had been turned into a gloomy day by clouds bursting with rain—
with her own thick mass of hair pouring down like a torrential downpour.
In some places, she was radiant with white silk and moonlight.
The tufts of hair on his head shone brightly for a moment as they scattered drops of falling, pure water,
appearing like the rays of light won by the conquest of the darkness-favoring fly-whisks.
Indeed, they were white, vomiting forth pearls of fame. ||23||
Made even more radiant by being wiped with a very soft cloth after bathing,
they shone intensely from being polished on a whetstone.
Like a golden ornament resembling a ray of light.
Then, that limb of hers bore the grace of an ointment emitting fragrance and shimmering with luster,
as if from the petal of a slightly opening golden ketakī flower.
If gold acquires fragrance through practice.
Her female friends, experts in all the arts, clearly demonstrated through long practice that she had been brought within the pure altar in a mere moment.
They fashioned it limb by limb and action by action. ||26||
Even without ornaments, this woman was adorned by her splendor; she was perceived by the wise as being even more beautiful.
It is not that she shines because of her ornaments, but rather that the ornaments shine because of her.
Who indeed possesses the skill of discernment to bring this about? ||27||
Having performed worship with bandhūka flowers and lotuses,
and having assumed the splendor of an offering of fragrant fruits to the Moon,
she put to shame the worship of the lips and eyes already received.
Having reached that face with realgar and yellow orpiment... [28]

The mass of hair on his head was bound by someone into a cluster of blossoms, soft as the smoke from incense, serving as the continuous thread for weaving the veil of darkness that blinds those who are infatuated with passion.
Again and again, attempting to restrain the smoke from the incense under the impression that it was a mass of hair,
her friend— her own confusion having been inferred by her smiles at last tied the chowrie to her hair.
The daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), wavy with thick ripples as if ploughed by Balarāma’s plow,
shines with the buds of *karuṇa* flowers offered there.
Her mass of curly hair laughed as it were. ||31||
Held by her upon her forehead was that golden fillet; it became like lightning from the cloud of her hair,
due to its proximity to the moon of her face which partakes of nectar.
The stability of that lifespan is certainly determined by its measure. ||32||
Upon the boundary of the forehead of the daughter of King Bhīma, the powdered curls shone clearly,
appearing as if produced from the lamp of a red arsenic painting.
The lines of smoke from the collyrium were swirling about. ||33||
The line produced by the collyrium, which shone brightly as it embraced her outer corner,
was like a second thread cast down to enlarge her two eyes for the sake of increasing the beauty of her youth.
Again and again, by the rays originating from the lineage of darkness— the sapphire-like pupils darting toward the corners of the eyes through the playful movements of the bodiless god of love—
Was her own path not adorned by those very collyriums? ||35||
The two eyes of the daughter of Vidarbha attained a peerless beauty when joined by a line of collyrium,
appearing like two lotuses made into arrows by the God of Love, which were marked by the scars of bowstrings upon his two arms.

That the Creator intended to extract the two eyes of the black antelope by driving his nail into it at the precise moment of its death was indicated by the fact that the wounds were located not far from those very eyes.
Then, their two ears, being excessively pained by her two eyes, truly placed upon them the pair of blue lotuses used as ornaments,
out of the thought that they were rivals to those very eyes. (38)
The pair of blue lotuses worn as her ear-ornaments shone upon her like two eyes fallen there,
as the God of Love looked on, rendered blind by passion.
Having clung to someone who was present and possessed of aesthetic sensitivity. ||39||

Within the interior of the *kiṃśuka* bow—the splendor of which served as the ear-ornament for the daughter of Vidarbha—Cupid, having gathered his arrows of blossomed lotus-eyes, beheld Nala as his supreme target. (40)
Did her two creeper-like ears, having conquered the two jeweled earrings, bind them to her face because they no longer practiced the discernment between truth and falsehood?
The two who were envious are described by means of the perception of two moons. ||41||

Having had her fastened with the two earrings by her friend, Damayantī was addressed: "The perfect symmetry of these two on either side of your moon-like face serves as a birthplace for the desire of your beloved."
He certainly bears this difficult burden. ||42||
The wax applied to the border of her lower lip to make the red dye glow shone right there,
as if eager to dwell in that very place.
Having shaken off the honey-like [impurities], they possess the same nature as the nectar of immortality. ||43||

Formerly, her throbbing throat-stalk indeed shone as a "lute" (vīṇā) by its sound alone, without further qualification; but now, having obtained the seven strings, it clearly shines as a "lute with a frame" (parivādinī), with its pearl-like veins. 44.
Then, as if being attended by a young lotus stalk to learn softness,
the two shone together with their auspicious union.
The arms of the fair-toothed woman [are adorned] with a bracelet and an armlet. ||45||
At that time, people observed that a fresh red dye had been applied to her two feet;
for she remained awake for a long while, embracing her lotus-like feet.
Like the fresh radiance of the sun at dawn, it shines forth after having parted from the night. ||46||
Having committed an offense against the fair-limbed maiden, the fire of the flower-arrowed god clearly consumed her immediately thereafter as she contemplated union with her beloved.
That redness on his feet is a sign of passion, not lac-dye.
When their limbs had themselves attained beauty and were adorned by one another alone,
what further purpose did those ornaments serve?
Indeed, their very act of creation was in vain. ||48||
This [city] nourished a splendor that increased progressively further and further through the contact of its ornaments,
as ever-increasing beauty stood before it.
By that [ignorance], the stream of the intellect's discernment was obstructed. ||49||
Beholding the reflection of her own face in the circle of the mirror’s gem-like center,
she placed her face close to the moon.
As it were, defining the distinction between these two. ||50||
Then the moon, defeated by her face, assumed the state of a deceptive object witnessed by the perception of two moons;
nevertheless, it was surpassed by her face, which multiplied through the two mirrors simultaneously presented by her two friends.
Was it her single face or another lotus that was reflected in the two mirrors offered by her two friends—
having been cooled during the nights by the meditations of the dew?
The attainment of residence in the same world as him was perceived. ||52||
Then, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of bows— whose flower-arrows were entwined with garlands of *palāśa* leaves and whose bowstrings were the rays of their jeweled ornaments—
that city appeared as if guarded because it was the very treasure of the Lord of Love.

Her exquisite beauty attained a state of great value through her ornaments, just as the daughter of Jahnu [the Ganges] does through special holy sites, as the natural ground for passion does through innate virtues, and as political wisdom does through brilliant fortunes.
The wives of the king, having come to the great festival of Bhīma, bowed down before Nala to avoid their own misfortune;
they thus received upon themselves the auspicious red lac from his feet.
Like vermilion upon their heads for the sake of their beloved’s long life. ||55||
Having attained kinship with the garlands of excellent syllables from the gracious gods by virtue of their unfailing nature,
she then approached, bowing down with modesty.
The guru, the guru-brahman, and the blessings of the devoted wife. ||56||
In the same way, at that time, his dependents—
who had reached the furthest limits of the arts of personal adornment— prepared for him the ornaments suitable for the moment of his marriage.
Thus was the ornamentation of the lord Nala also completed.
The king’s officials there, after deliberating again and again, had those peacocks bound, by whom that bird—
whose play was a treasure-house of plumage and who had abandoned his wings— had been made to speak of the splendor of peacocks.

The beauty of the blue lotuses was enhanced by their union with her hair, which possessed the splendor of being well-groomed, and with the bowstring of the Mind-born God (Kāma), which was endowed with the excellence of great length and joined to feathered arrows. ||59||
Adorned on his head with a crown composed of a flood of priceless jewels, the king shone resplendent;
for he was indeed a wish-fulfilling tree to beggars, as if shedding from it a cluster of beautiful blossoms.
At that time, the halo of the moon, clinging to Nala’s forehead in the guise of a jeweled hero-band,
shone as if unable to encompass his face, which had attained a beauty exceeding that of the moon.
Indeed, as the Mind-born God sought to destroy Damayantī’s mental abode of fortitude,
there appeared between her eyebrows a circular mark of variegated form.
She was gathered like a pellet near the bow. ||62||
That certain circle of sandalwood paste,
a companion to the stars, which had attained a certain splendor, was kissed by Nala’s face, which surpassed the lotus.
She was made to dwell upon the lap of the Moon.
Was that drop sent by Indra as the moon, out of a wicked hope that the daughter of Bhīma would not be wedded to Nala until the delusion regarding fire had passed? Or was she [the moon] herself?
Or rather, as if to read the script upon his forehead. ||64||
At that moment, the pair of circular earrings on Nala’s cheeks attained the state of the God of Love through their union with the reflections of his own knees.
Then, [he beheld] the beauty of the four shimmering wheels.
The pearl necklace, resting upon his neck as his head bowed in salutation to his preceptor and the Brahmins, kissed the tip of his chin;
it became like a multitude of swelling drops of nectar flowing from the moon of his face.
From whom Fortune was born, who became the powerful subduer of his foes in battles by means of his elephant,
and who fulfilled the desires of those clouds seeking water like lotuses.
That arm of his bore the nature of the ocean.
The hand of that celestial tree, which incessantly fulfilled the desires of those who sought its aid,
became as it were a second [hand] placed at its very root.
She firmly assumed the state of being a moat for her bracelet. ||68||
The circle of ornaments upon their breasts shone with the dark and crimson luster of diamonds and rubies,
appearing as if they were raining down [splendor] toward the faces of the ten directions.
Fame and majesty were acquired by him through his conquest of the earth. ||69||

Beholding the reflection of his own form in the circle of jewels belonging to the ornaments adorning all his limbs— which were densely crowded— Nala rendered useless the presentation of mirrors by those skilled in service. (70)
Not only was the splendor of her ornaments being bestowed observed by the world with joy as they moved,
but it was also beheld by eyes wide with the jewels [of their own] as they gazed.
Even by their ornaments, they seemed as if adorned by one another. ||71||
Thereupon, King Jayadratha, who had conquered the mountain-like enemies in battle, mounted the chariot driven by the son of Vṛṣṇi,
just as the son of Pṛthā had previously ascended his own.
The wearer of the diadem rejoiced at the departure of the procession.
Out of an awakening of aesthetic delight, the apsarases of the celestial realm named Vidarbha, having adorned themselves with ornaments,
came from house to house to behold that radiant one.
They then made the royal roads shine all the more brilliantly. ||73||
A certain woman, unaware and eager for a glance, even though her breast-cloth was half-blown away by the wind,
placed her bosom before him as he moved forward.
The women of the city [brought] the collection of auspicious jars. ||74||
As she was showing her friend Nala, the bracelets on her arms snapped unexpectedly from the force of her hands being raised swiftly as she leaped up.
She then fastened them with necklaces that had broken apart.
A certain woman performed the scattering of parched grain for a moment. ||75||

For that king who was desirous of departing, his youthful wives themselves became auspicious objects: their gleaming nails were mirrors, their lotus-faces were smiles, their speech was honey, and their sprout-like hands were flowers.
Desiring to eat the betel held in her hand, with her lotus-eyes fixed intently upon his gaze,
the playful woman cast the toy-lotus into her mouth as if out of anger at his double-facedness.
By some woman whose eyes were distracted by her glance,
the embrace of a paramour who had approached in the very midst of the assembly was rendered thick with obstacles through his bold advances.
At that time, the sight of him was experienced. ||78||

Desiring to see another woman who possessed a bodily splendor beyond the reach of mortal men— her gaze unwinking and her form such that she was unattainable by humans— she touched the earth with only the tips of her feet.
She did not become a mere celestial nymph by that alone. ||79||

In the past, another woman, unable to contain within her heart the intense longing expressed through the loosening of ornaments, the praise of her lover, the striking of his hands, and even the shaking of him, [was overcome].
She seems to distribute her joy among her friends. ||80||
Did their two ears become dejected as they gazed with eyes like decorative blue lotuses upon those whose hearts were captivated by the sight?
Because of that, they did not hear [the cries] of those fawn-eyed women.

Some lovely women, having fashioned [the sight] into a cupped handful reaching to their eyes, suspected out of innocence that he was covered from head to toe by the floods of the jewels of their ornaments; they wondered:
"Has he been embraced by thousands of glances that have become as if devoid of blinking?"
Through the delusion that the fruits of Vedic sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are universal sovereignty over the earth. ||82||
Your father Sudyumna was once a woman who became a king; he,
whose bodily luster surpassed even the life-breath of Urvaśī,
has now arisen as one whose splendor is fully capable of adorning the throne of Madana— the very fuel for the fire of Śiva’s wrath.
The Lord of all the gods, seeking this youth,
was abandoned for his sake by the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, who rightly discerned his excellence;
