for when he was chosen by her, even the gods, though they are "well-minded" (*sumanasaḥ*), became dejected.
It is not fitting for them to become dejected; rather, such despondency on their part is improper. //84//

Did not the soldiers of the quarters, bearing witness to the garland of choice that rolled upon his longing throat, tear open their own chests—which were already bursting of their own accord—even more so than by a weapon?
Alas! How is Indra to be propitiated today by him who has returned?
And Śacī, her lotus-like face turned aside, [was distressed] by his futile longing for the daughter of Bhīma.
Do not consider the daughter of Vidarbha to be ignorant; she is more renowned than Kīrti and more joyful than Śrī.
She has secured from Indra a blessing that he himself could not grant his own second wife, Śacī.
Tell us, who composed a poem on the life of Śacī? But as for her life, which would not be made into a vessel for the river of aesthetic flavor (rasa)? 86.
This youth, the flower-armed god who dwells upon the earth, delights the eyes with the beauty of his body— a work of art fashioned by the penance of many lifetimes spent in Vidarbha;
he is difficult to attain even for the sovereign of the abode of the gods through the weight of his prior merits.
Having experienced union with Bhīmajayā, may you today partake in the non-duality of splendors.
Did the Lord of Creatures, in bringing about the union of male and female, possess a fully matured practice for the sake of this perfection of their conjugal life?

For even through his play of bestowing mutual love upon men and women throughout the beginningless cycle of existence, the Creator of the Mind has extended this construction of intense passion between husband and wife.
He is seen by them on the path of his procession during the great festival of Jyeṣṭhī— a Supreme Person whom we consider to have been previously honored with hymns as he ascended the dais;
he is like a queen of women, with his fly-whisks of black and white falling in profusion before him.
In that month of Māgha, she joined the confluence of the Yamunā and Gaṅgā, which destroys the sins of the unrighteous.

The good fortune of this Indra over the entire circle of the earth was proclaimed here by the sequence of the meters and their themes, arising from the cultivation of a vast affection for the Vaidarbha style;
moreover, it served as a surety for the prosperity of our royal prince—the benedictory words bestowed by Śacī, who was propitiated by his choice of the Lord of the Gods. (90)
Until the gods were dismissed at the conclusion of the sacrifice, Damayantī alone— intent on complying with the purpose for which the assembly of kings had come— appropriately wiped away their shame;
for by her, she made herself the fruit of the favor bestowed by the gods upon her husband.
It was a situation where shame, anger, and talk of infamy had no place; it was something created even for the gods. ||91||
Beholding his body’s loveliness being enhanced by the splendor of the finest ornaments resting upon every limb, the beloveds of the citizens were filled with joy;
they boarded his chariot—which was as delightful as the pleasure-mountain of Indra or the moon—and followed him, whose hands were as beautiful as rubies. (92)
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this naturally radiant fifteenth canto in his composition, the *Nalīyacarita*, a great poem whose essence is the taste of intense emotion, has now come to an end. 93.
Canto Sixteen: Then that chariot-warrior, the lord of the earth, having chosen [the bride] and having taken auspicious objects, set out for the home of the King of Vidarbha,
placing the family priest Gautama— the foremost among those who know the Self— before him in two ways (as both his own preceptor and the bride's).

That Lord was clearly attended by the fawn-eyed women with chowries as white as the moon, which were being waved and reflected the brilliant rays of their ornaments— chowries that were, in truth, his own exceedingly pure virtues residing within him.
As the ruler of the Niṣadha land set forth together with his attendants, who were adorned with the most excellent garments and ornaments,
the enemy of Vṛtra (Indra) would have borne the title "Sunāsīra" (the one with a beautiful nose) by virtue of that name alone.

That bridal procession shone at night, its mass of darkness mingled with the dust raised by the army; it was as if the lamps were rendered superfluous by the jewels in the diadems of the kings who marched at Nala’s vanguard.

The King of Vidarbha, eager because the auspicious moment was drawing ever closer, dispatched messengers to the various rulers at every instant; meanwhile, the multitude of that king's army increased along the road in successive stages.

The forest became filled with the banners of the swift cavalry, which— like tigers and leopards with their golden-yellow cloths puffed out by the wind of the sky— were fluttering like waving creepers of variegated Chinese silk.

Then the lord of the earth beheld that courtyard of the palace gate, which, by means of the breeze from the flapping ears of the elephants playing near its arches, seemed to call out "Ho there! with its own garland of banners, like a messenger of Damayantī.
With her two plantain-stalks appearing like a pair of pillars with drooping leaves, she shone as if adorned with a *caṇḍātaka* garment;
she was like a dear female friend to his heart, her sound of musical instruments resonating like the joyful greeting of "Welcome! arising from the stirrings of his own state of mind.

At the gate, a meeting of the two royal armies occurred, which— restrained by the fear of both their leaders, the trainer and the master— did not result in mutual slaughter, yet produced a loud, swelling roar from their mouths.
Having pointed out his kinsmen with the words "from here," and having been honored by Dama who had come halfway,
the King of Vidarbha joyfully beheld him as he approached on foot, humble from the very gateway.
Then, rising up and joyfully extending his two arms, he welcomed his own son,
just as the lord of rivers, filled with waves surging from all sides, receives the approaching vessel of the celestial river.
Then that lord of many armies, the king of all monarchs, gave his auspicious daughter, who possessed the beauty of a virtuous woman, to this Supreme Person according to tradition,
for the sake of his own welfare, since He knows all things.
He made a conjecture regarding the honey-mixture (madhuparka) offered to him that was destined to be realized in the future:
that by intending to drink the honey, he would instead, under the pretext of the auspicious ceremony, consume the lip of the daughter of Bhīma.

The groom’s hand, eager for the destruction of others, and the bride’s hand, a thief of the luster of the lotus—were those two then bound there in the realm of Vidarbha by that virtuous king with harsh blades of *kuśa* grass? (14)
When the lotus-hand of the daughter of Vidarbha rested upon the hand of Nala,
her friends laughed at that moment, suspecting that it was the thread of her future role as a man in the act of love-making.

When Bhava indeed gave him that which had been obtained through his friendship with the Yakṣa under the name Bhīma, his father-in-law gave that very thing—exceedingly beautiful and fulfilling all desires—to Nala: a garland of wish-fulfilling gems.
In order to bestow upon her chosen suitor a great and rare object she had resolved to give, that [mirror] shone intensely while holding within itself, under the guise of a reflection,
the very thing requested and intended for the petitioner.
Bhīma gave that radiant sword, which had destroyed the demon Kāsara, to his bride;
for he had received it from Śambhu, who was immersed in union with her while she bore the name of Dhava.
The father-in-law gave him that very sword which had previously been held by the enemy of the Asuras [Indra] while he was wearing his armor;
for with its left half, it was abandoned by its master [Indra] when he cast off his skin, while with its right half, it remained capable of rending the bodies of enemies.
He whose forest-like body was thick with hair bore the vow of being a sunrise mountain for the sun of his own valor;
he possessed waterfalls in the form of the blood of slain enemies, which washed his blade to a keen edge and served as the twilight hues gathered upon him.
As if his own tongue had been sent forth by Yama, who was intensely desirous of begging for that daughter of his own,
he gave her to him— even the small sword (asiputrikā) adorned with its scabbard and worthy of being grasped by the hand.
When the two [arms] became the limbs of their own wives' breasts, serving as the decorative leaf-designs upon them and the collyrium for their eyes,
they were as if consecrated by the vows of sleeping on the bare ground of the battlefield.

The king bestowed upon Nala that very chariot— which, by one who feigned friendship, had already been promised long ago to his son’s suitor— that vehicle capable of crossing mountains, oceans, and difficult paths with ease.

Since even this great chariot, though its lineage is revealed by Nala and Kūbara, possesses the quality of being "born of a noble breed" (*prasūtavattā*), its excellence as a *puṣpaka* is therefore inferred from the analogy with Kubera’s [chariot]. (24)
Having deceived Mahendra by means of Uccaiḥśravas, Varuṇa previously presented that jewel of a horse to his own lord; now, he offers it to him to establish a bond of kinship with his kinsman.
He who did not grant joy to his pair of eyes by making their range of vision distant through his swift movement,
instead bestowed upon them the state of servitude born of longing and reverence, such that they themselves became like the withered stalks of their own throats.
That [king] caused Nala to accept a single, exceedingly lofty spittoon made of rubies, which Viśvakarman had respectfully presented to him out of respect for the Lord of Heaven (Indra).
For a long time, it was not discerned whether the face was filled with betel-nut fragments discarded after being flavored by Nala’s mouth,
or [the color] arising from his own circle of rays, which was exceedingly beautiful and intensely red.

O King, that worship which was performed by Maya while honoring the Lord Bhima under the name of the Master, Bhima himself bestowed it upon the prince of Niṣadha: a great vessel for food made of emerald.
The poison of serpents does not spread among peacocks, who always maintain their luster;
had the Lord not consumed the Kālakūṭa, he would not have attained his state as the "Blue-throated" one.
Did Indra’s elephant fall from heaven after offending Durvāsas while casting off his garland?
For it was that very elephant which he always gave to him under the pretext of rutting—a cloud-like beast that rains down [water] by its very nature as a sky-elephant.
"Either out of pride before me, or else out of fear, go far beyond the ends of the earth and live!
Thus did he address the elephants of the quarters with his own ears—without even a garland of syllables—as they came and went.
He truly bore his own fame as seed within his two tusks, while the showers of ichor from those tusks served to scatter the ill-fame of his enemies;
he, who for the sake of joy, attended upon the beauty of her head—her breasts like jars, adorned with the sweat of rut—as if she were the Goddess Śrī herself, weary from her ears.
No one, despite their efforts, was able to reach the end of the counting when the draft animals had been given as wedding gifts;
neither among the golden vessels, nor among the rutting elephants, nor among the heaps of jewels.
The Fire-god (Āśuśukṣaṇi), who had previously adopted an adverse attitude toward those two during the seizing of the hand, was propitiated by the daughter of Bhīma and circumambulated from the right;
thereafter, being placed at the forefront by Nala, he immediately became favorable to them by circumambulating them from the right.
Having offered the benediction, "May you be as firm as a stone," his mantra-utterance was immediately overcome by shame;
for while even a stone might move through human exertion, she could not be moved from her steadfastness even by Indra himself.
Then the family priest tied the garments of the daughter of Vidarbha with a knot of her beloved’s cloth;
he, the knower of all things, spoke as if to instill distrust in Nala, who was about to depart after tearing the fabric.
Pointing with her face turned upward toward Dhruva, the daughter of Vidarbha said to her husband:
"How could he not possess the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) witnessed by his own eyes? Nevertheless, the greatness proclaimed in the scriptures is likewise true. (38)

The husband showed his bride [the Earth] Arundhatī, saying: "Behold this virtuous woman who has, as it were, attained minuteness because she was previously placed in the heart of the king, while the Lord of Heaven was treated like a blade of grass by people."
On the road, the flowers placed upon her sprout-like hands, shimmering like stars as they traveled through the sky,
attained the splendor of parched grain (lāja) scattered by her— grain which possesses the brilliance of the rows of teeth in the mouths of the gods and the fire.
The trail of smoke from the oblations offered by her reached her cheek, taking on the beauty of musk;
it became collyrium for her eyes, served as tamāla-paste upon her ears, and acted as curls upon her forehead.
The weight of perspiration on the hands of those two, who were devoted to giving, was repeatedly wiped away by the waters of their charity;
likewise, the tears of emotion flowing from their eyes were suppressed by the thick smoke rising from the sacrificial fires. (42)

As Bhīma bestowed many riches as sacrificial gifts, the people’s hair stood on end at that moment; observing his courage, the beauty of the thorny buds upon their bodies attained a state of mingling with one another.
In those two, there was no haste for the succession of ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas that could overcome their steadfastness;
nor did the fire, though kindled with fuel and standing before them, rob them of their state of unwavering composure.
As he took the hand of Damayantī’s sister, the priest thoroughly performed the ritual for him,
just as the great seer Aṅgiras did for Indra when he married Śacī, the daughter of Puloman.
Then he went to the hall of curiosities along with the women, who had pierced it with a thousand holes in order to see;
for that hall, indeed, bore the likeness of the armor of the Thousand-eyed Indra, as it was presided over by that very Jiṣṇu.

Thus, for three days, they ate without remainder out of modesty, did not gaze directly at one another’s actions, and slept with longing yet free from carnal enjoyment, according to the prescribed rule for the bridegroom and the bride. (47)

In some places, the sprout of the Bhoja dynasty caused his subjects to engage in playful jesting with the common folk through his side-long glances; in other places, he fed those who had arrived for the bridegroom's procession with the celestial nymphs of the earth.
He said to someone: "Let them prepare here a suitable offering of sauce for the delight of his limbs;
let some women also offer, according to their desire, boiled rice to you who are thirsty from every direction."
Having requested permission, saying, "May he sit here facing you," the wicked man laughed once consent was granted;
for it is clear that the part of the body considered most excellent is indeed that by which one sits. (50)
"These two are my most beloved women," she said; thus addressed, one of them placed her own cluster of flowers around his neck.
"You who speak thus shall not shine, you whose neck is like that of a donkey! saying this, she then drew it away from the bridegroom.
While fanning Nala with a yak-tail whisk,

Damayantī’s maidservant was laughed at by the people for dropping her garment out of fear of a lizard that had been stealthily placed at her feet— a lizard whose speed surpassed even her own long legs.
The wicked woman offered a seat with its tail-end pointing forward; the upright, excellent Brahmin sat upon it.
She then pulled it up, saying, "Tell me your own intention," and afterwards she gave him one with the tail-end turned behind her.

While the fair-browed bride was having her feet steadied between [the groom's] hands by means of stories told by herself, the other man secretly placed his own pair of feet behind her; indeed, he saw the surface of the mirror and laughed.
Then, those women with beautiful eyes raised in amorous gestures, who had banished all steadfastness with their charms—
the very handiwork of the God of Love— repeatedly caused the world to laugh as they watched the transformations of the assembly of suitors.
When the young girl, whose lotus-face was turned away by a wall, smiled in response to the smile of the youth,
she indeed buried that smile within his heart and thereby achieved the skill of hitting a target from behind one's back.
That which the young woman did by casting aside her other appropriate tasks and restraining her eyes out of a desire to see—that alone indeed told the entire story to the lover within her heart. (57)
As she bent low while offering water, a reckless man kissed her face;
with his hand moving slowly as the water fell at his feet, he waited for the moment to deceive her other eye.

Beholding the youth, a friend of clever disposition fashioned a bracelet for him from the lotus-stalks of her own hands; though it was loose upon her arm—the very repository of all arts—it, lo, assumed a state of firm binding toward him. 59.

Under the guise of the reflection of her clear nails upon the feet of the lady with arched brows as she gave her milk, a certain man— possessing visible trembling and horripilation— entered that sanctuary, having been deeply wounded by the arrows of Love.
Whether the fair-browed maiden smiled with her face turned aside, or sat with her face bowed down in bashfulness,
or spoke in soft, faltering tones— the youth grasped that very thing as a pledge for his attainment of her.
Seeing her fanning herself, the youth, overcome by passion, perspired profusely;
then, having conquered his shame with a throat uplifted and feigning heat, he gazed upon her face.
Agitated by the breeze from the fan-like petals of his creeper-like arms, which moved as they touched her breasts,
the youth experienced the same agitation as a bird born in a nest bound by a net of various fires.

There was some indescribable flash of a sidelong glance, and likewise some particular artistry of speech, such that not even the slightest effort remained for the messenger in his mutual persuasion of the two youths. (64)
No one, overcome with joy, was able to drink even a mouthful of water brought to his lips;
instead, he kissed the reflection of the face of that woman whose eyebrows were like the bow of the God of Love, as it shimmered before him.
When a vessel of emerald was presented as a food dish, the members of the wedding procession reportedly fell into a rage;
they were informed that the dish was not filled with vegetables, but rather that this very object was "green" (harita). (66)

Dhruva, disciplined, speaking with a smile, and not looking at her face, asked something while standing before the young woman who was positioned on the crystal floor, his gaze fixed upon the ground between her two feet. (67)

With tears shimmering, these people ate their rice with relish— rice that was unbroken in every grain, separated from one another yet not devoid of tenderness, superior in flavor, white, and not too thick, all out of a sense of aesthetic delight.
While the handsome youth was kissing her slightly swelling breasts, which were blooming under the influence of youth, from the side with his gaze,
the girl of heavy breasts, feeling deeply ashamed, herself took back the garment that had slipped from her chest.
Since the very first cause of its origin was fragrant, the clarified butter produced from it was certainly fragrant;
therefore, when the young women distributed the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to them, it formed a sandy bank on the shore of a small river-like stream.
Even though the earth has been drunk by the inhabitants of the underworld, it is nevertheless inferred from this that [the nectar] is sweet;
for even those whose food is nectar feel a longing for it, despite its scent being scorched by the sacrificial fires.
"Did she not perceive my modest gestures, or did she disregard them?"— with such thoughts,
the young man’s mind was cut down by the arrow of the girl's glance as she turned back and looked with longing.

There, no one ate the mustard-ridden food; some made hissing sounds with their mouths while eating curd, shaking their heads as their palates were suddenly itchy from the intensity of its pungent flavor.

Like a fragment of the moon severed from its orb, its rays now becoming harsh to burn those separated from their lovers; first white and soft, it then bestows heat—just as a wicked person, having first been a friend, subsequently becomes an adversary.
Two young men, concealing their true feelings from the ground beneath them, performed a previously practiced dance-step;
by chance, they repeatedly cast three-quarters of their gaze toward each other’s faces. (75)
Having tasted with relish that soft sauce prepared from deer meat, their minds were most deeply pierced by the thought:
"Was this not perhaps eaten with the flesh of the deer from Śiva’s lap, along with the waters of nectar?"
Even for a moment to worship the bodiless god of love, whose messengers are their mutual inner intentions,
a decision was reached among the people regarding the two youths by means of a mere blink of an eye, which seemed so long-lived.

When a lover asked his beloved whether it was day or night by placing his hand— alternately warm and cold— upon her breast, the clever woman, out of modesty, refused his request and placed her finger upon her lower lip, which was as sweet as the twilight.

Gradually touching the hot rice and then the cold sugar while being watched by her clever lover, the clever woman, as if astonished by the thought of her own impropriety, placed her finger upon her reddened lip. (79)
Asking her by going back and forth, "How much rice are you discarding?
How much are you bringing?"—"Shall I come? Shall you come?"—she, it is said, lowered her face in shame. (80)
Just as those who had gone to the meatless [forest] fell into the delusion that there was meat, and those in the meatless [place] conceived the delusion that there was meat,
so too were these clever men made to laugh and fed various foods prepared through culinary artifice.
Under the pretext of making a piece of tender meat with its bone resemble a lower lip with his fingernail, the young man bit it with his teeth;
then, looking at the lips of the serving girl while laughing, he praised its flavor.

Having cut and crushed [the food] with many condiments, and having prepared it in such a manner, these people consumed the highly seasoned meal, marveling at the untimely nature of the dish they had made. (83)

Having been awakened by the words "I am thirsty" after gazing at her face, the young woman, though already satiated with water, intended to refill the water-dripper; however, she suddenly desisted from laughter upon seeing her friends. (84)

A youth, wishing to take some ghee contained in a vessel, saw there the reflection of a deer-eyed woman; he placed his hand upon her waist-knot [in the reflection], and it became covered with a profusion of clearly visible bristling hairs.
Under the pretext of eating, a certain man kissed the reflection held in the oil produced from the syrup;
having repeatedly touched it with the tips of his fingers, he then smeared his own face with the oil thus acquired. (86)

The soft, delicious, and fragrant sauce prepared from the flesh of fish, deer, goats, and birds, which the people were unable even to eat, let alone finish; it was impossible even to calculate its quantity. (87)
He whom she had previously surpassed with flattering words and gestures that were slightly frowning,
was now pitied by her as she smiled brightly and playfully tucked her fingers into her mouth while eating.
There, water resembling frost was prepared from the finest aguru wood and incensed by the wind; as it was repeatedly poured from golden ewers, those present described it thus:

89. "It has been made like frost, and it has been perfumed by the wind with the essence of aguru wood; having drunk of it as it rested in the golden ewers, they described the water there at every turn in this manner."
O Creator, that which was made by you as nectar and that water which was made as life itself were well done;
yet this [ocean] was begun in vain, for one who drinks from all sides like you ought to drink it.

While her husband stood there with his hand in the gesture of a lotus bud, repeatedly begging even though he was cruel, the two women did not give him the rice, for they argued with one another, "Friend, you give it! "No, you give it! (91)

"Is her breast so very beautiful?"—as he looked thus at the heart of the water-bearer, which was covered [by her garment], her two hands holding the pitcher surely gave this pleasing reply: "Certainly. (92)
In that house, they ate until their throats were full:
sugar crushed by showers of snow, and curds produced from the milk of young female horses, like mud dredged from a pool of nectar. (93)
The Creator, who fashions the interior of the hollow space with drops of water, was clearly plundered here and there by the Deceiver, who, observing it, assumed a tongue as restless as thirst. (94)
"You give me that which is not the object of my desire, nor is there passion for that which is not white—what is the use of that sugar?
To her who spoke thus, the fruit of the *bimba* was given under the pretext of being sugar; and she took pleasure in that very *bimba*-fruit of her lower lip.
Between those two friends whose gestures were identical, the one who perceived the inner state abandoned the friend who offered a reciprocal gesture;
she did not act with hidden intent nor was she restrained by that clever woman, for it was by her alone that the perceiver of emotions was gratified.
Observing the gestures of the youth, she said to her friend: "In due course, he will no longer tolerate your desire to give;
you are offering him a contrary sign—why do you not grant this to him who is so intensely a seeker?"

The interior of the leaf-plates, made circular by the act of eating as if by a concluding script, shone with milk-cakes that were adorned with the beauty of red chalk produced by the cooking process for those who were eating. (98)
The libertine, standing before the lady Urvaśī who was reflected in the mirror,
kissed her again and again under the pretext of drinking the beverage, even though she was situated far away.
A shower of hailstone balls rained down from these thickly surrounding attendants,
who bore rainbow-like flashes from the luster of the gems in their moving armlets and who possessed a fragrance like that of the moon.

To those who said again and again, "How much more of this condiment is being served to me? in their desire for satisfaction, she brought forth a great abundance of it as if by trickery, like a writing-stylus used to count them.

The lover composed a commentary on his own heart regarding its skill in concealing the gestures of the clever girl; he did so by means of hundreds of hints that touched upon her suitability for such a task. 102.

Placing two sweetmeat balls upon his chest—where the reflection of a young woman shimmered before him in a food-vessel drenched in ghee—the youth then scratched them with his nails and crushed them mercilessly. (103)
When her lover gazed at her with a smile and her female companions turned away in bashfulness, a friend brought a sugar doll from somewhere and, laughing, placed it in his hand.

Having gazed upon the lovely waitresses, these men must certainly have failed to eat even enough to achieve satisfaction; for, being unable to consume more due to having already eaten so much, they left behind heaps of piled-up side dishes.

Though he was tormented by that young woman who remained indifferent despite her intentions being signaled through various gestures, he became hopeless; then, reflecting upon another supreme woman, he was satisfied by her, even though she was full of wrath toward him.
With milk as her smile, pancakes as her decorative garment, the moon-like face of a banyan leaf, and large sweetmeat balls for breasts,
the act of eating became the beloved mistress of those enjoying the meal, captivating them with her radiant grains of rice.
For a long time he had been petitioned with hundreds of youthful entreaties, and for a long time he had been rebuffed by her angry gestures;
yet, as she performed the playful act of washing her hands, he was sprinkled by her with a slight spray of water from her slightly shaken palm.

The seventh flavor, consisting of boundless erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), arising from the playful charms of young women, brought great satisfaction to the lecherous folk during their meal—not in the way that the other six flavors did. (109)
Having placed a betel nut in her mouth, Parṇālī was abandoned by Nala’s followers when they saw a scorpion;
their faces clouded with fear and everyone laughing at their own delusion, they realized it was merely the fragrance from Damayantī’s mouth that had been infused within.

Saying, "Choose for yourself one of these two— between this collection of jewels that is both true and false, and this one which is beautiful yet utterly charming," he laughed and presented the pair to the one who wished to take the remainder.
Thus, for those who ate pure and refined food twice a day, several days passed in joy;
they attained satisfaction through the attentions of courtesans sixteen years of age during the night. (112)
Having married that slender-limbed maiden, Nala dwelt in the houses of the Vaidarbha for five or six nights;
then he set out for the Niṣadhas with her, in a chariot whose reins were held by the son of Vṛṣṇi.

Saying, "It is not appropriate for another to touch her; she is a child, yet she is tall," he himself mounted Bhaimī onto the chariot; it is said that he did not embrace her while being watched by the people.
Thus the quick-witted Smara made both him and the bride rough with a profusion of horripilation; [he thought:
"This beloved, though her body is smooth and exceedingly tender, will slip from my pair of arms which, though soft, fear to cause her pain. (115)

Likewise, did not his parents grieve more upon sending away their daughter—who had been raised on their own lap since birth—than they did upon dismissing that husband of their daughter, whose virtues were multiplied a hundred thousandfold by his humility? (116)

Having followed Nala as far as the boundary of his own territory, the King of Varāṭa, upon returning, assumed the role of a servant; like a wave on a lake turning back from the wind at the shore, he withdrew with his head bowed low.
"Merit is the father of the self; forbearance is wealth that wards off calamity; and contentment of mind is everything—Nala is all this.
Beyond this, my daughter, there is no one else for you but me," saying this, he shed tears as he released his own daughter.
Because he acted solely for her pleasure, the beloved husband eventually healed her mental anguish as she remembered her father;
yet, the submarine fire of separation from her mother continued to burn within her, even amidst that great ocean of her husband’s love.

That mountain, adorned with many minerals, bore an indescribable beauty by means of that earth—whose eyes were like those of a doe—which served at its feet, as if it were its own foothill (upatyakā). 120.
To protect the king’s single-minded devotion— which she had long cherished as if it were her own internal state—
the Goddess of Fortune abandoned her status as a co-wife and gratified the daughter of Bhīma by fulfilling all his desires.

Then the King of Niṣadha beheld the city, its archways adorned with garlands of emeralds, appearing as if its tresses were hanging down due to the pain of separation from him; moreover, he saw it as if it were his beloved, for its lofty houses stood with their necks craned upward as if to gaze at him.
The sidelong glance, cast secretly by Damayantī toward her beloved while her mind was slightly distracted by the sight of the city,
met suddenly on the midway path with her own returning gaze.
Then, on the road, that charming prince met with the jewel-like ministers who had been stationed in the city;
he was like the spring season accompanied by the beauty of flowers, joined by bees that had approached in succession and were eager with curiosity.
While they were restless with curiosity to hear his own life-story, he told them something of it;
and while leading their own country's history into the path of their ears, he entered the city. (125)

Then, along every path, young maidens approached the lord of the earth, honoring him with cries of "Victory! and offering parched grain from their own creeper-like arms—a cluster of buds as delicate as lotus stalks emerging from the nectar-water of the people's hearts.
Through their connection with the moon-like faces of the city women who were intent on beholding the mass of splendor of the newly arrived Damayantī,
the moon-chambers atop the rows of palaces throughout the entire city momentarily experienced a literal correspondence with their own names. (127)

The blue-lotus eyes of all the city women—dusty with the pollen of their insatiable thirst—drank in the nectar of the moon-like face of the King of Niṣadha, which was brought to them through the stalks of the rays of light entering through the openings of the palace windows. 128.

Receiving the showers of flowers rained down from above by the celestial beings— flowers which bore the guise of fragrant parched grain (lāja) fallen from the sprout-like hands of the women stationed on the palace turrets along the king’s path— he entered the grounds of the newly constructed palace for Damayantī.

Thus, having observed with curiosity from the heavens the wedding of these two, their journey together in a single vehicle, and their glances meeting with apprehension as they looked at one another from the window, the lords of the gods— [Please provide the remainder of the verse for a complete translation.]
Dense with bliss, they seemed to resolve to go to the celestial realm. ||130||
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the circle of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the collection of his senses;
in this *Naiṣadhīyacarita*, a great poem composed on his behalf by Kashmiris who have mastered the fourteen branches of knowledge, the sixteenth canto has come to an end. (131)
Seventeenth Chapter:
Then, having undertaken the largely futile labor of running across the earth, the gods, with their playful movements as restless as the waves of the Sarasvatī, departed as they had come.

They did not grieve after bestowing Bhaimī upon that lord of the earth, even though she had long been held in their hearts, just as one does not regret imparting sacred knowledge to a disciplined student.
The radiant gods occupied their beautiful celestial mansions,
like the reflections of the sun upon the slopes of Mount Sphaṭika.
By the wind generated from his speed, which forcibly drew the clouds along,
his own swiftness was proclaimed as if by the chariots of those [gods].
At that time, among those who were most distant, the power of atomization (aṇimā) appeared clearly, as if it were being fully manifested through his eightfold sovereignty.
In one place, a streak of lightning from a cloud, marked by the scraping of the tips of its banner, spread a yellow hue upon their chariot like a yellow flag.
As the rows of clouds repeatedly met upon the path,
the bow— serving as an ornament for the chariot of the Lord of Heaven— became their adornment.
I believe that at that moment, the masses of clouds in the water acquired their lordship over thunderbolts through the reflections of the thunderbolt-wielder’s own weapons.
The staff of the wielder of the rod (Yama), kissing the fierce-rayed sun in one place, clearly became the royal umbrella for the kings of Sāvarṇi’s lineage. 9.
To her, who was struck with wonder at the love between Nala and Damayantī,
the noose of Varuṇa bestowed the beauty of ear-ornaments as they slipped from her head due to her shaking.
Mounting a mass of wind, with his tail-feathers dancing like hands,
the peacock created the illusion among the sky-dwellers that "Bhaimī has been obtained by him."
On the road, Sarasvatī consoled Bhīma’s ears, which were pained by the absence of Damayantī’s words,
with the sounds of her lute that served as a poor substitute for them.
Then they beheld a mass of people approaching with dark luster,
appearing like the sky itself personified as it came to meet them out of affection.
The gods beheld Smara emerging at their head,
as if preceded by Kali himself for the purpose of instructing the senses in their lack of discipline.

Those who regard their lives as mere straw for the sake of forbidden women, who cast fear and shame behind them, and whose entire possessions have been consumed by procuresses—such people are his attendants. (15)
He who, as if in rivalry with the Buddha, assumes the state of a world-conqueror;
he whose agency here, though bodiless, is as if equal to that of Īśvara. (16)
He who, as if remembering his enmity toward the Lord—who had deprived him of his wife while creating this entire world in such a way as to confound her—now agitates this very creation. (17)
Smara brought about an aversion to food in the eyes of Śakra and the other gods— which possessed the luster of yellow and red—
that was incurable even by the two physicians of the deities.
The gods perceived that wrath which was casting [everything] away, trembling, rising up, and reddened, resounding with the cries and shouts of abuse.
Whom they worshiped with eyes that were pupils of disciples bitten by their teeth and lips, and with hisses of breaths resembling the hissing of serpents in the form of their knitted brows. (20)
Relying upon that fortress which is difficult even for the arrow of Kama to scale,
he seeks to consume the worlds, including Indra himself, with the fire of Durvasas’s heart.
He who produces intense detachment even while generating passion, and who generates the darkness that veils all the senses even while burning with light; (22)
When Bhava was unable to conquer the five-arrowed one (Kāma) and became enraged,
he achieved victory by resorting to the policy of striking at the enemy when he is occupied with conquering another.
Spreading out his hands in supplication, speaking with trepidation from the middle of the road,
and betraying his inner intent through his faltering tone, Greed was observed by them there.
His dependents were constantly characterized by wretchedness and thievery, afflicted by the disease of overeating, and watched with suspicion by those who ate with him. (25)
Alas, he who acts as a drought to the rain of the water of wealth-giving for the worthy recipient in his hand, sells his own destitute dependents to the wealthy like slaves! (26)
The two causes for committing one or two of the five great sins are anger and desire; he who commits all five does not consider them even as much as a blade of grass.
He who, though the abode of all the senses, relies excessively upon the tongue—let him seek instruction from that very tongue in order to acquire proficiency in eating. (28)
Alas, they beheld him embracing the void, failing to grasp what was beneficial and true, blind to the awakening of his kinsmen, and refusing to abandon his delusion.
Even when their lives depart day after day, the foolish who worship Him do not remember the Enemy of Smara, for they are submerged in the mire of family life.
It clearly causes the inner radiance of men—who possess the lamp of knowledge that has not yet attained nirvāṇa—to wither, just as soot does to a bright flame. (31)
Just as the three—the student, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic—depend upon the householder, so too do anger, greed, and lust depend upon him. ||32||
That which is sleep even for the waking, that which is blindness even for those who see, that which is dullness even when there is learning, and that which is darkness even in the light; (33)
The Kuru army did not feel shame before Arjuna, who was like Śiva;
for by him, as he conquered the world while abiding in the quality of darkness (tamas), desire was destroyed.
A few among these have been marked by the gods due to their former acquaintance; others, however, from the crown of their heads down, are darkened by the cloak of sin. (35)
There, as the army approached like a surging ocean,
they heard the ear-piercing words of someone.

The truth of the Vedic revelation that the fruit of sacrifice is like the surfacing of a stone—what faith can there be in that, O elders of intellect, since the path of desire has been rendered desolate? (37)
By some Bodhisattva, born with the motive of a sentient being, this world was declared unstable for the sake of piercing the vital points of the world. (38)

The Agnihotra sacrifice, the system of the three Vedas, the triple staff, and the smearing of ashes—these are the livelihoods for those destitute of wisdom and manliness, which they prattle on as their way of life. (39)

If purity consists in the purity of both lineages, and since each of those lineages must likewise be pure through their respective ancestors, then what caste could exist that is not tainted by the defects of infinite lineages? (40)
Who has not had sin transferred to them through contact with groups of lustful women?
Alas, the world, its vows emaciated by passion, neither eats nor bathes out of delusion. 41.
Fie on those hypocrites who, out of envy, protect women while failing to protect men, even though there is no difference in their blindness to passion! 42.

This very abstention from the wives of others was personally disregarded by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), who was infatuated with dalliance with Ahalyā; it was thus that Indra became a hypocrite.
O twice-born ones, abandon the conception of sin regarding the violation of the preceptor’s bed,
for you possess an exceedingly lofty zeal for seizing the wives of elders on behalf of your master.

"From sin come suffering and from merit come joys for one who has departed this life"—such is the Vedic revelation; yet the opposite is seen immediately. Thus, the relative strength and weakness of these two have been directly declared.
If even when there is doubt regarding the attainment of another body one must avoid evil,
then O Vedic scholars, abandon the sacrificial session (sattra) because of the suspicion that it is defiled by violence.
Even that Vyāsa, who is worthy of worship by those who know the three Vedas, spoke to you: "For Rāmā, who has conceived a longing for him, the grasping of the hand is prescribed. (47)
How can you have faith in well-performed deeds, and why do you not have it in sexual pleasure? A person should perform that action by which happiness increases in the end. (48)
"Commit sins by force; let them be as if uncommitted for you.
Manu declared that all faults committed under compulsion are as if not done. 49.
O heretics full of doubt, do not remain even regarding the meaning of your own scriptures;
practice whatever bliss you desire according to your own will. (50)
Where can there be unanimity among the great-minded regarding their understanding of the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti?
Exegesis depends upon the power of the intellect; therefore, one should not disregard it when it tends toward clarity.
If the notion "I am" resides in the body, then what sin would there be for its burning?
Or how could that [sin] not have some fruit elsewhere, given that the Self is witnessed by another? (52)
"The dead man remembers his births; when he is dead, there are waves of the fruits of karma;
the dead man is satisfied by what has been eaten by others"—enough with such talk of rogues! (53)
Alas, by the most deceitful Śruti, one is made to abandon the body with the thought "I am the person" and to grasp another as "this is not you."
When two things are equally doubtful, they say that the cause for the occurrence of the desired one is one's own mantras and the like; otherwise, they are merely lechers. (55)
O timid one, what burden would your own sin be to the Self taught by the Vedas, who alone sinks into infinite suffering through the sins of the entire world? (56)
What is the use of that flower plucked from its stalk? For it bears fruit only for him to whom it is offered;
if it is to be placed upon the head of another, then it should indeed be placed upon a stone.
Shake off these contemptuous words like blades of grass after your wife;
for one such as you, what lasting deception can there be toward people? (58)

"Carry out the command of Kāmadeva, which even Brahmā and the other gods do not transgress; for even the Veda is the command of the God—among these commands, which one is more worthy of being honored? (59)
If you consider even the portion of the Veda that is mere prattle, then by what misfortune do you not likewise desire the injunctions [of the Veda] as a means to end suffering? (60)

Though you possess intellect made robust by Mīmāṃsā, you yourselves believe in the Śruti while being distracted, and you yourself declare it to be interpolated— even that Śruti which [you claim] conceals the sacrificial post like a tiger.
For what Vedic revelation says, "Does this world exist?"—how can people believe in that world on the authority of such a [doubtful] scripture? (62)
Manu’s discourse on dharma and adharma—which are impossible to acquire or avoid—was accepted in vain by the wise as a pretext for seeking the power to punish the circle of kings. (63)
"By the word of Vyāsa alone you have faith in him; truly, you are experts in the Tantras!
Who would speak even to fish about those who are to be instructed by a Fish? (64)
That wise Vyāsa, the poet skilled in flattery among the Pāṇḍavas—did he not censure them when they censured, and praise them when they praised? (65)
It is said that Vyāsa did not indeed unite with his brother’s wife out of lust;
for if he had been devoted to a slave-girl, why would he have been instructed by his mother even in that matter?

For those who have made the books composed by gods and twice-born sages their path for veneration, has it not been made manifest that they, by bowing to the earth, have thereby actually humbled themselves? (67)
She was praised as a virtuous lover by those of tranquil minds intent on sacrifice,
who desired even after death to attain a heaven whose essence is the fawn-eyed woman.
O wise ones, what peace can there be? Why exert yourselves in the pursuit of pleasure and displeasure?
For once a being has been reduced to ashes, how can there be any return? (69)
The Sage’s mind holds that both natures may become attached in the realm of desire;
likewise, even Pāṇini, when stating that there is a third [nature] in liberation, expresses the same.
People who have never before experienced birth now carry him upon them for his journey;
he presents the appearance of a wild ram moving backward as he advances to engage in combat.
What kind of intimidation is this, saying "one will become an animal because of this sin"?
For even a water-snake is happy with its own causes of happiness, just like a king. (72)
If the Daityas, slain by the enemy of the Daityas in battle, sport in heaven, then let them fight with him there as well; even though they are slain, they remain exactly the same.

"In saṃsāra there is both the self and Brahman, but in liberation there is Brahman alone"—such is the cleverness of the proponents of the Vedas in asserting a liberation consisting in the annihilation of one's own self. (74)

He who declared the scriptures for the sake of liberation and for the attainment of a state like that of a stone by those possessed of consciousness—that Gotama is exactly as you know him to be, simply by observing him. (75)
The wives of Hari, Hara, and the other gods have their minds entirely absorbed in him; why then are they not liberated? For what reason does the Mind-born one remain in prison? (76)
If there exists a God who is omniscient and whose speech is never devoid of compassion, why does he not fulfill the needs of us seekers merely by the expenditure of words? (77)
If the Lord were to contemplate the suffering of living beings as being produced by their own karma, he would be our causeless enemy; otherwise, there would be other causes for it. (78)

Because reasoning is unstable and because [opposing views] cancel each other out due to their equality, there would not be a lack of validity for any of these doctrines, just as in the case of two valid counter-arguments (*satpratipakṣa*). //79//
Those whose wealth is austerity, yet who are prone to anger, teach others non-anger;
those who are themselves destitute teach the art of alchemy for the sake of wealth. (80)
What wealth has been given that this beloved of Hari is pleased with one who gives nothing?
By giving away all his riches, the foolish Bali obtained only bondage. (81)
Every person here is both a milker and a hater of the wealthy man in his heart; yet, having cast aside the agitation of greed, he remains indifferent toward them as if they were a single straw. (82)
Abstaining from theft prolongs life, while avoiding forbidden food is the deception of the belly;
for one who attains self-mastery, it is the sole root of the sprout of bliss. (83)
Having thus heard these harsh words, Śakra became filled with anger and spoke aloud:
"Who is this that cuts through the very vitals of dharma? (84)
While I, the subduer of Pāka, rule over the three worlds whose eye is the triple Veda, and while my hand flashes with the vigor of the thunderbolt—who could speak thus? (85)
O friend, whether there is no confusion of castes or even otherwise, you must accept as authoritative the failure of those such as the slayers of Brahmins in their examinations. (86)
That he does not see victory for one who goes to a woman renowned as a Brāhmaṇī or otherwise proclaims the purity of the entire lineage of castes. (87)
In the examination of water, fire, and so forth, there is agreement regarding what is known through the Vedas;
fie, fie upon that intellect which, having seized the neck of nihilism, does not bow before it! 88.
Even when a husband, wife, and so forth exist, since the arising of an embryo and the like is not certain, does the karma implied [by this fact] not pierce the vital point of you nihilists? (89)
Why do you not accept the various stories told by people from many lands concerning how they entered into someone else to perform a *śrāddha* for a deceased ancestor at Gayā? (90)
When those led away by the messengers of Yama have returned due to a confusion of names, why do you not believe the account of the next world as it is told? (91)
The fire blazed up in anger and, reproaching him, said: "What have you said? What is this that you have spoken so unrestrainedly before us? (92)

Do you not feel astonishment as you remember those who performed the Mahāparāka penance, who lived solely by the strength of the Śruti-dharma, and who were so overcome by fainting that they did not eat for a moment? 93.
Are the sacrifices, such as the Putreṣṭi, Śyena, and Kārīrī, which yield visible results, not suns that conquer the Mandeha demons of your doubt regarding dharma? (94)
Then the King of Dharma (Yama), making the sky embrace sparks through the brandishing of his staff, produced waves of words as if his very vitals had been pierced.
"Stop, sir! Stop! I shall forcibly blunt the throat and lips of you, a rogue, who recites the lesson incorrectly in this assembly. (96)
O Lokāyata, who could abandon the supreme world through mere words, when it has been firmly established by the Vedas, by those hostile to them, and likewise by hundreds of philosophical systems? (97)
Since you encounter disagreement among travelers on this path in this world due to their varying degrees of understanding, why would you not encounter it on that same path in the next world? (98)
For whom in this world or the next would the mind not be firm when they see that the entire universe consents to giving away their own daughter to another? (99)
If any one doctrine is true, then those who abandon all doctrines are ruined;
from that perspective, there is merely futility, but no harm arising from dharma. (100)
In some cases, because there is no disagreement among all [authorities], and in other cases because of the risk of falling [into sin] otherwise,
one must abide by the Vedic dharma alone, even regarding the remaining [dharma], since it was established by that [Veda].
Varuṇa, turning crimson with rage, spoke words devoid of compassion:
"O wretched heretic, do you not fear our fierce noose? (102)

How can this stone, which could not have been fashioned by a human and which bears the marks of a tortoise and other signs, fail to inspire faith in you simple-minded followers of the path of the heretics? (103)
How is it that the atheists were not made to feel wonder by the accounts of the Vedas, which correspond with the fame of those known as Śatakratu, Uruja, and others? (104)
Even while experiencing spirits who, possessed by various people, demand offerings such as *śrāddha* for their ancestors, how is it that you do not believe the Vedas? (105)
Having observed that living beings who were led away by the confusion of names and so forth have now returned to their own bodies and speak in agreement [with you], do not abandon the Vedas.
Then, as his strength was being crushed by the violent attacks of Indra and the other gods, someone with palms joined upon his head spoke thus to the deities: (107)
O leaders of heaven, this person is neither an offender nor dependent on others; I am merely a captive of the Kali age, my mouth rendered restless by its flatteries. (108)
Even as he was speaking thus, the gods perceived Kali and another Dvāpara approaching in front of their chariot-palace.
With his neck upraised, he gazed upon those celestial beings, who were rendered marvelous by their abundant splendor;
though himself overwhelmed by various sins, he looked at them as one in hell looks upon the denizens of heaven.
First, his head was bowed as he was licked by the Guru’s pride,
like Triśaṅku who was overcome by the splendor of Indra.
Like a jackal toward birds that have turned their faces away from him even to look at him, he approached those who were intoxicated with pride and addressed them with ease. (112)
"Hail to you, O Lord of the Dwelling! O crested one, you have no weariness.
O friend Time, you are at ease; O noose-handed one, you are uplifted. (113)
We are hastening to the self-choice ceremony to choose the daughter of Bhīma;
therefore, grant us your permission to set out upon that path.
Disregarding his groundless and excessive arrogance,
they looked at one another with smiles and, after a long while, spoke to him.
You will say again, "Do not speak thus; how indeed could he be carried away—he whom the Supreme Lord created as a perpetual celibate student? (116)
May Druhiṇa consider you a traitor upon hearing that you have broken your vow;
or else, was the Creator’s bridge not to be crossed even by your own people? 117.
That event, which humbles the pride of the youths of the three worlds, has already passed;
for us who are coming here, it is the svayaṃvara itself that serves as the point of departure.
While the affectionate nāgas and the gods looked on,
the daughter of Bhīma chose that protector of the earth, Nala, as her husband.
The daughter of Bhīma knew the lords of serpents as mere dwellers in holes, the monkeys as nothing more than men, and the gods as common folk; she knew only Nala, resplendent with virtues.
Having heard this, he, blinded by rage, assumed the form of Rudra at the end of the night of the world's destruction, and spoke thus to those who were in the final age: ||121||
Let Brahmā play with some woman; let you yourselves sport with celestial women! Let Kali practice asceticism, or let him go to the world of Brahmā for your great pleasure.
What kind of conduct is this of yours, who preach the Dharma to others while yourselves performing everything that your ears fear to hear? (123)
In that self-choice marriage, the Fortune of the Earth was won by the son of Niṣadha;
but the Shame of the world was won by you—your gain is indeed equal to his.
Having seen us from afar, this contraction of your faces is appropriate; it is as if out of shame you are unable to look upon our faces, for we are powerless. 125.
O sirs, how was that improper act committed while you stood looking on? Why was that wicked woman not consumed by your eyes ablaze with anger? (126)
Alas, disregarding her noble lineage and desiring something great, how could she have accepted that fickle Nala? 127.
How could Nala, who accepted as his own the deer-eyed woman sought after by world-protectors such as yourselves, endure being treated with such contempt as if he were a blade of grass? 128.
Did not this cruel fire, taking recourse to deception even while acting as a witness,
commit the act of being a false witness in that marriage?
Alas! Even for you, who possess such great companions, there has arisen this capacity for such a stain, just as it exists for the god of nectar-like radiance [the moon].
"Having abandoned him whom she chose, why do you remain here full of envy toward me? Speak!
From that abode of sin, I shall today destroy them by means of a stratagem. (131)
Strive to act together with me, as Pāñcālī does with the Pāṇḍavas;
she too should be enjoyed by us five, sharing her among us. (132)
Then, unable to endure that foolishness of the talkative man,
Sarasvatī struck him with her speech, which was as sharp and piercing as an arrow.
These [gods] came solely to bestow fame upon the daughter of Bhīma and a boon upon him;
for the intellect of a wise man, which delves into profound depths, does not savor the cleverness of the dull-witted.
Unable to respond to that eloquent woman, Kali, his tongue rendered dull, treated her with playful contempt and spoke only to the gods. (135)
We too have now expressed our desire regarding her;
yet, toward that Nala, we possess not even a trace of compassion. (136)
Now that the task is accomplished, what can we do? We were not present there at that time. Listen now once more to what is appropriate for the occasion and has been reflected upon. (137)
O wise ones, let this vow of mine regarding Kali be understood by Nala:
by him I shall cause both the daughter of Bhīma and the earth to be abandoned, and I shall conquer him. (138)
"Alas, let the worlds sing of my enmity with the King of Niṣadha—who is adorned with fierce splendor—as being like that of the sun toward the night-lotus! (139)
Dvāpara kindled that transformation with a cry of "Well done!";
then, placing his hand over his ear, the enemy of Namuci spoke.
With a mind full of wonder, you rightly observe our embarrassment;
for when one gives little to one who is great, that act brings shame upon oneself. (141)
Even a fraction of the devotion that Nala offered to us—which bestows the fourfold goals of life up to the very limit of its fruition—is now fruitless for him. 142.
O Kālī, your resolve regarding Nala, who possesses virtuous judgment, is not appropriate;
for he is the moon of the Niṣadhas, as vast as the world-protectors. (143)
We do not perceive any room for the Kali age in that mountain, nor do we see the emergence of the Dvāpara age in him who has accumulated all dharmas.
Alas! How can that most disciplined daughter of Bhīma be troubled by those like you who grasp at vain and harmful things, just as valid cognition is obscured by delusions? (145)
Neither the Kṛta age nor the Tretā age is capable of rivaling that [age], for its dharma is of a single, uniform radiance; nor are you two, Kali and Dvāpara. (146)
By saying "I shall certainly do it," you incur fault even while intending to act;
for the visible and invisible causes of your undertaking are not under your control.
Whoever should commit an act of malice toward him out of delusion will, before long, suffer the torment arising from that sin due to his own misconduct. (148)
O end of the age, this hatred of yours toward him is not appropriate;
this enmity of yours with Vairaseni will not lead to your welfare.
In that regard, the thought "I shall go" is false knowledge; it is passionate (rājasa), for it leads to ridicule in an assembly of the passionate.
Therefore, do not go to such a passionate assembly, lest you fall into ridicule. (150)
Having gone between Nala and the daughter of Bhīma, you shall not enter her unexpectedly;
for the wheel of the six [letters] is recited as unjoined, like the sound of the letter *ḍa*. (151)
The other lords of the quarters also approved these words of the Lord of Śacī;
however, he did not accept them for two yugas at once.
Kali spoke to each of the gods, and each god spoke to Kali;
thus they addressed one another with equal syllables and with derision. (153)
Since she has chosen the son of Vīrasena, your coming alone is appropriate;
what is the use of this chariot racing along in such agitation? (154)
If you were going to choose her first, yet she has already been chosen by another, this conduct of yours is laughable and brings shame. (155)
Since she has chosen another as her husband for the very purpose for which you have come,
your obstruction of his anger is in vain against one who is incapable of wrath and whose anger is futile.
O low-born man, you travel across a multitude of leagues on a great steed, captivating the world with your splendor;
yet when another has been chosen, why do you not feel shame? 157.
Perceiving that the pair of the third and fourth ages was not free from suffering regarding Nala,
the gods in heaven fixed their minds upon him.
Accompanied by Dvāpara as his sole retinue, Kali— stupefied by envy and truly obsessed—
undertook a campaign against Nala.
Because he was far removed from the fulfillment of sacrifices and charitable works (iṣṭāpūrta),
a dense obstacle arose to prevent the Niṣadhas from proceeding toward that inaccessible Durgā.
The wicked Kali, through his accumulation of sins, sought to cause the spotless circle of Niṣadha’s lord to fade, just as the sinful Rāhu seeks to eclipse the moon.
After some time,
the Kali age arrived at the capital of the king, the husband of Damayantī, who was full of self-conceit.
There, as he heard the words of the Vedas being recited from their mouths, the Kali age was unable to extend even a single step. (163)
As he heard the sequence from the mouths of those reciting the scriptures there,
that sequence became contracted and receded far away within his city.
He maintained a gait full of pride with his feet only so long as the *saṃhitā* had not been heard from the throats of those who recite the Vedas. (165)
His nose seemed to perish from the fragrance of the clarified butter used in that sacrifice; likewise, his eyes were distressed by the smoke of the ritual. (166)
In that place, on the courtyard of householders which was exceedingly slippery due to the water used for washing the feet of guests, this rogue stumbled. (167)
He underwent a process of slow roasting by the great heat of the sacrificial fires;
it was as if his very limbs were carved away by the winds from the fans of the waves of his meritorious works.
In every house, strewn with grains for the libation of the ancestors, he stayed far away from that black sesame seed as if from Death himself. (169)
He thought that his own heart had been rent asunder by the sectarian marks (tilakas) of the bathers, as if those marks had become swords and entered therein.
There he rejoiced upon finding a man speaking falsely;
yet, seeing him likewise regarding a woman, he then became dejected.
He perceived that city as having sacrificial posts for its fortifications and crowded with stakes;
it was filled with people whose wealth was dharma, yet it was embraced by predatory beasts.
That wretched man was unable even to move to the side of those who observe the *parāka* penance;
he stumbled heavily when attempting to cross the shadow of those fasting for a month.
Seeing Gāyatrī being invoked there by the twice-born from the solar orb as she drew near,
he vanished out of fear, having been seen and then lost to sight.
In a house filled with householders, in a forest dense with hermits, in a monastery serving as a refuge for ascetics, or in a celestial abode—he found no place anywhere to stay. (175)
Searching everywhere, he did not see his beloved Hiṃsā;
nor did he find his friend Kali there, even though Kali resided in the mouth of a fool. (176)
Seeing the sacrificial cow intended for slaughter, he ran toward her, desiring to sport with her;
she, however, being devoted to a gentle bull, drove that donkey away from afar.
He considered his own abuse as a mere silence from those intent on their vows; and he perceived his own head as being trampled by those who were saluting the one worthy of salutation. (178)
Seeing the grass mats of the sages in their hands, he took water for ritual rinsing and thought:
"These men are prepared to strike me with clods of earth and curse me with water. (179)
Wearing the girdle of muñja grass and carrying the āṣāḍha staff, he appeared to me like a religious student (brahmacārin);
"Therefore," I thought, "these men are coming to bind me with ropes and strike me with a staff. (180)
Seeing the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) before him, he became distressed with fear;
thinking that there were female serpents there, he shed tears from his sacrificial ladles (sruk).
He rejoiced upon learning that the twice-born man had obtained wine;
yet, seeing him performing the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, he was pained.
As many Veda-knowers as he saw with their hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture,
so many handfuls of tears flew up from his heart.

He perceived the Snātaka as a slayer; he recognized him, though self-controlled, as being like the God of Death. He was terrified by the mere sight of him, as if by Yama himself, who is ever restrained in speech.
Seeking out heretics, he encountered Vedic scholars;
like one seeking water who finds fire, the wicked man fled from them in distress.
There, seeing a slayer of a Brahmin, he experienced excessive joy;
yet, having gazed upon a performer of the Sarvamedha sacrifice, he was filled with feverish distress.
A threat was launched against him by the ascetics using their bamboo staffs;
the wicked man suffered distress from the Vedic staffs of the householders. (187)
Seeing those who slept on the bare ground, he desired only to abandon his royal circle;
by beholding their sacred threads (*pavitra*), he attained the state of being truly pure (*pavitrātām*).
Seeking the Conqueror while searching for the antelope skin, he who desired the destruction of his vows beheld instead the non-destruction of his consecration by a religious student.
Because he saw the drawing in of seeds upon the rosaries of those who were reciting prayers, he experienced the miseries of having his life-force drawn out by an adverse gaze. (190)
Seeing there, at the three junctions of the day, the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite performed by the Brahmins,
he would rather have chosen the removal of his own eyes than witness it.
Wandering there, Kali, desiring to inquire into even the slightest trace of a fault in Nala regarding Damayantī, did not see anything familiar anywhere.
That ascetic, who harbored an unprovoked hatred for austerity, Vedic study, and sacrifice,
felt intense burning anguish upon seeing the prosperity of those who were his own enemies within him.
Having seen her approaching there, he was pleased with the entire assembly;
but upon perceiving that she was a devotee of Vāmadeva, he became dejected.
Purity, acting as an enemy, granted him no entrance upon the earth, nor did the sound of the Vedas provide him any support in the sky. (195)
From the sight of the New Moon sacrifice he suffered distress, and from the Agniṣṭoma he was consumed;
he reeled at the Full Moon sacrifice and considered Soma to be Death itself.
Therefore, he saw those who were slayers of heroes, but not those who had themselves been slain by heroes;
he did not see those who had departed from life, but beheld those liberated while living. (197)
He was gratified seeing the Brahmins eating while touching one another;
however, upon seeing them consuming the Soma that remained from the oblation, he became distressed.
Upon hearing that the people were covered in dust, he immediately attained satisfaction;
yet, seeing them in the state of having performed purifying baths, he then became distressed.
Seeing a cow being slaughtered somewhere, he ran there with joy;
but, having learned that it was for guests, the dull-witted man turned back slowly.
Seeing the twice-born man who had abandoned his daily and occasional rites, he was delighted;
yet, observing that the sacrificer was departing, he ran far away with a dejected face.
Having previously observed this man who was intent on self-destruction, Ānanda now felt deep distress upon seeing him as one who had performed the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice.
Beholding the sexual union of a student and a courtesan during the Mahāvrata rite,
that ignorant man produced a sacrificial performance that was like an unseasonable, frantic dance of a jester.

Seeing that the wife of a sacrificer had attained the state of being the excellent private parts of a horse— the sacrificial animal of the Aśvamedha— by embracing a phallus, that unlearned man declared the author of the Veda to be a buffoon.
Then Kali beheld Nala, who was attended by Bhīmajā,
as one difficult to look upon with evil eyes, like a lord of radiance who is difficult to behold because of his own brilliance.
Beholding the density of their mutual affection, he felt as if pierced by a thorn;
he experienced, as it were, the cutting of his vital organs by the waves of their mutual jesting.
Due to his own indignation and fault, and because of their quality of brilliance, Kali was unable even to look at them with his eyes; therefore, he did not move from that spot either.
Sighing, that hater of Nala went seeking a refuge into the delightful palace garden of him whose splendor was equal to Rāma.
Because he was surrounded by a hundred thousand guards, the proud Kali thought that the ascetics there could not possibly cause him any harm; indeed, he considered it somewhat favorable for himself.
With the intention of worshipping the gods and the twice-born with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
he reached there the trees that had been gathered by Nala, which he was not permitted to climb.
Then, in order to fulfill the presence of all types of trees,
he saw a single planted *bibhītaka* tree that was useless even for the sake of dharma.
In that grove near the palace of the King of Niṣadha, Kali considered the banner of the pleasure-garden to be his own refuge.

Because it provided a place of rest for that fruitless Kali age, the *bibhītaka* tree was not merely a "tree of the Kali age" (*kalidruma*); rather, it was also a "wish-fulfilling tree" (*kalpadruma*). (213)
Since Kali gave him only one foot to stand upon by means of Dharma's foot,
I believe that at that time even that single foot of his met with its match.
Like a pigeon whose dwelling has been constructed by a woodpecker,
he experienced distress there from that king who was consecrated for sacrifice along with his sacred fires.
Occupying a *bibhītaka* tree and remaining there in such a manner,
that royal sage was not overcome by Bhīma’s son, despite the latter being full of desire.
Having taken hold of that very object [of dispute], Kali dwelt for many years, searching for a flaw in the conduct of the King of Vidarbha and the Lord of Niṣadha. (217)
Just as there was a creeper with blossoming buds in that forest,
so too was the creeper of Time (Kalā) with its buds blossomed by her attachment to Nala in disguise.
Desiring to discover a fault in Nala, Dvāpara wandered upon the earth with the wicked hope that there might be someone in the world who was entirely without blame. (219)
In this very grove, where blossoms are perpetually falling and remain forever in full bloom, rivaling the moon,
the Kali age has taken up residence; and the deer of its mark has acquired a luster so fit for anointing with the shadow of the wings of the kādamba birds.
In that vast city of Vairasena, which had become so full of prosperity through the merits of its people, it is said that after a long time, Kali finally found a dense obstacle to his entry.

Yet, in this very interval, Smara— his joy increased by the internal space [left open]— prepared his bow, whose tip was bowed in reverence to the crest of the Vedas, in order to win Damayantī and Nala.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
thus ends the seventeenth canto, naturally radiant, in the *Naiṣadhīyacarita*, a great poem composed on the earth by him for the sake of the eulogy of his sister Chindā. (222)
The eighteenth canto: Having thus obtained Damayantī, the essence of his wife, that King of Niṣadha then enjoyed her,
who was a boat for crossing the ocean of the third aim of human life.
Though he partook of enjoyments day and night with her, that knower of the Self incurred no sin;
for the state of being solely intent upon sense-objects, once drawn away, does not stain one whose mind has been purified by knowledge.

Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers with great care, he, accompanied by his beloved, devoted himself to the service of Madana upon that mountain-like palace, which possessed floors inlaid with millions of multi-colored gems and supported the weight of golden grounds.
By the power of the divine rows of jewels that served as ornaments for the necks of Vīrasena’s sons,
he treated like a blade of grass even the mountain of the gods, who possess the quality of providing whatever objects are desired.
Her interior had long been perfumed with dark, choice aloe-wood,
and was cooled by breezes rich with the powder of moon-like sandalwood held within latticed windows.

In some places, the wicks of the arrows of Kama’s shafts— possessing the splendor of sprouts from the mass of the prowess of Cupid’s throbbing arms— acted as great lamps of fragrant oil, rendering that place free from darkness.

The floors of his palace, paved with charming jewels, shone brightly; they were smeared with a paste of saffron and musk, washed with water scented by Himalayan sandalwood, and adorned with garlands of mountain flowers trailing along the pathways.

In certain places, the flower-bed of the earth attained the boldness of a forehead-tilaka by means of its soft and lovely-colored petals, which were made fragrant and supple through being rubbed against the limbs of the King of Niṣadha.
In another place, by means of the waves of fragrance from the multitude of blossoming buds in the nearby grove,
the daughter of Bhīma’s nostrils were made to feel as if they were living in a cozy cottage.
The swift wind honors that preeminent family with offerings of mango spray cut from the trees by birds in the groves where all seasons flourish in abundance—those who enjoy such a place. (10)

In some places it was entirely fashioned from gold; in others, it was said to be born of pure jewels. In one place it featured variegated painted galleries; in another, it was like a magician displaying unstable illusions.

Beholding him— who possesses many forms and similes that create the illusion of various things being imitated by their counterparts— the Creator, the king of artisans, was fashioned as one afflicted by the wind-disorder of old age, constantly shaking his head.
It was filled with the curiosity of wonderful stories told by people hidden within the interior of the walls;
it possessed many mechanical dolls that inspired amazement through their extraordinary movements produced by strings and mechanisms. (13)
Even during the dark nights of the month of Tāmasī, it possessed an intense moonlight through the rays of jewels set in its walls;
and even in the heat of summer, the fatigue of the sun's glare was dispelled from afar by the showers falling from its water-machines.
There, the ivory couch, inhabited by female sarika birds that recited verses from the treatises on the art of love,
observed the successes and failures in the amorous dalliances of the daughter of Bhima and the emperor of the Nishadhas.

Wherever the eyes fell upon those two ponds, which were like a repeated performance of amorous play by intoxicated kalaviṅka birds, there the festival of Love was witnessed in the form of pairs of swans—the ornaments of the pools. (16)

There, the cooing of amorous passion between the two of them was drowned out by the sounds of flutes and the notes of the bamboo pipes, by the "hum" cries of the cuckoos in the grove, and by the jingling of the bracelets of those who were dancing. 17.
As they listened with apprehension to the sounds of sighing, in which the worship of Rati and Smara was established,
those two were made to feel as if they were separated by a deceptive wall at night, even though they were inside the same room, by means of the latticed windows.

In his mouth, that warbling of the wild song of the kinnarīs—which was once as curved as the horn of the black antelope and which flowed solely with sweet and brilliant rasa—did not cease for a moment. (19)
There, the historical narratives stood with their entire sequence depicted as wall-paintings,
[narrating] how the God of Love laughed with bold audacity at his desire to sport with the daughter of the Son of the Lotus-Born (Brahmā).
There, on the walls, the reckless amorous excesses of the Lord of the Gods— who, desiring the wife of Gautama, acted like a drum proclaiming victory over the arrows of Puṣpaka— were boldly engraved.
Under the guise of rising grains of sandalwood powder, his fame— which had conquered the world through victory over Vaijayanta—
shone forth like the sister of the night of the full moon in the month of Kārttika.

In the courtyard of that palace, dramas based on the story of the amorous passion of the wife of Bṛhaspati for the moon— passion stirred by the memory of her husband— shone forth through their performances as nectar for the poetic speech of Bharata.

The golden pinnacle of his palace was marked by well-composed verses from Uśanas, which wove together the amorous dalliances of Śambhu in the Dāruvana forest and the playful sports of Mādhava with the cowherd women of Vraja.

One day, while wandering on the grounds of Bhānu, a parrot sang of his grandfather Śuka, who was longing for a maiden from the Daśa kingdom; for Śuka, out of passion, could not endure the lapse of time, the distance of the place, or the obstacle of the girl herself.
