Having failed to cross the ocean of austerity whose further shore is so difficult to reach, the sages remain depicted in paintings somewhere,
clinging to the jar-like breasts of celestial nymphs as their support.
"That very Love, who was conquered by me— both as a husband and as one carrying him— through the renunciation of sexual pleasure,
is now dancing in such a manner," [the peacock thought] as it danced to the deep sounds of the drums.

There, seeing Nala and Bhīma together, even Rati and the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva) became, as it were, through rivalry, the two wives of Kāma and Kāma for the sake of victory over those two who were already victorious. ||28||
Then, upon that mountain of white palaces, their amorous sports became manifest—sports which have never been beheld even by great poets, nor have they ever been learned even by loose women. (29)

How much trepidation was not experienced by Damayantī, the daughter of Bhīma, as she took refuge in Nala as her husband—a youth who had transcended childhood—while she herself assumed the demeanor of a wife? 30.

Reflecting upon that loss of decorum of his own, which she had previously heard from her beloved when they were united with a messenger, she was so overcome with shame that she did not know what she should do. (31)
Reflecting upon her own impulsive act of having suddenly chosen the Nishadhan prince herself in the assembly without shame, she was unable to look at Nala.
In whichever direction he stood, embracing that seat thick with the radiance of jewels,
this proud woman did not look even slightly toward it, as if she were resentful.

At the door stood that woman, possessing the splendor of a painted maiden, who maintained a deep bowing of her head as was fitting for immersion in the waters of modesty; she rendered a hundred calls from her husband’s side as if they were unheard.

Out of timidity, she did not enter her husband’s house; even when made to enter, she did not resort to the bed. Even when made to sit near him, she did not sleep; and even when made to lie down, she did not face him. (35)
Not only did the daughter of Bhīma not feel at all bashful toward the prince of Niṣadha;
surely even the God of Love was put to shame in the heart of the daughter of Bhīma, being utterly conquered by her modesty.
Even though Haradārasundarī herself desired to perform some action, if she was requested by her husband for that purpose, her effort was then stifled by him. (37)

As she turned her face away out of a weight of modesty, he— suspecting a lack of affection because she had been seized by fear— dismissed that apprehension from his mind by recollecting her intention as determined at the time of her mission as a messenger.
Then, having first approached her side with her companions,
that master of illusion subsequently employed one of them elsewhere, leaving her with only herself as his sole companion.
Although she was placed nearby by her female companions, he, who was well-versed in the science of the Flower-Armed God (Kāma),
brought his beloved into close proximity as if she were separated by a distance, using the circle of his own arm as a barrier.
First he kissed her on the forehead as she bent low with shame; then, in due course, on her cheeks as she bent even lower out of fear.
When her mind was thus reassured by him, he suddenly kissed her on the face and smiled. (41)

Having first approached with bashfulness, he was greeted with a "hum" sound; then, threatened by powerful trepidation, the god of love, though slightly revived, was once again suppressed within her heart.
During the festival of love, as the beloved’s two arms were eager to forcibly embrace her,
the young girl, finding no space between them due to their tight pressure upon her body, resisted each one for a long time.
Feigning some false curiosity while gazing at the movement of her necklace,
the husband touched the base of her neck with his hand, which was gliding toward her breast.
"Since you have honored me with a garland in this assembly, it is fitting that I too should offer something worthy of you.
Having spoken thus, as he presented his own necklace, he touched the bud-like breasts of her chest.
At night, he cast off the trembling garment placed within the folds of the girdle of the fair-browed woman, who had been deprived of consciousness by sleep,
as she regained her awareness through the swaying of the bed.
Then the king cast his gaze upon the silken garment covering the pair of his beloved’s thighs and smiled;
she, as if uncovered and shrouded in shame, covered them with the hem of her own cloth.
Gradually, this wise man made her somewhat free from her timidity;
moreover, in her mind, modesty was slightly bent by the god of love, as if by his bow.
Though she was delighted by his joking remarks, she did not smile or laugh;
for she reveals her own priceless rows of ruby-like teeth only to another.

Beholding the two breasts of the daughter of Bhīma, marked with the imprint of the gems from her necklace that had sunk into them, the fair-faced lady was inferred by her companions to have endured the intensity of her lover’s embrace. (50)
When she requested her friends to fasten her girdle tightly,
they laughed and inferred that the cause was the restlessness of her husband’s hand.
Closing her eyes somewhat out of modesty, yet revealing her fragrance somewhat out of affection,
she— like a lotus-pond frequented by both buds and blossoming flowers— triumphed as a lotus-woman.
Smara did not allow the fair-browed woman to remain without looking at Nala, nor did shame permit her to look;
then her glances moved toward the direction of her husband, but being bashful, they repeatedly shrank back from that path.
By this [woman], her husband was led neither to the range of sight nor to the state of being beyond it;
for while she looked here and there, he was indeed led away by her as she cast her gaze in those very directions.
During the day, unable to endure separation, she longed for the night as the time to be united with her beloved;
yet at night, ashamed before her husband’s dalliance, she desired instead the break of dawn.
"I shall do that which you most highly desire; do not be ashamed, abandon your fear.
Thus Nala spoke, constantly consoling her with the words, "I am like a circle of your friends. (56)
That fire of passion, which had remained with its power suppressed by the great herb of shame,
was kindled once more by those perfected ones through the incantations of their beloved’s endearing words.
Shaking off the hand offered by her beloved, she firmly covered her breasts with both arms;
having pushed aside the lover who was at her side out of shame, she embraced him as if he were situated within her heart.
"Otherwise, I have never asked you for anything; let me drink from your lower lip just this once.
Thus she tasted him with words that were whispered, plaintive, and full of forceful insistence, accompanied by a pressing embrace.
"Now that he has drunk the nectar of your face, this servant deserves his own duty;
therefore, I shall do it upon your thigh"—saying this, he placed his sprout-like hand there. (60)
"What indeed occurred during the kisses and such? Do not entertain groundless fear even here.
Having spoken thus, he first fashioned for the fawn-eyed maiden a girdle-string of jewels.

It possessed weariness, it possessed curiosity, it possessed the sweat of passion, and it possessed trembling; it possessed fear, it possessed delight, it possessed longing, it attained pleasure, and it possessed pain. (62)
This modesty of yours is indeed appropriate, that my union with you occurs only within your mind; yet, because of our constant union, my own shameless heart brings me to shame.
Thus he reproached her, who had been overcome by a profound shame that obstructed the commencement of their amorous union;
then, being so skillful, he acted in such a way that she felt shame only for following him in order to satisfy him.
Desiring the union of arms, faces, hips, breasts, feet, their various postures, fragrances,
and sexual delights with her eager lover, she made an appointment with him as the day was smiling and he was being watched.
By restraining her as she emerged from her bed at dawn— she who was otherwise impossible to reach—
he, the conqueror of Jambha, caused the Queen of the Earth to experience the pleasure of offering her face [to him].
Emerging at daybreak from the bedchamber of the hero, she beheld the joy of the fair-browed women;
thus, by her very self, she was herself made to remember the festival of her own recent love-making.

As his friend was thus conversing with her regarding the nocturnal activities of both her beloved and herself, he, who had been standing nearby, removed the veil granted by the chief of the gods; having heard their story, he was seen approaching with a smile.
At the moment she beheld the separation from the rim of the wheel, she became afraid for her husband’s laughter;
the mind, when its agitation arises from an omen, foretells the future regarding some matter. (69)
That she did not pull away her face when kissed by her husband rained nectar into his heart;
that she did not push away his arm placed upon her was what else could it have been but his being satisfied? (70)
With that [hand], he first placed his hand upon her two breasts to serve as a covering for them;
then, when the arms were removed, he placed it upon her chest even though only the garment remained, and finally, upon her two breasts themselves.
When she did not grant his request, he made her distracted by conversation and, placing his hand upon her breast to scratch it with his nails,
he rejoiced as he tore his own skin with those very nails.
He was able to forcibly remove the outer veil from the fair-browed woman's heart, but that lord, though powerful, was not able to dispel her inner veil consisting of modesty.
Though she was not deprived of her modesty and patience by the powerful god of love, that woman shone forth intensely;
for while one may indeed shine without clothing, a person does not shine by the total abandonment of shame and fortitude.
"You have said 'no' to one who seeks pleasure; you are clearly not in favor of me for this reason"—with these words, she rejected him, who was eager to speak further, by shaking her head. (75)
Was that shaking of your head which said "no" not clearly understood by me?
Its very equivalence in number to that negation plainly declares your desired affirmation. (76)
"There is none, there is none; listen to me—what is the use of that speech?
Having spoken thus to her, he related to her exactly what had occurred during his mission as a messenger, using those same gentle words she had spoken. ||77||
At first she firmly grasped his hand at the knot of her garment, but then she held it loosely;
speaking in a low voice, "No, no," she merely created an obstacle for him.

Constantly attaining a distinct cleverness in matters of form, dress, garments, bodily perfumes, ornaments, and the like—a cleverness capable of causing the delusion that she was some other celestial maiden—she appeared ever new to him. (79)
Having discerned his own ocean of passion through gestures, his appreciation of virtue through flatteries,
and his devotion through constant service, she brought him under her increasingly complete control.

Having approached her beloved who was provoked to anger by her refusal to offer her own body, she then conciliated him; yet she did not again consent to his request, which was characterized by an insistent desire for enjoyment.

Bestowing her limbs— which had become difficult to attain due to dense pride, perversity, and bashfulness— upon her beloved with great effort, she somehow maintained the same respect as at their first union.

That devoted wife, having fashioned for her husband a body like that of Giriśa up to his head, and for herself one like that of Girijā up to her head, and having fashioned for him all the appropriate [attendants], sported with them. 83.
Neither on dry land nor in the ocean, neither in a forest nor on mountainous ground, neither in a kingdom nor in the world at large—
there was no place where she did not play with him, nor was there any manner in which she did not do so.

As her beloved pulled at her modest garment, she extinguished the burning lamp with the breath from her mouth; illuminated by the crest-jewel of her husband, she gazed at the quarters of the sky in wonder. (85)
Placing an ear-lotus upon her beloved’s head with the desire to cover his crest-jewel, she performed,
as it were, a preliminary worship before the God of Love— the very body of her own lover— in order to sport with him.

Having covered that [lamp] and then seeing lamps on both her sides, she— her mind filled with curiosity, wonder, shame, and the agitation of fear— experienced a state in which the God of Love was lodged amidst a crisis.
When one [of the two] was pacified, she saw that the other had awakened again;
even though he too had been pacified, she merely closed her eyes, shaking her head as she recalled the excellence of the Fire-god.
"Look, O timid one! You are not even seen by me, since you have closed your eyes.
Having thus mocked her, he created darkness and enjoyed her while she was abashed. 89.
"You are being kissed, you are being marked with nail-scratches, you are being embraced, and you are being placed upon my heart!
Yet I will not again heed your words—'Hum! Leave me, leave me!'—for I am your servant. (90)

Thus, having deceived her beloved during lovemaking by feigning distress through false pretenses, that deceitful woman bestowed kisses and other acts; for what is beyond the reach of those with clever minds? (91)
In the dense darkness, by means of a lamp flickering and extinguished the very moment it was raised according to his desire,
he enjoyed the pleasures of beholding the intentions on her face born of their fearless dalliance.
When she knit her brows during love-making, that was the bending of the bow by the God of Love;
and when she then uttered "hum-hum," that was the "hum" sound of the God of Love as he discharged his arrows.
With her lower lip bitten by her lover's teeth and waving her hand, she seems to instruct the God of Love—who has just experienced joy at that moment—to dance. (94)
She was unable to embrace her beloved’s broad chest,
and he could not endure the distance created by her high, full breasts as she stood with arched brows.
The circular embrace of their creeper-like arms, which pressed them against one another,
remained as the very noose born of the lotus-stalks of the golden lotus-lake for the Lord of their Hearts.
Pressed by the embrace of her beloved, the breasts of the lover’s wife fell upon his chest; there, at the refuge of Love and the God of Play, they assumed the state of a pillow joined together.
Damayantī’s pair of thighs shone with the soft nail-marks impressed by Nala, appearing like a pair of golden victory pillars erected for the praise of Rati and Kāma. (98)
"Even by the Creator, your inner pair of thighs was highly esteemed;
it is for this reason that he fashioned them from gold of superior hue"—this is what he said to her long ago. (99)

Desiring to plunge those two soft breasts into the lotus-hands of her lover for the sake of pressing them, her breasts— plump as jars and firm— spread out a smile like a string of pearls across his hands.

Upon the chest of his beloved, he himself performed a worship with nail-marks like *kiṃśuka* flowers upon those two breasts of his wife, which were adorned with musk and saffron and possessed the luster of blue and red.

Then the orb of the moon-like face of the King of Niṣadha, as it kissed the lotus-face of his beloved, mocked the small portion of the moon that had risen from the ocean and was joined with its own reflection.

There, during their amorous dalliance, those two, with the nectar of their lips flavored by the abundant betel-nut and spices and perfumed by the rising sun, performed the graceful sport of an excellent drinking bout.

As her lord’s face was kissing her, that fair-toothed woman, manifesting audible *sītkṛta* sounds, then displayed a great trembling born of her inner emotion, thereby expressing his cool-rayed nature (his coolness) without words.

The orb of the face of Vīrasena’s son, having touched the breast of his beloved for a kiss, attained a state of kinship with the nectar-rayed moon through its possession of nectar-like [beauty], as if by means of a golden jar attached to it. 105.
Gazing again and again, she was gazed upon with joy;
embraced repeatedly, she was embraced; kissed again and again, she was kissed with devotion—and yet, no satisfaction whatsoever was attained. (106)
Although the broad circle of her necklace was broken by the playful dance of love-making, the innocent-eyed woman,
whose chest was covered in beads of perspiration, did not notice it even after a long time while it lay upon her heart.
That her necklace was made of pearls upon her heart was due solely to the thread;
otherwise, how could they have remained there at that time, having fallen away from their thread? 108.
Then, although it was but a single-strand pearl necklace, as their necklaces were broken and stretched out,
its reflection became an ornament upon the other's chest, which was drenched with the weight of perspiration from exhaustion.
With her pride in the beauty of her love-life eclipsed by the sole of his left foot, as he gazed incessantly at her face while enjoying her fresh youth, she reached the further shore of her joys.
Nala considered even his own internal limbs to be satisfied by contact with her body;
he imagined that beholding her was the completion of a feast of the essence of nectar for his eyes. (111)
At first, he was not satisfied with the ornaments worn by his beloved;
then, contemplating them, he became distressed, for they served as nothing more than obstacles when he wished to see even a small part of her body.
Even the space of a single hair’s breadth in their embrace seemed like a distance of many yojanas to them as they awakened;
yet, in looking at one another, they perceived even a moment as being separated by the interval of an entire year.
Seeing her eager to discover his true nature, he first showed her his own reflection in the smooth jeweled pavement, making her cry out in astonishment, "Who is this? (114)

At that moment, maintaining the state of the twelve-fold white-rayed moon through his intensely focused disposition, he dispelled the lightness of his beloved—who had appeared at his desired hour—caused by her recent attainment of his affection. (115)

In producing his own state of being, he made his beloved a sharer in the essence of the bliss that culminates the privacy of sexual union, through kisses upon the base of her arms, her breasts, and her navel.
With their limbs slackening, their eyes closing, and their hair standing on end,
they indicated through their sighs and whistling sounds that they had simultaneously reached a state of passion.

As the two of them reached the height of passion, the infliction of nail-marks during their bouts of rapture was clearly as desirable—even though it was sharp—as the sprinkling of pepper over molasses. (118)
With her eyes half-closed and their pupils flickering, she bore them for a moment while languid from the fatigue of lovemaking; yet that was not enough to satisfy her beloved as he gazed upon her.
His beloved, who was his very deity, for a moment incited her exhausted husband to move the palm-leaf fan; for a wife of such a nature would cause even the Creator to act with fickleness.

Her face, with its crest of hair and nose dappled with drops of perspiration, brought delight to the Prince of Niṣadha; it was a face where the lac-dye on her lower lip had faded from lying upon it, and where the horripilation on her cheeks was only half-effaced.

That face of hers—modest yet expansive, full of longing yet somewhat weary, and at once deeply contented and slightly despondent—attained a hundred thousandfold value in the heart of her beloved through his intense devotion. (122)
The more the eye of the King of Niṣadha beheld the multitude of his beloved’s pores filled with perspiration, the more strangely it failed to reach satiety.
Having seen that radiant base of her arm clearly revealed by her pair of hands as she cast aside her flower garland and restrained her hair, he sank into an ocean of bliss. (124)
Beholding her husband’s lip, which, like a bandhūjīva flower joined with a bee, was beautiful with its own eye-makeup, the slender-waisted woman was unable to conceal her smile. 125.
Beholding her smiling while averting her face as her lord asked the cause of her laughter, the modest bride gave this answer: she offered a mirror upon the lotus of her hand.

Beholding his face with its beautiful forehead kissed by her foot marked with lac, she, with her face bowed low in shame, remembered her husband who had risen at dawn, still possessing the residual glow of the night.
Seeing her beloved reflected as if embodied within her perspiring heart,
she dispelled the fatigue of their lovemaking with her own breaths, which were exceedingly soft due to her bashfulness.
Seeking to bite her lower lip—which produced a sensation never before experienced through the playful commands of her lover—the fly approached it softly; she touched it and was struck with wonder.
Having repeatedly observed the playful mark made by her lover’s fingernails upon her breasts,
she gazed at her beloved with a smile, the corners of her eyes slightly contracted with anger.
Seeing his beloved with a face as if stained by anger, her words trembling slightly from fear, he said to her:
"O slender one, I do not know who has caused this planting of wrath in you."
O slender-limbed one, your speech was slightly tinged with the scent of the saffron paste of your anger;
yet, O you whose face is subject to the moon, your countenance attained a redness that was entirely inconsistent with the occasion.
But let the pain arising from his nails and other parts quickly scatter your showers of nectar;
it is for this purpose that I have requested this wish-granting jewel-necklace to kiss my throat.
Your hand, acting as a maker of the divine bow (rainbow) upon my cloud-like breast, has stolen away its own offense;
let it once again attend to your feet through the service of fanning them.
O fair-toothed one, if it is improper for me to bite you mercilessly with my teeth, then tell me: why do you not avenge this enmity by biting his lower lip? 135.
This crest-jewel of mine, which brought about a result like the extinguishing of a lamp during the thefts of your garments, shall—
rather than being merely excused for that offense— now prostrate itself at your feet.

Having offered this tender speech, he— his hair touching the couch— pressed his head against her feet, which were like two crimson lotuses, with the rays of the gems upon his own crown flowing over them.
By the reflections of his own toes upon all the nails [of the other],
he attained equality with the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva), who had assumed ten forms in order to conquer the realm of Rudra.
"He has spoken; perform the appeasement of his anger. Behold, this slender night is perishing.
Yet, within this very night, you shall for a moment indulge in the remainder of your wrath. (139)

Then, with her own lotus-feet hidden by her hands, she led the Lord to fulfillment; the fair-toothed lady, displaying a smiling face whose pride was shaken by his prostration, [accomplished this]. (140)
Through the elixir of mutual passion, their minds became desirous of enjoying each other once again;
yet the wicked night, short-lived as it was, could not tolerate their longing.
When they had both attained sleep upon their bed, the lover spoke these words freely to his beloved,
interspersed at intervals with celebrations consisting of the drinking of the gift of her lower lip.
Since he has committed such an offense out of fear of dharma by mercilessly acting as a messenger for the gods,
let this subjection of Nala last until the end of his life serve as the expiation for that transgression.
O fair-faced one, that moment of beholding you is a true instant; that wide sovereignty by which you take delight is vast indeed;
and that embrace of your limbs, with its graceful movement, is Nala’s consecration in nectar. (144)

O slender one, I desire that [union] of yours in the great festivals; for is it not this very union of the river and the ocean that constitutes the bliss of Hari in his heart, the offering of the beloved to Śiva, or the joining of half of Śiva’s body? 145.

What opportunity is there even to say "Let the firm thought 'this is mine' be fixed upon me," since you have cast aside the Lord of Heaven like a blade of grass and purchased me with the price of compassion? (146)
While you were repeatedly listening with composure to the playful charms of your speech through your companions, I, it seems,
observed you trembling with fear as you overheard the words of Jānakī, which were destined to be fruitlessly rejected by Rāghava.
From the shrub whose leaves were closed by a touch, from the frog that held a blade of grass as a bow,
and from the lizard whose head was shaken by your friends— all these, among your companions, proclaimed their own majesty while expressing their fear.
"You expressed your fear of separation from me when we were in private; that was overheard by me.
Therefore, I have not abandoned you"—thus spoke this excellent man, who is afraid of untruth.

"Having united us, why does Sleep not approach us today, as if angry, saying: 'Since you have given me this very livelihood at that moment for the sake of pleasure, I shall remain in separation from you'? (150)
When her beloved spoke such words, she closed her eyes for a moment out of joy,
just as the night-lotus closes its petals at dawn when the cuckoo warbles sweetly, as if from exhaustion after a sleepless night.

With thighs entwined and lips joined, performing for one another those actions they had seen in their dreams, they thereafter fell asleep while pressing each other within the hollow embrace of their arms. 152.

That couple entered into a sleep of bliss, their mutual identity proclaimed by the continuous flow of sighs from the fatigue of passion—artfully concealed by the momentum of their coming and going—which clearly dispelled any notion of a difference between their lives; a state in which both hearts became one, as evidenced by the marks of the elephant and crocodile on the king’s chest and the sprouts of leaf-designs upon the young woman’s breasts.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond ornament upon the crowns of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this is the eighteenth canto in his composition, the great poem *Nalīyacarita*, which is auspicious through the brotherly affection of the sisters Śiva, Śakti, and Siddhi. (154)
Nineteenth Canto:

When the night had reached its tenth watch, bards sang songs— thoroughly imbued with the intense, manifest aesthetic flavors (rasas) revealed by their poetic skill and composed of strings of words sweet to the ear— for the sake of awakening the King of Niṣadha, who was reclining on the lap of his beloved like the fish-marked Moon.
Victory, victory to you, O Great King! Make this morning’s exquisite beauty fruitful for me by bestowing upon my eyes—whose lashes are slightly heavy with sleep—the gift of your gaze.
May the daughter of Vidarbha be your first omen upon rising from bed; for, my dear, what auspiciousness could be greater than the lotus-face of one so beloved?

The quarter belonging to Hari’s queen, as if beholding that moon— who has reached the direction presided over by Varuṇa and is becoming naked through the gradual falling away of the fragments of his mass of radiant garments— now displays her own face, smiling here under the guise of its serene clarity.
The stars, no longer exceedingly large, have ceased to be within the range of vision; the rays of the sun, moving one after another, gradually pervade the sky.
This beloved of the darkness, the moon, whose life-force is now impoverished, proclaims the exhaustion of the night by its feeble light.
A mass of darkness throbs intensely like a vast expanse of mud, clearly kissed by the rapidly flapping beaks of cranes with white-feathered wings;
even the female bee, imagining it to be a crow, shines with a smoky hue as the sun’s exceedingly swift rays cast the splendor of lac-dye upon it.
The clear water droplets resting on the tips of young *kuśa* grass blades— gradually accumulated from the frosty spray of the night’s dew—

rendered the pearls within them utterly insignificant, as they were surpassed by those transformed into something indescribable through their union with the sharp points of iron needles, fashioned by one skilled in piercing gems.
The stars are gathered in the sky to provide the clear and pure *bindu* (dot) for the *oṃkāra*s of the verses of the Sun’s rays;
undoubtedly, the rays have been drawn from the orb of the cool-rayed moon to serve as the high-pitched *udātta* accents for their composition.
Seeing that the night-lily has departed, that Nala— who was the very veil for her eyes— has vanished far away, and that the moon, the lord of stars, has lost its luster,
the sun, the king of rays, destroys the night by seizing it by the hair of darkness, as Rāvaṇa’s son swiftly seized the illusory wife of the Lord of the Raghus.

In the sky, which serves as a couch for the dalliance of the throngs of gods, the moon—a collection of planets—plunges in; it bears a profusion of beauty from the portions of garlands shaken off during amorous play.
Yet, being filled with its belly by masses of cotton-wool in the form of its exceedingly soft rays, the moon cannot serve as a pillow for the cheek of the goddess Lakṣmī.
Surely the rays of the sun now grace his vicinity, for he is the very embodiment of the unfolding of the ten hundred branches of the four Vedas;
even within the cavities of the mouths of those who study them, there rises on the path this very echo of their sacred words.

The Blessed One, the kinsman who requires no external support, leads the lotus to the state of being a resting place for the portico of Indra’s palace—a glory resulting from his tireless circling of the golden mountain, which touches the circle of the western sky as it drives away the darkness of poverty. 11.

Observing the hawk-like flight of the sun’s rays as they roamed through the sky—those arrows that strike down the crows of darkness—the moon fled toward the western quarter out of fear of being slaughtered; and upon reaching it, the stars took flight like pigeons.

The stars shone intensely, like pearls fallen from a necklace; the courtyard of the sky of the gods had been stripped bare by the play of divine amorous dalliance, yet now, after the morning sweeping performed by many hands, it is seen again, distinguished by the splendor of its own natural, unadorned state. (13)
Having first offered the guest-offering (argha) with stars as unbroken grains of rice, variegated by rows of dūrvā grass-blades that dispel the assembly of darkness,
the sky now offers a hospitable reception to the rays of the sun with water-flour made from the series of cool dew-drops moving within it.
Even when the Sun, the benefactor of the Asuras, has met with calamity, why would the preceptor of the sons of Diti not join him with his life-breaths like a wick of darkness?
He recites the life-restoring spell from his throat while rolling about, were it not for his fear of violating the vow of silence during the twilight hours.
On this battlefield, during the moment of nightfall, the plateaus of the Sunrise Mountain bear streams of bitumen melted by the heat, as the sun wanders there;

does this occur because of the respectful prostration of the rising Aruṇa [the Dawn], or perhaps due to contact with his younger sister [the Sun], resulting in a coating of fresh bricks out of apprehension? 16.
Surely the mares dwelling in the powerful army of the sun’s chariot horses neigh as they behold those standing nearby;
meanwhile, the female ruddy goose, her heart dependent on the arrows of Love and filled with deep affection for her own lord, now lusts after him.

At night, deprived of food and parched with thirst from hunger, the young foals whinny most sweetly with their tails swaying; the herd of horses, rising from their place, longs for salt, being eager to lick the stones produced on Mount Manthāna which resound with jewels.
Is it that the assembly of stars lacks the status of Arhats, or is it that the Night lacks propriety, since their lord, whose host of rays is countable, is not seen by them?
It is clear that the chest of the Moon-lord is made of stone, possessing the luster of shimmering dark stone, for alas, even upon separation from these two, it does not melt quickly.
I recognize this twilight as the jewel of heaven, for she who leads [the bride] around the fire—into which the dawn rays have poured parched grain—is that very same one.
Since she formerly caused even the sun to appear like a flickering flame, who would not be eager to gaze upon her hand with curiosity?

We bear the burden of being the foremost among those who possess the glory of being non-dual with Rati and her husband [Kāmadeva], because we speak most excellently in pleasant words; yet we know that even for one who is not angry, such harshness—even if composed in jest—is indeed harmful to merit and does not arise for the delight of either of you. (21)
O you who are pure through austerity, become light-hearted and beautiful; perform your twilight devotions. How is it that this twilight, the younger sister of Night, does not hasten you?

For the Lord of Light (the Sun), who makes things inevitable, must surely remain until the break of day—how many moments will he wait while appearing like a full embryo in the lap of the eastern quarter?
O daughter of Bhīma, it is truly strange that even the lord of the Niṣadha land has become so utterly slack in his devotion to the moon today, his mind stolen away by you, who are a treasury of arts.
He did not consider it a fault to render the twilight fruitless; for he is now intent on bowing to the sun, whom he would otherwise never worship.
O wise lady, there is no one more knowledgeable than you; therefore, do not become the cause of your husband’s downfall into the sin of failing in his prescribed duties.
Indeed, because of your constant abandonment of him, people will surely call this man "the lover of a wanton woman," and others will speak of him with unrestrained and shameful words.
O King, even this most excellent woman, the sky, abandons her companion, the night, for a moment; with the rays of the sun slightly released, she bathes herself.
The glories of the lotuses, departing from the lilies with joy, display a longing to behold the golden water-pot of the sun emerging from the ocean. (25)
The rays of the Lord of Heaven, having clearly beheld Indra—the first Kakubha verse—as their traveler, will perceive you immediately thereafter;
alas, may they display the skill of discerning your respective splendors as they proceed with the capacity for reasoning, deliberation, rejection, and acceptance.
Not too loosely held by their masculine strength, the bees—possessing bold power—having forcibly entered the face of the lotus, emerged;
then, having taken something from its mouth and brought it forth at the junction of dawn, they presented that honey, like fresh food, to their wives.

At the break of day, with one of her petals already opened, the lotus plant creates a thought in the mind of the observer: "Has she begun to consume the full expanse of the sun's rays, having first taken a mouthful of water for the ritual rinsing (āpośāna) in order to receive him? (28)
Now, as if by the clamorous cries of the flocks of birds on the trees along the bank, the lotus-pond has emerged from the seal of its slumber;
the bee drinks the nectar of the day-lotuses with great relish, savoring it repeatedly with the ambrosia of the women’s lips obtained in the interval.

Now, as the life of the departed day comes to an end, the bees—having sought refuge within the hollows of lotus buds that close out of compassion—are seen here, along with their companions, breaking their fast upon the honey as they settle among the blossoming lotuses. (30)
The quarters of the sky grow pale as they part from the darkness, their stars becoming thin; what lake is not revealed like a hawk by the laughter of lotuses?
Only the peak of the sky turns blue with its own burden of infamy, for it bore the weight of the light that destroyed the darkness seeking refuge within it.
Let the groves of day-lotuses laugh, as they are awakened by the rising sun; let not the night-lotus succumb to drowsiness before its friend, the moon of waning luster.
Let this smile of the forest of night-lotuses, whose beauty is the heir to the rocks of the Himalayas, be recognized; meanwhile, let the day-lotuses be overcome by their own sleep.
Let the swarm of bees that has newly arrived here drink honey from the lotus, or let them fill their bellies with the abundance of nectar from the night-lilies;
but here, the cakravāka birds lick the honey called "lip" upon the lotus-face of their own mates to quench their thirst for the night.
In this world, there were two couples who, like the two wheels [of a chariot], had mastered the scriptures of love; they enjoyed each other’s company anew by repeatedly parting from one another.
Because the gods, whose food was nectar, constantly suffered from a distaste for that nectar, the all-pervading Lord Śambhu, the master of those who consume nectar, consumed poison.

As the young woman departs for her husband’s home, the night-fading moon, possessing the luster of mist, desires to leave from its own heart; and as the sun-gem wishes to depart from the heat within the mind, the cakravāka birds, their tongues trembling with the pain of separation, call out here in great agitation, addressing their mate by name.
Does a person, becoming blind through eyes that are like closed buds, falsely accuse the moon-lily of not looking at the sun?
Listen, listen! Those who are the wives of kings in the imagination of poets are said to be "not seeing the sun" (*asūryampaśyā*); it is certainly not the moon-lily who is so described.

The sky appears as if purified by bees that have emerged from the hollows of the lotus-stalks like drops of water falling from the hand of the Lord of the Day, who has swallowed the ocean of darkness;
yet, because they embrace both banks of the stream of honey from the hundred-petaled flowers, these bees repeatedly create in me the suspicion that they are merely masses of mud. (37)
By the youthful rays of the Lord of Light, who move about the vicinity of the lake and disregard the splendor of saffron and rows of jasmine flowers, the bees—
leaping up in joy at the fragrance of the lotuses— were made to assume the beauty of clusters of *guñjā* berries due to their dark, shimmering hue.

Since the very youthful red glow of the sun strives to dye this lake blue as the swarm of bees prepares to alight, the lake has surely become variegated, its central expanse turned pale by clusters of white, blossoming *kavala* lilies. (39)
Oh, how great is the vow of the sun toward the lotus, the abode of merit!

For he benefits the eyes of men, which poets—desiring to express his status as the very dwelling place of splendor—have likened to lotuses through comparison; yet even he abandons the eyes of the owl, since they do not possess that same nature.
O traveler on the path of sacrifice, since you possess such immense devotion to the Sun, approach him quickly while he is still rising;
for at this very hour, it is said that handfuls of water thrown up during worship turn into thunderbolts against those who travel with sluggish camels toward the Sun.

I know not by what person this circle of sun-stones has been opened—having cast off the dark stone of night that served as its lid—to reveal the mine situated on the plateau of the mountain of sunrise, where the rubies of the young sun’s rays are preserved. 42.
It is said that the lord of the gods accepted from Karṇa a pair of earrings and, being their owner, joyfully gave them to the East;
for there, one was seen as the moon at the time of its rising, while the second was perceived as the jewel of the day, streaming with the gold of its newly risen rays.

When her passionate husband, the sun, had set and reached the time of the day’s cessation, his radiance entered the fire. Having forcibly extracted him from the lower world, this flame has been made to reach the city of the Lord of the Immortals; thus, it bears the very form of a chaste wife’s vow.
This saying of the wise is indeed true: that the dark complexion of a son arises from the food of his father’s white and green [vegetables] and so forth;
for even from the sun, whose body possessed a stainless luster, darkness was produced by Yama, Yamunā, and Kṛṣṇa, who drank from it. 45.
The Sun-god has long practiced this habit: at the end of every night, he brings forth this very time consisting of day;
yet it was not possible for him to abandon this nature born of Time, just as he could not avoid giving birth to Yama and Yamunā when producing them in the past.
Ruciracaraṇa, whose chariot was graced by the great beauty of his charioteer Sūta, begot two sons—Śani and Śamana—to protect the worlds.
Since even the Sun, that kinsman of the eyes and ocean of compassion for those who travel, was mocked by the wicked, what villain will not mock us? (47)
He who provides heat to those suffering from the ailments of winter so that embodied beings may find the rise of comfort, and who gives water to those whose mouths are parched by harsh rays,
and who bestows warmth upon those afflicted by cold and coolness upon those tormented by heat— this Sun rises, his activity revolving around the pursuit of the welfare of others.
In this world, what wonder does it not display? For the darkness, having taken refuge in the hollows of the four quarters, was about to consume them in an instant;
yet, seeking shelter among the trees, that darkness dwelt in the form of shadows, for the rays of the sun were rendered powerless to dispel it. (49)
Having studied under this very father of his—who, like the Sun, cures the darkness and fainting of the world and even of the lotus-thickets—these two Aśvins practice medicine;
moreover, since Yama is his father, is it not fitting that he rises mercilessly to bring about the untimely death of the night-lotuses?
That the lord of the stars (the moon) tormented the lotus plant—though it was free from disease—and that the night-lily laughed at the sun’s consort (the day-lotus):
I suspect both of these have now contracted out of their own apprehension, as the new sun rises with a luster as red as the *karkandhū* fruit. (51)
I know that the Sun, whose body consists of the Vedas, has ten hundred branches of light extending through the path below the earth;
every night, the Lord of Serpents hears their resonant sounds with his two thousand eyes, and perceives their radiant splendors simultaneously.
Those before whom the state of having many claws truly appears are these rays of the sun, the friend of the lotus, possessing the luster of coral.
It is most fitting that the grace of their fingers has been embraced by certain elongated parts entering within the lattice-work.
Behold these rays of the sun, like fingers, which have entered through the lattice-windows of the palace as if to be drunk at once by the eyes;
they appear to be whirling rapidly, overtaken by a swarm of circling atoms—were they not perhaps fashioned anew by the carpenter of heaven upon his lathe?
Like a barber, the day, having shorn the braid of darkness with the sharp razors of the sun’s rays, has brought the night to an end;
consequently, the surface of the earth now surely appears white from all sides due to the mass of falling hair, under the guise of various shadows.
O Nala, we declare that your fame is a conch-shell created for the sake of prosperity, its sound being its sibling; that king of birds (the swan) is clearly inscribed in heaven.
Behold truly here the cutting off of his hand, which inspires faith; yet even that, though a cause for withering, is exceedingly beautiful as a spot upon him who is so captivating.

The moon, half-set and bearing the likeness of a saw with its rays for teeth— pale as the silt of the powder from conchs whose water has been swept away by those very rays— is being subjected to a firm pressure by the trunk of the elephant of the ocean, which moves with great effort to shatter the lotuses that obstruct the path of the sun’s sharp brilliance.
Desiring to split the lotus, the hot-rayed sun presses upon it with his hand, destroying the array of star-conchs;
now, because the moon—the lover of the night—has been forced to hide behind half the mountain of setting, his orb acts as a saw for cutting through the conch-shell.

Since the sun awakens the eyes [of the lotuses] by opening the petals of the day-lotuses, and since Hari filled the thousand eyes [of Viṣṇu] with day-lotuses, there is indeed a real kinship between the lotuses and the eyes;
it is because of this that the metaphor of the lotus for the eye is so highly cherished by poet-men. (59)

I recognize that very same night-lily, which formerly possessed the splendor of a watchman over the entire lotus-pond with its interior as wide as a blossoming petal-eye, now, having reached the day, falls into the bliss of sleep, thickened by the fierce humming of bees wandering within its heart.

Here at dawn, questioned by a crow whose speech was restricted to the form of the interrogative word "kim" (what), he replied with the words "tātaṇau" (the *t* and *ṇ* sounds) according to the rules of the grammar of the Serpent-born (Patañjali): "Tell me, which two are the substitutes for the original sounds? Thus, the cuckoo gave its answer in the form of the word "tuhi. 61.

In the grammar of Pāṇini (the son of Dākṣī), there was surely some student who became a pigeon; his throat followed the ornament of the few remaining hard pens, which had been worn away by the effort of mastering the flood of sounds.
Having forgotten everything, yet by chance remembering at dawn the technical term *ghu* that he had once memorized, he still shakes his head today with the vigor born from reciting the wooden slates.
In the eastern direction, with its rays like the voices of young cuckoos, the sun—possessing the smooth splendor of saffron and bearing the Vaijayantī banner of the dawn—steals the heart;
this golden-bodied sun is truly the pinnacle of Indra’s palace, and it is fitting that the ocean of darkness drinks from it through the waters of his own radiance.
With only two or three rays, which act like a conflagration for devouring the dense thickets of *tāmatamāla* trees, he has bestowed a festival of days upon this assembly of thousand-petaled lotuses.
Now, the sun’s heat, having pulverized the mass of darkness over the earth, the quarters, and the sky, spreads forth its touch with such speed that it is rendered utterly futile.

This sun, the submarine fire of the ocean of darkness that has long since ascended [to the sky], the laughing-stock of the sporting lotus groves now languishing—why does he not yet assume his own brilliant whiteness? Even today, the rows of rays from the jewel of the sky continue to redden the heavens.

"By this morning description, the Goddess, being thoroughly pleased, has bestowed upon you the grace of ornaments for her own body"— with these words placed before them by the women of the inner apartments,
the bards donned a circle of ornaments that dispelled poverty, which possessed the luster of eyes reddened by the surge of anger at the brilliance of the rubies.

As they approached, saying "Wait a moment," the king received their hospitality in the form of a glance; having performed his morning ablutions in the waters of the celestial Ganges, he ascended with joy the Puṣpaka chariot—which had been obtained as his wife's dowry—and departed from the palace unnoticed by those who had arrived later.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crowns of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this nineteenth canto has reached its conclusion in his work, the *Nalīyacarita*, a great poem consisting of a single, uninterrupted composition of new themes. (68)
The twentieth canto:
Like a cloud of a chariot with the speed born of the wind, he reached from the sky the plateau of the mountain-like palace, which possessed various minerals upon its terraced slopes.
Then the daughter of Bhīma went out to meet her beloved as he approached nearby,
like the wave of the western ocean meeting the moon at the sound of "Om" at day's end.
With his gaze fixed solely on her face, he perceived from afar a profound reverence,
as if it were the splendor of the golden lotuses of the Mandākinī.
Holding that message from her own country within the hollow of her hand,
she shone like a lotus bearing a lotus, she whose eyes were like blossoming lotuses.
She valued even a small gift given by her beloved as exceedingly great;
for she contemplated that single cowrie shell as being equal to a hundred thousand.
That beloved said to her, "O slender one, this [act] is an obstacle to your embrace;
let the remaining ritual be completed, if there is no distress in your mind."
"Where is there such a rule today that pierces the very vitals of your jest?"—
thus she spoke to him in her mind out of anger, but not in words.
"O innocent one, you grow weary of the ritual precisely because it involves a momentary interruption;
yet he who shall cause your separation will not do so for long"—thus did Kali speak then from his heart. (8)
Then, as if with disdain, she approached the king’s lotus-faced friend,
just as Lakṣmī leaves the bed of night-lotuses to go near the day-lotus.
"May he not become like another Kali or Dvāpara age for me," thinking thus, he satisfied that Tretā age with his own perpetual sacrificial session.
Having performed the morning rites and restraining her friend with his hand,
he stood behind her and closed her eyes with both hands.
He was gazed upon by Damayantī’s companions with smiles,
as if they were measuring the extent of their beloved’s eyes with their own outstretched palms.
Thinking, "Are you perhaps my husband?", she spoke these half-words as he released her hand;
perceiving the difference in his touch, she who cherished her pride fell silent.
"O Sāvitrī, daughter of Sutanu, this anger of yours is not appropriate;
for what reason, O beloved, do you disregard that asceticism by whose grace I obtained you? (14)

If you intend to harbor resentment because I did not greet you with a formal salutation after bathing—even though I had become your slave during the night—then speak that resentment; you are worthy of being honored.
To prevent her from stepping upon this [spot], he pressed her hands with force;
then, restraining her with anger and apprehension, he bewildered her with his sidelong glances. (16)
Then the lord of the Niṣadhas, captivated by the shimmering flash of her tremulous side-glances, spoke to that slender maiden. (17)
Has your gaze, having begun with the deceptive speed of a sidelong glance to leap far away, turned back out of fear upon perceiving the well of your ear? 18.
O lotus-eyed one, even when angry, you arise for my delight;
even when scorched, the sun’s radiance exists only for the fragrance of the hundred-petaled lotus.
I suspect that the Creator, having fashioned the moon, repeatedly broke it apart because its beauty was eclipsed by the delusive splendor of the orb of your face.
Your letters, which are clear, sweet, and exceedingly competitive with pearls produced on the banks of the Tāmraparṇī and born from the womb of the moon, [are truly excellent]. 21.
O wonder! Your words have arisen together with the nectar itself from the ocean of milk;
even today, they bear the traces of a smile like a smear of running milk.
Like the moon embracing the eastern mountain with its moonlight,
he adorned the couch, having transferred his beloved onto his own lap.
Like a cloud at the onset of the rainy season embracing the glossy sky, he long embraced his beloved to release her from the exhaustion of their separation.
His face was like a cucumber, and he was immersed in her essence, resting upon a smile,
just as the sun is reflected in the midst of the honey of a lotus.
Then, calling his dear friend named Kalā by the hand,
he seated her before him and spoke, making her a witness to his jesting.
O lotus-faced one, why does your friend not show us favor?
I think that, being attached to you all, he does not hold others in high regard. (27)
"This beloved has been favored by me through my own surrender during the night"—
this woman of false speech does not yet deceive her friends.
As for her saying, "I do not cherish anyone other than Nala even in my mind," that was rendered false by the god of love, whose presence in her was inferred from her youth.
If you were to speak of the beauty of her face,
we would still not perceive it now, for our heads are bowed in shame.
With her full gaze she looks upon this row of friends, but with a mere atom of a sidelong glance, she looks at me as if I were guilty of an offense.
She does not regard me as she does now; therefore, let her imagine that I, who was seen by her while acting as a messenger, have been forgotten by her in such a manner. (32)
This very friend reveals her passion to me with words that are pleasant and like nectar; yet, though she says "you are mine," the proud woman remains silent toward me once again.
Which female friend does she not address by name, calling her by name? Yet, O Kali, she does not touch our name with her tongue, nor does she call us "Nala. (34)
In her heart, which is occupied by full breasts and is merciless toward us, there is not even a tiny fraction of space; where, then, shall she bear us? (35)
Having understood her heart to be such, we indeed perceive the aversion of her breasts, which have cast off softness and maintained their proper conduct.
Having spoken thus to her with a taunting jest, while his throat was thus silenced, he was addressed by her, who had learned a smile from the face of Damayantī. (37)
This [affection] has been well cultivated by you; indeed, you possess a fresh passion toward us, while our friend maintains a long-standing attachment toward you. (38)
"O you who are learned in the science of love, how can this young bride of ours be enjoyed by you? How can she speak to us? Tell us. (39)
O Lord, the worlds sing of you as one whose speech is never false;
therefore, a woman who speaks otherwise would not be dear to you, even if she were beautiful in form. (40)
"O Lord, the Mind-born (Cupid) exists within her heart, yet he is none other than you;
for her friend, the mind, has you as its place of abode day and night. (41)
Then, that Love-god became a reflection within the heart of your friend;
otherwise, how could he, being bodiless, possess a form identical to his? (42)
"Who is Smara? Who are you?"—in this doubt arising from the beauty of both, she holds either of you in her heart because of her longing for you alone. (43)
Because she perceives that a mind once placed upon you is difficult to draw back,
this lotus-eyed woman touches you with a mere glance out of apprehension.
From the moment you beheld her, you have been fixed within the very grip of her eyes; look for yourself, for if you have doubt, what confidence can there be in another's word? (45)
"By beginning with the transfer of the saffron from her breasts during our embrace, she has already uttered these very words: 'Such is the passion of my heart for you. (46)

This man, observing a vow of muttering prayers from the *Kāmasūkta* hymn that bears your name with his mind, kisses the rosary on his friend’s neck under the pretext of it being a single-stringed necklace. 47.
Since your great heart has been occupied by my friend, we say that her breasts, no longer finding room within, have emerged outside. (48)
Her two breasts, free from blemish, have been pressed and wounded by you;
how can those large ones show their faces, covered as they are with shame? (49)
Thus, having been sprinkled with these hymns that showered nectar by means of his artistic skill, he asked his beloved, who had raised her face, "Is it indeed thus? (50)
And the husband’s hand, raising his beloved’s face,
shone like a lotus that has finally attained union with the moon after a long time.
Then Damayantī, both bashful and smiling, turning her face back again,
became a source of great joy for her husband.
Once again, the king, together with his beloved and longing for the playful sport of jesting, spoke with a smile to her friend.
Let this friend of ours resolve to forgive the offense of this day;
for she does not perform here toward us that which is characteristic of the night, namely the act of "niśi" (to destroy). 54.
If, by day, the moon—the friend of this face—is eclipsed, then the splendor of the lotuses, which are its friends, is likewise diminished. (55)
Shame was conquered by her while she played with me;
now that it has returned, ask whom it belongs to.
"Even though she bit my lip at night, let her not be angry with me;
for does the *bimbī* creeper ever feel resentment toward the parrot that eats its fruit? (57)
The beauty of the frontal globes of the elephant has been stolen by her breasts, which bear the beautiful marks of the goad; behold, O King, that I might not crush those two!
Let my mouth be at fault for drinking the nectar from her lower lip;
what offense has my head committed that it does not obtain to kiss her feet? (59)
"Ask me what offense I, who have listened to your words, have committed, that the lute speaks so harshly to me and the sweet-voiced cuckoo so cruelly? (60)
Let her speak to you, having placed her trust in you as she did with Āliñjana;
why then is that affection of hers toward us now forgotten? (61)
Then, under the pretext of bringing her own ear near the ear of Damayantī for the sake of whispering,
she drew her own face close to her [the princess's] ear and spoke to her.
"O rogue, you have not said anything at all regarding my private conduct! Stay here; I shall cause this gentleman to report that very matter to the King. (63)
"Even though you have studied the science of love under my very instruction,
why have you committed this perversion of the marital bond by doing something that should not be done?"
While she remained silent, as if listening to her words,
she repeatedly uttered the sound "hum-hum" at intervals during the debate.
Then, having approached and taken her seat— her boldness suggesting a desire for pleasure— and having experienced the blow from her friend’s playful lotus, she addressed the king.
It has been seen, O Great King, it has been seen: that he strikes me thus, or else threatens me with his brow, out of anger at my pleading for your sake. (67)
"This Nala speaks without any identifying mark; by what sign can he be recognized?
I suspect that Śakra himself, having created an illusion, has come here."
This gift of lotuses from the golden lotus-lake of the celestial river brings about both your status as Indra and your arrival here from heaven.
"I have perceived the illusory shadow of the King of Niṣadha in Hari;
and having heard of his misconduct, I spoke to Ahalyā. (70)

The princess of Vidarbha, whose intellect is as sharp as the tip of a blade of darbha grass, honors your status as the slayer of Jambha as it emanates from your lotus-hand that embraces the thunderbolt.
If you are truly the Prince of Niṣadha, then by personally revealing her secret deeds—which have no other witness—you will pierce through her agony of suspicion. (72)
Having heard these words, which concealed their well-executed deception, he, being filled with doubt as to her true state, spoke. (73)
Do you remember how, while you were feigning sleep, I placed my hand upon your navel, causing your hair to stand on end with joy as you became "Lotus-navelled"? (74)
O tender one, overcome by shame and fear, you were released by me halfway through this new festival of love, for I was distracted by my own exhaustion and dread. (75)
Remember how, having conquered you in battle, I kissed you on the crowded street as you ran toward my feet, while your two fingers were joined together.

Do you know how, even while intoxicated with pride, she—dejected by her lack of affection for me—looked at herself and me reflected in each other’s eyes and was pained by the line that stood between us? (77)
It has not been forgotten by you that, deluded by infatuation, I drank from your tongue while insatiable for drinking from your lips. (78)
Remember in your heart the impression of the moist nail-marks upon your breasts, arising from our embrace—the very craft of which I spoke to your smiling friends. (79)
While you were sporting with other women in the midst of a wine-party, you looked at me with anger;
do you remember how I, before them, indeed stumbled with my head at your feet? (80)
"Do you know what happened when I returned from my journey and saw you, O tender-hearted one?
You surely kissed the female bee while embracing her with playful joy. (81)
There, the refined impression remains awake, for from my own mouth to yours, I have scattered and offered those pieces of betel-leaf according to propriety. (82)
Is there in your heart that wound born of a nail which was inflicted by you in anger upon Śambūka, who stood guilty of an offense committed in a previous existence? (83)
Even in dreams, when we turn our sides at night by merely exchanging our respective directions, there is happiness for us two in that friendship which remains free from aversion.
Having found a moment when my gaze was averted, you showed me your bitten lower lip and, meditating upon me, threatened me. (85)
Having observed her thus, through the graceful movement of whirling the lotus-stalk, she joined her hands and said, "Please grant me your grace, for I have propitiated you. (86)
"You likely do not remember my offering betel-leaf with my hand placed upon your lotus-hand; nor indeed do I remember that. (87)
For it was indeed false that you, my friend, left me—who am speaking the truth—and went to your companions;
even there, as I approached, you playfully plucked a blade of grass from before me. (88)
Do you remember, my beloved, how you were once reproached by me as you cried out like a female cuckoo, saying, "O pure night, you who cannot endure a second round of love-making"? (89)
While I am eating fresh neem, she serves me honey; remembering this, you should consider that my passion exists even toward my co-wives, despite your own anger. 90.
Remember how I praised you, saying, "This has been prepared by you after tasting the sugar-candy," and how I was afraid of your lower lip, which was reddened by the anger of that self-reproach.
Kissing again and again from the mouth down to the navel, I was never satiated;
yet there is that which I could not reach to kiss—may my memory kiss that blessed thing. 92.
Remember that certain amorous sport wherein you, having been addressed by me as "bhavān," were embarrassed and smiled. (93)
Remember how, at that very moment, your own face—its chin darkened by sweat moistened with passion—was seen reflected in the gem of your necklace. (94)
"Remember that nail-mark on my thigh; why do you say 'He gave it' falsely?
For I have violated the vow of modesty, which is the deity of our secret tryst. (95)
When, during our forest play, you were made to feel bashful by my words—"Throw this leaf of the *smarāśvattha* tree that has fallen to the ground toward me"—you were truly put to shame. (96)
While her lover was thus recounting her secrets with pauses, she,
overcome by shame, covered her friend’s ears with both hands.
Seeing her friend’s eyes, which were like blue lotuses, pressing against her ears, Damayantī’s two hands, resembling red lotuses, also pressed them [the ears]. (98)
The speech of her husband, having entered the ears of her friend, the princess of Vidarbha seemed to cover it over with shame, as if intent on concealing her own secret.
Seeing Nala laughing with a sarcastic smile at his beloved’s playful jest,
her other friends also laughed, even though they did not understand the true nature of the situation from afar.
Out of affection for the couple, those celestial nymphs of the earth showered fragrant flowers of smiles upon them with the breezes from their mouths. (101)
Then, born from his smile, a radiant smile shone upon them, like the blossoming of a cluster of night-lotuses from the light of the cool-rayed moon. ||102||
Having recognized the voice of her friend, which was radiant with a smile,
Kalā became empowered among those women who were her own partisans.
Then the merchant called out loudly to her: "Come, O beautiful one, you who have been deceived by heaven; drink the nectar-streams of the words of this moon among kings! (104)
The slender-waisted Badarī heard a portion of his voice, though she was not very close, just as a small village hears the faint sound of thunder at the end of an aeon.
Then, as she listened to the words concerning Niṣadha, the clever Damayantī perceived her inner state from the gem upon Nala’s head resting against her own back.

Having inferred [the truth] from her friend’s facial expressions as they were observed in a reflection, she, imitating that friend’s bashfulness and other gestures, was herself inferred by her friend as if she were listening.
Having repeatedly made such gestures, she spoke; he heard her words clearly:
"You understand these words falsely, or else my deities would be rendered powerless. (108)
O King, since my beloved’s hands will be pained by the tight pressure of my ear-ornaments, it is fitting that you restrain her.
Thus she caused her friend's ears to be released from the husband's grasp,
as she was proceeding to obey her husband while vainly attempting to prevent his exertion.
Then, the sound of that sudden renunciation reached his ears like a rhythmic clapping, severing the continuous stream of noise born from the obstruction of his hearing.
Having retreated a short distance, she rejoiced and then smiled; and approaching her friend, Kalā entreated her with plaintive tones as follows: (112)
"I shall tell you the secret that was heard by me from those two; describe what you have heard to me, come, friend, let it be exchanged. (113)
At the request of her friend, she first feigned the hearing of a secret;
at this, the couple were struck with wonder and shook their heads. (114)
To her who was thus speaking to him, the Lord of Niṣadha replied:
"If you two have been deceived by me through the rashness of false oaths, then remain [as you are]. (115)
The peacock replied to him: "Whence could this suspicion of a blemish arise?
Today, you yourself have uttered a falsehood regarding what was said by your beloved's attendants. (116)
It is indeed true that I heard a great humming sound;
I said only, "I hear," but not even, "Your voice. (117)
Having thus addressed you, O Lord, I maintain that such an oath—even if true—is indeed futile when it results in a harsh consequence through the power of fate. (118)
How indeed can you deceive me with discourses on non-enjoyment?
Alas, it is unworthy of you that I should not be led astray by you both! 119.
Then, whispering from ear to ear, the two friends told each other what they had heard;
and they marveled repeatedly, smiling much.
Then Kalāsakhī said: "O Damayantī, do not be angry with me;
for I spoke thus only after concealing [the truth] even from her second ear. (121)
Then the lover said to his beloved: "The proficiency in deceit of these two female friends of yours has been witnessed; therefore, do not place your trust in your companions alone. (122)
Even though she conversed with him, her husband did not speak at all;
he kept his secrets from her in private, yet behaved with such confidence toward her in public that she was like a member of his assembly.
As she was thus rising up, Nala said to his beloved:
"Speak, O daughter of Bhīma; shall I cast this ill-behaved one out of the house?"
Then, gratified by the fair-toothed woman’s consent signaled by a nod of her head, the beloved cast a handful of water from his cupped hands onto the two friends. 125.
The sprinkling of water from the garments by Citradatta and Acitta was performed loudly;
even from afar, they were drenched by those waters which fulfilled Nala's desire.
By the boon of Varuṇa, this [ocean] made the hearts of these two still with its easily obtainable loads of water, and even with its wonders.
Even by that [means], Damayantī and her friend did not retreat;
instead, he showed them with joy, saying, "Look, O slender one, here before me! (128)

Having soaked her garment with water for the sake of becoming a Jaina female ascetic, the two friends— though still wearing their silk garments— were able to see each other’s breasts without obstruction.
This very illusion has manifested itself as the water of Śambara, since it reveals their limbs even though they are covered by a cloth. (130)
This [splendor] of yours, appearing as the garment of the sky, has arrived, characterized by beautiful necklaces, rows of gems, and the gaze of the sun. 131.
Seeing their own condition, the two of them departed from there in shame; out of curiosity to see them, all their friends followed one after another and went outside.
Stepping outside, they said to the princess of Vidarbha, who was skilled in policy:
"Your two friends, who know your secrets, must not be neglected by you even now."
Then the king spoke aloud to them: "This friend has told you this;
her secret was heard by these two, but their secret was seen by me. (134)
One should not place trust in the words of these two, who are my adversaries;
for Brahmā has consecrated them upon a throne of illusory falsehood.
Even when his enemy’s beautiful conduct has been washed away by the streams of his fame, who are not skilled artisans at painting the mark of falsehood with the soot of calumny? (136)
Those two friends said: "We shall not say much;
we will speak only of that for which we have all been exiled. (137)
The architects did not perceive her due to her great height and her steady hands;
even when she spoke in such a manner, they were prevented by the trembling of their own hands.
"Depart from here, O bold one! Fie upon your habit of lewd and unseemly speech!
When this was said, they too spoke [in response] and fled away in fear. (139)
Nala said to his beloved, who was bashful at those words and had her face cast down:
"There is no friend so shameless as this certain buffoon, not even in the slightest degree."
Ah! This face of yours is truly golden, yet devoid of shame;
for even when subjected to extreme heat, no discoloration emerges from it. (141)
Then, placing her upon his heart, he laid his body upon the surface of the bed;
and closing his eyes, he relished the delicacy of her limbs.
Placing his hands upon her pair of breasts and inserting them between her waistband,
he made the labor of grasping her hand truly fruitful.
Carrying her, who had been placed upon him, with joy in his heart, he clearly proclaimed his own status as the one who carries her. (144)
With the seal of musk-paste wiped away by his perspiring fingers, he caused his beloved’s breasts to cry out in pain before her friends. 145.
Placing his fingernail upon her breast and feeling a thrill, he was watched by her;
he said to her, "Why does this [nail] not pierce me, who dwells within your heart?"
"Ah! What impropriety is this in your heart, which, though pure, has been treated as if impure—marked by my sharp-pointed nails as if by villains! (147)
O lady with beautiful hips and thighs, that garment of yours, which kisses your buttocks and embraces your breasts, enjoys its own virtuous nature, worthy of an auspicious fate. 148.
Beholding her perspiring and slightly visible lower garment clinging to her hips,
he sighed and lamented the length of the day.
He bit her very lip right at the edge of her beloved's lower lip;
there, he feigned the restless playfulness of drinking from her lower lip. 150.
"O girl with tremulous eyes, I am unable to endure the agony of Love's arrows;
therefore, be gracious, be gracious!"—saying this, he provoked her to anger even though she was already pleased.
The eyes of the Lord of Niṣadha went from the lotus-face of his beloved to her two breasts, and from those two they went to her full hips. (152)
Thus, out of impatience and fearing his forceful conduct, she rose suddenly and followed her friends with longing. (153)
As if restraining him to the best of her ability by extending a slow vibration,
the breasts and hips of Damayantī, longing for union with Nala, held him back.
Even though his arms were as thick as the pillars of an elephant, he was unable to support her, who was languid from the weight of her hips, for he was paralyzed by the touch of her limbs.
"Embracing me again and again, O slender-limbed one,"— having spoken these half-finished words to her beloved,
she smiled, turned back, and gazing at him, went to the far side of the doorway.
Having begun to speak unpleasant words to her beloved, she—feeling inward remorse and being modest by nature—was unable, before her friends, either to go on or to turn back. (157)
Then Bandisundarī, approaching the presence of the gate, spoke to Nala at midday:
"Victory to you, O King! Your land, scorched by the heat of the day's youth, thirsts for the waters of a bath. (158)

The water offered from the Ganges, possessing the luster of a conch shell, desires through contact with the curls of your hair to experience immediately thereafter the beauty of being mixed with the Yamunā, whose waves are unrivaled in their tranquility. (159)
Having ascended to the very summit of the world, the sun now blazes with a wondrous majesty like you;
behold him, surpassed by the merits arising immediately from your service to the Destroyer of Cities.

As if forcibly summoning joy despite the absence of initiation for the meditation and worship of Hara, the king—exhausted by the grief of separation from his beloved—repeatedly cast his gaze toward the direction of the side door; then, with the thought that his beloved had suddenly returned, he rose to go out. 161.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crowns of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered the host of his senses;
this naturally radiant twentieth canto in his great poem, whose poetic descriptions are to be measured by flavors untrampled by others, has thus concluded in the *Nalacarita*. (162)
The Twenty-first Canto:
As he was ascending from the jeweled palace of the queen of Vidarbha, followed by the kings who had shown their service,
his own status as a tributary king was once again proclaimed by those other monarchs through the gesture of their hands.
Thinking that even a path bound with Chinese silk was too hard for her pair of feet,
the row of queens bowing down on all sides indeed bore her upon their heads with garlands of flowers.

O King, his own unprecedented jewel—variegated with qualities enhanced by diligent craftsmanship—was then quickly brought forth by those who had been made content by the great honor of receiving his glance. (3)

Other kings received that jewel presented by another monarch as a mark of his favor, while others obtained it through gestures such as the movement of fingers, the play of the eyes, or the undulation of the eyebrows. ||4||
Then, having dismissed them like a father after they had been nourished by the sprinkling of wholesome and truthful words,
he of immeasurable luster trained them— who were brought near as pupils— in the practice of missiles and weapons.
Having instructed his circle of excellent disciples in the science of weapons, which is difficult for mortals to master, he—
his brow marked by beads of sweat and breathing heavily— became desirous of bathing.

Women with lofty breasts sprinkled him— his limbs already softened by being rubbed with *yakṣakardama* paste, his head previously anointed with deer-musk— with fragrant waters that attracted swarms of bees.
The pure domestic priest bathed that king, who was a bearer of the earth and possessed a mass of vast ascetic merit,
by pouring from above waves of water from sacred fords whose currents fell like those from a rain-cloud.

The pair of his lotus-hands, as he bathed, shone like two blades of *darbha* grass held within them, bearing, as it were, spreading trails of smoke born from the fire of separation from the breasts of his beloved.
The water of the Gaṅgā, kissing the interior of his cupped palms as he imagines it for the purpose of sipping,
brings the sky— filled with reflections merged in its own purity— into his very hand.
Having obtained her brother Damanaka’s release, the Earth, still filled with passion,
embraced him limb by limb as he was eager to take her, she who was once soft as mud now softened by water.

With pure *darbha* grasses placed upon his head by Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra—standing respectively at the base, the middle, and the peak [of the mountain], and stationed at his hands, feet, and head—they poured water over him as if it were the waves of the Gaṅgā disgorged from their mouths. (12)
As he held his breath within the water,
his face took on a loveliness like that of the moon, which had previously dwelt for a time in the belly of the lord of rivers.

Wearing a garment as bright as a cloudless sky and radiant with stars, he who brings delight to the world of mortals put on the attire of the moon-crested Lord, as if in rivalry with him whose raiment is the ten directions.
As if wishing to join her at every step as she followed Bhīmajā, that lord of royal sages did not cover his heart on all sides under the pretext of the fold of his upper garment.

The auspicious splendor of the bath attended upon him: its breasts were the jars filled with bathing water; its moon-like face was marked by a spot of white clay; and its teeth were the drops of water remaining in his hair. 16.

Seeing her who was white, cool, divine, possessed of mantras, sweet, and joyful— she who possesses four eyes— his sense of smell, having vainly harbored a longing for fragrance, became like one that inhales water.
As the queen sprinkled with her own hand the water she had taken for the arrival of the sun,
the flickering illusions created by that shimmering radiance caused people to suspect that the sun was moving across the lathe of Tvaṣṭṛ.
As he recited them correctly, the Vedic mantras came to reside within his lotus-like hand;
with their pure seeds and clear, distinct syllables, they assumed the guise of beads upon a crystal rosary.
Furthermore, he described the offering of barley for the libations to the gods as being upon the joints of his fingers;
with the masses of sesame seeds mixed with the water being poured out, he became one whose hands and time were doubly marked by sesame.
With hands and feet purified, he entered the temple of the gods attended by celibate students, proceeding along a high, clean path untrodden by the feet of others— this royal seer.
