Somewhere in the sky, by means of the swarms of bees produced from the smoke of incense made of dark aloe-wood,
a veil was formed over the mass of light belonging to the garlands and wreaths of beautiful flowers.

Those very rays of light, which previously made the night as yellowish-red as a sprout with its intense glow, were held there by them to be offered to the gods like golden tilaka-marks; they appeared like lamps.

There, the oyster shells shone as they experienced within themselves a filling of saffron— red like fire— which, in the absence of the pearl-gem, was held by the "fire-footed" (Cupid) as a token of love.
There, the vessel made of emerald stone, its surface kissed by the paste of rich sandalwood,
found comfort in the mouth of Rāhu as he swallowed the moon during their amorous play.
There, silver vessels, thick with the mire of musk from the bellies of deer,
attained a resemblance to the moon whose interior is clouded by its own dark spot.
In that dense thicket of Dharma, where there was indeed the suspicion that sprouts of merit were emerging,
he offered rows of oblations consisting of abundant sugar and parched grain, which resembled the palaces of the Sugata.
In one place, a profusion of campaka flowers made the mountain—once known as the abode of the hosts of immortals—seem short;
and there, a heap of jasmine blossoms drew up the lofty peak that was like crystal.
He disregarded the noble wife who was guarding even her own beloved husband;
for there, the ground was so crowded with offerings to the heart-pleasing deities that it lacked any space at all.

Where, upon the paved floors, the reflections of the dancers' heads shone with a rhythmic beat (*kuṭṭimita*), as their hair— composed of rays from blue gemstones pressed by the hands of their lovers— gleamed.

There, that lord of the earth sat upon a spotless gem-stool, which was filled with ornaments of many-colored jewels, provided with faultless offerings, and beautiful with a profusion of variegated cloths.
While Nala worshipped the Sun with steady devotion, Karṇa, whose heart was tainted by malice toward him, mocked him;
meanwhile, the sun, as if reflecting the faith in the heart of Śraddhādhana, shone resplendently upon Sāmba.
In the mutterings of the secret mantras of various deities, the rosaries took on his luster,
as if the clusters of seeds from red sandalwood were striving intensely to learn that very crimson hue.
Tryambaka, having performed worship with the blossoms of the tree named *heman*,
shone as if with a flower-trumpet, having conquered the Lord of Rati in battle by means of that very [trumpet] he had assumed.
Worshipping the hand of Hara with a smile and a flower from the *nāgakesara* tree,
he bestowed upon it the white splendor of the skull of a directional guardian (Dikpāla) that had been turned sideways.
Having placed a garland made of blue lotuses as an ornament for his neck-stalk,
he rendered even his crystal body consistent with the title "Blue-throated" (Nīlakaṇṭha).
The enemy of the cities (Śiva), the foe of Madana, will find delight in this deed performed by me;
for he previously burnt that city with water in the form of smoke, and then [consumed] the arrow of Kāma.
Unable to endure even for a moment more the separation from the daughter of Bhīma,
he closed his eyes in a swoon of meditation, as if terrified by the moon upon the crest of Śiva.
Rolling on the ground like a staff, he prostrated himself before Tryambaka like Kāma seeking refuge,
having laid down his own weapons— the bow and arrows— in place of flowers at the pair of the god’s feet.
Having placed flowers resembling his own weapons at the feet of Tryambaka, did Kāma, rolling upon the ground like a staff, approach that refuge and bow down? 40.

As he was engaged in the recitation of the Śatarudriya, the row of Rudra’s eyes— belonging to one who is devoted to Rudra— took refuge upon his hand, which was like a fresh sprout, just as a swarm of bees takes shelter on a blossoming leaf.
That king worshipped the Supreme Person with the rites prescribed in the *Puruṣasūkta*,
and he also paid homage to the twelve forms of Keśava while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
He beheld him seated upon a throne fashioned from a circular wreath of jasmine flowers, appearing like the very embodiment of the Lord of Serpents wearing his own earrings.
A garland of blue lotuses belonging to the binder of Bala (Indra) shimmered upon his chest,
its millions of filaments acting as the wide-eyed side-glances of Śrī, who resides upon the jeweled floor known as the Kaustubha gem.
With hundreds of golden *ketaka* flowers, a lotus fashioned from gold, a garland of silver, and a *karavīra* flower of red gemstone, he rendered the decoration upon his head superfluous. (45)

By means of small offerings of food, oblations of grain, and presentations of food, that Kṛṣṇa was not captivated; rather, his worship through the water-offering of conches and discs resulted in his form appearing like one born from the water of conches and discs.
O Queen, as the smoke from black aloe-wood incense was offered here in worship to the one whose banner bears the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa),
the snakes held by you emerged through the lattice-windows as if stained by the ill-fame born of fear.
Covering him with thousands of smiling jasmine garlands interspersed with priceless gems and flower wreaths,
he made him appear as if submerged in an ocean of milk filled with many jewels.
The row of lotus seeds on his rosary, having come into contact with his hand as he recited prayers,
returned once more to the lotus-dwelling to enjoy its long-term residence.

With her head bowed at the feet of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, she shone like the daughter of Jahnu when she was honored by the Lord of the World with a garland of *vicakila* flowers, as he humbly entreated her for his longed-for purpose.
The sinless one, indicating his own passion for Kamalā by placing her upon his heart,
nevertheless showed respect for the Goddess of Speech by placing his own throat above her, the abode of Śrī.
Realizing this, he did not find joy even in receiving great wealth through worship;
instead, he sought to cultivate devotion to Hari with offerings consisting of the pearls of well-spoken verses.
"Praise from afar is beyond the range of words for you; our description of your form is your censure.
Therefore, forgive me for what I babble"—saying this, he spoke as follows. (53)
O people, this world is insentient and self-luminous; yet you desire to provide a description of it.
But surely, can darkness ever possess the nature of illumination toward the light of the sun? 54.
May you never become an object of speech and mind; otherwise, how could they not direct themselves toward you?
For even a cloud that does not reach them might bring satisfaction to a pair of cātaka birds with their necks upraised.
Like the water of the ocean tossed up by the lashing of the tail of you who possess the form of a deceptive fish,
the Gaṅgā of the abode of the gods becomes manifest, attaining whiteness through contact with the courtyard of the sky.

May your tortoise-form protect the world—you who are skilled in the task of guarding the earth, whose back is kissed by the wheels [of the universe] like calluses formed from supporting the circle of the earth through manifold creations. (57)

May the tusk of you, who possess the body of a boar, bring satisfaction to me— or indeed to the entire world— since I perceive even the four oceans as the impression of your four hooves upon the quarters of space.

O Mother, because of your embrace as you stumbled while rising up, with your hairs standing on end in great joy and bristling outward, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) became like a *nīpa* tree laden with fruit; yet, O playful boar, it did not crush it there.

O Lion, you who originate from the dense forest of the Dānavas and other foes, protect me with your deep and terrible roars; you whose half-body is that of a man, born from the collection of weapons fashioned by the gods for the destruction of your enemies.

May the five mace-like hands of you, who were extracting the wealth of Indra as it lay within the cave of the belly of the Lord of the Daityas— its entrails clinging to them like severed ropes— protect us.
"O Bali, this entire world is being filled by you; what is it that you lack?
You are but a boy, though clever in deceitful speech; O Vāmana, grant us the joy of our hearts. (62)
"I am exceedingly desirous of receiving from you, who possess the power of the nectar of generosity, the realization [of my request]"—
to you, thus addressed by Bali with hair standing on end in thrill, I bow, O you who employed the artifice of becoming a dwarf.
"O Vāmana, you shall dwell for a long time on the surface of the earth or in heaven, bound by those who enjoy [the world];
with these deceptive words, 'Stretch out this hand to take the universe,' you have indeed deceived the whole world. (64)
"An opening of my intention is being made; for I desire to give the entire universe to your feet. Thus addressed by Bali, O Vāmana, purifier of those who bow, may you protect us. (65)

May those two arms of yours, who were born from your very own arms as you were creating the world in the past— those arms which took the form of Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni)— be victorious, for they are now fit to effect its dissolution.

May your devotion to performing what is appropriate be victorious— you who caused that earth, which was divided into nine portions by the Creator out of anger because she was dusty and had many husbands, to be enjoyed by the twice-born.
O son of Reṇuka, since the ten-faced Rāvaṇa— who was difficult for Kārtavīrya to pierce— could be easily destroyed by you,
I praise your repetition of the name "Rāma," which, due to the absence of any difference in time, constitutes a non-concentrated redundancy.
O Rāma, the Creator himself—having surpassed all other scribes—indeed fashioned you, whose birthplace is the dust of Janaka’s lineage, as a masterpiece for your own sake from the very beginning. 69.

O Unborn One, O Ornament of the Universe, let there be as much passion as you wish arising from the body; there is no fault in this, for it is by that very means, O Lord, that Your majesty alone is capable of quelling all faults.

O Hero of the Raghus, if you do not grant me the wisdom of reality, then grant me even that delusion by which the army of Rāvaṇa, bewildered in battle, perceived the entire world as being composed of you alone.
Twice the Fortune born of the earth has departed from you: once through the command of your father, and once out of fear of your ignorance.
And was not the ocean, whose city of Laṅkā rests upon its waters, twice transgressed by you? (72)
The Rākṣasa did not slay Janaka’s daughter with the arrows of Kāmadeva,
for he purified himself by his own weapons because the boon granted by the god— that he would not die at the hands of an immortal— was true.
Does not the fame of Śambuka, which kisses the ocean, mock that cluster of conch shells?
For he, having been reduced to a mere name along with his army by the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), met his end at your hand.

Having acquired that fame born from bestowing gifts that strike fear into Death and terror into the lords of the Puṇyajanas, how is it that you did not feel ashamed to abandon your own wife out of fear of mean and wicked men? (75)
O refuge of the world, may you become my shelter, for you are an ocean of fire born from the separation from my beloved wife;
you are the sacrificer who offered his own life as a blade of grass into the sacrificial fire of the loss of Lakṣmaṇa.
Having witnessed even the sorrow of the Krauñca bird, that primordial poet composed a single verse out of grief;
moved by compassion arising from you, he indeed composed this worthy poem, an ocean of verses.
Knowing what was appropriate, did you not, by means of Lakṣmaṇa’s body, cut off both the ears of Śūrpaṇakhā—who was unworthy of attaining fame because her father was Viśravas—and her nose? (78)

May those arms of yours, with which that wish-fulfilling tree was uprooted by your body disguised as a Yādava—as if competing with the pride of its own generosity—carry away for me the creeping vine of my misfortunes. (79)
May that which you performed during childhood sports— striking the waves with shards of pottery—
protect us, as if it were the preliminary sketch for the playful act of piercing Bāṇa’s arms in the future.
Salutations to you who prepared Arjuna’s chariot to render Karna’s spear fruitless;
by placing a monkey upon his banner, you rendered Lakṣmaṇa free from the dart lodged in his chest.
The son of Apageya did not, by his boon, send even his devoted Bhakta to heaven with his physical body,
lest he become an expert in the amorous dalliances of celestial nymphs even in the divine realm, which would result in the violation of his vows.
Compassionate toward Karṇa, the son of the Sun whom you caused to be slain, and having fulfilled the purpose of Arjuna of the Lunar dynasty whom you conquered,
you brought about a state of half-sorrow and half-joy, with the Sun as your tearful eye and the Moon as your smiling eye.
O Rādha, your devotion to Prāṇa (the vital breath) is like that of Rādha; your friendship with Śatru (the enemy) is not at all like that of a son.
For you, who are dear to Śrī, it is indeed fitting to bear the Śrīvatsa mark eternally upon your own heart. 84.
It is said that you, Halin, possess white hair upon your body, and he is indeed Śeṣa;
yet this incarnation of yours bears the grace of a withered lotus-stalk, resembling those grey hairs.
You are the lord of Bhogavatī, who carries delightful fragrances; though you are Śeṣa, you are yet without end.
You possess a splendor charming with the wine of worldly enjoyment, and you shine with the luster of the moon, the friend of the night-lotus. 86.
O Kāmapāla, the exquisite beauty of Revatī, which rivals the splendor of the dark blue sky, is indeed fitting for you, whose own bodily luster causes the moon-lotuses to bloom with delight. 87.

O proponent of non-duality, you whose mental continuum is singular; O wise one, well-versed in the three Vedas; O victor over the five-arrowed god, possessed of the six superknowledges; protect me, you who have shaken off the four alternatives. (88)
There, as you, the conqueror of Māra, were directly realizing the momentariness and the negation of a self,
a rain of flowers fell from the hands of the gods— not merely a continuous stream of arrows from the flower-weaponed god of love.

Having struck you in the heart—though you have donned the firm armor of fortitude—the God of Love has rendered his flower-arrows utterly blunted; thus, the very faces of his companions serve as parasols for those shafts.
That Brahmā displays such eloquence in the composition of your hymn is due to his four faces;
for while you, the knower of all, remain awake, Śarva is called "blue-throated" merely because he claims to be omniscient.
O Kalkin, who in battle reckons time like the earth and wields a sword that is a fire for the destruction of barbarians,
may you, through your tenth incarnation, cast away my tenfold impurity.
As you wandered over the earth with your fame— white as the dust raised high by battle—
your name became true to its meaning, "Viṣṇuyaśas" (Fame of Viṣṇu), just like that of your father.

I bow to you, Dattātreya—the seed of the fame of Maru and Arjuna, who conquered yoga, known by the name Anagha, and who are the sun to the darkness of worldly delusion for Alarka—on this path consisting of the peaceful non-dual reality. 94.
O son of the slayer of Vṛtra, you who have slain Rāma in the form of a boar, be victorious;
O Kṛṣṇa, you who have destroyed the son of the Sun, I bow to you, even though you possess the same wings as Indra’s son. 95.
Salutations to You who, as Vāmana, were smaller than the smallest; who, assuming the body of Trivikrama, pervaded the quarters of space;
who, as Buddha, were free from any talk of violence; and who, as Kalki, have destroyed all [evil]—homage to You! 96.
O Trivikrama, purify me! When you took your stride, did Rāhu become your sandal as he clung to your foot?
And when you bound Bali, did Jāmbavān offer you the noose of his whirling circumambulation? (97)

What need is there for a mere half-cakrin’s axe when he who [easily] lopped off Arjuna’s thousand arms with his own [single] axe now strides forth against the multitude of Bāṇa’s arms, which have been severed by the complete cakrin? (98)

Having seized the Pāñcajanya conch with your hand, you call out to the Asuras as "O you who are not Pāñcajanya! Are you truly conscious? Behold! Why does even that which is insentient not cease its hostility toward me? (99)

Upon your chest, O Lord adorned with a shimmering forest garland, Lakṣmī remains— her breasts heaving as they thrill from your constant touch— as if upon a branch bearing both a *śrīphala* fruit and its two-fold stem.
Your hand is not released by the lotus, as if to learn intensely the state of being most beautiful;
and the moon, whose rays cause the night-lotuses to smile, attends upon your face, its reflection acting as a pair of eyes.
Victorious are those yogic powers of yours, as well as those of Nara and Hari, which were able to slay the enemies Hiraṇyakaśipu, Rāvaṇa, and the multitude of Kuru heroes! 102.
O Illusionist, is this state of being only half-existence for you, since you are indeed existence in its entirety?
For people with eyes of knowledge know you as the All, even while you assume the state of being a remnant. 103.

Since the application of liberation is obstructed here by the weaving together of successive births from previous existences, no other means of concentration manifests for anyone at all, except for your own meditative absorption. (104)
Did you split your body twice upward into two 'a' sounds to become Hari-Hara?
And why did you split it crosswise to become Nṛhari? For one who is independent, what question can indeed be asked? 105.
O You whose desires are fulfilled, why do You create the three worlds? Why do You destroy them if they were already created?
And why, descending again and again, do You protect this world when it is inevitably destined for destruction even by Your own self? (106)

Having emerged from the waters of the ocean, the fickle Goddess Śrī remained with you, having reflected upon those she had known well— the Gaṅgā, the lotus, the Kaustubha gem, and the moon— residing respectively in your foot, hand, heart, and eye.
The reality of the substrate (vāstu) cannot be established through various distinctions due to logical contradictions and manifold refutations;
rather, the definitive explanation of reality is that this [substrate] manifests as those various distinct forms through the unfolding of the intended reality. 108.

Having seen the entire universe within your belly as if it were external, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu departed without being able to distinguish his own self from that which was mixed with both; who do you consider him to be? (109)

Whether you reside upon the head of Brahmā as the creeper of his power, or upon the head of Śiva as the consort of the Lord, or within the belly of Viṣṇu as he assumes the form of a child—in every way, you are the support of the worlds. (110)
The river of the seeds of Dharma flows from your feet; Fortune, the root of all prosperity, throbs within your chest;
you are the progenitor even of the god of love; and you yourself are Brahman, the bestower of liberation. 111.
Even those people who utter your name, which destroys hell, as if in mere play—for them alone do hells have cause for fear; how then could they themselves be afraid of the hells? (112)
A person devoted to you need not fear even the falling of a thunderbolt among the causes of death;
for at that moment, your name issues forth instantly from the throat of a Vaiṣṇava, even without effort. (113)

In every way, even when purity is being practiced, those refuse-like impurities that arise within the hearts of living beings—like debris inside a palace—are cleansed by the stream of mindfulness of you. 114.
Even regarding that particular excellence which is beyond the reach of those such as us, your name "Rāma" is the abode of all virtues;
yet why was it bestowed by you alone throughout even three lifetimes? Indeed, [if it were not so,] how could this be otherwise? (115)
Bestowing grace upon me with your solar gaze, O Lord, make me free from the darkness [of ignorance];
do not dispel my heat with that moon-like eye which has been fixed elsewhere. 116.

Alas, I am shameless; though I daily transgress your command consisting of injunctions and prohibitions, I still desire your favor—which is difficult to obtain even through asceticism—by mere words alone. (117)
O you who possess all forms and have created the universe, how great is your wondrous power; I place that jewel within my heart.
For does a poor man, having reached the Golden Mountain, ever bind his own rags with gold? 118.
Having spoken thus to Hari, he became thoroughly permeated by conscious meditation (*saṃprajñāta-samādhi*),
moving about with actions consistent with his love and devotion toward Viṣṇu, who was beheld through the power of his contemplation.

Having showered a profuse rain of wealth upon the hands of the Brahmins and having offered the ancestral rites and *kavya* to the worthy recipients, he worshipped Hari and Hara with supreme merit and, bowing low, entered for refuge. 120.

Following the midday rite, the sun—the moon of the earth—rejoicing in the nectar-like rice he had tasted, adorned with his own rays the eastern mountain, that palace-mountain which rivals the Vaijayanta palace in its splendor. 121.
The daughter of Bhīma, having performed her devotions and worship to the deities, ate after her husband had finished his meal;
she then sat upon his lap, her limbs rendered languid by the excessive weight of her ornaments and her waist yearning for the embrace of his arms.

Following her was a certain female friend carrying a single cage, which resembled a mass of beauty in the palm of her hand; it clearly belonged to a parrot whose beak was as red as the ripening of a *bimba* fruit and whose feathers were suited to the maturity of a young fruit.

One female cuckoo followed her with a cry that was clearly joined to the word *kuhū*—the very name of the new moon—at the boundary of the dark fortnight, through the mutual connection of word and meaning;
she was accompanied by a male cuckoo of excessive passion, holding a crystal staff held horizontally.

Those daughters of the Gandharva king, who were the disciples of Bhīma’s daughter in the arts and her companions proficient in the art of playing the soft-sounding lute, went to play the lute for this seated sovereign of men.
The lute of those gazelle-eyed women resounded slightly before them with a perfectly pure and low-pitched drone;
it seemed as if it were initially lacking the confidence to sound forth in the presence of Damayantī’s throat-creepers, which were so exceedingly sweet.

Because she had previously associated with him in order to attain equality with Damayantī—the ground of all arts, virtues, and excellence—she incurred the reproach of "immodesty" (avinaya) in the world; thus, even now, she is known as "the lute" (parivādinī).

The lute, displaying a marvelous agility of hand, emitted a resonant sound sweet with the *niṣāda* note; it was like a female elephant who, shaking her head in accordance with the sacred scriptures, utters a cry sweet with the *niṣāda* note, belonging to that elephant among the mountain-dwelling sages who possessed the fruit of long practice.
Did the Creator extract the entire essence of lutes to fashion her soft-voiced throat?
For, having found an opening through that [throat], the lute became so ashamed of its instability that it abandoned its plectrum even among the fingers of young girls. (129)
Then the lutes sang sweet songs of praise for the couple, with verses of such perfectly clear syllabic arrangement that the parrot,
who was exceedingly fond of the Earth, uttered all those melodies while scattering joy.

You shall indeed understand the depths of our intellect through our words; nevertheless, we praise you both as being possessed of supreme intelligence, for otherwise, even this much knowledge would not have been grasped by you from our speech delivered on this occasion. (131)

On the lap of the mountain, that [Pārvatī] was the consort of the crest-jewel of kings; you, likewise, are the equal of this lord who is blessed with enjoyments. That this is the same sequence—that even in this birth, you are the chaste wife of a husband adorned by the status of being a guardian of heaven—is the only difference.

In whose heart does this passion flash forth, from which it produces delight, or who extends it toward you? And who could harbor the doubt that the god of love—whose life as a celestial being was rendered useless by the glance of the Three-Eyed One, and whose progress along the path was thwarted—is now restored? 133.
Bearing this earth— which possesses necklaces gliding like rivers and which, through the radiance of his own moon-like face, displays the splendor of the inner altar—
you shine like a mass of water, beloved by the minds of the people of the Middle Country, which holds the beauty of the inner sanctum.
This slender maiden, who has made the moon-faced one her witness, grants victory to the God of Love by the mere placement of her leaf-like eyebrows;
what else is this but the fruit of your extreme weakness as a mediator, that you have been humiliated here by him whose banner bears the fish?
O Queen of the City of the Mind’s Being, surely you are the city whose banner is the sea-monster upon your breasts;
O young woman, do they not call your two eyebrows the triumphal archway for the fish-bannered God of Love, who touches the great prosperity of this city? 136.

As desire moves incessantly between you and her, how is it that it does not incur fatigue? For you two who are constantly engaged in coming and going, it serves as the shade that removes the exhaustion of the journey for that fish-bannered god of love.
O Lord of Men, when the new line of hair, fond of being bathed in perspiration, performs the vows of wakefulness for the sake of love,
it appears as if its body were bristling with the filaments of the arrows of the God of Love, thick with honey and smeared with sandalwood paste.
O King, this lotus-eyed goddess of your life has now reached you, drenched in a spray of perspiration;
for as those various flowers were the arrows of the Lord of Rati, is her sweat perhaps the blood from the wounds inflicted by his shafts? (139)

Depending upon this passion of yours, have both the western quarter and the sun become red? And seeing that, are the lotuses of the pleasure-lake here practicing the art of assuming faces suited for the arrows of Love directed at you two? (140)
Let this circle of friends depart, for it interrupts the uninhibited play of you two who are under the sway of mutual passion.
How could Madana be truly intoxicating if he did not cause one to cast off one’s garment or provoke a battle with teeth and nails? 141.
While the parrot was thus reciting falsely, they departed at the hour of twilight, perceiving the many royal duties [to be performed];
their eyes were half-seen by their own angry female friends, as if they were lotuses closing up out of shame.
The cuckoo, whose beak was eager to repeat the garland of words it had heard—saying "Praise! Praise!"—seemed as if it were reciting a hymn to Nala;
likewise, the parrot, its eyes filled with passion toward the king, appeared as if it were looking toward that very bird.
Then, from her residence in the lofty palace, the daughter of Bhīma beheld the pleasure-pool becoming exceedingly thin, shining with a gem that resembled the orb of the rising sun;
it was clearly indicated by pairs of ruddy geese fleeing from the banks in mutual alarm, crying out in distress as they thought, "A female serpent is approaching!"—moving in a winding, zigzag course.
Then, beholding the two wheels of the chariot red with blood as if struck by the inability to endure their excessive separation,
she made even that time of the lotuses' sleep fragrant with the scent of lotuses scattered by her sighs.
The daughter of Bhīma spoke to her husband: "Look with compassion upon the condition of these two cakravāka birds!
Alas, what man would not weep upon seeing her [the moon] who pierces both my heart and these two? (146)
The sun, unable to endure the joy of the night-lotuses as they were about to bloom, spread abroad his desire not to linger;
do the birds cry out at every tree because the pangs of the female cuckoo have entered their own hearts? (147)
Even these two birds, performing every action preceded by their mutual understanding, yet practicing what is undesirable— separation—
is indeed a striking illustration for inferring that the movements of conscious beings are governed by destiny.

Is this sword, clearly red from the scattering of bricks that are the crimson of his feet, being sharpened by Fate—who desires to sever the pair of wheeling birds—on the whetstone of the sun’s orb, which possesses a handle shining like a staff and upon which the rotation has been incessantly set in motion by Garuḍa, the elder brother of Aruṇa? 149.
Having thus drunk the nectar-essence offered by the face of that moon-faced woman, he, his own face shimmering with a variegated smile, said to her: "It is clearly exactly as you have described it."
I recognize your two eyebrows as the two bows of Rati and the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma), bent low to conquer all men and women by means of their respective appropriate charms;

I recognize your nose as a double-reed flute concealed under the guise of a nose for those two who desire to release their arrows; and I recognize your two breaths as the wind-god’s weapon (the Vāyavya-astra) born from the spring breeze for them.
Yellow is a quality of color, yet it is exceedingly sweet even in your body; for who, beholding this gold upon you, would not praise it as "excellent gold"?

What need is there to describe other colors? Among forms, whiteness alone reigns supreme, such that even silver acquires the ill-repute of being "base metal" (*durvarṇa*) merely through association with it. (152)

If a *puṇḍraka* sugar-cane grows on ground made of powdered sugar-clay, ploughed by the watering of honey and milk-clouds, and nourished by a paste of milk as its special treatment (*dohada*), and if it then bears fruit through the sprinkling of grape-juice—only then does the superlative suffix *-tama* arise to express the sweetness of your words, surpassing even that. (153)

If Cupid, who is himself nourished by nectar, were to churn the newly risen cream of the ocean of sugarcane juice using a rope made of threads from boiling molasses—thereby crushing the mountain of sugar within the gift-offering—he might produce a nectar that could rival the supreme composition of your tongue and serve as a feast for my ears. (154)

In Your mouth, O Bhāratī, where dwells the Goddess of Speech—whose dwelling is the shimmering play-lotus, whose nectar is the grace of Her voice blending with the sweet resonance of the lute, and whose lips are the palaces fashioned from the red chalk and lime fit for Her amorous wanderings—is it indeed a string of pearls that these two rows of teeth shine as? 155.
Your speech is a certain river of the Manmatha-tirtha, flowing with the currents of radiant aesthetic flavor (rasa); every fragment [of this speech] is spoken of as the sand of its banks.
Are these pure white sugar-cakes fashioned from the very mud of this shore? Are these waters nectar? And are those two lips of yours truly the banks of this river? (156)
O young woman, your voice—which is like a stream from the ocean of nectar—does not come easily to the throat of the female cuckoos;
yet how many times have they not practiced it in order to place it upon the throats of connoisseurs, by repeating it within the mango trees of your grove? (157)
Your upper lip is a bowstring made of a garland of bandhūka flowers for the bow of Love; there, upon the lower edge of your lower lip, is the creeper of the boundary line.
Even this speech of yours, my dear, is surely the science of the god of love’s archery, which is now fittingly practiced by lutes acting as bow-wielding instruments.
That man is vulgar and always excluded from the assembly of the learned; O charming girl, even the arrows of the God of Love recoil from touching him.

For when he asks, "Is this honey?", he does not touch your lower lip; when he asks, "How is this gold?", he does not touch your body; and when he asks, "What is this nectar?", he does not offer you a word in reply. (159)

O Goddess, you who have bound the power of *aṇimā* within yourself; you who possess *garimā*, *mahimā*, and a pair of hips and breasts; you who hold the mastery over the awakened mind (*vaśitva*) and maintain the power of *laghimā* through your smile;

you who are delightful through *prākāmya* in your speech and have attained the fulfillment of all desires through your fame in every direction—O Sovereign, the Lord, being delighted, has bestowed upon you these eight supernatural powers (*bhūti*) as his own handiwork for your sake.
We are not clever enough to praise your speech; rather, we praise nectar itself for that purpose, knowing it was fittingly born from the battle between Garuḍa and Indra.
For by her who created the grape-juice and crushed its pride, this very nectar was favored with the grace of having her own feet washed in it, while she maintained a firm disdain for milk.

O fair-toothed one, if grief torments you for the two *kokas*, then speak; your command shall be carried out. I will go and entreat the sun, reflected here in the water, not to set. Even if I join my palms in supplication, he might remain averse to my plea, for he is single-mindedly intent on his course. Therefore, give him this handful of water, and then behold me as I return to you.
"Then, for the sake of your joy, let your ladyship seek for a moment here the absorbed state of your own friends who are absorbed in the bulbous roots of your jests.
Having thus, under this pretext, caused his companion’s mind to waver among her friends, he himself went outside, desiring to perform the ritual of the *yantra*. 163.

This [work] has entered into the twenty-first poem of his very new collection, he who was begotten by Śrī Hīra and Māmalladevī as their son— Śrī Harṣa, the diamond that adorns the crown of the circle of king-poets, and who has conquered the host of his senses.
In this work consisting of a description of the life of the husband of the daughter of Bhīma, the naturally radiant canto [fifteen] is concluded. 164.
Having performed the evening rites, his heart longing for the lip of his beloved,
that lord of mountains reached the palace of Damayantī situated on the seventh level.
Having occupied the couch— its bed prepared and ready— upon which his beloved had been released as she rose to meet him,
and having perfumed her as well, he now offered verses of praise to the evening twilight.
First, favor the quarter of the lord of waters with a glance—
she who has been washed as if by lac-dye, yet remains unfilled, as if by saffron-paste.
The sun has fallen from the lofty summit of the mountain of the sky like a boulder of red chalk;
by its very fall, as it is being pulverized, this line of twilight dust rises up here.
Is this the village of a mere low-caste man living on the peak of the sunset mountain—a mere coop of cocks?
For by the masses of its crests, shimmering with the crowing at the end of the watch, this western quarter has been instantly turned crimson.
Behold how, here at this place where the sun has swiftly set, the twilight— acting as a staff-bearer with its fingers in the form of the rays emerging from the setting sun—
is exercising authority in the office of the night's doorkeeper by warding off the day.
O friend, why does the Great Actor, reflecting upon the passion of the assembly and even upon the twilight— the mistress of the mineral pigment—
now fashion for himself a necklace with his slender body as the thread and the rows of stars as the garland?

Behold how the evening dancer, whose crown is the king of stars, adorns the circle of the quarters here with fragments of his bone-ornament necklace that has snapped during his dance, while he bears the guise of ten million boats.
Time was a Kirāta who brought about the slaughter of that day-elephant whose temples were clearly marked by lotuses;
its twilight was the stream of beautiful blood, and the stars were the pearls from its frontal globes.

I believe that this very division of the quarters, now flushed with the glow of twilight, was formerly worn by the Lord clad in space (the naked one) at the marriage of Śivā on the occasion of the Puṣpasindūrikā festival.

O fair-eyed one, when he married Satī and Umā, what did the two directions—resplendent with passion at the two twilights—lack that they had to become naked, as if for the sake of a flower-sindūra mark upon their garments? 11.
Having taken up his staff, this mendicant Sun wanders through all directions;
now, as if plunging into the ocean, he has donned the saffron robe of the twilight clouds at evening.
The sky, having sold that mass of gold—the sun—which was tested by the streaks of the twilight upon this touchstone-like western mountain, has now received cowrie-shells in exchange: the stars. (13)
The twilight, having removed the ripe pomegranate—the orb of the sun—seems to have cast off its skin;
it is like a heap of bones spat out by Time, who devours the seeds consisting of the stars.

This multitude of stars, having devoured the mass of bones as if they were seeds, has stripped them of their pulp; now this skin, cast off at twilight, resembles a ripe pomegranate devoid of its fruit.
And from the impact of the falling feet of the Lord of Caṇḍī, who performed a frantic dance at the end of twilight—
Behold, the sky is adorned by fragments of crystal stone from Mount Kailāsa that are flying upward.
Thus, perceiving that the twilight had departed as if out of shame born from his description,
he gazed again at the sky, bristling with stars and darkness, and spoke once more.

O lady with eyebrows like the bow of Kāma, this ocean did not previously leap up into the sky—filled with crocodiles and variegated with fish and conchs—out of the intensity of pain from the wound to its vital parts inflicted by Rāma’s arrow. 18.
I suspect that the stars released by the Flower-Arrowed One as arrows for the sake of deluding the gods and their celestial nymphs are indeed those very stars;
for the word "five" in the name of the Five-Arrowed One surely signifies his manifold manifestations, just as the word "five" does in the case of the five-faced one. (19)
For the flocks of cakravāka birds nesting on the banks of the celestial river, distressed by their nightly separation,
the stars are the teardrops in their eyes, and the showers of rain are the streams falling from them.
I believe these to be the aquatic creatures—the crocodile, the shark, and the crab—of the celestial river;
for we clearly perceive them here below, submerged because they have long since fled from the fear of the gods sporting in its waters. (21)
Does this conch-shell of Smara shine in the sky as a trumpet for his victory over the three worlds?
For what other warrior would the power to play such an instrument be possible with flowers made of moonlight? (22)
Is this night a yoginī who has revived the Lord of Pleasure and bewildered the lotus?
This conch shell, kissing the sky, proclaims her great power of yoga, for it remains unattached [to her]. (23)

At the time of awakening during the day, this night-like yoginī on the path of emptiness demonstrates that the stars are like flowers in the sky—sublated; thus, even though the world appears clearly, it is seen as false. (24)
This deer, made of your very limbs by the god of love and struck through with an arrow by the bow of your brow-pair,
has now gone to your moon-like face, followed by the rows of flower-arrows shining like stars.
The universe, the pavilion that serves as the refuge of the worlds, shines forth at every moment;
its stars appear like the openings of worm-holes, emitting clouds of dust-like radiance.

Behold in the quarter whose consort is Śacī, the daughter of Bhīma; like a flood released from its banks due to the destruction of the dam of day, the darkness flows forth unchecked like the torrent of ichor from Indra’s elephant.
The mount of Antaka, whose rows of hair-like rays extend in all directions, acts like darkness;
seeing it from afar, the Sun fled, as if terrified, taking his own horses with him.
The orb of the sun was, as it were, a ripe mahākāla fruit upon the ridge of the western mountain;
I know for certain that its seeds are the very darknesses produced when that fruit was split by the falling of the stones.
The disgrace of her husband, the Sun— who was disregarded by Sumeru due to its circumambulation—
was like musk upon the quarters of the sky, which were otherwise devoid of the name "Caitraratha" because of the splendor of his rays.
The sky held aloft by the thousand-rayed sun during the day was as if supported by a thousand hands;
yet that very same sky, when falling without the sun, has come to be so near—whence indeed could darkness [otherwise] arise? (31)
Was it the soot of darkness, heavy as it met the earth, that was deposited by the sun—the lamp of the day—upon the sky which resembles an inverted cauldron placed above? 32.

At night, when the moon is absent, the quarters of the sky— darkened by the sky’s black antelope-skin garment, with the stars as the arrows of the flower-arrowed god, and marked by bashfulness— approach me like women going to meet their lovers out of jealousy.

O slender one, we declare that the eyelashes of the Primordial Being, whose eyelids meet as he quickly closes his sun-like eyes, are the very darkness that has surpassed the beauty of the moon’s spot with its own blackness.

As if Vivasvat had brought together the eyes of the people along with his own thousand rays, even the cows—whose other name is "eyes"—have been gathered; thus, this blindness is surely due to those [rays], and not by darkness. (35)

O lady of beautiful thighs, upon investigation, the Vaiśeṣika system is considered by me to be the most excellent; indeed, they call that philosophy the "Aulūkya," and it alone is capable of defining the true nature of darkness. (36)
This very prosperity of his, which touches upon withered things and belongs to a realm where touch is forbidden— like that of Triśaṅku—
brings delight to nothing else except for these two eyes of Kauśikī.
Indeed, that which is the consecrated lord of the planets eclipses the splendor of the stars;
it is a darkness by day, yet its form is clearly perceived, while the world of owls beholds it as light.
During the day, in order to ascertain the conduct of those who were his enemies,
the darkness, having fashioned shadows as its spies, caused them to enter while clinging to every object, as if to question them.

Then the moon, its beauty as red as a hibiscus flower, rising up as if desiring to appease him, was praised by the king with a description that provoked the anger of his enemy who was thus causing darkness. 40.
O beloved, although the moon is veiled for even a moment by the curtain of the mountain’s plateau,
it rains down beams of moonlight into the hollows of the beaks of the cakora birds.
In the darkness, suspect that the women going to meet their lovers have reached the trysting place at the edge of the trees;
having cast off their blue garments under the guise of shadows, they move about in silken robes suited to the moonlight.

O lady with thighs as full as the trunk of a plantain tree, drink with your eyes— beautiful as night-lotuses— the moon, which is the mirror for the beauty of your face and which the cakora birds delight in as their own moonlight.
Without doubt, this moon formerly rose from the very mountain that churned the ocean;
for even now, though he resides in the sea, we perceive his rising from a mountain. (44)
Having been received as a guest by his own younger brother, the elephant that serves as the vehicle of the Lord of the East—
was it because of this that the splendor of dawn, thick with vermilion, now rises upon its head?

Because this [orb] was not kissed by the faces of the celestial ladies— who were filled with joy due to their own similarity to it— this very orb now rises, red as a bimba fruit, from the lack of contact with their lips.

Does the Creator fashion the faces of young women with the moon as a golden mold, using the eyes and other features visible through the difficult-to-perceive [reflection] produced by the reverse engraving of its parts? (47)
(With this [face], whose limbs are fashioned with marks produced in reverse form, the Creator has made your face a mere semblance by means of eyes and other features that are not truly visible.
That sky which formerly belonged to this direction of the Lord of the Gods was drunk by the night.
By that [light] now surely kissed by the powder of moonbeams, it has become non-red.
Having gone there, those very [sacrificial offerings] which that son of Jamadagni had offered pleased this world of the ancestors;
having severed the heads and armor of the thousand-armed one, he bestowed them as gifts upon his forefathers.
Deprived of its ears and nose, your face does not shame itself as it gazes upon Sītā’s lovely countenance;
alas, overwhelmed by Lakṣmaṇa, the moon—resembling the face of Śūrpaṇakhā—is shedding a stream of red blood.
When that rogue of evening gave him the blazing jewel of the sky and took from him the gold that was but a counterfeit of the glowing moonlight, it instantly turned into pale silver.

The silver [disk], released by the child-like night-time, like the shimmering orb of the moon, sheds its redness as it abandons the covering of the silk thread through the sequence of its revolutions. (53)
The moon, as if erasing with its rays that eulogy of darkness which the night had inscribed upon the sky with chalk-like white letters,
has become pale even in its red glow.
When this [sun] shines white here, it gleams with a reddening luster as it rises in another place;
thus, who can truly know the reality of passion and dispassion in this treasure-house of the arts?
The limbs of the women who are the quarters of the sky were gradually adorned by the rays born of Kashmir at twilight, which had wiped away the musk of the darkness,
and by the moonbeams as lovely as sandalwood paste.
Fate fashions the days of the dewy season again and again, using those very same materials;
otherwise, how could these moonlit nights be its counterparts, or how could those [winter days] be so short? (57)
When these words had ended, he spoke to his bride, who remained silent due to her absorption in listening to those eloquent sayings:
"O beloved, why this seal of silence upon you, as if out of resentment toward the moon because it rivals your face? (58)
Fill the wells of your ears with the garland of syllables from the nectar-moon of the vessel of erotic sentiment;
for the silkworm that weaves your beautiful speech is surely but a mere imitation of grass.
"Right here, I now desire to hear from you as well words that are kin to honey," thus urged by her beloved, she then began to offer a panegyric of the moon. (60)
I suspect that this moon, in order to increase the fullness of the ocean, milks from the moonstone how many waters,
and from the eyes of the female ruddy goose— eyes filled with grief at separation from her mate— how many more.
When the darkness has withdrawn, mimicking the flood of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) during the night,
the sandy island, with its lamp of shimmering, stainless luster, becomes clearly visible amidst the moonlight.
I suspect that by the mere luster of her laughter, the entire universe, along with all its night-lotuses, was made as pure as milk;
for when those lotuses have their mouths closed during the day, the world does not shine in such a way even though the moon is present.
Residing in the matted locks of the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya), this [skull] does not decay, for death remains far off due to fear of him;
nor does it grow, as it is utterly terrified of the Rāhu-like emergence from the garland of heads whose life-force has been seized by his own nectar.

Bestowing his splendor upon the cakora bird, nectar upon the gods, and even a single digit of himself upon Śiva, this moon—brother to the wish-fulfilling tree—triumphs; yet all this is but a trifle for him.
Though he bears a poison-blackened throat on his lap, is purified by attaining nectar, and is pale with the ashes of the *kaṭa* plant,
even the Arhat Mṛḍa does not deserve the sixteenth digit of the moon, for that [digit] resides upon his own head.
O best of birds, the Lord of the Twice-born (Brahmā) fashioned his white and black splendor from the half-burnt bones of the Flower-Armed One (Kāmadeva);
for even though he was borne upon the head of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), he extends blessings of prosperity and nourishment to him.
Indeed, out of greed for the deer, the son of Siṃhikā swallows the moon;
yet, by giving it away even to his own self while it sleeps in his lap, he does not abandon it, and because of that, he is released.
That the nectar-eaters, having drunk this [ocean] which is now empty, spread abroad [their fame], is indeed fitting;
for in the past, even its father, the ocean, was made empty by the one born from a jar (Agastya) after he had drunk it.
Filling all four quarters of the horizon, this entire expanse of moonlight, the kinsman of the celestial river,
dispels the heart’s distaste for dwelling within the belly of the ocean of milk.
She is the daughter of the Moon, the dancer of the Ocean, and the companion of the eyes of the Cakora bird;
yet she is some indescribable being to the night-lotus, for her very name proclaims her as "Kaumudī."

Upon the earth, the rays of the bright-rayed moon shine forth, appearing as if they were the earth itself—possessing the appearance of a ground made of moonlight-water and the substance of the surface of the land, while bearing gaps under the guise of shadows;
their radiance is a mixture of the white luster of the moon and the dark glow of its spot.
To what extent has this region been made clear by him through the removal of darkness from the divisions of the sky?
Likewise, even though it was dark, it was illuminated by the splashing waters of the salt ocean.

The moon cannot undergo decrease or increase of its qualities, for its own cause—the ocean—is subject neither to loss nor gain; yet it is a wonder that this very moon attains those states after a long time, while the ocean does not do so constantly.

Though he relies upon that which is visible in a mirror, he does not bear a form visible in a mirror; though he is born from the eye of Atri, he is a marvel, for he was produced even from the eye of the Three-eyed One (Śiva). //75//
This pure orb of the moon, which possesses the splendor of a sacrificial feast for the assembly of gods,
bears only a single dark spot as its blemish, just as that very sacrifice itself bore violence as its sole stain.
One of these steeds, thirsty and dislodged from the chariot by the driving wind, remains in the waterless sky with its tongue lolling, drinking the multitude of nectar-drops from this [cloud]. (77)

I suspect that the deer was not merely present in this infant; rather, it was placed upon his lap by the Moon, who offered it as a gift to his beloveds, just as the forest is placed in the embrace of medicinal herbs with their messages.
Tasting the sprouts of medicinal herbs and drinking the nectar-like waters of this very [moon], the spotted deer dwells here in happiness, having come for the sake of serving him alone. (79)
Seeing the distressed lunar deer fleeing from afar in the sky, pursued by Rudra,
I think this other deer, trembling with fear, has entered the moon as a refuge, believing it to be the crest-jewel of Śiva.
"O Lord, does a deer still remain on your back like the spot on the moon?"—such was the doubt;
to resolve it, he stood right in front of his own face, for in that duel of chariots, he had seen the enemy's back.
The reasoning that the moon’s pale belly is the very lap of this god declares it to be turned upward;
therefore, may I have even greater faith in the Vedic account of the gods as being situated with their faces turned upward.
When objects situated at a distance are observed as red or blue, only the quality of blueness is perceived;
indeed, the portion consisting of redness remains beyond our perception, even though it resides in the hairs on the back of the hare. (83)
This world is capable of shattering the pride of grammar regarding the path of word-usage;
for while it says "this has a hare, therefore he is the Moon (śaśin)," it does not say "she has a deer, therefore she is the Deer-woman (mṛgī). (84)
Whatever measure of the moon the first day of the lunar fortnight brings forth, that much was poured out by the ocean as well;
yet, the fact that the moon remains so small when held upon the head of the Lord at that time is here a sign [of its true nature].
If the nature of a *ketaka* flower were attributed here to the moon— with its collection of digits shaped like petals—
then that would accord with the musk-like fragrance of the musk-deer dwelling in its lap.

This lunar orb, which once existed according to the celestial luminaries, has now become visibly flattened, like a dregs-cake of nectar pulled out by the pair of Rahu’s fangs acting as a mechanical press. (87)
Because of their lack of similarity, camphor is not our friend; indeed, the moon is its friend.
For both of them, when burnt, retain an even greater potency than their original forms. (88)
It is fitting that the Moon should have friendship with Madana, for he was absorbed when Śambhu’s eye blazed;
and this [Madana] now goes to his dissolution when the eye of the Primordial Being, consisting of light, encounters the new moon.
In ancient times, when the moon became the lotus-eye of that Primeval Puruṣa,
it was at that very moment that this [spot] became the beauty of the bee-like pupil within his mark.

Having observed that both were equal— this one and Kāśyapi— and seeing that they shared the same wings and were both resorted to by hawks, the god Indra appropriately appointed them both to the task of guiding his eyes.
I suspect that those who imagined fire to exist within the frost for the sake of explaining the cause of the withering of the lotus plants,
have thereby also justified the existence of the spot on the moon as being a mass of its smoke.

Pervaded by streams of perspiration like flowing rivers, the Earth, distressed by the fatigue of bearing the burden of the world, plunges here into the ocean of nectar under the guise of its shadow and thus casts off her exhaustion. (93)
It is my own inference that the Golden Mountain (Meru) has indeed become dark blue by the long-term settling of indigo;
for even its yellow portion must be reflected in the world’s shadowy image of the moon.

I think that the moon, whose splendor is eclipsed by the lotus when it closes, does not attain the glory of worshiping the blossoming lotus; yet, adorned by the lap of his own consort, he attains that very glory through his two eyes alone. 95.
That this hare awakens within the moon—what wise man would consider this a marvel?
For indeed, within the ocean that is its father, there were once both horses and elephants as well. (96)
Since both the beloved Gaurī shines most brightly as the dark night and his beloved Nīlā as the moonlit night in him,
he assumes a white and black form out of a desire for both of them to attain beauty.
Among the young star-mushrooms that have arisen here for a long time, clinging to a mass of wood as a shelter from rain and sun, I perceive the moon alone to have blossomed into full bloom. 98.
At the close of day, because the sun suddenly sinks from view, the eyes of the world cross the island-filled river of the calamity of darkness during the night, thanks to the grace of this moon.
Is this moon not also a momentary, minute speck of light—a mere drop of radiance—even in our own eyes?
Yet it was fitting that in the eyes of Atri it became a great mass, which perished after only a month. 100.

Neither could the medicinal herbs save their husband by their own power, nor the Brahmins by their mantras; neither did the ocean with its jewels, nor nectar with its potencies, save this wasting son, nor even their own refuge.
Either this moonlight is false, or it is nectar;
otherwise, how could the cakora birds, having drunk the rays of the moon, not become free from old age and death? (102)
With these words, full of eloquence, Damayantī rendered the king motionless with the weight of wonder;
for a moment, she made him stiff with the sentiment of astonishment, like a shower of gold.
Saying, "From this mouth has emerged this speech, sweet as a stream of nectar," he kissed her moon-like face,
which shared the radiant beauty of blooming lotuses.
Thus addressed by her beloved, that pearl of the lineage of the King of Vidarbha offered a web of smiles like rays; she was like a shimmering star descended from heaven to earth.

"Self-praise is not worthy of you," having thus enjoined me, she said: "It is only fitting that my face, which has the form of the moon, remains indifferent during the praise of the moon, thinking, 'I am but a servant of the earth.'"

Thus urged by his beloved, that essence of the world of mortals—whose speech was equal to his very life and who was about to address the moon with words dripping with the essence of jesting and a smile upon his lips—spoke these charming words: 107. Having drunk in the song born from your mouth, this deer—eager to hear it—I imagine that he desires to abandon the moon at all times, mistaking it for your face. (108)

May your tongue in your mouth, by means of song, draw toward you the moon-dwelling deer that is worthy of being approached due to its delusion regarding the moon; for what purpose has your pair of ears become like a noose, as if intending to bind it? 109.
Whether due to being nourished by the rays of the moon, or because of the coolness born from the forest of darkness,
the traveler of sound does not traverse the day as long as he remains distressed by the heat during the night.
Even from afar, having found its limit in the enjoyment of the sweet flavor through drinking your song, the Lord of Night indeed casts aside his own nectars with utter disdain. 111.
"O slender one, this does not cause us surprise, since he became the eye of the Primordial Being;
for his form is indeed consistent with his lineage, having arisen from the eye of Atri. (112)

O lady with the belly of a lioness, by these moonlights, as if by streams of milk, this night— this washerwoman composed of darkness— has instantly washed away the dark indigo dye clinging to her beautiful garment.
The autumn season completely dispelled the deep blackness of the clouds;
yet, O lady with beautiful thighs, she was unable to wipe away even a small portion of the blackness of his spot.

Since the eleven digits [of the moon] set into the crests of the eleven Rudras, do they enter him so that the remaining five become the crescent-moon arrows in the quiver of the five-arrowed god? (115)
O slender one, if another moon were created by placing thousands of stars without any gaps between them,
then, being free from its dark spot, it might attain the splendor of your face.

O fawn-eyed one, I suspect that the conflict between the moon and the lotus arises from their desire for the same object: the moon wishing to seize the beauty of your face, and the deer-marked moon wishing to seize the splendor of the lotus. (117)
Even the Lord of the Written Word (Brahmā) could not obtain to drink the nectar of your lower lip, which is like the moon of your face;
having drunk it, he now feels loathing for the nectar of this moon, which was made into mere leftovers by the gods.
Bearing this moon, the lord of herbs, upon his head, the husband of the daughter of the mountain king consumes the terrible poison born of the ocean and wears the serpent without any fear. (119)
Behold, there was no downfall for this lord of the twice-born even as he went toward his wife;
for even worldly activities do not harm those who have attained their final body, since they shine with the light of the Self.

The water, purified by faith and variegated with sesame seeds, which had been offered by the sons to the ancestors with the utterance of "svadhā," approached the moon as its abode; it was indeed nectar itself, inlaid with the luster of its [the moon's] rays. 121.

Behold how the female royal swan, mistaking the reflection of the moon in the water of your pleasure canal— which is visible through the bliss of its position atop the lofty palace— for her beloved who has long been submerged here, kisses it.
During the day, this moon, marked by a hare, was rendered insignificant by the gods who drank its nectar;
now, at night, it has become full of nectar and has submerged itself here in your river under the guise of a reflection.
When the moon’s ray and the night-lotus, both with hands of flowers, have come together in union,
the sprinkling of water from the honey that flows out seems to proclaim their wedding ceremony.
This doe dwelling in the forest, her eyes like blossoming, long blue lotuses, gazes here above at her beloved; she beholds your deer, who dwells within the moon of your face.

I perceive the face of Night— her lower lip being the moon— to be beautiful with the smile of its rays, as she breaks the meditative concentration of the night-lotuses performing penance in the water.
This lunar orb is a lake of the God of Love, with its slight spots as its mud and its nectar as its water;
from drinking the nectar, it bears the sign of a fish born therein, which signifies immortality even in the absence of water.

Adorned with the bones of stars, bearing the daughters of the Moon and Jahnu, its luster sprinkled with the dust of moonbeams, and wearing the lord of serpents as a necklace under the guise of the Milky Way, the sky clearly proclaims itself to be the embodied form of the Eightfold Lord (Śiva). 128.
It is said that for that father, the sage, there was but a single star in his eye;
yet for this [son], this wealth has become even greater than his, in that he possesses twenty-seven of them.
O fawn-eyed one, this orb of the moon is the white parasol of the God of Love;
that its waning occurs immediately after the full moon is indeed the collapse of Manmatha’s royal canopy. (130)
O proud lady, even he who formerly conquered the worlds with ten faces was never able to conquer this moon;
this is the fading of his luster now that he has been surpassed by your singular face alone.
You have seen this moon for these many days as it overcame its former state;
if it should now attain equality with your face when full, you will immediately witness its decline.
Just as that lord of the twice-born was humiliated by Rāma after having overcome other warriors,
so too does he suffer humiliation from your lotus-face after having surpassed all other lotuses.
"Look, the moon's interior is being made beautiful by the form of the deer; look!
Thus he sometimes saw the end of the moon and sometimes its interior while gazing at Damayantī.
Since he was born from the ocean, from the belly of the sage’s eyes, and from the two [Atri and Anasūyā], is he therefore a twice-born (dvija)?
And since he likewise becomes twice-born (dvija) in this very way, is the moon not truly the son of Atri (atrija)? 135.

O slender one, by that very merit performed in the abode of the Tārā monastery— which created a lunar orb upon the snowy land and made it the dwelling of musk-deer— under the guidance of the Jina, [the world] became a realm of frost and musk.
The Creator attained the status of being the ornament of both the heavenly world and the earthly world.

O lady whose face mocks the beauty of the moon’s orb, they say that the deer [Indu] finds abundant grass in your mouth; yet he does not abandon it, as if by a deer-thirst for a mirage. The power of delusion does not pass away in the perceptions of bound creatures. (137)
Having cast aside this nectar-moon— which was made miserable by Svarbhānu through the terrors of his forceful drinking—
the moon conceals its own dark mark by clinging to the redness of your lower lip, which is coppery like betel-juice.
When you became a lion, having cast either a deer or a rabbit into your belly,
your wife, the daughter of Hari (the Earth), gave birth to this one whose body has grown so vast;
yet, from your lotus-like face, there arose a defeat for that solitary lotus.
But there might be one opponent for him, namely the son of Siṃhikā. (139)

O beloved, if the lotus-born Creator, whose splendor transcends speech, fashioned Your face as a lotus to serve as a pair of lotus-eyes for worship, then who is this cool-rayed moon? It is but a crane dwelling in the reeds on the banks of the celestial river that rests upon the head of the Hunter of the Sacrificial Deer.

I suspect that the spot upon the lap of this stainless moon—born of the greenery of Indra’s quarter and wandering through it, whose every digit was fashioned with a singular consistency of non-darkness—is a fragment of the ichor from the temples of Airāvata, the preeminent elephant of Indra, which fell as he strode. Its luster is like that of a blue lotus. (141)
They declare that the sixteenth part of the Lord of Night is its *kalā*; fifteen such parts, increasing from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*rākā*), constitute its orb.

But as for that remaining part which is extracted apart from the lunar day—is it not the ornament of Śiva? Is the dark spot (*kalaṅka*) here merely the hollow of its location, appearing with its blackness? (142)

The moon, O charming girl, desires to consume the moonlight with his young cakora bird; longing to subsist upon it as its very root from this leaf-like orb that he has made his own, he stretches out his eyes to a great length.
And, disregarding you, he places the deer in his lap to stroke it, wishing to surpass even the beauty of your eyes—which are no more than a mere likeness of his—with the splendor of his own.
By means of your face’s abundant loveliness, the moon was fashioned from the remainder that touched only its rim and became soiled by the wiping away [of the beauty];
having created these two, the Creator surely washed his hands in the waters.
Even now, by means of mere fragments of that [ocean], water-dwelling creatures begin to produce lotuses.
The moon was fashioned from the remainder of your entire loveliness after it had touched only your face; yet even that crescent became the crest-jewel of Śiva, who was arrogant because of its beauty.
Consequently, the lotus, which once touched his foot, has now lost its splendor, while the moon has become the very seat of Lakṣmī.
Behold, my dear, how the moon— the gemstone of the sun for the assembly of stars— was born from their intense delight (sapītiḥ) as he was surrounded by them;
it is easy for poets of metaphorical fancy to describe this.
Holding a cup made of blue sapphire in the form of the moon, he [seems] to be lifting up the nectar.
O beautiful one, I suspect your face was fashioned by the Lord of the Night after extracting the qualities of the cool-rayed moon’s orb; for that very reason, it is a mine of faults (the moon).
Yet, I see that the essence—the two eyes—was taken even from the deer within the moon and placed here.
When your face exists, or when the moon exists, how could one who is not blind maintain composure? (147)

O slender-bodied one, do you not perceive this multitude of pure and radiant stars beyond counting, as if they were the mass of hoof-marks from the host of horses of the sun’s chariot, filled with the nectar dripping nightly from the cool moon? 148.
Let this person, with the moon-like flowers of his hair brought near,
become your attendant; let him serve you,
bearing the moon which resembles a parched grain cake speckled with sesame seeds.
Offer the sacrificial oblation and worship the five-arrowed one.
May the Moon, whose stream of nectar-like rays falters as it falls into the chasms produced by the mass of teeth meeting during his eclipse by Svarbhānu,

and who has attained the splendor of a thousand-streamed vessel at the consecration festival for the joy of the marriage of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) and his beloved— may he grant us satisfaction. 150.
Śrī Hīra, the diamond that adorns the crown of the assembly of king-poets, and Māmalladevī gave birth to Śrī Harṣa, who has conquered his collection of senses;
this naturally radiant twenty-second canto in the *Nalīyacarita*, a great poem composed in the Campū style, is the work of that author in his *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*. (151)

Just as a most beautiful woman does not captivate the hearts of young boys, even so my speech, though exceedingly lovely, does not steal away the minds of the wise; yet, if it becomes like nectar within, it intoxicates the intelligent.
What could her name be, she who is filled with disregard for men devoid of passion? ||152||
Let the mountain boulders in every direction vomit forth their own Sarasvatī; let them compare it with hers, whose grand display of sound flashes forth at the very outset—
for that other, supreme Ocean of Milk is what is being manifested by her.
The nectar churned from it was a dispeller of fatigue, a source of joy, and a delight.
I have here and there, with great effort, untied the knots of this work; let not the wicked man, whose mind fancies itself wise, read it with force.
Let the virtuous man, who has loosened his firm knots through faith and service to his guru, attain the joy of immersion in the waves of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of this poem. 154.

May this work of the illustrious poet Śrīharṣa arise for the delight of the learned—the work of him who receives two betel leaves and a seat from the Lord of Kānyakubja; he who realizes the Supreme Brahman, an ocean of bliss, within his meditative absorptions; and whose poetry showers nectar, while his utterances have triumphed over rival systems of logic. (155)
